editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: THE LAW: Children shall maintain their parents, or be imprisoned. THE THEME: A man who had two sons disinherited one of them. The disinherited son was adopted by a rich man. He grew rich, and his natural father, falling into poverty, was maintained by him against the order of the rich father, who therefore disinherits him a second time. — I lay it to luxury: whatever we ever poured out in immoderate bounty is all consumed in the keep of two old men. When my father forbade me, he kept saying: "He himself would give me no maintenance, if I were in want." He had already come to such a pass that he placed all his hope of a last subsistence in that one house alone, in which he had both a son he had disinherited and an enemy. Behold, death overtook him in his need: what will you do? Your brother is more to be buried by you than maintained. Whoever was asked said: "What of it? Can so wealthy a brother not maintain his brother?" The wretched old man lost, through your riches, even the coaxing tone that might have begged a coin.

THE THEME: A man had three rich sons. A poor man, with one son, disinherited that son, who was adopted by the rich man and grew rich. The rich man, having disinherited his own three sons, wished to adopt this man too. He refuses, and is disinherited by his father. — Is this my fortune — that at one and the same time I am both disinherited and adopted? That house, of course, which has no room for me as a young man, made you an old one. Quieter times we had as poor men; the civil wars we waged with the Capitol gilded. Do you call gold and silver riches — the playthings of fortune, which sometimes are sold along with their very masters? I give you notice, rich man: even if I come, I shall take pains — which in your house is most easy — to be disinherited. Though many things happen contrary to expectation, yet I never thought it would come about that either my father should hate his children or a rich man covet them. I do not long for a patrimony: happiness is fragile and fleeting, and all the showy gleam of flattering fortune comes with peril: often without cause she has cherished, and without reason forsaken. I have seen the general of a great army fleeing without a companion; I have seen the thresholds, once thronged by a crowd of clients, deserted and put up for sale under the master who was their agent of ruin. For why should I speak of men rolled down from the height of wealth to beggary? Many examples will occur to you, even if you seek them in a single house.

OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. Of my brother I dare neither to judge nor to speak: on one count I both thank him and congratulate him, that he could save our father though ordered to die. Confounded by so great a storm, I could neither weigh anything nor make anything out. I will reveal to you, father — fortune torturing me — more charges than you yourself seem to know. Whether you handed my brother over to me bound or unbound I do not know: so far as my stupefaction goes, he could even have fled; nor did I well remember whether father or stepmother had charged me with such a service — whether they had wished it a service or a punishment, a vengeance or a parricide. You bid me sew my brother into the sack? I cannot, father. Do you not forgive me? Or do you not believe me? I maintain that not even you could do it, if some tyrant had said to you: "Come, sew your son in with your own hands." In this work can you use your own eyes, can you use your own hands? Can you bear to hear the groan of your enclosed son? If you can, I fear you have condemned an innocent man; if you cannot, then to show what a brother could not do against a brother, I have given my father as witness.

OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. My own peril does not move me: always in our misfortunes we have looked not to fortune but to the cause. I do not doubt that Callias would have ransomed Miltiades, if he had then had a marriageable daughter. OF MUSA. One man cannot endure one thing, another another. For me adultery is a prison. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. "Nothing," he says, "can I give my daughter greater than Cimon for a husband. When shall I have grandsons from him?" Shall I throw away the sword handed me by the law for the avenging of chastity? You have lost your money, Callias, if you freed such hands. The man condemned for embezzlement left his heir nothing else than himself for a father.

OF VIBIUS GALLUS. I thank the rich man, because he is content to make those whom he hates defendants. By day we are forbidden public ground; ask what is done by night. "You shall not walk," he says, "by the same road as I; you shall not tread in my footsteps; you shall not present a squalid garment to my delicate eyes; you shall not weep against my will; you shall not be silent." We were lost, if he were a magistrate. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. That I went in mourning is grief; that I wept is filial duty; that I did not accuse is fear; that he was repulsed is your doing. Shall I not keep silent, who still live because I kept silent? You know the suspicions of a talkative people. Why did that man, while my father lived, never seek office? But I beg all men to help me in the inquiry into my father's death; and I should have come to your knees, rich man, did I not fear lest you should say that ill-will was being stirred up against you; and long since I follow you with this mind: I watch by talking for an occasion; nor, by heaven, can I say that it is your inhumanity that makes me not dare, but my own fault pursues me: I am silent. Would that my father too had had this fault! While he speaks freely, he offends many: for I do not think he had you alone for an enemy in the state.

"He himself," says he, "forbade me to maintain him." Do you call the imitation of another's fault innocence? Do you not even reckon how great that cruelty is — that if a man does not maintain his brother, he is not even to be maintained by his son? Why do you boast of the adoption? I came to you only when I had a rich father. Spare me, I beg, father: we have the gods present among us. You know you act in safety: even if you disinherit me, I shall maintain you. My crime must be confessed: I was too slow to pity; and so I pay the penalty — I am in want.

OF VIBIUS RUFUS: That children are to be kept, even he judges who keeps them with no great gladness. I invited those children of mine to share my trifles: shall I, who promised them my house, snatch away their own? What shall I do? If I obey, I shall be disinherited; if I do not obey, I shall be disinherited. I love my father: this is my obstinacy. The rich man has no son: will you give me? The rich man may recall his own: will you take me back? Thus I refuse not to be adopted, but to be lent out.

Why do you accuse me of having granted my brother impunity, when my purpose was overcome by fate? My brother did not obtain from me that he should live, nor that he should flee: he obtained nothing else than that he should die otherwise than in the sack. My case is a bad one — as is fitting between brothers. Where was hope? In the rudder? There was none. In the oars? Not even in these. In a companion? No one was found to be the companion of a shipwrecked man. In the sail? In the topsail? All the gear was cut away; there was no support for hope. Must I excuse myself to my father or to my brother? Of your son I make this answer: as long as he is allowed to remain on his native soil, he is a citizen; cast into the sea, whatever after exile and shipwreck he does or suffers, torn away from every bond of common life, is part of his punishment, not also a work of wickedness. But to others who complain I will give you yourself as witness that he is no pirate.

OF CESTIUS PIUS. A high-born spirit cannot endure insult. Rightly did you long to have grandsons from Cimon. What did you approve in me more than the prison? I am no more innocent than my father — nor even more fortunate; this one thing is the difference between father's fortune and son's, that for him the prison was the end of his calamities, for me their beginning. I will set out to you how toward none of my own kin I am ungrateful. Cimon, a son, was found to be Miltiades's whole estate; not even he had anything to give for his father except himself. I could have hoped for marriage in the house of Cynegirus, I could have hoped in that of Callimachus; nor did I fear

As that man says, I have approved my case to the people. OF JULIUS BASSUS. But when have we not been in mourning before these rich men? "Accuse," he says. Shall I, a poor man, accuse a rich one; I, a mourner, a candidate? I am not allowed to walk by my own choice. He has summoned me to court: "Carry me through as defendant," he says, "plead it out." Who would dare to accuse a man saying these things? "Why," he says, "do you follow me?" — as though the poor had one road, the rich another. OF CESTIUS PIUS. I should not be a defendant, if I could accuse. With beard let down, in mourning, with my charges I have come to you. Let everything be done — I will not cease to seek out the slayer, and perhaps I have already found him. When suddenly my father, in the midst of the city —

My parents, though their hatred is mutual in all else, agree only in branding me. O happy spectacle, if I can bring you back into harmony; and let me try, for your very faces urge it. Rise, fathers; come forward, judges: of my two parents the one has been saved for me, the other is yet to be saved. Stretch out your hands to one another in reconciliation; add me, as a mutual pledge, in the middle of the bond. Between you as you contend, I, in the middle, am crushed. Shall I then watch starve to death the man by whose ashes I am to swear? All happiness is unstable and uncertain. Who would have believed that Marius, lying upon the mud-bank, had been a consul or would be one? But why fetch examples from so far off, when one is present who saw him? What do you think the fortunate need not fear?

OF CESTIUS PIUS: Receive a witness to my life — one whom you value highly: a rich man whom it is hard to please. Do you wish to know why I will not leave my father? Because he begot me, because he reared me, because he disinherited me. Long I doubted whether the one was testing a friend, or the other a son. "I disinherit you," he says. Is this a true father? What can I hope from the man who will adopt me? THE NARRATIVE OF CESTIUS PIUS: The rich man raised one son: he was not content; for what was one to a rich man? He raised three; he might have given one in adoption: he disinherited one, a second, a third. Do you think now there is nothing left to the rich man? He disinherits a fourth.

I robbed him of the sight of the land, of the light, even of the means of a human death; fortune herself, who took pity on him, yet left him nothing but the sea. "I must die," he said; "my father has ordered it: neither do I beg you that I may not die, nor is it lawful for you not to do what you were ordered. Between an angry father and a brother about to die, take up the choice that your duty makes necessary: render my blood to my father, but spare me the sack; I am willing to die, but by your pure hand; this gift of your devotion I will carry down to the shades — that it was granted me, through my brother, to die otherwise than as a parricide."

that Cynegirus would value his own hands more highly. Cimon ransomed is the happiness of his ransomer. OF VOTIENUS MONTANUS. You are now making me say it: I did not receive a kindness, or I repaid it. I shall repay it the more surely when you are missed as honourably as you gave. Shall I let adulterers go? What else should I do, if I still had my hands bound? Grief drove me on, thunderstruck. By Hercules, Miltiades my father would not have won me over. I owe Callias nothing — except that I am free. Callias is an excellent man, he is merciful; but would that he were so only toward the good! The injury is greater if Cimon's hands are now bound than was the kindness when they were then loosed. He did not lose his daughter with a more unfair spirit than I my wife, but with a fairer spirit he chose to endure an unchaste woman. Will you hide your riches, when they have fallen in with men who are reckoned by their beggary? Our house has nothing better to show than its poverty. Give money to Miltiades to pay off his condemnation, and he will be guilty; give it to Cimon to ransom his father, and he will not be dutiful.

why do you gaze at me? Why do you watch what I shall say? — was carried off. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS. To go about with a great train, in splendid dress, is not of my fortune; that the rich can do; it is enough if we live. Since my father's body was found unspoiled, who was the slayer I do not know: whoever he was, like a rich man he despised the spoils. "Why," he says, "do you follow me through the public street?" An unworthy crime has been committed: rich man and poor have walked by the same road. OF OSCUS. "Accuse," he says. Where is he who had begun it first? I could wish my father too had not parted from you: he would be alive. "Why," he says, "do you not make me a defendant?" Because, my father being dead, you do not fear me as an accuser — for I fear lest anyone think a wrong is done him, if I say "slain."
My father was slain —

What must the unfortunate despair of? OF JUNIUS GALLIO: I will declare why you disinherit me: do you declare why you adopted me. Some things come about as new. For my part, I do not wonder that pity is laid to my charge; I wonder that this man lays it to my charge; for I have so borne myself that by this crime I bind two fathers to me. Each loves me, each in his misery longs to maintain me, each forbids it. He is not at peace either with himself or with fortune. Reconcile at last these men — good men, indeed, but stubborn. Do not require of me which of them gave the cause of the quarrel: each is an uncle, each is a father. Both his brother's fortune and his brother's temper have passed over to this man. I am compassionate: I would not have changed my father, if I could have changed my nature. OF PUBLIUS ASPRENAS:

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: Whoever you are, greedy keeper of money and worshipper of measureless lands: when you have got much, will you be able to enjoy it all? You seek a son: behold, here is a crowd of young men without a father. Command what you will: I will sail, I will serve as a soldier, provided that, wherever I am, I am yours. Are we poor, who have what rich men beg for? Whence such a father? You are not angry, save to show love. And further, are those patrimonies, into which in your madness you rush headlong, the joys of their masters, or their burdens? You used to recite a thousand examples of men crashing down amid their own riches, and among them you placed the rich man's house too. Did you disinherit deservedly, or undeservedly? If undeservedly, I hate a father who casts out so many innocents; if deservedly, I hate a house that makes so many guilty. Something not to be done I shall do in a wealthy house. What with us is frugality, with them is meanness. You ask back your sons rather than take them back.

OF ASINIUS POLLIO. Lend me fair ears: I will give you even one condemned to be acquitted. "He lives," he says, "my brother." I do not believe it. "He saved me," he says. You have made me believe it. This is the sum of what was done: in that house in which a parricide was readily believed, I could not kill my brother, nor my brother our father. "What have I to do with that ship? I wish to die only once." OF Q. HATERIUS. Lightning flashed out on every side from the thick clouds, and with terrible crashing the rough storms had hidden the day: rains everywhere, and everything raging with squalls. The sea, I say, awaits the parricide. The sea had swelled with sudden tempests, fearful even for lawful vessels. "I confess, I confess," I said: "my brother, Fortune, if he is innocent, I commend to you." I found, abandoned even by the shipwrecked, a vessel — a wretched fragment and already an omen for those about to sail, which, if any helmsman had seen it,

OF VIBIUS GALLUS. In nothing do I seem to myself more fortunate than that I was the price of Miltiades. Bound there lay the avenger of Persia's power, the champion of public liberty; bound there lay the reproach of an ungrateful city. Shall I dismiss an adulteress for my father — I who do not so much glory that I am Miltiades's son as that I am his substitute? What? Do you think it a punishment to be bound for Miltiades? If I kill only one of them, I must go into exile. What shall I do? Shall I kill? You demand more than you bestowed: for a prison, exile. Shall I not kill? You demand more than you bestowed: you gave one kindness, you ask two. The whole throng of my ancestors seemed to me to murmur round me, saying: "Where are those hands that loosed Miltiades?" There came not into my mind my wife's indulgence, nor Callias my father-in-law, nor the memory of any thing or any kindness;

by whom? If you permit me, I do not know. OF JUNIUS GALLIO. "You are in mourning," he says; "you weep." What else can I do, the son of a poor man slain? My father was slain in the midst of the city, the laws being safe. Who could tell this without tears? I will not lay aside this squalor, until I have found one on whom to put it. Who slew my father? I do not know. You can bear witness to nothing more than this my own voice: as yet I do not know. Meanwhile I deliberate, and shall put on that garment which the slayer left to my father. "Why do you follow me?" Magistrates do not clear away those behind their backs.

It is the law of fortune to furnish what you demand. Have pity: chance is changeable; victors have turned their backs to the vanquished, and those whom fortune had advanced she has forsaken. Why should I cite Marius, in his sixth consulship begging at Carthage, in his seventh ruling at Rome? But, not to send you among more examples of unstable fortune, look who it is that is asked for maintenance, and who it is that asks. OF JUNIUS OTHO THE FATHER: Fear change: he too lost nothing from his goods sooner than his son. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER:

Even now the people, conqueror of all nations, keeps a cottage on the Capitol — a people whose great good fortune no one wonders at; deservedly is it powerful: surely it is sprung from one who did not leave his father. As you go out from your house and return, I at least will attend you, nor will I leave you save at the threshold: I shall be a son in public. I love poverty as much as my father: to both I am accustomed. I cannot play the son in a rich man's house. If you were selling a slave dear to you, you would ask whether the buyer were cruel. By Hercules, I value one single hour in which I may satisfy you when you are angry, at three times more than the whole patrimony. This thing alone, of all — that you so wish to lose me — I cannot love enough. What shall I do, adopted? Shall I speak well of his sons?

he would have put off his voyage. The shipwrecked man is sent off from the shore. OF MARCELLUS AESERNINUS. "You have, brother," I said, "if you are innocent, a ship; if guilty, the sack." I did not commit parricide — and, how easily we men err, I thought it done; I was deliberating whether to obey my father. "Brother," he said, "you will be the first in the house to commit parricide." OF ARGENTARIUS. What you had ordered was done: my brother perished. "He lives," he says, "and let me go." By a fine argument he is proved to live. He raised both hands to heaven: "If I never plotted impiously, if even condemned I love my father, immortal gods, judges of all things, be present." Had he felt otherwise, he would have called down upon himself the cruel seas: thus he steered his ship. OF BLANDUS.

I did what I am wont: I looked to nothing else than my father. OF MENTO. Consider that they are adulterers for whom you plead; consider the sort of people you are wont to pity: it is shameful to have both the adulterers and Cimon dismissed by the same man. I am one who does not cease to return gratitude even to the dead: so may it befall me to have true children — which Miltiades has learned how great a thing it is. OF PORCIUS LATRO. Shall I dismiss the adulterers?

OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. What would that man do to one accusing, who persecutes one silent? "Why do you not bring suit?" Because you are so far from being afraid that you would force suit to be brought against you. Do I now do you any wrong by being in mourning? Is what is allowed to a defendant not allowed to a mourner? What less could I render to my father? In his honour I changed my garment. OF ARGENTARIUS. Do you not wish me to weep for my father? You did not used to provoke us unprovoked. OF CLODIUS TURRINUS the father. "Why," he says, "have you taken up squalor?" What then? Shall I not even mourn him whom I cannot avenge? I do wrong to no one but my father, whom as yet I weep in silence. OF PORCIUS LATRO.

Will you not open to me your household gods? I am no burdensome guest; I bring but one old man. By this fault, father, I won your favour. An unknown old man comes; I wish to pass by in silence; he entreats me by his father. Shall someone, then, perish of hunger who prays that his son may survive him? What shall I say this is, that they disinherit me so dangerously? That these men change their fortune as often as I change my father? Be reconciled: amid funereal battle-lines armed hands are stretched out in pledge of peace. The whole world had perished, had not pity ended its wrath; or, if hatreds so stubborn please you, spare me. Tossed between two fathers, the son of each, yet ever disinherited by the more fortunate, set between two perils, what shall I do? Those who maintain are disinherited; those who do not maintain beg.

Of the disinheriting? Shall I enter your house, as though I had cast you out? Shall I seize your ornaments, so that, if I commit any fault there, neither your father nor mine may take me back? What is there that I must either deny or excuse? You do not charge your son with the most insane evil of extravagance, with shameful loves, with a luxurious dress, or with drinking-bouts. If you cannot bring these charges, copy at least some from your friend's notebooks: dripping with foreign unguents, riddled with lusts, walking, that he may please women, more softly than a woman — and the rest, which belong to disease, not to a judge.

The vessel lay on the shore, which even whole had borne men unhappily. I will believe him a parricide if, as you set out, he gave you his own ship. Suddenly, while I was not aware, the iron fell from me together with my courage; my hands grow numb, and by some confusion darkness is poured over my dazed eyes. I understood how hard it is to commit parricide, even what one's father commands. So may you succour me, Fortune — you who alone look upon the wretched in our house — so may it befall me to live or die honourably, so may I be the last accused in our house, as truly he swore that he had had a better stepmother than a brother. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS.

My spirit burns with desire for vengeance. These hands Miltiades could not have held back, which he was able to bind. If you freed them for this, give me back to the prison. That savior and champion of Greece, that tamer of the Persians and the East, on whom fortune had but now conferred so signal a triumph over the enemy, was condemned for embezzlement — for this very purpose, no doubt: that his innocence, which otherwise could have lain hidden, might by the very condemnation be displayed. An innocent man was condemned. Who in the city is merciful? Now the occasion for mercy has come: Miltiades must be ransomed. I ransomed your body, Miltiades, though I was not to be present even at your funeral, on which I had spent myself. I pity my accuser, not because he lost his daughter, but because he had her. Callias was worthy to have such children as he ransomed. But if you ransomed me into this endurance of defilements, I prefer the prison to marriage. It is more honourable to be bound for a father than freed for an adulterer. When I heard that there was a man counting out money, I wondered that there was anyone in our city who would rather ransom Cimon than Miltiades. I would not have ransomed even my own father, had he not been innocent.

Amid the grief of a father so cruelly slain, what is braver than that he groans? "Accuse me," he says. Whence are you so free of care? You seem to have found out who else did the slaying. There was no booty in him for a footpad to pursue, but there was the highest virtue, but there was a most firm bulwark of poverty, an innocence defiant against the disdain of riches: these were the spoils sought from an enemy. Somehow it gladdens a man to be wretched amid wretchedness, and for the most part all grief flows out through tears. He exults too much at our funeral: while that man lived, he was not wont to provoke us into becoming defendants. If anyone, amid the tears for a slain father, has marvelled at the inertia hitherto so trusted of one most wretched of all mortals, let him lay all his wonder upon this indignity of the present peril. Do you marvel that a poor man has not taken up the spirit of accusing a rich one? Because he is silent, he is made a defendant.

This one thing, father, I call the gods to witness: I leave you rich. OF CESTIUS PIUS: For such a work I had prepared myself: I wished to bring the brothers back into harmony. Is this what you reproach me with? But unless I obtain that they be good brothers, I shall obtain that they not be bad fathers. Each loved me, each made vows for me: how much would it be if I said, "Each maintained me"? What the cause of their quarrel was I do not know; I fear that this man did the wrong first: he was the first to fall into want. What do you reproach me with, father? Pity, I think. I know of a man in this city who was adopted for that very crime. "He refused," says he, "to maintain his brother." You have found something I might defend. Can I raise children, if the first thing I must tell them is that their grandfather perished of hunger? You were not deceived as to what I am: you knew, when you adopted me. I have been twice disinherited: I wish to plead both my cases, neither by myself; let the other stand by me — my cause shall always have a father for its advocate. Let each love the other: each loved me. Do you wish that man to pay a true penalty? Let him feel what a wrong he did to so good a brother.

Disinheriting is a talkative thing: how I love you, poverty, if by your kindness I am innocent! I have no accuser; nay — wretched me — I even have a praiser, and one whom not all men please: for I would rather say this than "one whom all men displease." Yours is not a house propped up by many children, nor does a crowd stray about your side, nor is there a host of heirs within your threshold, nor would you keep someone in reserve after me. And yet not even thus ought you to have given me away, when you had seen the gods contending with a father's vows. For he is safer against fortune who has something left after his loss, and we have the example: that a man can lose three sons. That Croesus, richest among kings, remember, was led off with his hands bound behind his back. And you, Crassus, after you had tracked out those arms of the runaway slaves, the richest man of the Roman city — what now? Among the Parthians you lack even a tomb.

I confess, I wished to kill him; but then I understood how hard parricide is. "I," he says, "wished to kill my father? Not even now could I." Our father sailed on a clear day, a calm sea, with auspicious voyage, in an undamaged ship. What is this? The condemned man sailed more luckily than the man who had condemned him. "Go," he said; "I was not permitted to have you as a father; I will have you as a patron; come back." A great proof of devotion: a father dear to his son even after punishment. Which do you think — that he learned innocence among pirates, or that he did not lose it even among pirates? OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. He could kill his father: what witness did he fear? Disowned by my father, where shall I betake myself? To the seas? I cannot: I have the pirates angry with me. When my brother was handed over to me and I was ordered to exact the penalty, if there is any faith in me, I thought I was being tested, whether I could commit parricide. OF PORCIUS LATRO.

OF BLANDUS. Let him cast chains in my teeth: never will he bring it about that I do not glory more in the prison than in marriage. Men's feelings differ: you perhaps, Callias, cannot bear chains, I cannot bear an adulterous wife. Shall the adulterers then escape, as though Cimon's hands were bound? OF ARGENTARIUS. Ransomed, he at once began to address me about marrying his daughter. "At once," I said, "Callias tests whether I am grateful: you have Callias without Cimon." He asks for one, he snatches two. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. Say now, "I took you from prison," while I answer, "I gave myself to prison." Never will it be brought about that I think it better done that I was ransomed by Callias than that I was bound for Miltiades. Your daughter robbed you of a son-in-law, Cimon. My father was led to prison, even now full of his own captives.

By these tears, by this squalor, by these instruments necessary to all in peril, we ask no invidious reward of your pity — only that, being acquitted, it be allowed me to live as though a defendant. That man is powerful and in favour, and — what not even he himself denies — was rich, and one who thought he need never fear anything, even as a defendant. Then day by day the hatred grew, through the violence of the one, the freedom of the other. The rich man held us, the poor, to be nothing but poor; we held him to be nothing but innocent, amid daily battle-lines ever unconquered. Who in the meantime planned our death I do not know: what cannot be dissembled I do know — who wished it. That man came with a crowd of clients and parasites, and poured out his whole household against poverty. "Why do you not accuse me, do not summon me?" Scarcely did he refrain from saying: "What would I, an accuser, not dare against you, who had him put to death who had only gone to law with me?"

OF POMPEIUS SILO: Of your father I deserved well, though through my age I cannot have known him; yet he too has a benefit of mine: I maintained his two sons. Rise, unhappy old man. What? Do you think he weeps because he is in want? No — because he disinherited, because he did not maintain. OF ARGENTARIUS: You see — I began to be generous in your own house: it was because of me he took a wife, when perhaps he might have adopted a young man. These were the words of the man as he disinherited me: "Go to the man you love more than your father." Not all a father's commands are to be obeyed. I do nothing new in your case: you know that I did not obey my former father either. He came, with beard unkempt and hair foul with squalor, his limbs trembling not from age but from hunger, his face half-eaten and thin, his voice crushed by fasting so that it could scarcely be heard, his eyes sunk deep within and scarcely lifted —

I pass over the . . . thousands of examples of men crashing down amid their own riches: I do not relate how often, among these, you have set the rich man's house, losing its better sons by its riches. This I know our ancestors fled; this Aelius Tubero, whose poverty was a virtue; this Fabricius, refusing the gifts of the Samnites; this the rest of our fathers, whom, at the very plough, as they goaded their cattle, lictors stood about. Rise, rise, most wretched young men, and by entreating my father learn to entreat your own.

You would have perished, father, had you not fallen in with a parricide. OF TRIARIUS. He was sailing in a shipwreck. It is too little that he did not kill our father; nay, he even let him go in an undamaged ship — and is called a pirate too: a second time, on a false charge, he is ill spoken of. OF CESTIUS PIUS. There was a ship — or rather there had been, but a rotten one, its joints loosened, an unlucky omen for the voyage. "Sew me into the sack: at least I shall feel the seas, and not also see them." The torn sails too had made hollows of wind, and the shipwrecked raft had outstripped armed fleets: you would know that he sailed who was destined to save his father. Cruel and obstinate, the stepmother, after all is overcome, none the less rages. The seas are now at rest, the brigands now pity, the pirates now spare. We were passing by our mother's tomb, he fearing death, I crime: wait, judges; soon fortune will hurl a crime upon us.

OF JUNIUS GALLIO. "I did you a kindness," he says, "in that I gave you my daughter in marriage." Now indeed, Miltiades, you bear a fortune heavier than the prison: Callias has deigned to share it with you. I thought myself ransomed; I was bought for his daughter. The images of my ancestors stood before my eyes, and Miltiades, sent out from his place, shone with the majesty of a commander, and again called upon my hands. OF JULIUS BASSUS. I married Callias's daughter: this injury, father, I did you while unwilling to be ungrateful. Please yourself, if you like, and parade those riches: yet I ransomed my father at the same price for which I was ransomed by you.

Cities for the most part, neighbouring ones, swell with war amid a sudden quarrel; amid civil strifes there is enough for vengeance in whatever each man has seized for railing. With what violence Macerio storms against the absent Metellus! M. Cato heard charges of theft flung at him by Pulcher. What greater indignity could there be of that age than either Pulcher an accuser or Cato a defendant? Against Cn. Pompeius, conqueror by land and sea, there was one to compose a lampoon — one scratching his head, as is said, with a single finger. There was one who, by the license of song, despised three gilded chariots. There was one to mangle the empty boasting of the most sacred M. Brutus . . . saying that his hands were not only unstained but steeped in the blood of fellow-citizens; yet he, though he was tearing at three consulships and three triumphs, was so far from fearing to become a defendant that he even took pains to be eloquent. This man alone, in our state, is more innocent than Cato, more noble than Metellus, braver than Pompeius —

— I maintained him. How, you ask? As I maintained you. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: Suppose me to be today not disinherited but adopted. I wish to foretell certain things to my future father: this man whom you wish to adopt maintained his father's enemy against his father's will. He left a wealthy house with an easy mind, to live with a beggar. You ought to know this fault of his: he is obstinate in showing pity to the wretched. Nor yet have I any cause to complain of this fault of mine: by it I found one father, by it I lost another. How many fathers pray for a son like me! By these I am disinherited. He is a man: will you not have me maintain a man? He is a citizen: will you not have me maintain a citizen? He is a friend: will you not have me maintain a friend? He is a kinsman: will you not have me maintain a kinsman? Thus one comes to "father." He is a man, he is a citizen, he is a friend, he is a kinsman. On this condition, then, it will be no fault to have held out a coin — unless I shall have said:

OF BLANDUS: He begot three, he disinherits four. "I disinherit you," he says. It is plain whence you come. OF VIBIUS GALLUS: If anyone hears that I am to be adopted, he at once thinks me disinherited; if anyone hears that I am being disinherited, he at once thinks me adopted. Why . . . I answer: lest I take from a father his son, from sons their father. Will you not be corrected even by so near an example? He who disinherits his own seeks others. No happiness is sure: a little while ago I envied the rich man's sons, now they envy me. My father praises me while he disinherits, I praise my father while I am disinherited; this is our one debate: he thinks me worthy of a wealthy father, I think myself worthy of my own.

The vessel lay, very old and worn by the salt sea, scarcely able to hold one life. I came to you about to seek a fair victory — to prove myself a parricide. "You did not kill," he says, "your brother." Stepmother, hear a most welcome word: I confess I am a parricide, I killed my brother; am I safe, father, if I prove this? I placed him in an unrigged ship: is this not to kill? For a stepmother, indeed, a stepson is never killed enough. Nature has opened many roads to death, and the fates run down by many paths; and this is the most wretched condition of the human race, that we are born in one way and die in many: the noose, the sword, the steep place, poison, shipwreck, a thousand other deaths lie in wait for this most wretched life. And this is called killing — only it takes longer. If anyone now stands in the crowd, he says this: "Shall anyone spare this man, who killed his brother and proves that he killed him?"

The division. Latro divided into these questions: whether everyone who has not returned a kindness, when he could, is liable for ingratitude. "Many things," he says, "intervene, on account of which I ought not to do it, even if I can." If a man is not liable simply because he has not returned a kindness when he could, whether this man is liable. This he divided into these: whether he cannot be condemned for what he did by law; then, whether he ought to have done it; lastly, whether, if he was carried away by feeling and indignation and was not in his own control, he ought to be pardoned. This not as a question, but, as was his custom, by way of treatment or commonplace.

Latro divided thus: whether there is a wrong in the matter. "There is no wrong," he says: I am in mourning; how many do this! All kinds of wrong are comprised by the law: to strike is not allowed, to revile against good morals is not allowed. In this place SCAURUS said: a new formula of wrongs is being framed — "in that one man reviled another against good morals." Even if there is a wrong in the matter, whether, if he does it with no evil intent, he is safe; or whether he does it with evil intent. This Latro divided into two questions: whether, if he believed his father was slain by this man, and for that reason followed him, he should be forgiven; then, whether he did believe it. GALLIO made this the first question: whether, if a man does what each is allowed to do, he is not liable for wrongs. "It is allowed," he says, "to weep, allowed to walk where you will, allowed to take up what garment you will. But nothing," he says, "is allowed to be done to throw ill-will upon another. You are in mourning — I do not complain; but if your squalor stirs up ill-will against me, I complain."

— "He is my father?" OF VIBIUS GALLUS: I shall go the rounds with you, father, from one strange door to another; I shall show to all both me, who gave the maintenance, and you, who refused it. OF ROMANIUS HISPO: I know, father, that what you say is better: if I could do that, I should never have been disinherited. I confess it is a fault. This too my former father wished to mend in me, and could not. You drove me into the trap: the man who was disinheriting me kept saying, "This ought not to be done"; you said it ought; I believed you. "He gave me no maintenance," he says. Did you lack it? Whoever is asked for maintenance by a beggar does nothing more than point: "Go to your brother, go to your son." Already some pray over us the same fortune. Believe me, the tongue of the people is holy. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS: Take away your riches, which the surge of uncertain fortune drives now this way, now that; be reconciled:

OF PAPIRIUS FABIANUS: Behold, drawn-up armies, often of fellow-citizens and kinsmen about to join battle, have taken their stand, and the hills are filled with horses and men, and presently the whole region is strewn with the bodies of the slain; amid that multitude of corpses, then, or amid the plunderers, someone might ask: what cause has driven man against man into wickedness? — for neither do wild beasts wage war among themselves, nor, if they did, would the same beseem man, a kind gentle and nearest to the divine — what so great wrath bears you on, when you are one stock and the same blood,

You arrange a pair in your house, so that one is a parricide by crime, the other by service. My brother was placed in a ship: what sort of ship? You know that nothing is more dangerous than even well-equipped vessels: a little timber keeps fate apart. But what if that life is committed to no oars, defended by no sail, no rudder? The ship is unrigged, open on either side; the poor wretch is put aboard a wreck, and adds his weight besides to a vessel destined of itself to go to the bottom. Behold a ship armed by divine power: suddenly sails appeared, suddenly the ship began both to steer itself and to lift itself up. Great is the protection of innocence in dangers. The savage sea rolls, the squalls press the ship's sides with foaming onset, the ship is battered on every side by perils: yet innocence is safe.

MONTANUS VOTIENUS added this question: whether Cimon returned the kindness to Callias. "I took your daughter," he said, "to wife; your daughter became Miltiades's daughter-in-law. Do you not count grandchildren shared with Miltiades a kindness?" GALLIO raised that hard question, but pursued it carefully, which is wont to be first in controversiae about an ungrateful man: whether he received a kindness. "It was no punishment," he said, "for me to be in prison: I had come there of my own will. Do you think I lay more gladly in my own bedchamber? There was then no more honourable place in Athens than the one that had held Miltiades." Then he subjoined that question too: whether he is liable who has received a kindness he did not seek. "I did not ask you," he says; "you gave it to your own ostentation; you thought it pertained to your glory. So would you not have received a kindness if it had fallen to you to free Miltiades?"

About the colour there was inquiry: some openly inveighed against the rich man, some said nothing at all against him, some followed a middle road. Since beyond these there is nothing, Latro wished to seem to have found a fourth kind, so as to speak against the rich man in this fashion: "You indeed did it not, yet I had reasons for which I might be deceived and suspect something of you in vain: because you were an enemy, because my father was found unspoiled," and the rest. But this is that middle kind, neither of dismissing the rich man nor of accusing him: for he ought neither to dismiss the man whom he has put off, nor to accuse him for this very reason, that he has put him off.

— I am innocent. THE OTHER SIDE. OF VALLIUS SYRIACUS: He has resolved to grow great out of my unpopularity: shall we old men follow where a young man's ambition calls, and lend him an audience? He can boast of himself better than he can defend himself. Is my fear a just one — that I may write down as my heir an ingrate, and leave behind an enemy? Among the other things I confess I have in common with my enemy, this too is one: we have both led the most unhappy and the most wretched of lives, save in this alone, that each of us has seen the other in want. He ordered me to be cast out, with insults of words added; he raised his hands to heaven, confessing himself debtor for this spectacle, and then for the first time prayed his brother for his life. From the patrimony made ready for me I took no joy — as one stunned by such a stupor of calamities — save that I was to give everything to this man here, and refuse everything to that one. It is plain to us that there are gods: he who did not maintain is in want; he who did not receive his brother into his house remains out of doors. Fortune has now made my power equal to his power, save only that I cannot be the first to act.

or what furies have driven you to mutual bloodshed? What so great an evil has been laid by fate, or by chance, upon that race? Was it, that banquets may be furnished for peoples and roofs may gleam with gold, that kin-murder was worth so much? Great, forsooth, are those dainties, for which men would rather, as parricides, look upon their own table and panelled ceilings than, as innocents, upon the light. Or, that nothing be denied to belly or to lust, must the slavery of the world be sought after? To what end, in fine, are these pestilent riches sought, if not even to this — that they may be left to children? What, in the end, is there that riches have not corrupted? First, if you wish to begin from there, the very houses, which men have built up so high that homes, made ready for use and defence, are now a peril, not a protection: so great is the height of the buildings and so great the narrowness of the streets, that there is neither defence against fire, nor any escape, on any side, from the ruins.

O seas more just than judgements! O storms gentler than the father! The life that he cast out, you saved. Nor was this only done by divine power, that he reached harbour safely: he is taken up by a fleet of brigands. Let the father have a mind to sail: he will be captured — that he, the judge, may come to regret his own sentence. "The stepmother could condemn me for parricide; she could not make me a parricide even by condemning me. Recognize my innocence on the sea, which at home you would not." With embraces, with kisses he saw me off: did a parricide thus dismiss his father?

SILO POMPEIUS, on Callias's side, said that he had given two kindnesses: that he had ransomed him, and that he had given his daughter in marriage to one in want. This second one no one else reckoned as a kindness, in which it so far is none, that, as it is doubtful whether he did not give a kindness, so it is doubtful whether he did not receive one. BRUTUS BRUTTEDIUS besides made these questions: whether, if Callias did this for his own sake, in ransoming Cimon it is a kindness. "For a kindness," he says, "is what is wholly bestowed for the sake of the one on whom it is conferred. Where a man either hopes or prepares something for himself from it, it is not a kindness; it is a calculation." And he pursued this at length, with both arguments and examples. Then, whether Callias did it for his own sake. "You wished," he says, "to escape the reputation of meanness by a brilliant deed; you sought from this an everlasting memory. The man by whom Cimon was freed could no more be unknown than the man for whom he was bound. You wished to have a son-in-law noble and dutiful." HISPO ROMANIUS made a hard question: whether he returned the kindness by this very act, that he killed the adulterers. "I freed you," he says, "from the greatest disgrace; I gave you a kindness against your will. There is no reason for you to wonder; for you too ransomed me when I did not ask." Here he cited the Virginiuses and those fathers who killed their violated daughters, who shut them up.

ALBUCIUS said nothing against the rich man; he declaimed in this colour: "He commits a wrong," he says, "who accuses one whom he has not summoned." "Why," he says, "do you follow me?" That you may at last pity me, that you may cease to persecute an afflicted house, that you may know I cannot accuse in this garb, that you may conceive a desire for the glory of an avenged death. You alone can, if you will, find out who slew him; you can accuse. "But some hold me suspect for this." You can scatter that suspicion: ask who did it. "That you may know," he says, "that you are throwing ill-will upon me: when I had said, 'Accuse me,' you did not deny that you would accuse, but answered, 'I will accuse when I am able.'" Forgive me — I can no more accuse anyone as yet than acquit him: I am asking who did it. These are slight arguments, they are empty, which touch others: that you are an enemy, that he was found unspoiled — there is no reason why I should accuse, there is reason why I should suspect.

I adopted you when you were disinherited: now that you adopt, I disinherit. OF VIBIUS RUFUS: When I was in want I would say: "He has avenged himself enough, in that I, the partner of a wealthy enemy, now ask a steward for my day's keep." OF MARULLUS: Will he dare to beg his life, who would rather die than have his own words said to himself? To many I owe pity, to many I have given it. Whoever it is that any calamity makes like me, I hold him exactly as though he touched me by a degree of kinship. I know how bitter it is to entreat strangers; I know how grievous it is to be driven away by one's own. I know how cruel it is, day after day, both to pray for death and to beg for life. Even if you do not hate the man who wronged me, I hate the man who wronged you.

To the delights of mad luxury every stone is dug out, the woods are felled in all lands of the earth; bronze and iron are used, now gold too, in building and adorning houses; merely that men may anxiously, both by day and by night, dread ruin and fire — which, whether thrown upon roofs or fortuitous, makes those panelled ceilings and chambers the very destroyers of cities: for men do not defend their own, but in the common peril seize what is another's, and in their own houses the stronger ownerships fall to others, and they themselves, while they are most ablaze, carry off plunder from another's ruins. To these ends, then, is that veined stone cut, and covers a wall with a thin facing — and the floor is laid in mosaic and gold is poured upon the ceilings?

OF JUNIUS GALLIO. Many things I do not recognize: my brother was condemned at home, I in public; against him it was charged that he had committed parricide, against me that I did not commit it; he denied his charge, but I must use a strange defence: "I killed my brother"; in that house in which parricides are condemned, this is innocence. I see, judges, that you are unwilling to hear this kind of defence: so I would rather prove myself innocent to you than to my father. I did not kill my brother, I could not kill my brother; we feared the same things, grieved over the same things, wept the same tears, had the same father, the same mother, the same stepmother;

The colour both to GALLIO and to Latro and to Montanus seemed best: that nothing be said insultingly against Callias, both ransomer and father-in-law and unhappy man. CESTIUS said many things against the miser and usurer and money-changer and pander, while he wished to prove this, that he had returned the kindness in having endured to have such a father-in-law. Latro said: "I will dismiss your daughter; what shall I do about the adulterer? You ask for one, you snatch two." This HYBREAS put differently: "And to you, adulterer, what shall I do? Is not Callias your father too?" This whole sententia is different from the former, even though it is drawn from the same material. The other is not like, but the same, which ADAEUS the rhetor said first — one of the Asians, of no mean repute — and then ARELLIUS FUSCUS: "Do I seem to you ungrateful, Callias? You do not know where you bestowed your kindness on me."

RUFUS VIBIUS put this for colour: "I am in mourning, I grieve; I follow you that I may be the safer; I fear that unknown man, whoever he is, who slew my father; I know that, as long as I am with you, I cannot perish." While MURREDIUS followed this colour, he said most ineptly: "Why do I follow you? My father, because he walked alone, was slain." The colour of OSCUS did not please Gallio: "I follow," he says, "that I may find who did it; this I reason with myself: whoever it is that did it will wish to charge it upon this man as his enemy; he will come to the rich man." "Much more wrongful," he says, "is this, if he does it for the sake of inquiry, if he follows the rich man not only for reviling but for peril." GALLIO thought one should plead subtly, and direct the colour of one's pleading to the position of the controversia, so as to say: "I suspect my father was slain by you. For who else hated him more? Who else is so powerful? The garment, no doubt, some other unknown slayer had coveted. Someone will say: What then? If he is an enemy, is he straightway the slayer? No; therefore I do not accuse."

THE DIVISION. The division of controversiae of old was simple; whether the recent kind is more subtle or only more laborious, you yourselves will judge: I shall set out both what the ancients devised and what their successors added. Latro made these the questions: he divided into law and equity — whether the son could be disinherited, and whether he ought to be. Whether he could be disinherited he asked thus: whether it was necessary for him to maintain his father, and so whether he cannot be disinherited for having done what the law compelled. This he divided into these questions: whether a disinherited son ceases to be a son; whether he ceases to be one who has been not only disinherited but also adopted by another. Even if he was a son, whether anyone who has not maintained his father is to be punished — as in the case of one sick, bound, or captured; whether the law admits any excuse for a son; whether this man could admit it. Whether he ought to be disinherited he asked through these: whether, even if the man was unworthy to be maintained, this son nevertheless acted rightly in maintaining him; and then whether the man was worthy to be maintained.

O poverty, how unknown a good you are! Nay, men imitate mountains and forests within their decaying houses, and in shade and smoke counterfeit green things, or seas and rivers. I can scarcely believe that any of them has seen the open forests and the plains, through which a swift river, whether headlong from a precipice or, when spread over the level, gently flowing, runs between; that they have ever seen the seas wide from a hill, or in winter, when stirred to their depths by the winds. For who could delight his mind with imitations so perverse, if he had known the true? Evidently, just as to infants the things that can be touched and grasped by hand or in the lap . . . for a small mind cannot hold great things; hence to the shores too masses are carried, and, heaping up earth in the deep, men build out their bays. Others let in the sea by channels: so unable are they to take joy in anything true, but, against nature, things displaced — earth or sea, exchanged — are a delight to their sick minds. And do you wonder if, to men suffering from a loathing of the works of nature, now not even their own children, but only others', are pleasing?

I am of a gentler heart by nature, of a softer soul. Nature has not given the same disposition to all mortals: one is harder, another more merciful; even among pirates one is found who cannot kill. I thought I had been chosen so that no other should kill him. If our mother were alive, I think he would have handed him to her; what was next to that, he handed him to me. Which seems to you the case — that he wished to punish his son by his brother's hands, or to send away his stepson? I am ashamed of my own defence; I fear that, when I begin to relate what I did, you will say: "Surely you were denying that you could kill a man."

ARELLIUS FUSCUS altered it thus: "You will not call me ungrateful, Callias: consider whence you ransomed me." I remember then that Fuscus, when this sententia of Adaeus was cast in his teeth, did not deny that he had transferred it into Latin, and said that he did this not for the sake of recommendation or theft, but of exercise. "I take pains," he said, "to compete with the best sententiae, nor do I try to corrupt them but to surpass them." Then he quoted some sententia of Thucydides: "For prosperity has a strange power to cover over and overshadow the faults of each man"; then the Sallustian: "Prosperity is wonderfully a screen for vices." Since brevity is the chief virtue in Thucydides, by this Sallust surpassed him and overthrew him in his own camp; for in the Greek sententia, brief as it is, you have what you can take away with the sense unimpaired: remove either "cover over" or "overshadow," remove "of each man"; the sense will hold, even if not equally polished, yet equally entire. But from Sallust's sententia nothing can be taken away without loss to the sense.

HISPO ROMANIUS accused openly, and said that he lacked not a case but power; and this epigram he said in the proem, with great applause of men: "I have that man for accuser who marvels that he is not a defendant." JULIUS BASSUS in this controversia said: "Why do you follow me through the public street?" An unworthy crime, judges, has been done: poor man and rich have trodden the same ground. He was wont, however, to pursue squalid matters, and found those who admired them above all else. I remember him declaiming the controversia about the pander who summoned ten young men to come to the brothel, and covered with thrown-up earth a pit filled with fire, into which, when the young men had slipped and been consumed, he was accused of harming the state. ALBUCIUS heard him declaiming — a fastidious hearer of those whom he could envy; he admired this epigram of BASSUS: "By heaven, I could not endure you, had you tied a dog at the door."

The modern declaimers added to the Greek authors that first question: whether an adopted son can be disinherited. This Cestius used. Gallio added another question: whether, if even an adopted son can be disinherited, it can be for that fault which was known to the adopter before he adopted him. But this hangs on the side of equity, and is more a treatment than a question. Gallio doubled Latro's first question thus: it was lawful for me to maintain you even though you forbade it; and then, it was not lawful for me not to maintain him. In the first part he maintained this: that a son cannot be disinherited for what is within his own power; and that no one can be forbidden to show pity. What if you forbid me to weep, when I have seen a man in calamity? What if you forbid me to favour one in peril for some honourable deed? Our feelings are within our own power. For there are certain laws unwritten, yet surer than all that are written: though I be a son in a father's power, it is lawful for me both to hold out a coin to a beggar and earth to a corpse. It is unjust not to stretch out a hand to the fallen: this is the common law of the human race. No one asks for a grudging right by which he is to benefit another.

OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: I alone of all men am disinherited because my own father loves me, and another seeks me. What does he charge me with? Do I love harlots? Have I run into debt? Speak — let the rich man hear. "I wish you," he says, "to be rich." O me, worthy to be disinherited, if I leave such a father! My father used to praise poverty to me, used to tell me of the discomforts of the rich, used to say that many rich men were accused; I, at least, remember that they were disinherited. "I disinherit you" is not a word of my father's.

OF MUSA. My brother was handed over to me, of all people, to be punished. With what intention you did this, father, is matter of dispute among most men: as for me, if you wished anything gentler to be done at that time, I did not understand it; I placed him aboard, much resisting, and sewed him into the sack, while he begged for it. You charge me with too soft a soul: one man is gentler, more than he ought to be, another more severe than is necessary; another, placed in the middle of the passions between the two, is wholly in his own control. Some men can both accuse and condemn and kill; some are so gentle that they cannot even give testimony against a man's life. I cannot kill a man: this fault is found even among pirates. Some men cannot live without administering the state; for others, the chief tranquillity is to lie hidden in private life and to have withdrawn beyond all envy; some cannot be persuaded to bind themselves in marriage, others to do without it; there are men who fear the camp, there are men who rejoice in their own scars.

T. Livius, however, was so unfair to Sallust that he charged Sallust with this very sententia both as a translation and as corrupted in the translating. Nor does he do this out of love of Thucydides, to prefer him, but he praises the man whom he does not fear, and thinks Sallust can more easily be conquered by himself if first conquered by Thucydides. CESTIUS had this colour for Callias: he charged Cimon, unbidden, with this — that he had allowed his wife to become an adulteress, that he had not guarded her, that he had waited until the father should come upon them, to become a spectator of his own calamity. "Now," he said, "even if you dismiss them, you are ungrateful. I had not waited until I should be asked."

The same man used to say that those epigrams of Latro were swollen rather than strong, which were carried about with the highest admiration of men: "the fathers read the proofs and divide the bones of their children by guess"; and that one: ". . . brought forth your priestesses"; and that one: "Over the ashes of our children the brothel must be leveled to the ground." But he himself praised these things, at least those which he had taught. For in this very controversia, lest Bassus should seem to have said something more squalid, he himself said: "Shall ten young men so perish for your two-pence?"

Latro pressed this point vehemently: I did not act by reason, I was conquered by feeling. When I had seen my father in want, my mind did not stand firm in me; what you forbade I do not know. He said this was not to be treated as a question; yet it was more powerful than any question. Arellius Fuscus the father moved this, at the end, as though a question: I thought that, however you forbade it, you nevertheless wished your brother maintained; with that look you forbade — or so you seemed to me. Cestius more boldly: not content to say, "I thought you wished it," he added: "You did wish it, and to this very day you wish it." And by his own figure he said all the reasons why he ought to wish it. "Why then do you disinherit me?"

OF TRIARIUS: Why do you disinherit me? Do I spend day and night in base banquets? Do I live mostly in a brothel? If you do not know what crimes are charged against me, learn them from a friend. If all men are bad, what is more wretched than this father? If they are good, what is more bloody than this father? OF ROMANIUS HISPO: Shall I go into that house, in which either a father so often runs mad, or a son so often sins against his father? When I come forth suddenly rich, all will say: who is this whom great fortune does not become? This is the rich man's fourth disinheriting. OF POMPEIUS SILO.

Amid so great a variety of characters, see how small is the thing I am excusing: I ask pardon not for ambition, not for sloth; I am merciful, I cannot kill a man. Congratulate yourself, father, on my nature: never will such a son commit parricide. This fault I seem to have drawn from you. Or do you not think him merciful who gave to a brother, to be punished, the one he had condemned? Lucullus's centurion could not kill Mithridates — his right hand and his resolve failed together — Mithridates, by good Jupiter, so undoubted a parricide! OF POMPEIUS SILO. Rejoice, father: neither of your sons committed parricide. I sent the shipwrecked man away from the harbour. Tell, father, how the man so dismissed dismissed you. Do you wish, father, to know whether the accuser or the accused is the more guilty? Cast the stepmother into another ship; let her make her vows, let her pray: if she never accused an innocent man, if she never crushed an undeserving stepson, she will fall in with such pirates as do not know how to dismiss their captives.

HISPO ROMANIUS followed this colour: he said that the young man, swollen and made insolent by the thought of his own nobility, held his kindnesses in hatred, taking it ill that his father-in-law was called Callias; and so he gave all his effort that the girl's morals should not only be allowed to slip into vice, but that he himself should drive them on, so that he might have just cause for divorce. Having got his chance, he did not slay her, but waited until the father should come upon them. He had thought this: "He is waiting for me; he wishes to settle accounts equally with me. He would have done so, had he not shown the father the adulterous daughter." GARGONIUS in this controversia, using a foul kind of false brilliance, said: "That is public adultery — to lie together beneath the trophies of Miltiades." DORION, when he had described that the prison had been a glory to him, said that he had never failed to parade that fortune: "When Callias came in, I uncovered my fetters." HYBREAS said: "I forgive myself."

EUCTEMON, on the son's side, when he had told that his father, alone and without a companion, had been set upon and slain, said: "For this reason it is safest to walk with the rich." And the same: "Why am I silent? My father died while speaking." HERMAGORAS said: "Let us found a city of our own, you poor; for the rich men . . . their own." This in the narration: "By whom he was slain, I do not know. He had enemies by nature . . . able to accuse." ARTEMON said: "When I find the slayer, then in turn will I prosecute; and then indeed, if I find a poor man."

"I think it is because you are vexed that the duty was snatched from you." LATRO gave a plain colour for the young man: he had nothing whereby to excuse himself, but something whereby to glory. I could not, he said, endure that hard spectacle. Do you think it was only my composure that escaped me? My mind escaped me, my spirit did not stand firm in me, my feet did not suffice to the service of holding up my body, my eyes grew numb with a sudden darkness. Otherwise, if I had then been in my right mind, should I have waited until I was asked? FUSCUS introduced that colour which he often used to employ, the colour of religious awe: nature moved me, he said; piety moved me; the changefulness of human chances, so plainly proved by this example, moved me. Fortune seemed to stand before my eyes and to say such things as these: "These are the men who do not maintain their own."

However much there is, it is enough for me; I am an only son. Bravely will I bear my fortune; this is not the first time it has happened to me. I am an only son, and already I am disinherited. What you would have me seem, I do not know: innocent? But I am disinherited. Guilty? But I am adopted. Yet, however that may be, disinheriting is the more bearable: it disinherits one; adoption will disinherit three. It cannot be said to me what is said to other disinherited men: "It was in your own power; had you obeyed your father, you would not have lost a father"; for even had I not been disinherited, I was to lose one.

The other side. OF MUSA. My parricide reigns on the sea. OF SEPULLIUS BASSUS. Deny that he was a parricide at home, you who know that he is a pirate. OF GAVIUS SABINUS. An outrage! A condemned parricide, after his punishment, could say to his own father: "Die." The division. Latro divided into these questions: whether it was lawful for him to do what his father ordered. "It is not lawful," he says, "to kill a brother; nor had he been condemned: for he had not fallen by a public trial." Forgive me if I am too scrupulous, when I see a man so easily condemned: I fear lest someone arraign me for parricide. It is easy. If the case is to be pleaded at home, even the guilty can hope for acquittal; in the forum what shall I answer? "I killed my brother"? Certain men call me a parricide because I was not present to my accused brother. Whether, if it was lawful, he ought to have done it.

ALBUCIUS with this colour: my father, he said, came to me, and spoke no submissive words; he did not entreat, but, as one must deal with a son, ordered me to maintain him; he recited the law, which I always thought was written even for an uncle. And then he said: I rendered not as much as I owed to a father, but as much as I could steal from one who forbade it. BLANDUS with a different colour: he came suddenly, hideous with squalor and tears. O Fortune, how grievous are your turns! That man, rich and proud but a moment ago, begged maintenance, begged his son, begged the son he had disinherited. You ask how long he begged? May the gods not suffer that wickedness, that he begged long — yet longer than you did. You ask what I did? What I was wont to do.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF PORCIUS LATRO: If I did not know what an evil poverty is, I should now understand it: my son does not fear disinheriting. The images of the Fabricii lay open to the Metelli; adoption mingled the families of the Aemilii and the Scipiones; even names abolished for ages shine again through new successors. So that nobility of the patricians, by the foundations of the city, has stood firm down to these times. Adoption is the remedy of fortune. I am not ignorant of those whose poverty, in idleness, in corners, rails at the convicted prosperity of the rich, and pursues them with accusations, and lets them have no peace. But no material in human affairs displays virtues more brightly: the census ascends to the senatorial rank, the census distinguishes the Roman knight from the commons, the census advances a man's standing in the camp, the census chooses the judges in the forum. Have I not persuaded you? Go, then, to those whom you would rather follow than bring back. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER.

"That man is guilty, but he is my brother. The laws of nature are sacred even among pirates." What will you judge of me, if I do it? I think you will hereafter find it hard to believe parricide of me. And, even if he ought to have obeyed his father, whether he is to be pardoned if he could not. "I will confess," he says, "what perhaps will offend the ears of brothers, will offend my father: I wished to kill my brother, I could not. Darkness suddenly came over me, my courage stiffened, my body sank as my breath was cut off. I cannot kill my brother." Set a pirate in this place: he too will be unable. Some men only cannot kill a man; some men's hands fail against the enemy. The brother's kindness too is not so great, father, as you think: he did not refuse to kill you, but was unable. He made those last divisions: although he did not kill, yet whether — if he punished the condemned man — he ought not to be disowned. For the father says: "If you could not, you should have refused and sent word to me that you could not."

POMPEIUS SILO with this colour: it moved me, he said, that he came with no claim of his right, nothing in his power, but as an uncle would come. I, for my part, did not wait for words, did not wait for prayers: I embraced my father and kissed him, and gave him maintenance. In this one thing I acted cruelly — that I said his brother had given it: I seemed not to maintain but to reproach. TRIARIUS with this colour: I feared, he said, that if I had not maintained him, I should be disinherited by my father; I knew how I had pleased him. ARGENTARIUS with this colour: my father came to me, overwhelmed with squalor, trembling with failing limbs; he begged maintenance. I ask you, judges: what ought I to do if these things should happen? For that man I do not ask: he knows what I shall do. Will you suffer me to do a wrong to one father, and bring odium upon the other? When he forbade me to give maintenance — if there is any faith in me — I did not think he forbade it from the heart; he is acting, I said, as a procurer of my own glory, that I may seem to have maintained my father even though forbidden.

I can more easily praise poverty than bear it. Why do you speak to me of Phocion, why of Aristides? Then poverty was the fashion of the age. Why do you speak of the Fabricii, why of the Coruncanii? Those are the examples of a procession, where the gods were of clay. It is easy, where you have never known riches, to be poor. What you wish for your children, I command of mine.

At this point Latro said a thing much praised: "You should have said," he said, "that you could not." So you did not know? You thought I could kill? What then? You spoke as though you had condemned one parricide. Then, whether he punished his brother. Here there was a description of the punishment, which he said was worse even than the sack, and he added that even today the man is paying the penalty, shut up among barbarians, through whom he must of necessity lack his country, his people, his hearth — yet not even through them is it necessary to commit parricide. This division was used by those who chose not to defend the condemned man's cause and only to plead their own; others were used by those who chose to defend his cause too, among whom was GEMINUS VARIUS, who said that the young man had the best case if he did not kill his brother even though guilty, but a better one if he did not kill him innocent; and the material allows this.

MARULLUS pleaded with a new colour: an old man fell at my feet, squalid in beard and hair. Some man or other, I said, knew not who he was, knew my disposition to pity. I raised him up, though I knew not who he was: do you wish me to thrust him off, because he is my father? CESTIUS with this colour: I reasoned thus with myself: he is my father; his brother sees him in want, does not pity him, does not furnish maintenance; this means, I said, he does not wish to snatch the duty from his son, he knows that in this fortune of my kin this is now my part. In this I erred — that I did not go to my father of my own accord; but I kept saying: I do not wish to render this man anything more than I rendered the other; I waited until the uncle should come to me, and now too I shall wait. My father came to me: what was I to do? Lead him to his father? I did not: he is rightly angry. For if he had maintained him, he might indeed have lightened his brother's fortune, but aggravated his cause.

THE DIVISION. I do not think you ask how this controversia was divided, since it has nothing of difficulty in it; yet FUSCUS divided thus: I say it was lawful for him to adopt; I say it was lawful for me to refuse the adoption; I say that, even were it not lawful, I yet rightly refused: for both what is done by right is true, and what is done without right, provided it have reason, is rightly done. When he treated of right, he said: "you are," he says, "under your father's discretion." If in this I am made subject to my father, because I am dutiful, then surely it is for this — that I may be dutiful; and the argument is at hand: surely I am answering one who disinherits me. What, then, do I answer him? Plainly I am acting that I may not cease to be a son; and the same I do when I answer one who emancipates me. For what difference does it make, as to losing a father, whether I am cast out or transferred? If it is not lawful to refuse, I ask: why do you rather disinherit me than hand me over? When he treated of duty, he divided into these: I say a son ought not to have been given in adoption without great cause; I say much less by you; I say least of all to that man.

So Geminus made these questions, and those who agreed with him: whether he ought not to be disowned even if he did not kill his guilty brother. Here he said: it was not lawful, I ought not, I could not. And whether if he did not kill him innocent. A pretty thing Geminus said here, when he had begun to defend the brother through all the points as though he were a defendant: "Someone will say: 'Do you defend him so late?' I could not sooner: today the matter has first been brought into the forum." Lastly: whether he punished even a guilty man sufficiently.

Latro did not approve the colour of BUTEO: he said that he had furnished but little, only enough to keep breath in him; and when he had described his pallor and his leanness, he added: it is plain that he is maintained by enemies. When LATRO disapproved this colour, he used this epigram: nothing, he said, is to be taken from a disinherited man's glory in his crime. HISPANUS used this colour more gracefully; for he added something to the pity due to one not maintained most kindly, and took nothing from his own piety: how, he said, do I maintain him? I send him scanty food by stealth, and whatever I can take from my own table I hold out to the hungry old man. Do you not believe it, you who know how you maintained me?

SILO POMPEIUS divided thus: he began from the old and exploded question, whether a father is to be obeyed in all things; even if in all things, whether he is yet not to be obeyed in that whereby it is brought about that he ceases to be a father; then he asked whether an unwilling son can be given in adoption: if he cannot, he cannot be disinherited for this — that he used his discretion: yet so that he can be, not when he uses his discretion against his father's will, but when he uses it ill. Here he subjoined, whether this man used it well. Then he treated the part of duty, and divided thus: that the adoption is base, that it is useless, that it is dangerous. When he said it was base, he said: how inhuman it is to invade another's goods, to lie in wait for three sons, and to snatch from children the hope of reconciliation with their father! When he said it was useless, he said it was useless to the father, useless to the adopter, useless to himself. When he said it was useless to the father, he treated how grievous a thing it is to be deprived of an only son, how much more grievous to be deprived of one whom another covets; and when he said that the rich man himself too, who had so many consolations, sought a son, he said: it will not be easy for you to adopt. When he said the adoption was useless to the rich man, he treated thus:

Concerning the colour, there was debate among the greatest both orators and declaimers, whether anything ought to be said against the stepmother or nothing. PASSIENUS and ALBUCIUS and, besides the orators, a great band of new rhetors went over to this side; there were also those who inveighed against the stepmother; there were also those who did not indeed speak openly, but by hints and figures — a thing Passienus did not approve, saying that it was less decent, or tolerable, to defame a stepmother than to accuse her. Some had only the openings within their control, then were carried away by the impetus. But it is more excusable to fall into a bad colour than to cross over into it. Latro introduced that straightforward colour in the narration, which he used throughout the whole pleading: "I could not kill." And when he had described, with mighty spirit, the man wavering and collapsing in the midst of his thought about killing his brother, he said: "Stepmother, seek another charge against your stepson; this man cannot commit parricide."

As for the colour on the other side, which is the harder, LATRO said that this was to be followed: that we should bring on inexorable and burning hatreds, born of the gravest wrongs. After the manner of Thyestes, he said, the father ought not merely to be angry but to rage. He himself in his declamation used, to loud applause, that line of tragedy: "Why does he flee his brother? He himself knows why."
