Following this colour, SYRIACUS VALLIUS seemed to set down a harsh thought not harshly, in his narrative, thus: we have both led the most unhappy and the most wretched of lives, save in this alone, that each of us has seen the other in want. With equal effect he seemed to have expressed the brothers' hatred by this epigram:

that it would come about that his own sons would return to him, if he had not adopted. Here he seemed to say prettily: if you understand the father's mind, he gives you a hint how to reconcile his own: he declares that he cannot bear solitude. When he said it was useless to himself, he praised poverty, inveighed against riches; he said he could be corrupted by riches, by which even armies can be corrupted. When he inveighed against riches, he said: they say the rich have many vices, but this is the gravest — they do not love their own. And there is no reason for anyone to think himself firm enough to repel vices: by their very touch they harm the passer-by. I fear lest I should learn to sin. See how quickly you have learned to disinherit! He said that the man would come to displease the rich man when more closely inspected; that his very love of poverty would be loathed by them; he said it would come about that he would be disinherited, if he displeased his adopter: I do not even please my own father. He added that the adoption would be dangerous for him too, in a house that longs for its own masters, and where the whole household desires to expel a grafted heir:

CESTIUS used another colour. "We were passing," he said, "by our mother's tomb." He began to call upon her shade. "I was moved." And with a boyish touch he ran through the colour: "What was I to do?" he said: "my father bade me kill, my mother forbade." And he said, with the colour: "This I thought to myself: I have not been ordered to kill him with my hand, nor with the noose, nor by the sea; the choice of the manner of death is free." ARELLIUS FUSCUS used this colour: "I thought I was being tested by my father; with one and the same punishment," I said, "he wishes to punish one son and to try the other." ALBUCIUS set out more in his arguments and handled almost all the colours. In the narration he used this colour and said: "Grant me this one favour: let me not die as a parricide."

Hear, judges, how greatly I was in want: I begged my brother. This part I remember being declaimed at Cestius's by ALFIUS FLAVUS, to hear whom report had drawn me; who, though he still wore the toga praetexta, was of such repute that as a boy he was known to the Roman people for his eloquence. Cestius always both praised his genius and feared it: he said that so great a genius, so untimely ripe, was not likely to live long; but he was heard amid so great a concourse of names that Cestius rarely dared to declaim after him. He himself did every harm to his own genius; yet that natural force shone out, which, after many years — though buried by sloth and unstrung by verse-writing — nevertheless kept its vigour. But something outside his eloquence was always commending his eloquence: in the boy his very age lent a charm to his genius; in the young man, his idleness.

Latro placed last the question he was generally wont to use: even if he did not act rightly in being unwilling to be adopted by the rich man, whether, if he did this with a good mind toward his father, he is yet to be pardoned; and then whether he did do it with a good mind toward his father. In this question the cause of the young man, who loves his father and prefers him to riches, is good; yet Latro denied that the father would yield, granting that it was done with a good mind toward himself, but would say it was a collusion of sons against a father.

ARGENTARIUS, as though the brother were not the deviser of this plan, said: "I considered what I should do; at last I found how to avenge the parricide without parricide." PASSIENUS used this colour: "I did not think my father wished his son killed at all costs. It seemed to me that he had prepared everything for mercy: that he had heard the case at home, that it was among his own people. He handed him to me, his brother," I said: "come, if he had wished to spare him, to whom would he have handed him?" ASINIUS POLLIO spoke against the stepmother; and so he used this colour: "I considered with myself what was lawful, what was fitting. If so great a crime," I said, "has been committed, it is no part of mine to expiate the age; there is need of the triumvirs, of the comitium, of the executioner. The punishment of so great a crime can no more be private than its trial." MARCELLUS said: "So, if he committed parricide, shall I commit it too?" — and that sententia which I reported above: "You have, brother" — and so on.

He, declaiming the part of the disinheriting father, delivered to loud applause this epigram: Who are you, to pass sentence on a father's deed? He sinned then; you sin now. We do not refer our hatreds to you as arbiter: we have the gods for judges. And that epigram: We hear of brothers' fabled struggles, incredible had we ourselves not been alive — impious feasts, a day made dark by detestable kinslaying: in this one way alone did that brother deserve to be maintained by his brother. How innocently do I avenge myself against kinslaying! I give him back his son.

. . . some unspoken thing or other it had seemed to BROCCO, a certain not bad rhetor, who had said that the young man seemed to him to have certain capital vices; that a man thinks ill of himself who is unwilling to go before a judge strict toward innocence. ARGENTARIUS passed over all the earlier parts, and came at once to this: whether or not he ought to have obeyed his father; and he cast the declamation into a figure. "I wish," he said, "that someone would disinherit a son who has asked his poor father to give him in adoption to a rich man; how good a cause the father will have! He will say thus." Then, when he had declaimed that controversia which had not been set, he passed on thus: "if that son had a bad cause, I have a good one."

VARIUS GEMINUS too said: "I did not wish to kill." "Splendidly," I said, "the stepmother divided her hatred between the stepsons; she attacked each differently: against one she brings the charge of parricide, to the other she entrusts it." And he defended him in the narration by this figure: "I asked my brother: 'Before what praetor did you plead your case?' 'Before none,' he said. 'Who was the accuser?' 'No one.' 'Who the witness?' Nay, what witnesses? For even of a lesser crime one man's word is not believed. 'No one,' he said. 'Who pronounced sentence upon you?' 'No one. And besides,' he said, 'if I had been a defendant, would I not have sent to you?'" SEPULLIUS BASSUS used this colour: "I had not a parricide's instruments — no sack, no serpents; yet I cast a parricide into the seas."

CESTIUS did not approve this colour as too tight-drawn, but said it must be tempered; and he himself used this colour, which he introduced at the very beginning: someone wonders that, when we two — I and my son — have received the gravest wrong from my brother, I alone am angry. There is no cause for wonder: my son has already been satisfied. You ought, he said, to have begged me to furnish it myself; you ought to have led him to me; you ought to have attempted a reconciliation, not to have hunted a reputation for piety out of our quarrel. Perhaps, when I was in want, I would have begged my brother, had you not been there; perhaps he would have begged me, had you not been there; we may yet come to agreement, if there be not in the midst one whom we wretched, stubborn men may prefer to beg.

He compared his own cause with that one. There was more inquiry about the colour — whether the young man ought to say anything against the rich man. For what shall he do? Shall he speak against the man who shows him such honour, and against his father's friend? Shall he not speak against the man he flees? And yet even those who had imposed on themselves abstinence from abuse did not keep it well: the sweetness of some epigram crept up on them, before which they could not stand fast. The dry declaimers more faithfully maintain the colours they have set up: for nothing tempts them, no figure, no epigram. So women who have an ugly face are oftener chaste: it is not the will they lack,

HISPANUS used a harsh colour: "This punishment," he said, "I chose as the heavier. What? Shall that man be sewn up and at once escape all sense of the punishment? No: let him hang in suspense, anxious, and — what not even sewn-up parricides endure — let him himself watch his own penalty; let him hope nothing, fear everything. He ought to die worse than other parricides: he was condemned by his father." And he used this colour throughout the whole declamation, saying that he had chosen this as the heavier. This colour displeased the prudent. For what hope of acquittal has he, if he neither obeyed nor spared? HATERIUS used this colour: "Long I disputed with myself. Is he a parricide whom no witness drags forth, whom no judge convicts? What then? Is he innocent whom his father condemns? And I find a penalty most like the man on trial — a raft sunk yet not wholly destroyed, which could either punish or absolve my brother."

HERMAGORAS in this controversia passed from the proem to the narrative elegantly, in a very rare manner, so that in one and the same thing there was a transition, an epigram, and a figure; but, as it pleased Latro, a figure that wounds, not one that tickles: . . . On the other side GALLIO too passed from the proem to the narrative by an epigram thus: why should I not be unwilling to have a son in common with this man — with whom I would I had had no father in common either? DIOCLES OF CARYSTUS expressed that thought, bandied about by the Latins, most briefly, in a very rare manner whereby an epigram is completed in two words; nor indeed can it be done in fewer . . . EUCTEMON, a slight declaimer but a sweet one, expressed nobly and charmingly that thought, harassed equally by all, by which a reconciliation of the brothers is attempted . . .

but a corrupter. FABIANUS the philosopher used this colour, so as to say: even if I could bear to be handed over to someone, I would not to a rich man. And he spoke against riches, not against the rich man: that they were the things that had stormed frugality and piety, that made bad fathers, bad sons. GALLUS VIBIUS was once of as great eloquence as he was afterwards of madness — he being the only man, I know, to whom it happened to fall into madness not by chance but to arrive at it by judgement; for while he imitated madmen, while he thought frenzy the allurement of genius, what he so often feigned he reduced to reality. He declaimed this controversia the day after it had been delivered by Fabianus;

TRIARIUS too pleaded as though he had wished sentence to be passed on his brother, and said: "At last, lifting my hands to heaven, 'Whatever it is,' I said, 'that rules the lands, that reigns over the deep, whatever it is that from on high looks upon human affairs, I invoke you: the condemned man is committed to the deep; gods, judge after the father!'" This sententia was said to be translated from the Greek, but the Greek is more corrupt: "Poseidon, lord of the unmeasured depths, you who were allotted the kingdom of the sea, a father-slayer is being launched out: judge after the father." From the father's side — namely, that he was dismissed by the pirate-chief — CESTIUS thus: "He thought," he said, "this punishment harder for me than death." And he put it thus in the narration: "I begged that he would kill me; I did not obtain it."

and he was wont to come to his commonplaces in such a way that, about to describe love, he would say, almost in the manner of a singer: "I wish to describe love," just as one might say "I wish to rave." Then he would describe it, and as often as he was about to begin he repeated: "I wish to describe love." In this controversia he plainly attained what he wished — to bring riches into hatred with us. For often he flung out: "I wish to describe riches," and unfolded many things eloquently, more corruptly than Fabianus, but more sweetly. This one thing occurs in which there is a little madness: "the unknown herds of slaves do not delight me, nor the resounding workhouses of a wide estate:

VARIUS GEMINUS said: "In this he dismissed me — not because he wished me safe, but for his own defence, so that, since he had not killed me now, he might seem not to have wished it before." Latro said: "Who, moreover, is more wretched than I alone, who owe my life to a parricide?" DIOCLES OF CARYSTUS placed an elegant thought in the proem on the young man's behalf, saying that he could find no grounds for being disowned: that he had had no occasion for extravagance, that no parricide was charged against him, that he laboured even under the opposite reproach. "Perhaps," he said, "he complains that I did not ransom him when captured." He added: "There was no need of ransom: he was my child." And when he treated, in the last part, that a father ought to bear even the faults of his children — above all of an only child — he added: "You have learned, father, that even a wicked son is sometimes useful." ARTEMO was praised in the description of the storm and approached it elegantly: "Hear the launching of the man who sailed well." And when he spoke of the vessel itself, he began beautifully: "A hull deserted by a fortune that knows no return." And he set out the last sententia of the description: "A shipwrecked man was launching out from the harbours." And he passed elegantly to a part of the narration: "Tell now, father, how the man so released released you." GLYCON said: "The judgement of a single judge does not suffice . . . set aboard a ship he finds his innocence in fortune."

for nothing I love my father." FUSCUS ARELLIUS spoke this colour too: I am offended by omens. When first I began to think of this adoption, three disinherited men came to my mind, and I hear that in that house there were three sons, and are no more. I fear a house unhappy in its children. And he gave other causes too — for a disinherited man may say more things on account of which he would not [choose] — but I now relate the one point on which each man chiefly insisted. Latro used this colour: that he had been a companion to the rich man's three sons. "I always," he said, "cultivated them; nay, I cultivate them still. When they were disinherited, I advised them to keep silent and soften their father by yielding; I said: as soon as you think the time fit, my father will entreat yours. See — they remind me that the time is most fit. It is true; the father can find no fitter time for reconciliation: a rich man seeks sons." CESTIUS with this colour:

I am accustomed to tell you that CESTIUS, a Greek, laboured under poverty of Latin words but abounded in ideas; and so, whenever he ventured to describe something in a richer style, he came to a stop — especially when he had directed himself to the imitation of some great talent, as he did in this controversia. For in the narration, when he was describing his brother handed over to him, he pleased himself in this one — unhappy — elaboration: "It was the dead of night, and all things, judges, that sing beneath the stars were mute." JULIUS MONTANUS, who was a companion . . . an outstanding poet, used to say that he had wished to imitate Virgil's description: It was night, and over all the lands the weary creatures, the race of birds and of cattle, deep sleep held fast. But that Virgil's imitation had turned out well, since he had expressed for the better those excellent verses of Varro: The dogs had ceased to bark, and the cities were silent; all things were of the night, composed in peaceful quiet. Ovid used to say of these verses that they could have been made far better, if the last part of the second line were cut off and it ended thus: All things were of the night. Varro expressed the sense he intended most excellently; Ovid in Varro's line found his own sense: for the line broken off is to mean one thing, the whole line means another.

those whom he could not terrify by disinheriting, he thinks to chastise by adopting. He does not covet your son: he is correcting his own. When he thinks them corrected, he will disinherit me, having threatened me enough. "He will not do it," he says. And yet he has had no one until now in whom he could do this either more easily or more justly. FABIANUS pleaded with this colour, as I said: I do not wish to be rich. RUFUS VIBIUS with this: I do not know how to be rich. When he said these things in this place, they were taken up with applause: there is no reason for you to think riches suit all men; for nothing is more harmful than a newly-rich man. And he said this: let another man speak high words and seek glory from contempt of riches; I do not say, "I do not wish to be rich," but "I do not know how."

ALBUCIUS too attacked riches, and spoke a fine epigram about Fabricius: "he spurned royal gifts," he said: "with the gold he would have received a master too." And he treated that commonplace excellently: I shall hold all my food suspect, all my drink; three sets of tutors are there; whoever is most frugal will wish to kill me. The poor do not fear poison, do not fear an heir; until now we did not even fear disinheriting.

SILO POMPEIUS pleaded with this colour: no one can please him. Not even in this did he keep anyone — that he should not disinherit all. "Behold now," he said, "he has found a new kind of disinheriting, that they may not hope anything from a return." And when he had said much against the rich man, he said: there is no reason for you to wonder if I hate you: I love those whom you have disinherited. The colour on the father's side requires some care. Some brought on a father greedy for riches — which seemed invidious in this case, because he wishes to give riches to a son in such a way as to snatch them from his sons. And so LATRO used the best colour: "for this reason," he said, "I wish to give you in adoption — that through you the disinherited may more easily be reconciled."

CESTIUS: "I fear," he says, "I may be disinherited." I should wish you to fear it. ALBUCIUS used this colour: that he had the closest friendship with the rich man; that he had said to him, when he doubted whether to raise a son: "raise him," he said, "into my patrimony; I shall judge that boy a brother of my children." And so, when he was disinheriting even his third son, he said: why do you mock me thus, as though I were childless? Even now I have a son. He came to me and said: give me back the one you reared: if my children are reformed, I shall have this one with them; if they persist in their madness, I shall have this one in their stead. I tried at once to bring him back into harmony with his sons: it was untimely. I tried to compel him by withdrawing my own: he answered, as though a rich man could not lack a son. SILO said:

"I am," he says, "the friend of the disinherited." What then? Would you rather he adopt an enemy? If you enter the house, you will see whether some men turn the father's mind away from his sons. "If he takes them back," he says, "what will become of me?" The rich man's house holds even four children. If they grudge to have you for a brother, I shall most gladly take you back. So well has the rich man deserved of me, that I am ready both to give him a son and to lend one. BLANDUS pleaded with this colour, so as to say that the rich man was inexorable toward his children. That he himself had done everything to appease him; that the causes seemed great and grave; and so that the adoption was certain to come about.

OTHO JUNIUS the father was wont to deliver difficult controversiae prettily — those in which one needed a middle path between silence and significance. He published, indeed, four books of colours, which our GALLIO prettily used to call the books of Antiphon: so full of dreams are they. And this fault he had drawn from the ancients who handed down the art of speaking; for they approve those colours which cannot be refuted — not, as dreams, that they should be . . . but that they should not be offensive under any name. But it is ridiculous to affect what cannot be proved false. It makes little difference, in one's own case, whether a man produces a false witness, or himself:

for the one ought not to be believed, the other is not wont to be. Yet OTHO JUNIUS spoke well these controversiae which had to be spoken with insinuation. And so I remember him speaking excellently for that woman, accused of adultery, against whom SYRIACUS VALLIUS, an eloquent man, had sworn a charge. The nature of the trial was such: a master swore that he had caught a handsome young man with his wife in the bedchamber, and on this account put away his wife. The slave being prosecuted for adultery on this charge, the master did not defend him, and the woman against whom the action was brought guarded the precedent. There was need of some colour, since she had been seen in the bedchamber with the slave and the husband.

OTHO JUNIUS laid down nothing certain, but only treated excellently of a woman ensnared by her husband; how useful his pleading had been at once appeared when NIGER BRUTTEDIUS spoke, who used this colour: that the slave had been summoned by the master to recline between himself and his mistress; that she had not suffered it; that the husband, indignant, had leapt up as upon a corrupter. He used a more corrupt colour than . . . : for he said the slave had been summoned to act as pander to his master's lust. SYRIACUS, when in his second speech he pressed this colour, said many eloquent things, among which this too: "the accuser brought the adulterer right into the bedchamber, the patron into the bed" — and almost carried off the case. And Syriacus did this slyly too, and answered prettily: when he spoke in his first speech, he did not lay down a case, but argued; he said he would prove she had been caught in the bedchamber with the slave.

NIGER BRUTTEDIUS, when he pleaded, objected to Syriacus that he had not laid down a case, and pressed him persistently as to why it did not appear how the slave had been solicited, how brought into the bedchamber. When Syriacus answered, he said: first, we did not study under the same teacher: you had Apollodorus, who always wishes a narration; I had Theodorus, who does not always. Next, if you ask, Niger, why I did not narrate: I did it that you might narrate those things. And against Maximus Stertinius, by whom he was pressed, though he had been his companion, he said: for twelve years I was in your service; tell me, what did I do wrong in your house? But this is your custom: you call the end of servitude an injury. We are dear to you only so long as we are useful. These sayings of Syriacus, taken up with great applause, occurred to me, and I could not pass them over: I return to OTHO, from whom I have wandered too far.

He was wont to maintain these colours that require silence and significance; and so he spoke this controversia too with this colour, as though he did it for the correction of the disinherited and for the sake of reconciliation. This he did not disclose, but used all his epigrams to tend toward it, as: "I cannot," he says, "endure life without my father." And do you think I can endure life without you? And do you think any father can endure life without his children? And this: believe me, two fathers think nothing impious about their children. And this: "let him take back his own," he says; "I cannot bear life without you." This perhaps will please him — that you will wish to return to your father. And this: do you not love the disinherited?

Then take possession of their house. Do you love them? Then save it. He said this too: "gladly," he says, "am I poor": and so am I. Someone will say: "why then do you give your son in adoption to a rich man?" He will admit the excuse if I say: I do it for my sons' sake; even so I act more honourably than if I handed my son over to him. And this: this is either my plan, or his, or our common one; grant that you agree: he is joining two old men. And this: O the rash and incautious obstinacy of youth! Perhaps the adoption would now be superfluous, had he not resisted. And this: I do not take you back; do all you will, I shall not be the father of a childless rich man. And this at the end: you know that I too am not poor against my will; I begot you, I taught you to despise riches; follow my authority. I advise nothing base, I covet nothing sordid; trust my good faith, it is expedient that this be done. "For whom?" he says. For me, for you, for the rich man; I say no more.

He spoke the whole controversia well, indeed, but in such a manner that, while he was speaking, you would think it ought to be spoken so, and then would wonder what need he had of an insinuating delivery, when he might have used an open one. Prettily about this fault of his Scaurus used to say that he read the records into his own ear. GLYCON SPYRIDION, on the other side, spoke an epigram sweet enough: "Let us save those whom you disinherit, confessing that you have loved them." ARTEMON said: "Riches, father, are no sure possession, where three secret rich men meet you." HERMAGORAS said: "We shall go the rounds, four men secret from one."

THE LAW: A priestess must be chaste and of chaste stock, pure and of pure stock. THE THEME: A maiden was captured by pirates and sold; she was bought by a procurer and set up as a prostitute. She begged of those who came to her the price of her chastity. A soldier who came to her she could not move by entreaty; he used force; she killed him. She was put on trial and acquitted, and sent back to her own people. She seeks a priesthood. — Your priestess would still be living in a brothel, had she not killed a man. What she suffered among the barbarians I do not know: what she could have suffered I do know. To a priestess not even a clean master fell by lot. Let the procurers be absent from this forum, let the harlots be absent, lest anything too little holy meet the eye while a priestess is being chosen. If nothing else, at least everyone who thought you foul has kissed you. O excellent defence of chastity: "She killed a soldier" — but, by Hercules, you did not kill the procurer. You were led into the brothel, you received your place, the price was fixed, the placard was inscribed: thus far inquiry can be made into you; the rest I do not know. Why do you summon me into the little cell and onto the obscene couch? It is of a priestess's chastity that the question here is asked. "No one," she says, "robbed me of my virginity": but all came as though to rob you of it; all departed as though they had robbed you. What good to me is a priestess whose chastity is held on sufferance? If your mother had been a prostitute, it would harm you: for your sake the priesthood would not be given to your children. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS.

THE THEME: A man and his wife swore that if anything happened to one of them, the other would die too. The husband, while abroad, sent a messenger to his wife to say he was dead. The wife, hearing this, threw herself from a height; she was picked up, and, being restored, was bidden by her father to leave her husband. When she refuses, he disinherits her. OF PORCIUS LATRO: Immortal gods, with what providence as you ought you rule the human race: you brought it about that this was not the peril of a loving woman, but the proof of her. OF CESTIUS PIUS: Before we swore, this was long an unspoken law between us. If she is disinherited, she will not live. This her father does not believe. It is nothing new; her husband did not believe it either. You ask what the oath was? "So may I please my father." OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: Now, wife, I shall not sail, I shall not travel abroad. Your good faith has made me timid. "He lied," he says; this is the way of lovers; that is why we believe none but those who swear. Does my father-in-law wish to part those whom not even death will part? "I shall die," she says; "I have both a cause and an example: some women have thrown themselves upon the burning pyres of their husbands, some have ransomed their husbands' lives with their own as a substitute. How great a glory is bought with a short anxiety! O happy you, wife! Among these you are numbered while still alive."

If Cicero had accused Popillius, he would be alive. Popillius killed Cicero: I think you now believe that this man killed his father. That he may perish at a single blow, I will give so much: may I be allowed to make this bargain on Cicero's behalf? OF GAVIUS SABINUS. The one thing we could do, we have done: that there should come a time when Popillius would miss Cicero. "Popillius," he said, "you can kill Cicero; you can even kill your father." OF PORCIUS LATRO. About to kill Cicero, he ought to have begun with his father. "Antony," he says, "ordered me." Are you not ashamed, Popillius? Your commander believed that you could commit parricide. He severed the head, cut off the hand, contrived that the smallest part of his crime should be that he killed Cicero. An outrage! Let the action go most successfully; we shall achieve only this — that the man who killed Cicero merely blushes.

OF MENTO. Already even men about to die were asleep. The whole sequence of the punishment is gone through, lest the courtesan should claim she had not seen something. O wretched is he who offends a courtesan! O wretched the matron whose beauty a courtesan envies! The praetor will deny her nothing she asks. OF MUSA. This is Flamininus, who, when about to go out to his province, sent his wife away from the gate. OF ARGENTARIUS. Do I charge him with extravagance, do I charge him with the jokes of actors? Or do you, at a banquet, do nothing else but kill? Men who lived in prison perished at a banquet. OF BLANDUS.

OF JUNIUS GALLIO. I am in doubt what to wish concerning the outcome of this trial, since my crime is to have conquered. You see how in this trial too he boasts of his own works: and does anyone marvel that, born of such a father, I am too eager for glory? Your part is easy: join the brave men. We disagree because we are too much alike. When we went out into the line of battle, he used to say: "If I were a young man, no one would fight more bravely." He told too the virtues of his ancestors, but set himself before them all. "When I have come to your age, I will not contend with anyone — though, if I choose to follow your example, I will contend even with my son."

What you did shut up within, we ought not to ask and cannot know. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: You killed a man. What do you answer? "He was offering me violence." Yes, I suppose vows are to be made that a priestess may keep her freedom — will you entrust them to a captive? Vows are to be made for chastity — will you entrust them to a prostitute? Vows are to be made for soldiers — will you entrust them to this woman? That was all that was wanting — that the temples should take back those whom either prison or brothel has cast out. OF MARULLUS: That we may know she was in a procurer's house, she is winning; that we may know she was among pirates, she is bloody. "No one," she says, "touched me." Give me the procurer's accounts: the takings will agree. Come now — what if someone came who was stubborn? What if someone desired this very thing, that you were a virgin?

OF MARULLUS: There were constant contentions: "I love more"; "no, I do more." "I cannot live without you"; "no, I without you." The end that contenders usually come to — we swore. You looked upon us, gods, whom we never violated. OF ROMANIUS HISPO: It is hard, judges, to render the reasons for those secrets which are pleasant to lovers even without reason. And there is no cause for you to think that today it is only her disinheriting that is at stake: it is her life. You know how she loves her own: she can no more live without her father than without her husband.

Good gods! I call the killing of Cicero bad morals. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. He smites the neck of so great a man and cuts off the head, severed at the shoulder. Go now and deny that you are a parricide. This one thing, however, you did happily — that you killed your father before Cicero. He moved the judges more easily on a parricide's behalf than, as a client, on his own. To you, advocates, this example belongs: Popillius hates none more than those to whom he owes most. Wherever you are, judges, who sat in judgement on this defendant, do you repent at all of having acquitted him? OF ARGENTARIUS. He is impious, he is ungrateful; I dare to say, he is a parricide: the man who had defended him felt it. Look upon the forum: here you sat beneath Cicero; look upon the rostra: here you stood above Cicero. How much your eloquence availed, Cicero! Popillius is on trial for his morals. He cut off the neck of the speaking man: this is the greeting an acquitted client gives after a long time. Spare him now, I beg, Popillius: Antony charged you with nothing but the killing of Cicero. He committed two parricides, one of which you have heard, the other you have seen.

Let him be struck in the forum; let all see, let the courtesan hear. The leavings of the praetor were dragged off with a hook. I should have said his majesty was injured, if, as you went out, your lictor had not removed the courtesan from your sight. OF VIBIUS RUFUS. The accuser stood ready with his notebooks; he said whatever the courtesan desired. Was it for this that we did not send your wife out with you? That, to keep the province safe, we should pray that the courtesan come to a good mind? We gave you a lieutenant, we gave you a quaestor, that you might dine with a courtesan? The courtesan reclined in the wife's place — nay, in the praetor's. OF P. ASPRENAS.

Because I have the judgment of my country, I have lost that of my father. Shall I say to him who disowns me, "I will not be wanton, I will not love"? This amendment of my crimes I cannot promise: but I will fight, and bravely, and most bravely. I saw my father, already old, putting on the breastplate: it is much to fight against such an example. Does he call it a trial in which father and son together brought in the spoils? Behold, I, a fellow-soldier, can yield to a young man, to an old man I cannot. That I contended is the law's doing, that I conquered the judges', that I fought my father's. I wished to yield: the young men rushed together; the cause of age was being pleaded; I conquered — not a son a father, but a young man an old one. I conquered, but all congratulated my father.

What if someone, that you might not be able to refuse, brought a sword? OF PUBLIUS VINICIUS: Make her a priestess who may either honourably remain what she always was, or feel the penalty if she has ceased to be it. Of what boldness are you, girl? Even if we did not fear for ourselves, you ought to fear for yourself. Each man's conscience is subject in one way to the godhead's power, in another to our estimation: we have seen only what you did openly, they see even what is secret. I should call you unworthy of the priesthood, had you merely passed through a brothel. Shall the lictor going before clear the way for this woman? Shall the praetor yield her the road, shall the consuls yield their supreme command? Shall every prostitute that plies her trade flee at your approach? It would not be lawful for a priestess to have a maidservant like you: let it not be lawful for such a one to be made priestess. For as to what concerns the lot — that the rest of the maidens might not be defiled, this one was set apart. Do you think yourself chaste, because you are a hated prostitute? She stood naked on the shore for the buyer's disdain; every part of her body was both inspected and handled. Do you wish to hear the outcome of the auction? A pirate sells, a procurer buys, nothing is held back. You were brought to a place where you could do nothing more honourable than die. You begged for alms more earnestly than you now beg for the priesthood. "Fortune," she says, "forced me to suffer these things; all ought to pity me." And I do pity you, girl; but we do not make priestesses of women to be pitied. With us the highest honour is not the solace of the worst misfortunes.

OF JUNIUS GALLIO: Father-in-law — for so I shall call you as long as I live — what mean these deeper groans and these stronger sighs amid your tears? You seem, girl, to promise something stronger. I am not worth so much, that you should risk yourself twice for me. OF ARGENTARIUS: The indulgence of her family harms her. The woman fell into two perils, neither of which she would have known, had she loved her husband less or her father less. OF ALFIUS FLAVUS: And there is no cause for you to think her longing for him is the easier to bear: she loves her father too, as though she had sworn to die.

OF CESTIUS PIUS. If I say, "His youth was base, his boyhood infamous," he will answer: "Cicero already defended all that." Are you not ashamed, Popillius? Your accuser is alive. "What is so common as breath to the living, earth to the dead, the sea to the storm-tossed, the shore to the cast-up?" Parricide, thus would you too have perished. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. Antony would not have believed that Popillius did it, had it not come into his mind that the man had also committed parricide. An outrage! Cicero is defended by me, when Cicero defended Popillius. OF MENTO. No more could any other than Popillius have killed Cicero, than no one but Cicero could have defended Popillius. The parricide whom Cicero, living, had denied, Cicero, slain, revealed. The fortune of Cicero! Antony proscribed the man who was prosecuted; Popillius killed the man who was defended. If you had been condemned, the executioner would then have sewn you into the sack. I see what he will answer: Antony would not believe Cicero had been killed by Popillius, unless he brought him a token.

With a single kiss, perhaps, she bestowed a murder. Even executioners, about to dine, wash their hands. OF PORCIUS LATRO. Not even by a sober lictor was he struck. I do not inquire into the whole year; I am content with one night. "Drink, lictor, that you may strike the harder." Do you at all understand how a man was condemned who was killed thus? How do I know whether, in whose favour he was killed, he was also condemned by the same person? As much as the Roman people had given you, so much you gave to a courtesan. If she had denied it, what witnesses should I have? For who was at that banquet who deserved belief? It is easier for a man who has given a courtesan other things to deny a murder, than for one who has given her this too to deny anything. Of course this is never wont to be shown before women's eyes — or she would have seen it often already.

As a young man I obeyed great examples. I was deceived, while I thought to myself of Horatius warding off the Etruscan ranks with his body, and of Mucius burning his hand on the enemy's altar; and while I thought of you, Decius, who yourself too were unwilling to yield to your father. I will pass over into your benches, I will embrace you against your will: though you fight back, I am the stronger. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS.

OF MENTO: I would have you respect your ears and your majesty, since in this case I must of necessity name a brothel, a procurer, harlot's earnings, a homicide. Who would believe it? Amid these things a priestess is sought. But, by Hercules, a future priestess ought to have heard nothing of all this. The chief thing known of your priestess is that she stood for sale; her chief virtue, that she killed; her chief good fortune, that she was acquitted. A priestess cannot be hoped for in one in whom a prostitute can be hoped for: with different eyes does the procurer appraise a maiden, with different eyes the pontiff. OF BLANDUS: "I am a virgin," she says: "ask the pirate-captain, if you doubt; ask the gladiator whether, when asked, he spared my virginity." I do not refute it — provided you know that the temples are closed to such witnesses of yours. At the auction no one would bid, once it became known that she had been a slave to pirates. That was not the face of a virgin, that firmness, that boldness fearing not even an armed man.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF PUBLIUS ASPRENAS: Surely, if anything happens to her husband, the wife will perish; and if I know my daughter well, she will perish if anything happens to my son-in-law. My daughter is going to die: I will add what is shameful — if anything happens to my daughter, her husband will live. See by what a law you have bound yourself: if you obey your husband, you will die; if you obey your father, you will live. OF BLANDUS: O a fair bargain! To the one she owes her life, to the other she devotes it. OF PAPIRIUS FABIANUS: "I cannot," she says, "leave my husband." Is there anything you cannot do, who can die? He who had sent the message of a false death almost received that of a true one. The husband, while he loved his wife too much, was almost the cause of peril; the wife, while she loves her husband too much, was almost the cause of mourning; the father, while he loves his daughter too much, disinherits her. Gods, save a whole house labouring with mutual love. "I shall die," she says: this you threaten your father, you promise your husband. You can bear life without your husband; you bore his absence abroad. She can more easily do without the one to whom she owes her life than without the one to whom she devotes it.

OF TRIARIUS. Grant to Cicero what the kinsmen of Catiline, what the friends of Verres, what the clients of Clodius granted: pass by the proscribed man. Not even from a dead man does he keep his hands; he mangles the slain. Popillius, this is your third parricide. OF POMPEIUS SILO. Can I unburden you any further? Grant Cicero what Antony did. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. Say: "Antony, I can do that crime: I have even killed my father." Cicero's friends were untroubled after Popillius was sent to him. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. Could you kill Cicero? Yet how well Cicero had persuaded us that you could not commit parricide! You killed Cicero as he spoke. "Is there any informer of yours," he says, "to be feared?" Or is no one to be feared by Cicero who comes with Popillius?

OF JULIUS BASSUS. Amid the drunken leavings of a most lavish dinner and the food that loathing for drunkenness leaves behind, a human head just severed is carried in; amid the sweepings and the leavings flung from the diners and the sawdust strewn at the feast, human blood is swept away. I congratulate you on your lot, province, that, when a courtesan desired such a spectacle, you had a prison full of the condemned. If you had wished a slave whipped, you would have led him away outside the banquet. OF ROMANIUS HISPO. Who would endure you, if you had convened a court in your dining-room? It is a crime to condemn a man at a banquet; what is it to kill one? At a courtesan's pleasure you pronounced judgement on defendants — unless perhaps you behead more readily in her honour than you judge.

It was necessary for me to fight bravely: I had to fight not only for my general but for my father. If you had conquered, it would be said: "He yielded to his father; for he feared to be disowned." You always used to wish that it might fall to you to have a son better than yourself. Do you call a trial the double triumph of our house?

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: Do not fear, girl, you are chaste: but praise yourself thus to a husband, not to a temple. You were called a harlot, you stood in a common place, a placard was set above your cell, you received the comer. The rest — even were I in a common place, I would rather be silent. OF POMPEIUS SILO: She is received with the kisses of harlotry, taught its blandishments, and fashioned to every movement. Turn away your ears, you who would seek the priesthood, while I tell the rest: I shall bring to you nothing doubtful, you shall hear nothing but what the neighbouring city saw. You, a priestess? What if you had only been captured, what if you had only been prostituted, what if you had only been a homicide, what if you had only been a defendant? OF ROMANIUS HISPO.

This controversia too needs no division; for besides that one question — whether a father can disinherit on account of marriage — the rest, since they pertain to equity, belong to treatment. Yet Latro made an excellent conjectural question; he propounded this: whether, even if the husband acted with no bad mind toward his wife, he is yet, being so rash and inconsiderate, to be left; then, whether he acted even with a bad mind toward his wife. ARELLIUS FUSCUS subjoined to the question of law that she could not depart from her husband: for the oath bound her to this too. For without doubt this was the mind of those who swore — that they should not be parted while living, since they had even provided that they should not be divided by death.

OF Q. HATERIUS. The man who but lately was borne back on the shoulders of Italy — is he now brought back thus by Popillius? When Cicero's head was set up on the rostra, although all were held by fear, yet the people's groan was free. OF JULIUS BASSUS. "Proscribed," he says, "was Cicero." Your father, certainly, was not proscribed. OF BLANDUS. The shades of old Popillius and the unavenged spirits of your father, Cicero, pursue you, so that you may feel the man whom you denied to be a parricide. OF CAPITO. I have brought before you a defendant the most guilty of all that the earth bears — ungrateful, impious, an assassin, twice a parricide; nor yet do I fear; let the advocates see to it: no one is killed by Popillius except after a kindness. I do not even despair of his condemnation; for he is not defended by Cicero. I fear lest I fail to do justice to my cause. It is a greater cause to lament that Cicero was killed by Popillius than it once was to prove that he had not killed his father.

OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. I speak of a table stained with human blood, of axes drawn in the dining-room: who would believe that a courtesan desired such things, or that a praetor did them? I speak of a corpse, of axes, of blood: who, amid these, thinks of a banquet? "A man," she says, "I never saw killed." Then under the praetorship of Flamininus did you see everything else? OF SILO POMPEIUS. A most noble man, one who had held such offices, a courtesan would basely have made merciful: she made him cruel. "I never saw it." Add, if you like: "Nor, under another praetor, shall I be able to see it."

OF CLODIUS TURRINUS. Would you say to Mucius, "There is no need for you to show that hand"? You to Scipio after the destruction of Carthage, "Be silent"? Virtue is talkative, and not only shows itself but thrusts itself forward. Behold, some now say: "The father yielded to the son, and in this he disowns him — that the contest may seem to have been real." Wish, father, to be conquered by your grandson too. "Afterward," he says, "you will be able to fight bravely." How do I know? With wounds I have made myself old. Who is happier than you? You conquered all, your son conquered you. How much more honourably did father and son contend with each other just now — destined to make the more honourable whichever conquered. I am in doubt what to do. Shall I be silent?

Do you at all deny this — that you yet wrestled with the man, who in that struggle must of necessity first have been on top of you? The procurer added that the soldier was rightly killed, since he had dared more than was permitted against a prostitute. You won over the people: did you win over the procurer too? Did you win over that pirate whom you could not kill? OF ARGENTARIUS: "I killed an armed man," she says. What of the unarmed? She glories in the killing of one whom I am not sure she did not kill too late.

To LATRO it seemed the contrary: that the odium of the oath was being loaded on, when it ought to be lightened: that oath seems against fortune, this even against the father. CESTIUS did the contrary and said outright that by that mischance she was freed from the oath; that they themselves were released from the bond of the obligation, and therefore there would be no peril to the wife if anything happened to the husband. SILO POMPEIUS said the contrary — that she was bound by the oath — and added that, even if she were parted by divorce, the compact of the agreement would yet not be dissolved; "and therefore," he said, "I claim an honourable title for our death, lest, if anything happen, either I should die for another man's wife, or she for another woman's husband." HISPO ROMANIUS used this colour:

Could anyone have killed Cicero who had heard him? The marsh of Minturnae did not swallow up the exile Marius; the Cimbrian, even in the captive, saw the commander; the praetor turned his journey aside from the sight of the exile; the man who had seen Marius on the river-bank set him in the magistrate's chair. We cannot complain of Popillius: he held his patron in the same place as his father. Gnaeus Pompey, tamer of lands and seas, gladly professed himself the client of Hortensius; and Hortensius had defended Pompey's goods, not Pompey. Romulus, founder of these walls and a parent consecrated to heaven, did not make so great a city as Cicero saved.

OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. But if there is anyone, judges, who would wish me to recount the praetor's cruelty — how many besides this man he butchered, how many innocent men he condemned, how many he shut in prison — to him I do not promise that I will satisfy him: in one banquet, with his praetorship, I will unroll the whole defendant. A feast is set up by this man in the province, and with magnificent equipment a banquet is built up; golden cups are set off by silver ones. In short, judges — the province felt the equipment of his banquet. A certain man is dragged out of prison into the praetor's banquet, and at him, stupefied and wretched, the courtesan smiles. Meanwhile the rods are brought out, and the victim of cruelty is butchered before the table and the gods.

But silence seems a confession. Shall I tell my virtues? But this too befalls me as something new — that to me alone, disowned, it does not profit to tell them. I went out into the line in my father's presence: "Fight bravely," he said; "it is base for a young man to be conquered by an old one." I am greedy of glory: if this is a vice, it is my father's. I am brave: do you blame it, father? But you will disown me now, if I say: "I am most brave." Yet I will say it boldly:

THE NARRATIVE OF CESTIUS PIUS: She was so guarded at home that she could be seized; so dear to her own that, once seized, she was not ransomed; the pirates so spared her when seized that they sold her to a procurer; the procurer so bought her that he might prostitute her; she so begged those who came that there was need of a sword. Her name, cast into the urn, did not come out — it was cast out. It was time now to draw lots: the urn was purged. You stood, girl, in a brothel: already, though no man violated you, the place itself violated you. You stood among harlots, you stood adorned so as to be able to please the people, in the dress the procurer had given; your name hung on your brow; you received the wages of unchastity, and the hands that were to offer holy things to the gods bore takings to the procurer; when you besought the embraces of those who entered — that you might win all else — you begged with a kiss. Maidservants are not bought for a priestess out of brothels; in a priestess's presence men abstain from obscenities. Not without cause does the lictor attend a priestess: had you met her, he would have driven you off as a harlot.

that the oath was a jest; that, as lovers swear many things daily, so she too had sworn; and so that, forgetting she had sworn, he sent the message, to test whether his wife's affection still held; that the wife understood the message was false, and threw herself from that place from which, when thrown, she could not perish: "so that, just as I," he said, "had frightened her with a false message, she might frighten me with a false peril." MARULLUS, our teacher, used a word freely enough that expressed the sense, when he said that the wife understood her husband's falsehood: and she herself played back against her husband's rash jests. This controversia I remember being declaimed by OVID

Metellus put out a fire for Vesta, Cicero for Rome. Let Scipio boast of Hannibal conquered, Fabricius of Pyrrhus, the other Scipio of Antiochus, Paulus of Perses, Crassus of Spartacus, Pompey of Sertorius and Mithridates: no enemy came nearer than Catiline. They say that the head, seized by the hair, with the blood flowing down, befouled this very place in which Cicero had pleaded for Popillius. OF BUTEO. Of how great eloquence he was! He proved that his father had not been killed by the man by whom even Cicero could be killed. OF MARULLUS. If I were an enemy to advocates, I should wish the defendant to be acquitted. I judge it base that in that city Cicero should not be defended, in which even Popillius could be defended.

Wretched me — you mocked the terror of the Roman empire! O you who in cruelty surpassed all tyrants! To you alone, amid the feasting, the groans of the dying are a delight: this was the last course of the dinner. In the same dining-room I see a praetor, a lover, harlots, slaughters; and the courtesan commands the praetor, the praetor the province. Into the banquet is brought a man in chains, who, when he saw the languid eyes of this praetor, thinking that he himself was being dismissed by the praetor's kindness, gave him thanks and, holding the table with both hands, said: "May the immortal gods return you like thanks." Whoever reclined in the same dining-room — one let his head fall and wept abundantly, another turned his eyes away from that cruelty, another laughed, that he might be the more pleasing to the courtesan.

I am most brave, nor do I fear this charge in a state in which we have known even old men to be brave. OF JULIUS BASSUS. To you too part of my disgrace overflows: be ashamed, father, if you are conquered by disowning a son. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the father. Forgive me, young man as I was, I erred: I will not be ambitious, when I am old. OF GAVIUS SILO.
Which do you think conquered? I have only the reward, you have both the reward and a brave son.

It is not credible that the pirates restrained themselves from lust — pirates wild with every cruelty, to whom all right and wrong is a sport, brigands at once of lands and seas, whose every assault upon another's goods is made by arms; cruel in their very brow and inured to human blood, carrying before them fetters and chains, heavy burdens for captives. From their lusts could you keep them off — men for whom, amid so many far greater crimes, to ravish a maiden is innocence? But the brothel received you. Every sordid and injurious throng flows in there, nor does any man come there to judge. But did all favour your stories? Were all persuaded? Was no one found, in so great a throng of men coming and going, who would mock your fortune? So then — when you have lived as innocently as you claim, do you, who suffered these things, believe there are gods? "I suffered nothing," she says. This is enough for a bride, too little for a priestess. Where have you been until now? Begone, you are unknown. Where have you not been? Begone, you are too well known. OF PUBLIUS

NASO before the rhetor Arellius Fuscus, whose hearer he was; for he was an admirer of Latro, though he followed a different style of speaking. He had a polished and graceful and lovable talent. His prose even then could seem nothing else than verse set loose. And so studiously did he hear Latro, that he transferred many of his epigrams into his own verses. In the contest over the arms Latro had said: "let us send the arms into the enemy and seek them." Naso said: "Let the arms of the brave man be sent into the midst of the foe; thence bid them be sought." And another thought from that suasoria he likewise borrowed from Latro. I remember Latro saying in a certain preface what the schoolmen had learned as though it were a poem: "do you not see how an unstirred torch lies dull, but, shaken, gives back its fires? Leisure softens men, iron is worn away by rust and gathers corrosion, sloth unteaches us." Naso said: "I myself have seen flames grow when the torch was shaken, and again die when no one stirred them."

Few of the historians have handed down Popillius as the killer of Cicero, and these too say that he was defended by Cicero not as a defendant on a charge of parricide, but in a private trial: the declaimers chose that he should have been a defendant on a charge of parricide. But they accuse him as though he could not be defended, when he can so well be acquitted that he could not even have been accused. It did not please Latro that he should be accused as some accused him: "I charge you with this, that you killed a man, that you killed a citizen, that you killed a senator, that you killed a man of consular rank, that you killed Cicero, that you killed your patron." For by this method the indignation is not aggravated but worn out. One must at once come to the point at which the hearer is hastening; for in all the rest Popillius has so good a case that, with the killing of his patron set aside, he will have no difficulty; his defence is the necessity of civil war. So I do not wish to lead the defendant through those stages which he can so often escape. For in war it was lawful to kill a citizen and a senator and a man of consular rank; it is not even a charge that he killed Cicero, but that he killed his patron. And it is natural that what ought not to have been done to any patron should be more disgraceful when done to Cicero as patron.

Then this man, amid the varied faces of the guests, bids him be removed, and the wretch stand to offer his neck, motionless; meanwhile his death is set off with cups. Not even by the hand of a sober executioner was a Roman citizen killed. I do not forbid that he be struck with the axe; this I ask: that he fall by the law rather than for a harlot. Remember that terror is sought for the empire's sake, not entertainments for little women. Why should I now recount, judges, the kinds of games, the dances, and that contest of disgrace — whether the praetor moved more wantonly, or the courtesan?

THE DIVISION. Latro divided thus: whether the son can be disowned for this — that he did what the law allowed. "No one," he says, "in the same matter both has the law and fears it." On the other side he says: if he does anything which is not allowed, the law will avenge it; if anything which is allowed but not fitting, the father will. The question is not of the son's crime, but of his duty. Then: let each use his own law; that was allowed you, and this is allowed me. Let it be permitted to disown one's children. Is there any law that prefers the son to the father? If he can be disowned even for what he did with the law's permission, whether he can be disowned also for this — that he received the prize. "He cannot," he says, "be privately punished in that matter in which he is publicly honoured. To the same thing cannot both a prize be given and a mark of disgrace announced. Suppose the other rights to be subject to paternal authority: this right is greater than the rest, in which there is question of victory, of the highest virtue. You cannot disown your son under this law, by which you were conquered by your son."

ASPRENAS: I speak against her, driven by enmity towards no one; for what hatred, what enmity can anyone have toward a woman whom no one of her fellow-citizens knew before she stood for sale? I am moved by regard for all the maidens, on whom a grave sentence is passed today, if in the city there can be found no woman chaster than a harlot, none purer than a homicide. Did the pirates keep you inviolate? A pirate, a procurer, a slaver would not have abstained from a priestess. Are we to believe in a priestess's chastity on the security of such sureties? You lay in a pirate's skiff; you were handled by someone's hand, kissed by someone's mouth, embraced by someone's arms. Did a pirate keep you better than your father? You consorted with men bloody and smeared with human blood: thence, surely, comes your power to kill a man.

At that time, indeed, when he was studying, he was held a good declaimer. This controversia, at least, he declaimed before Arellius Fuscus, as it seemed to me, far more ingeniously, except for this — that he had run through the commonplaces without any fixed order. These sayings, as he spoke, I remember being taken up: all the labour lies in this — to grant that a wife should love a husband, and a husband a wife. Then you must allow them to swear, if you have allowed them to love. What oath do you think we had? You were to us a holy name; if we should lie, she invoked her father angry with her, I my father-in-law. Spare us, father: we did not forswear ourselves. See how our reproacher is borne on by an unbridled love! He complains that anyone besides himself is dear to his daughter. What is there that can call him away from his indulgence?

Latro accused him of his morals: first, that he had so lived as to plead a case of parricide; then, that he had killed his own patron. And he made these questions: whether he can be accused under that name under which he was acquitted. "If anyone," he says, "wishes today to arraign me for parricide, he will not be able. How can the crime that cannot be charged be punished?" Whether acts done in civil war can be charged. Honourably did VARIUS GEMINUS say, when he treated this commonplace: "If you call those times to account," he said, "you speak not of the man's morals but of the state's." If what was done in civil war can be charged, whether this ought to be charged. This question he divided into this: whether, even if it was necessary for him to do it, he ought nevertheless not to be pardoned. For to certain things no necessity ought to compel us. Here Latro said, amid the loudest applause: "So you, Popillius, if Antony had ordered it, would even kill your father?" Then, whether it was necessary for him. "You could have excused yourself, you could have sent someone ahead to Cicero, so that he might know and flee;

OF CAPITO. Rise now, you Bruti, Horatii, Decii, and the rest of the empire's glories: into how great a disgrace, by good Jupiter, have your fasces, your axes, fallen! With these obscene girls make sport. But if, by the immortal gods, on no solemn day, in the people's sight, you had held a banquet in the forum, would you not have lessened the majesty of our empire? And yet what difference is there whether you drag the banquet into the forum or the forum into the banquet?

If he can be disowned, whether he ought to be. This he divided thus: whether, even if he ought not to have contended with his father, he should nonetheless be forgiven, if as a young man he slipped through eagerness for glory; then, whether he ought to have contended. "For you," he says, "the contest was both honourable and safe: for what is more glorious than either to conquer a brave man or to be conquered by one's son? If he ought not to have contended, he would not have conquered. And it could have come about that, had he yielded to you here, some other man would have come forward to the contest who now did not come forward, because he knew it would profit him nothing if he conquered you, since he must be conquered by your son. There would have been no praise of yours: for it would have appeared that that victory was not of a brave man, but of a father. In silence your virtues would have passed away:

Proclaim that you are freeborn: what do you expect, once you have come into a brothel? Already every temple is shut against you. She is fouled by the kisses of fellow-slaves, tossed about amid the jests of drunken banqueters, dressed now in a boy's, now in a woman's attire: from there you are not to be ransomed even by a father. No woman about whom a question is asked is chaste enough. I would not choose you priestess, even if you had been a slave to a priestess. To whom do we owe it to believe that our priestess is a virgin? To a harlot, a procurer, pirates: for this is the sum of the witnesses. A priestess would have deserved the chief pontiff's chastisement, had she ransomed you from a brothel. The whole crowd of the lustful gathered and ran together to the new harlot. This at least you will confess: your chastity is held on sufferance. So many gladiators entered your cell, so many young men, so many drunkards — and all of them, before the soldier, unarmed? I say she stood for sale; she says she even begged. The chastity of my priestess I owe even to the executioner.

Good gods, how did this man love his wife? He loves his daughter, and disinherits her; he grieves that she has been in peril, and takes her away from the man without whom she says she cannot live; he complains of her peril, which this man, who bids her love cautiously, has almost lacked. You may more easily obtain an end of love than a measure. Will you obtain this — that they keep the bounds you approve, that they do nothing but advisedly, promise nothing but as though about to perform it, weigh every word by reason and good faith? So old men love. Few crimes you know, father: we have sometimes quarrelled too, and made it up, and — what perhaps you do not think — have forsworn ourselves. What concern is it of a father's that lovers swear to believe one another? Nor is it the gods' concern.

it was certainly not necessary to cut off the hand and head of a dead man." Latro's colour for Popillius was a simple one: that he had acted compelled by necessity; and here he said that sententia: "Do you wonder that it was necessary for Popillius to kill at the time when it was necessary for Cicero to die?" ALBUCIUS said that, for Cicero's punishment, the man most friendly to Cicero had been chosen, as though Antony meant by this to reproach him with his fortune. "He will bear it," he said, "more grievously to be killed by Popillius than to be killed." MARCELLUS AESERNINUS introduced the same colour differently. "Antony was considering with himself," he said: "'What punishment shall I devise for Cicero? Shall I order him killed? Long ago he fortified his mind against this fear; he knows that death is neither untimely for a man of consular rank nor wretched for a wise man. Let something new be done that he does not expect, that he does not fear; he does not scorn to offer his neck to an enemy, but he will scorn to offer it to a client.' Let someone summon Popillius, that he may know how much the defendants he defended profited him." POMPEIUS SILO used this colour:

Then he described how differently a man is beheaded in the forum. The praetor ascends the tribunal while the province looks on; the guilty man's hands are bound behind his back; he stands while the faces of all are intent and sad; silence is made by the herald; then the lawful words are employed; on the other side the war-trumpet sounds. Do I seem to you to be describing the jests of a banquet? Alas, how unlike are your ends to your beginnings! A Roman knight accused you, Roman knights judged you, the praetor pronounced you condemned, a courtesan killed you.

now they are made illustrious, while they are compared." TURRINUS in this place said neatly: "More men began to envy you, after you were conquered." And so a thing of a new kind happened: the son had conquered; all said, "O happy father!" He made the last question: whether, even if he sinned in some way by the judgment, he amended it by the prize. In this place GALLIO said that epigram which was much applauded: when he had long pleaded for pardon, he said: "If I cast away nothing, what do you think I will do? Go to the temples to supplicate the gods? I will flee for refuge to your statues."

OF JUNIUS GALLIO: The law is exacting: to the priesthood it admits none but women of unbroken — not holiness only, but good fortune; it inquires into ancestors, into the body, into the life: see how you can satisfy so fastidious a law. You were captured by pirates; among slaves, among homicides, in the narrows of that skiff you took your walks: let us see what the savagery of enemies, the lust of barbarians, the licence of masters, could have dared upon you. I am sure, judges, that when you hear of this barbarian savagery, you wish her well, that she may change her servitude as soon as may be. The pirates kept her safe as men do who mean to sell to a procurer; the procurer kept her safe so that she should be forced to stand in that rank, to feed at the same table, to live in a place where, even if you suffer no outrage, you see it.

There is no cause for you to plume yourself, wife, as though you were the first to sin: some woman has perished with her husband, some has perished for her husband; yet those every age will honour, every genius will celebrate. Bear, father-in-law, your good fortune. How great an example it costs you, and for how little! For the future we are made more careful, as you bid; we confess our error; it had escaped us, when we swore, that there was a third party who loved more: so, gods, may it ever be. Do you persist, father-in-law? Take back your daughter: I, who sinned, am worthy of punishment; why should I be a cause of disgrace to my wife, of childlessness to my father-in-law? I will depart from the city, I will flee, I will go into exile, and however I can I shall, wretched, bear my longing with a cruel patience. I would die, if I were the only one to die.

"I was offended," he said, "by the proscription, and spoke certain things too freely. 'I do not wonder; you are Cicero's client: so much the more, kill your Cicero.'" And he said a sententia not lacking in force: "Each of us," he said, "but in a different way, was punished: for Cicero the proscription was to be killed; for me, to kill." MARULLUS, our teacher, told the tale thus: "He ordered," he said, "the commander ordered, the conqueror ordered, the man who was proscribing ordered: could I refuse anything to him to whom the state could refuse nothing?" BLANDUS used this colour: "I wished," he said, "to excuse myself; I said, 'Cicero defended me'; he answered, 'I know; he accused me. Go therefore, that he may know that Antony's accusation harmed him more than Popillius's defence profited him.'" BUTEO used this colour:

OF BUTEO. That this man might dine more pleasantly with his mistress, a man was killed. "Did you, judges," he says, "ever see before the rostra a praetor dining with a courtesan?" OF VOTIENUS MONTANUS. The man who feasts thus, how does he show anger? Those about to condemn swear that they give nothing to favour, nothing to entreaty: I demand that you swear to this law. The majesty of the Roman people, spread through all nations, through all provinces, lies in the lap of courtesans; she commands our praetor who once stood for sale, from whose kiss no man abstained except the one who spared his own lips. Recount your own guests: there were, I suppose, tribunes, there were prefects, there were Roman knights:

SILO POMPEIUS attempted in this controversia too that question which he thought should be attempted in all disownings of brave men: whether a brave man can be disowned; he said that in no controversia could it be handled better. "You cannot," he says, "disown one who can conquer you. Do you marvel that under this law a man is taken from a father, who is both matched with him and preferred to him?"

Perhaps someone was found whom this very thing inflamed — that you begged. But did the procurer himself spare you? Do we not know those men to whom, in such a trade, this is especially pleasing — that they pluck untouched virginity? Did the procurer keep you, whom he meant to prostitute to the people's lust? Did the procurer keep you so, as we keep a chaste woman among the chaste? "I won them all over," she says. If anyone doubted whether she was a harlot, let him hear how coaxing she is. You clung in embraces, you bargained with a kiss, so that — most fortunate as you were — you begged unchastely for your chastity. What shall I do with a woman skulking within her own crimes? When I say, "You suffered violence," she says, "I killed"; when I say, "You killed a man," she says, "He was offering me violence." Our priestess defends her unchastity by homicide, her homicide by unchastity. THE DIVISION. Latro divided into these questions:

Naso, however, rarely declaimed controversiae, and none but ethical ones; he more gladly spoke suasoriae. All argumentation was a burden to him. He used words with no great licence except in his poems, in which he was not unaware of his faults, but loved them. This can be made plain by the fact that, being once asked by his friends to remove three lines, he asked in turn that he himself might except three, over which they should have no power. The condition seemed fair; they wrote down in secret those they wished removed, he those he wished kept safe: in both tablets were the same lines, of which Albinovanus Pedo, who was among the arbiters, used to relate that the first was: "the half-bull man and the half-man bull"; the second: "and cold Boreas and unfrozen Notus." From which it appears that the man of supreme genius lacked not judgement but will to curb the licence of his verses. He used to say that a face is sometimes the more comely for having some mole upon it.

"'Let that Ciceronian client, that friend, be summoned,' he said; 'I have devised how Cicero may perish by his own hand.'" CESTIUS used this colour: "Most harsh," he said, "was my service in Antony's camp, for this very reason, that I was Cicero's client; the hardest expeditions were assigned to me. Then too I was summoned as though to punishment: 'Go,' he said, 'kill Cicero; and I will not believe it,' he said, 'unless you bring the head'; and he marvelled the more at his own power, that it was not permitted to Popillius not to kill Cicero." ARELLIUS FUSCUS used this colour: that he had followed Antony's party so that, if he could do anything, he might help Cicero; that when the proscription was made he had fallen at Antony's knees and begged for Cicero; that Antony, offended, had said, "So much the more, kill the man you do not wish to die." This colour displeased PASSIENUS, because it leads to a witness; for if Popillius did this, he not only has something to defend, but something to boast of.

with these, then, the praetor . . . OF CASSIUS SEVERUS. Not even of a slave or a captive is it lawful to take punishment in any place or in any manner or through whomever one pleases or whenever one pleases; and a magistrate is brought in for these things for custody's sake, not for merrymaking's. OF TRIARIUS. On what charge had he been condemned? Murder. Yet he had not killed at a banquet. Take careful heed, courtesan, lest you ask for a second murder.

As colour for the young man GALLIO brought in this: "The young men," he says, "stood round me; the cause of age seemed to be pleaded. While I hesitated, I heard someone, I know not who, saying: 'You do nothing; I yield to you, to him I do not yield.'" CESTIUS used this colour: that he had thought it more honourable for the father himself, and certainly for the house, that the praises of both should be seen in the forum. MONTANUS VOTIENUS said:

"I considered not what you commanded, but what you had taught; for you had always said, when you urged me to glory, that I should yield to no one." Your fortune seemed enviable to all in that trial, when it was asked whether you had fought more happily or begotten. There is no reason for you to think that I seemed braver to them: they were deceived, father; they judged not what was, but what they believed you would rather.

whether by the law she cannot become a priestess; and even if the law does not bar her, whether she is fit for the priesthood. Whether she is barred by the law he divided into these two: whether she is chaste, whether she is pure. Whether she is chaste he divided into these: whether chastity refers only to virginity, or to abstinence from all base and obscene acts. For I grant that you are a virgin, but one handled by everyone's kisses; even if short of unchastity, you have still wallowed with men: are you chaste, such as she can be thought to be whom the law wishes to be harmed even by an unchaste mother? Even if chastity refers to virginity alone, whether this woman is a virgin.

HISPO ROMANIUS used a vehement and harsh colour: for he gave Popillius an advocate, and said that he would plead Popillius's case in one way, Antony's in another; for Popillius he would say: "I did not wish to kill; I was compelled"; for Antony he would say: "Cicero ought to have been killed." And he stated the commonplace, that the state could not otherwise be pacified than if that disturber of peace were removed from it. Alone of the declaimers he inveighed against Cicero. "Did not he," he said, "when he judged Antony a public enemy and all Antony's soldiers, understand that he had proscribed himself and Popillius too?" This colour at first sight is rather harsh, but by him it was handled admirably. VARIUS GEMINUS said: "When Antony had ordered me, I allowed it, lest some client of P. Clodius be sent — one who would afflict him with insults before he killed him, who would tear him living."

MONTANUS VOTIENUS thought these were the questions: whether whatever a proconsul did wrong in his magistracy can be punished by the law of treason. For a defendant who cannot defend himself by the fact takes refuge in the law and says he is not bound by this law. Not whatever a man did wrong in his magistracy injures the majesty. Suppose someone, while he is a magistrate, kills his father, kills his wife by poison: I think he will not plead his case under this law, but under those — of parricide and of poisoning. Do you wish to know that it pertains to the matter not by whom a thing is done, but what is done? A private man can be accused of injured majesty, if he did anything by which he injured the majesty of the Roman people. Suppose a proconsul has a mistress: will he therefore be condemned for treason? What is more, suppose he corrupts a married woman while he is proconsul: he will plead a case of adultery, not of treason.

ARGENTARIUS said: I sought the chance of a kindness, I did not covet to receive the prize. The honour came to both: one has the prize, the other received it. FUSCUS ARELLIUS the father said: had you bidden me sail, I would have driven the bark through wintry waves; had you bidden me travel abroad, nothing would have been hard at your command. This thing you bade me, hard for a brave man: to be conquered. BLANDUS narrated with this colour: "My father objects to me that I did not yield to him in one matter; I will multiply my crimes: never, as often as a thing was rightly to be done, did I yield to him; always I wished to seem more frugal, I wished to seem more laborious; for when it came to a matter of strength, even he himself used to yield:

He said that the school of Apollodorus, indeed, holds that the themes should be fixed and safe, but that here the controversia does not resist this suspicion; for it is not yet laid down that she is a virgin, and there are many reasons why it is credible that she is not.
