He added this: in short, even if I do not bring it about that the judges believe she is no virgin, I shall yet attain this — that they think her unworthy of the priesthood, since it can be doubted whether she is a virgin. Whether she is pure he divided into these: whether, even if she rightly killed a man, she is nevertheless not pure, being defiled by homicide; and then, whether she rightly killed an innocent man wishing to make use of a prostituted body. She was acquitted: she showed not that she was pure, but that she was safe. Whether she is fit he divides into such treatments as each man pleases: whether she is fit — so unhappy as to be captured, to be sold, and sold to a procurer of all men, to be prostituted, to be forced to kill a man, to plead her case.

ARGENTARIUS said: "Summoned, I came; after the proscription Antony had become more terrible even to his own. I was ordered to kill Cicero. What was I to do? I could disobey in one way only — by killing myself: not even Cicero could do this." On the accuser's side, in that place where Popillius arrives, everyone wished to say something new. Latro said: "He had shut the doors; no one was admitted to the proscribed man; Popillius, as soon as he came, was let in." CESTIUS said: "When it was announced to Cicero, he said: 'For Popillius I am always at leisure.'" CORNELIUS HISPANUS even made Cicero complain: "Popillius, so late?" ALBUCIUS said: "What is it, Popillius? Do I lie safely hidden at all? Must I change my place?" Foolishly † SABIDIENUS PAULUS, who brought Cicero in at the very moment reading aloud his speech for Popillius. And MURREDIUS did not allow this controversia to pass without some mark of his stupidity. For he described Popillius carrying Cicero's head and hand, and gave a Publilian sententia: "Popillius, how differently you held Cicero's hand as a defendant!"

"Weigh," he says, "each thing severally that you charge. If he had only had a mistress, would you accuse him at all? If he had executed someone with no one's bidding, could he be accused?" If not every wrongdoing can be punished by this law, then whether what is done under public authority. For when he commits adultery, when poisoning, he sins as a citizen; when he executes, he uses public authority. But in that which is done under the pretext of public majesty, whatever is done wrong must be punished by the action for treason. "For tell me, if, when he ought to execute, not using the lawful dress and solemn manner, he ascends the tribunal by day in banqueting attire; if, when the trumpet ought to sound, he orders music to play — will he not injure the majesty? And yet what he did is fouler":

it was not I who conquered him, but his age." TURRINUS used this colour: "I wished," he says, "to yield, but there were those who said it was not allowed; that thus a most wholesome law was being abolished. They seemed about to argue against the father's prize and to say: it is not allowed to brave men to yield to each other; the matter is not pleaded for their sake only, but the public's; it concerns all to know who is bravest. By these utterances of men I was sent to that contest, in which either victory would belong to him. What do you think I will say? That I seemed braver? It is false, since this too — that I was brave — was his. What then? You ask why I conquered? It seemed to concern the blush of all our youth that no one fought more bravely than an old man." And when he had said that he had conferred the prizes upon his father, he said:

CESTIUS went deeper still, and objected that she had been held so cheap by her own people that she was not ransomed. SILO POMPEIUS, while following the precept by which we are bidden to make, as often as we can, a controversia of all the words of the law, raised this question: "chaste and of chaste stock." The law, he said, when it says "of chaste stock," refers this not only to parents but to all with whom the maiden has consorted; for it does not add "of chaste parents," but when it says "of chaste stock," it means that those from whom the maiden comes should be chaste. I understand, he said, many things under this word. When it says "of chaste stock," I understand "from chaste household gods" — you come from unchaste ones; I understand "from chaste teachings" — you come from the most obscene ones; for what have you learned? — and whatever could be said in this place. The same he did with that other part, "pure and of pure stock."

and he made a comparison. Then, if what a proconsul did wrong, using public majesty both in right and in equipment, can be punished by the law of treason, whether this can be. "It cannot," he says; "for nothing has been taken from the greatness of the Roman people. He injures the majesty of the Roman people who does something in the public name: as an envoy who brings false instructions — they are received as though the Roman people had given them; a commander struck a treaty — the Roman people seems to have struck it, and is held bound by an unworthy treaty. But now nothing has been taken either from the strength of the Roman people or from its repute; for it is charged to the proconsul if he did anything, not to the Roman people. But from you the rest are judged. No: for both before this man there were others by whom they could be judged, and after him there will be, and no one ascribes the faults of individuals to the cities."

"I conquered you, father, but surely I conquered for you." ALBUCIUS narrated with this colour: "I did not wish," he says, "the title of bravest man to seem to have fallen to my father by collusion: I did not yield before the trial, that in the trial I might yield, and I did nothing else than praise my father, recount his virtues;

ROMANIUS HISPO, using an accuser's pugnacity, denied that she was pure, referring this not to the killing but to the body; he argued that she is impure who has given a kiss to the impure, who has taken food with the impure. ALBUCIUS divided the controversia by a figure; for he said: let us suppose three women seek the priesthood — one who was captured, a second who was prostituted, a third who killed a man: to all I say no; and so he pleaded the case against each one. ARELLIUS FUSCUS divided thus: I shall prove her unworthy of the priesthood, first even if she be chaste; next, because we do not know whether she be chaste; lastly, because she is not chaste.

"And yet the deed itself is base. But so are many other things, and majesty is not therefore injured by them. Almost no one is without fault: one is irascible, one lustful; yet not, if you should wish something in someone changed, is majesty thereby straightway injured." Then he comes to the estimation of the deed itself, and said that these things were charged: that he had a courtesan, that he killed someone in his house, that it was by night, that it was at a banquet,

and for this very thing I seemed worthy of the prize." SILO GAVIUS said: "You used, father, to tell me examples of distinguished men, some even of our own house; you used to say: 'You had a brave man for grandfather; see that you be braver.' I went out with you into the line, nor there . . . When we returned, all the glory was in one house. The state wished to recognize its brave men. O what eagerness for glory I saw in my father, and how youthful! He forbade me to contend by his command, he bade me by his example. It came to the trial: the most enviable of all the things I have known was asked about my father — whether he were braver or happier."

FUSCUS introduced this colour for the girl: the immortal gods wished to show their power in this girl, that it might appear how no human force can resist the divine: they thought nothing could be more of a marvel than freedom in a captive, chastity in a prostitute, innocence in a homicide. Latro said: some captive was more fortunate, none more brave. MARULLUS, when he had described how great the girl's dignity was, with her very face displaying something loftier and prouder, added this epigram, which Latro used to admire, or rather, as he himself said, to kiss with delight: let all relate, if you will, that they came to her as to a prostitute, provided they departed as from a priestess.

that it was at the courtesan's bidding. SILO POMPEIUS added these questions: whether, if he did what was lawful for him to do, he cannot be accused by the law of treason. "He can," he says; "for this law asks what is fitting, others what is lawful. It is lawful to go into a brothel; if a praetor be led into a brothel with the fasces going before him, he will injure majesty, even though he did what is lawful. It is lawful to wear what dress one will; if a praetor administer justice in slave's or woman's dress, he will violate majesty." Then he made that question: whether it was lawful for him to do this. "It was not lawful," he says, "in that place or at that time or for that cause to kill. Some things which are lawful, when the time and place are changed, are not lawful."

OSCUS narrated with this colour: "There were those who came up and said: 'Ask your father to yield to you; it is not useful to the state that the enemy's spirits be roused; they will be roused, if they learn that no one in this city is braver than an old man.' They forced me, as though even then I should render some service to the state, to come to trial: in which what do I have? I am judged the younger." MENTO said: "I fear lest for this very thing I become cheaper to my father; we know how proud of glory he is."

ALBUCIUS said: some man of fierce and violent spirit came — driven, I believe, by the gods themselves — to violate not the chastity of the future priestess, but to behold it. He told her beforehand to keep his hand from her sacred body: "There is no reason for you to dare to harm a chastity which men preserve and the gods await." And to him as he rushed to his own destruction she said: "See — here are arms which you know not how to use, for chastity," and, snatching his sword, she drove it into the breast of her pirate. That this deed of hers should not lie hidden was the care of those same immortal gods: an accuser was found to render in the forum testimony to her chastity. No one believed that a man had been killed by a woman, a young man by a girl, an armed man by an unarmed one: the thing seemed too great to be believed done without the help of the immortal gods.

"As to the colour," he says, "the question is which the man who speaks for Flamininus ought to use. There are certain controversiae in which the deed can be defended but cannot be excused; among them is this one too. We cannot bring it about that on this account he is not to be blamed; we do not hope that the judge approve him, but that he dismiss him; and so we ought to plead as for a deed not corrected, yet not criminal." And so MONTANUS used to say that for Flamininus he would not narrate, but would answer the charges. And he said that this sententia of RUFUS VIBIUS was the colour of the pleading:

TRIARIUS used this colour: "In the trial I wished to yield to you, that you might seem not to have commanded but to have conquered, and I yielded: I pleaded my case perfunctorily; but let it be known that he yields because it is too little for him not to think . . ." NICETES in this controversia said: "If the grandfather, restored to us by nature, stood by that tribunal of old, would he not have said:
SCAURUS said this thought in another way:

CESTIUS feared to descend into the narrative, and ran past it thus: he said that these things ought above all to be valued in a priestess — chastity, innocence, good fortune. How chaste she is, the soldier showed; how innocent, the judge; how fortunate, her return. We have, too, a certain prior claim given to the priestess by the godhead itself: though they object that she was a captive, that she afterwards served a procurer, that at last she pleaded her case — amid so many perils the gods would not have kept her, had they not meant to keep her for themselves. ARGENTARIUS said this in the narrative: the accuser pressed the defendant hardest on this point — he said the man was killed while still within his words, before he offered violence.

that he had good hope for a defendant in whom all lust was confined within a courtesan, all cruelty within the prison. Montanus himself handled most beautifully that commonplace — how many things the Roman people had borne in its commanders: in Gurges extravagance, in Manlius an unbending sternness — whom it did not harm to kill even his son and a victor — in Sulla cruelty, in Lucullus avarice. "In a praetor," he said, "when his self-restraint, his diligence have stood firm, do not sift out how he dined on a single night." "Yet which," he said, "is the more unfair: what they charge — that a condemned man perished for a courtesan — or what they demand — that a proconsul perish for a condemned man?"

"O if my grandfather were present at the trial, how gladly would he watch even our discord! He would have cried out to me: 'There is no reason for you to yield; he never yielded to me himself.'" LABIENUS declaimed the father's part and said: "What is allowed even to worse men — I do not wish to dwell with my adversary: the same lodging does not hold a brave man and a conquered one. 'I have set up a statue to you,' he says: nay, that I might never be able to forget that I was conquered, you have cut my disgrace in bronze."

SILO POMPEIUS narrated with this figure: I promise you a priestess whom no fortune can make unchaste. Slavery can compel some: she served both barbarians and pirates, and among them remained inviolate. The perverse habit of an age fallen into vice can corrupt some, with even matrons' great tutorship in lust: she will remain chaste. Set her in a brothel: even through this she has had the fortune to bring out her chastity untouched. She was in a base and shameful place; the procurer prostituted her, the people adored her: there was no one who did not contribute more to preserving her chastity than he had brought to violating it. Much, too, can an enemy, a sword, do to bend even the resolve of a chaste mind: she will not yield — nay, if need be, she will avenge her chastity. Do I seem to promise an incredible thing in a girl? She has already furnished it: a young man trying to defile the gift of a pitying people she repelled with the sword. There was one to accuse her of killing: she was acquitted. That there might be no room for doubt in you, whether she who was to come to the priesthood was pure, was intact — it has already been judged.

The colour FUSCUS ARELLIUS introduced was this: that he had been drunk and did not know what he did. SILO POMPEIUS used this colour: "He did not think," he said, "it pertained to the matter where or when a man perished who deserved to perish." TRIARIUS introduced a foolish colour: "There was talk," he said, "at the banquet that the praetor's excessive leniency was despised; that there had been other proconsuls who executed daily, but in this man's year no one had been put to death. Someone of the guests said: 'I have never . . .'; the woman too said: 'And I have never.' Angry that his clemency was held in contempt, 'I will see to it,' he said, 'that they know severity is not wanting in me.' A criminal is brought in who ought not to look upon the light any longer. Was someone killed? A condemned man. Where? In the praetorium. At what time? Is there any time at which a guilty man ought not to perish?"

TRIARIUS said: the girl denied she had done it; she denied he had fallen by her own hands: a shape, she said, loftier than human seemed to tower around me and to lift girlish arms above a man's strength. Whoever you are, immortal gods, who willed that chastity should emerge with a marvel from that infamous place, you brought help to no ungrateful girl: to you she dedicates the chastity which she owes to you. The colour of the other side has no difficulty: it is plain from the epigrams I have set down. One must speak vehemently against the girl, not sordidly nor obscenely. Sordidly, as JULIUS BASSUS, who said: "this virgin from outside the gate," and "show that rusty hand of yours"; VIBIUS RUFUS, who said: "she still smells of the smoke of the arch." Obscenely, as the rhetor MURREDIUS, who said: "How do we know whether, with those who came, she struck a bargain for her virginity by some other kind of lust?"

GALLUS VIBIUS said: "The courtesan begged. I feared, by Hercules, lest she should win the request either that an uncondemned man be killed or that a condemned man live." On the other side many good things were said, many corruptly: in the description of the punishment, those above all who wished to drag all the lawful words of the punishment into sententiae fell into faults; as TRIARIUS said: "'Remove'" — do you hear, lictor? Remove the courtesan from the praetor. This is not bad. He added: "'Scourge,' but see that your rods do not upset our cups; 'strip him.' Courtesan, do you recognize this word? At least the province recognizes it."

This kind of thought I remember a certain ex-praetor uttering, when he was declaiming the controversia about the woman who brought an action against her husband for ill-usage, because she was a virgin, and won the case; afterwards she sought a priesthood. "We know," he said, "that restraint of husbands who, even if they spare timid virgins the first night, yet sport in the neighbouring regions." SCAURUS was listening to him — a man not only most eloquent but most charming, who never let any man's folly pass unpunished. At once came the Ovidian "foolish in her place," and the man broke down and said no more. This fault, Scaurus said, was derived from the Greek declaimers, who allowed themselves anything and obtained anything.

SILO POMPEIUS, a man esteemed for judgement, himself too approached this description, yet did the least harm. He said: "The courtesan executed; 'come, by the law'; for is anything here done by the law?" HISPANUS said: "'Come, by the law' is said to you, Flamininus: live without a courtesan, dine without an executioner." ARGENTARIUS broke up the most violent treatment into the minute figures he was wont to use: "'Come, by the law' — do you know what he says? Come by day, come in the forum. The lictor is stupefied; he says the same as your courtesan: that he has never seen this." MONTANUS VOTIENUS said: "The lictor, about to strike, looked to the praetor, the praetor to the courtesan."

HYBREAS, he said, when he was delivering the controversia about the man who caught and killed two women in unnatural love, began to describe the husband's feeling, in which no shameful inquiry ought to be demanded: "I should first have looked at the man, to see whether he was born so, or was stitched together." GRANDAUS, an Asianic declaimer likewise, when he spoke on the same controversia — "Did I kill them, then, so as not to suffer them to be adulterers?" — said: "But what if I had caught a counterfeit-male adulterer?" In this controversia about the priestess MURREDIUS said, no less obscenely: "perhaps, while she repelled his lust, she caught it in her hands." One must keep far from all obscenity, both of words and of thoughts. Some things it is better to leave unsaid, to the harm of one's case, than to say, to the harm of one's modesty. VIBIUS RUFUS seemed to have spoken not amiss, using everyday words: "How much that priestess took from the soldier!"

VIBIUS GALLUS said: "To the lictor, because he had struck well, a toast was drunk." That which is bandied about as Latro's I declare on my testimony is not Latro's, and I clear Latro of a sententia foolishly turbulent; for I myself heard a certain FLORUS, a hearer of Latro's, say it — not at Latro's. For it was not his custom to hear anyone declaiming; he declaimed himself only, and used to say that he was not a master but a model; nor do I know that it fell to any other than, among the Greeks, to Nicetes, and, among the Romans, to Latro, that his pupils did not wish to be heard themselves, but were content to listen. At first, by way of insult, Latro's pupils were called by mockers "hearers"; then the word came into use, and "hearer" was put indifferently for "pupil." This was to sell not one's patience but one's eloquence. To return to Florus: he said in the Flamininus case:

amid the private cups the edge of the public axe flashed; amid the drunken leavings of drunkards a human head is swept away. Never would Latro have so composed that, because he was about to say "public axe," he should say "private cups," nor would his sententia have evaporated into so soft a composition; nor did he ever conceive figures so incredible as to describe a man struck down in the very dining-room amid couches and jests and tables. He, when in this controversia he had described the atrocity of the punishment, added: "Why have you shuddered, judges? I am speaking of a courtesan's sport." And he said that less-known but no less good sententia: "Against our ally a praetor of the Roman people executed in a private house, by night, at a hasty tribunal, drunk perhaps, not even shod — unless, that the courtesan might watch everything, she carefully required it."

RUFUS VIBIUS was one who spoke in the old style; that sententia of the homelier stamp came off well with him: "The praetor, to kill a man, called for his slippers." Another of the same kind, but not of the same success: when he had bewailed the condition of injured majesty, and described the custom of the ancestors by which they had always wished men to be summoned to a punishment, he said this sententia: "But now by a praetor justice was administered by lamplight." Yet Pollio Asinius used to say that he accepted this sententia.

LIVIUS, about orators who hunt after old and mean words and think obscurity of speech to be severity, used to say that MILTIADES the rhetor elegantly remarked: "They go mad after the dictionary." Still, in these men, even if there is less madness, there is less hope; those who swell, those who labour under excess, have more frenzy, but more body too; for it is always easier to come to soundness in what can be cured by subtraction; but no help can be given to the man who is at once mad and feeble.

But, lest I seem to shield this kind of frenzy, MURREDIUS spoke most bombastically of Flamininus: "Our praetor, gorged in that deadly feast in the courtesan's bosom, the axe roused." And that tetracolon: "The forum was slave to the bedchamber, the praetor to the courtesan, the prison to the banquet, day to night." The last part was said without sense, that the number might be filled out; for what sense has "day was slave to night"? This sententia I have reported for this reason: that both in tricola and in all sententiae of this kind we take care that the number be complete, we do not care whether there is sense. And all kinds even of corrupt sententiae I set down on purpose, because we are more easily taught by example both what to imitate and what to avoid.

Behold there is this kind of false brilliance too, which seeks the bitterness of words as though it would aggravate the matter; as in this controversia LICINIUS NEPOS said: "The defendant was condemned by the law, he perished for the brothel." And what SENIANUS said has its own kind of insanity: when he said that punishment ought not to be exacted by night, after a long description he concluded: "By night not even the sacrificial victims are slain."

To this controversia the Greeks too stretched out their hand. NICETES said in it: "When he heard that it was a banquet, he hoped." EUCTEMON said: "All thought that he was being let off." GLAUCIPPUS the Cappadocian, when he had described a luxurious dinner unworthy of a praetor's majesty, added: "Now even the revel-rout!" This same thing ADAEUS said more elegantly, when he had described a nocturnal dinner: "How amorous the revel!" NICETES said: "I have never beheld a man taken off. If the city is fortunate, you will not see it either." ARTEMON in the same place said another sententia: "I have never beheld a man taken off. Woman, there is no need of a revel." GLYCON said: "When it was announced to those in the prison: 'There is a drinking-bout and a summons of a mistress' — someone cried out: 'Wretched me! take me off; for I was unjustly condemned.'"

THE LAW: An unchaste priestess shall be thrown from the rock. THE THEME: A certain priestess, condemned for unchastity, before she was thrown down, called upon Vesta. Cast from the rock, she lived. She is demanded back for punishment. — Was this what you expected — that, hanging her head, she would, before she was pushed, of her own modesty cast herself down? That was all that was wanting — that she should be more modest on the rock than she had been in the shrine. She stood, and casting her eyes round upon the crowd, began to violate that most holy godhead in the very punishment by which she was being avenged — as though she had violated it too little among the altars: this was a second act of incest in the condemned woman. She was condemned because she was unchaste, thrown down because she was condemned; she is to be demanded back because she is both unchaste and condemned — and was thrown down. Can it be doubted that she is to be thrown down again and again, until what she was thrown down for is brought about? She calls her ill fortune in perishing her defence. What shall I pray for you, importunate woman, but that you may not perish even when thrown down twice? Shall she come to tend the pledge of the Roman empire — unchaste, if not by debauchery, at least by the executioner's hand? "I called upon the gods," she says. Standing on that rock you named the gods, and do you wonder if they wish you thrown down a second time?

THE LAW: A ravisher, unless he wins over within thirty days both his own father and the father of the woman he ravished, shall perish. THE THEME: A man ravished a maiden. He won over her father; he asks his own father; his father delays. — Tell me the truth, then; I will not weep. Why do you tremble, old age? Why, tongue, do you falter? Why, eyes, are you struck dumb? It is not yet the thirtieth day. Do you beg for your life? I gave it, and you have lost it. "You wish," he says, "your son to die." Do I wish you to die? No — your madness, that blind and rash desire, and, amid these, that other father of yours, who was won over too quickly. Why did that old man so quickly remit the wrong? Not even with a sadder face did he bear the storming of his daughter's chastity. I fear that what I hear may be true — that, by a new and unheard-of custom, the ravisher was won over to the marriage of the girl.

OF CESTIUS PIUS. Say what I have done. You do not know? Surely even secret things do not escape you. Let him dismiss me: you will understand for whom I prepared it. Say what I did before: unless perhaps you are content to charge the defendant with parricide, the parricide with nothing. OF ARGENTARIUS. I wished to die because I was a defendant. What then? Shall no defendant live? He shall live, beside whom his father will sit in mourning. I shall return to poison, since unfair fortune did not allow me to be rid of danger by a single peril. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. Why then do you not die? It does not please me to die if it pleases anyone else. When he interrupted me, I fell into these thoughts: "Was anyone ever so wretched? Does anyone hate me more than I do myself?" I began to pity myself.

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. Is it fair that we should divide children with strangers, whom we do not divide with their mothers? "If you do not take one away, you shall have both." What shall I do? I begot both, I longed for both, for both I made the bargain. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. Together they were born, together exposed, together reared; given back, they are above all torn apart. Fortune once tore them from their parents, never from each other. Take pity, judges; the verdict is grave.

OF PORCIUS LATRO. Not even as victor did he wish satisfaction made to himself: he excused the conquered, nay he restored them. Since you demand back the life you gave, take it. There was no woman's head in the proscription. OF OSCUS. You have defiled your household gods with your daughter's blood. And yet why do I say "household gods," as though she perished in the house? When Pompey's head was brought to him, Caesar wept: this he granted him for the sake of his daughter. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS. "How do you wish me to make you satisfaction?" By this very thing he should have made it. He had a daughter dutiful both toward her husband and toward her father: the one she followed even to death, to the other she made satisfaction even through death. How dangerously do I offend him, who, when once he has begun to be angry, knows not how to forgive?

If nothing else, you stood in the place of the unchaste. THE NARRATIVE OF CESTIUS PIUS: What shall I do? Shall I set forth when she committed the unchastity, with whom, with what accomplices? These things, because I proved them, she was condemned. What was added afterwards that should make her a virgin? That she lay in prison, that she was led to the rock, that she was hurled from it? She says she is innocent, because she could not perish. So then — did the law mean that an unchaste priestess be examined in trial, but the judges in the punishment? Is the case adjourned by the judges into the penalty? She demands that, since her cause was not safe against the penalty, the penalty be safe against her cause. Do you not think the law took care that you should perish, which took care how you should perish? Shall we entreat you, woman, to be acquitted a second time? Either you violated the priesthood, or these men a priestess. You think ill of the gods, if they so late come to the aid of their own priestess. Sentence was passed; the verdict was pronounced; you were condemned: I ask about this place, woman, answer me:

OF CESTIUS PIUS: That you may judge the better of the old man, I shall narrate of myself as a young man. I had a father of sound mind, neither so severe as to be cruel, nor so indulgent as to be incautious. I married the wife my father had bidden, and yet I repent of my marriage. Son, did I not often flare up, often relent, often give what I had refused? You yourself parcelled out the thirty days, that the father-in-law might have the first, the defendant the middle, the father the last. Not to recount all his vices from his earliest youth: he ravished a maiden, he accuses his father — and all within thirty days. Do you think I will promise the accuser what I refused the son? "I won him over," he says. Others say he won you over. In the middle days you accuse me. Why did you ravish a maiden, if you so gladly chose to live?

OF VARIUS GEMINUS. "Three times," he says, "you have been disowned." You seem to me, father, to reproach me that I live so long. That I come, that I speak for myself, do not wonder: it is as pleasant for the innocent to be defended as for the wretched to die. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. I know that certain men in peril boast of this: "Now for the first time I plead a case." This I cannot say; three times I have been a defendant, nor do I doubt that I have come to be hated by you, since I hate myself. OF PORCIUS LATRO. Three times I have pleaded; to these punishments of mine poison was added; I hold it; if this is not enough for you, I will live.

OF JUNIUS GALLIO. I exposed two because I could not choose one. I am in danger of, having come into court with two children, returning with none; for I cannot choose whom to lose. The cause of my bargain was that I might have sons; its result is that I lose them. For my sons I owe you, not my sons: ask as much as you wish for their schooling, charge what you wish for their food; you may ask more, provided you do not give back less. Our ancestors saw how unbounded was the indulgence of those who feared for their own, how ready to give whatever was demanded; and so, on behalf of the father, our law has bargained with the rearer.

OF CLODIUS TURRINUS the father. "Die." What else had she deserved, if she would not make satisfaction? Had you not forestalled her, sister, perhaps the father would have made satisfaction to himself. This, I am certain, each of you urged upon the girl: "You come to an angry father; compose yourself into what blandishments you can; ask, beseech; if you accomplish nothing, you have the means of forcing him: declare that you will die." This which you have forgiven, victor, pertains to the men: they thank you; for the women you would not have proscribed even had you been angry. "Why did she follow her husband?" Have the old examples of good wives so slipped from you, to which, when sane, you used to urge your daughter? One redeemed her husband's breath with her own, one cast herself upon the burning pyre. The girl would have spent herself for her husband, had she not been keeping herself for her father.

are there gods? OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: Let us try again: why do you fear the gods, when they are favourable? "It was," she says, "a sheer place, of measureless height, grim to behold." I told you: the law wished the unchaste woman to die. There stands a mass cut sheer into the deep, roughened by close-set rocks, which either dash the body to pieces or strike it more grievously down anew; the sides bristle with jutting crags: the place was chosen of all places that the condemned might oftener be thrown. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS: Cast down from above, not received below — a woman for whose punishment a rock must be built.

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: "I shall die," he says: do you even now threaten? Do you not yet entreat? "How long," he says, "shall I entreat?" You are already weary, and have not yet entreated anyone. "I cannot," he says, "win you over for so long." By a new custom he charges a madman with constancy. "What then? Will you be able to watch your son die?" Perhaps I shall not, and therefore I am angry while I may be. OF POMPEIUS SILO: This boldness of his is in part my own fault: he was reared too indulgently, he thinks all things lawful for him, he has never asked anything of me. "He has pardoned," he says. So has anyone been asked before me? You do not know the condition of your own law: in this offence, those who have equal votes perish. He sent himself to another's discretion; the law admitted him to mine. "Let the ravisher perish, unless he win over both his own father and the father of the ravished woman." Do you wish to know which the law preferred? Not to be won over: it is angry. Of his two fathers the ravisher accuses the one who follows the law.

The other side. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. I call the immortal gods to witness that, by three disownings already, I took care lest I find poison in my house. The defendant on a charge of parricide lives, who, disowned, wished to die. In how narrow a compass is the fortune of my house set! Either the father must perish or the son. What have you, that you should wish to die? The childless live, the shipwrecked live, even those live to whom thrice-disowned children have fallen. When he says he wishes to die, he asks for life. I hold a parricide — what is plain — most ready even for his own death. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. Do not wonder if I do not show the strength due to my grief: by three trials you have learned that fathers cannot accuse.

I could not be bound for those who were not in my power. If we divide on fair terms, let account be taken of both: let me have two as long as you have had them. At an auction the spear, however hostile, does not divide brothers; it is something more to be twins than brothers: each loses his charm unless he is with the other.

OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. The daughter rolls before the paternal threshold in her own blood. Why have you shuddered? It is a father's satisfaction. You know the law of our house: I must either conquer or die. What kind of satisfaction is this, by which the daughter does not perceive that the father has been won over for her? OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. Which were the better side, the gods alone seemed able to judge. "If you wish to make satisfaction to me, die." So far as concerns me, I had rather you were angry. If it were parricide to have been on opposite sides, Cicero would never have defended Ligarius before Caesar. M. Tullius, how light a crime did you judge that of which you confessed! Give the daughter — if you are merciful, to her prayer; if an enemy, to the edict; if a father, to nature; if a judge, to her cause; if you are angry, to your brother.

OF JULIUS BASSUS: I had thought nothing more could be added to her boldness than that on that cross she had named Vesta: but lo, rolled back from the very punishment all the way into the temple, she has polluted by her touch whatever is, after the gods, most holy; and she who may never return from the rock save to the rock — how much less may she rebound into the temple? Come rather to where she is condemned, than to where she is acquitted. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS: If anyone still doubted about the woman thrown down, let him come and believe his own eyes. Is this a virgin's modesty? In so blessed a city, where so many maidens overflow, where there are so many daughters of leading men, she demands that, passing these by, you should of all women raise up from the underworld this one for your priestess. "Why then, if I am unchaste, do I live?" I do not know; this one thing I know: neither does what cannot be come to pass, nor is it a portent that can be. Far be the wickedness that that rock should acquit which receives the condemned alone. THE NARRATIVE OF ARGENTARIUS.

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS: Do you wonder that I doubt? The law itself is in doubt between death and marriage. Why do you betray me, untimely tears? It was not yet the time for confessing. There is no cause for you to think my tears have promised you anything: I weep because I must watch my son die. What I shall do I still do not know; at any rate you will not know before the thirtieth day. "I won over," he says, "the father of the ravished woman." Why then are you troublesome to me, if that is enough for you? OF OSCUS: He broke down the doors and forced her, calling again and again upon the laws, to suffer outrage: unless he won over the girl as easily as her father. By outrage he deserved death; by accusing he begs it off; meanwhile the days are spent. Which of us spends them? "I entreat," he says. It is not my fortune to entreat; now it is I, who am in peril, that ought to have been entreated. OF PAPIRIUS FABIANUS.

OF VIBIUS RUFUS. When what you confess is so great, how great is what you deny? You sought poison, you bought poison, you brought poison into that house in which you had a father for an enemy. You would rightly have hated your life, if even then I had charged you with parricide. Do you wish to know what your fault is? Reveal who sold it to you; it will be said to him: "Did you sell poison to anyone? Did you sell it to a thrice-disowned man? No doubt you did not know for whom he meant to use it." So do I by this trial delay my son's death? If you shut me up with him, I will die, that I may bring upon you the odium which he wished to bring upon me. OF VARIUS GEMINUS. You ask for whom my son prepared poison? He did not drink it. OF POMPEIUS SILO. "For myself," he says, "I prepared it." And this is to prepare it for one's father. Acquitted, he wishes to die; a defendant, he lives. OF MUSA. "Mithridates had an evil drug." Who else ought to have it than a parricide? "Demosthenes," he says, "had poison and drank it." Am I to you, father, what Philip was to Demosthenes? OF PORCIUS LATRO.

OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. My opponent ought to forgive me for keeping my own, when he himself covets another's. He asks back those he has had till now; I keep those I have just recognized. Shall recognition divide those whom even exposure joined? OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. Say which is the more obedient, which the more affectionate. "Both," you say. Do you wonder if I cannot divide twins so alike? Everything for my son I bargain — except my son.

OF BUTEO. Before the very threshold of the house she died, that it might not be doubted whether she had perished for her husband or her father. Where did you see that? Where hear it? I deny that you learned that in war. OF MARULLUS. "She had deserved," he says, "to die." Do you still accuse? Surely satisfaction has now been made you. O new monster! With the victor angry one must live, with the father appeased one must die. OF PASSIENUS. Would that I had intervened: you would not have made satisfaction to your father alone. I should call you mad, had you not asked on your son-in-law's behalf. The son-in-law followed the opposite side, the wife her own.

I had almost begun, judges, to narrate what kind of woman the defendant was; but what shall I accomplish, when I have proved her unchaste? Surely that she be seen as one to be thrown from the rock: she has already been seen so. I shall not imitate her shamelessness, so as to seem, by reopening a judgement already passed, to have condemned it. What was demanded, I proved; what you judged, I carry out. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: I call upon the gods and goddesses, whom in the former trial I did not call upon in vain, that the unchaste woman may perish as slowly as may be. "I called upon the divine powers," she says. What do you call upon, woman? If you are innocent, there are no gods. See how greatly the priestess has sinned, who could neither be acquitted nor die. Either you violated the priesthood, or we violated a priestess. You are mistaken, if you think it enough for the priesthood to be unable to die. OF ROMANIUS HISPO.

I am mad. Of course I live basely, I love a harlot, I do not know the law, I do not count your days. To the judges he summons his own judge. "Then I shall die," he says. If you say this to a defendant, I do not care; if to a judge, I shall see; if to a madman, I do not understand. "You are mad," he says: and can anyone pardon a man who entreats thus? You are my judges; he has his own judge, and cannot complain that he is inexorable whom he has not yet tried.

When I was disowning him, if I had charged anything, he would say: "Did you catch me at it?" Yet you will not have grounds for much doubt about him: what he denies is parricide, what he confesses is poison. "I wish to die," he says. With his father living, even this is parricide. Wretch that I am, I feared equally lest he drink the poison and lest he give it. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. "For myself," he says, "I prepared the poison" — that no one may doubt whether he can kill another. OF JUNIUS OTHO the elder. He is a defendant on a charge of parricide who would rather die than see his father. How do you wish me to prove to you more fully that he wished me to die? He does not wish to die. "I wished to die," he says. Why? Because three times you conquered? If you believe me, he wished to commit parricide; if you believe him, he wished parricide to be committed by me. What sort of defendant is he, whose one defence is that he was unworthy of life? I say that his father was so hateful to him that he wished to kill him; he himself confesses that he was so hateful to himself that he wished to kill himself.

OF VOTIENUS MONTANUS. I shall not even have a defence: if I give up my children so easily, I exposed them gladly. Is this to give children back, or to snatch them away? They had to be lost either way — whether I bargained or refused. I made the bargain weeping, trembling, as when I exposed them. OF CESTIUS PIUS. That I might not divide my sons, I exposed them together. This man too took up two, who is content with only one.

OF LABIENUS. By this compliance let him obtain at least this — to die within the house. M. Cato, than whom the civil storm carried off no more splendid man, could have lived by Caesar's kindness, if he had been willing to owe it to anyone. The best defense of a civil war is forgetfulness. OF MUSA. When Cn. Pompey's head was brought to him, Caesar is said to have turned away his eyes — which you did not do even at your daughter's death. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. That cruel fortune of war ranged through every rank, descended even to the punishment of the lowest plebs: nothing in our state was immune from the victor's anger except women: this praise the wretched city was permitted to keep. Either our father is mad, or the victor is.

From the Tarpeian rock to Vesta, whose fillet the executioner tore; from the temple to the rock, from the rock to the temple: this is the running to and fro of the chaste priestess amid punishments and prayers. Tossed between the upper and the lower world, you have come back to life for a new punishment. THE NARRATIVE OF POMPEIUS SILO: As to the setting forth of the facts, judges, I will not, by words, delay the vengeance of the immortal gods. Let the unchaste woman be thrown from the rock. She was condemned by law: you have the judgement. She was thrown down: you have the precedent. THE NARRATIVE OF VIBIUS GALLUS: Brief is the setting forth of the facts: I charged my adversary with unchastity, accused her, condemned her, handed her over to the executioner: do you now permit the accuser to depart? Let us come back to your acquittal. Did the gods then prefer to acquit a condemned woman rather than a priestess? Too late, when condemned, did you crave innocence; when thrown down, life.

OF JUNIUS GALLIO: "I entreat," he says. Now, here, thus? If you wished to entreat, you would have brought up kinsmen, friends, the images of your ancestors, tears, groans fetched from deep within. I call the gods to witness, I was prepared to entreat the girl's father thus. When you have lowered your unwilling face into a suppliant's posture, when you have said: "I repent that I ravished her, that I did not entreat you first"; when you have said you were mad, I shall deliberate with my friends, deliberate with my kinsmen, deliberate with your mother. Wretched me, how nearly I promised! Hold firm, my heart, hold firm; yesterday you were braver. And I have much to deliberate on; diverse feelings pull me apart, I am torn between defendant and son; on this side is the wrong, on that, nature. Why do you hurry? You have no one to entreat but me. "Then," he says, "will you have pity?" I shall promise nothing before the thirtieth day. Wretched me, that I can be angry for only thirty days! There was need of a longer time.

I do not think you require a division, since the controversia is conjectural. Yet it has a conjecture unlike the rest, and a double one; not as is usual either between two defendants, when we convict one (so that this becomes the proof against the other), or between two charges, when we prove one — as when we say a woman was an adulteress, so that on this ground she may be believed also a poisoner: in one and the same man the conjecture is double. For we ask whether he prepared the poison for his own death or for his father's.

A second time I am forced to expose. OF JUNIUS GALLIO, the other side. Your part is easy: you can dismiss the father from this trial with both. OF MENTO. This man is used to being without children; I, even if I receive one, must still be tortured: I have grown used to two. Whatever I ever did — and you have at home those you may question about me — I never did anything without them except this disclosure. Do you call that violence which made you a father? Shall I be without an heir, who a little while ago had two sons so fine that of them even one would be enough for anyone? OF POMPEIUS SILO. See how modestly I plead:

OF MENTO. Once repulsed she returns; again repulsed she asks a third time; she is not wearied, she knows that even enemies are won over. O cruel man, unless satisfaction has already been made you even for your son-in-law! I am not ignorant in how great peril I stand: an angry man knows not how to be appeased, and he grew hot even at his daughter's voice. OF TRIARIUS. Would the victor not be won over, when a father asked for his daughter? "Die." Even those who must punish the condemned do not say "kill," do not say "die," but "proceed by law": they withdraw the cruelty of command under a milder word.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS: Condemned, she was thrown down; acquitted, she descended. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: You would think the girl was being let down, not falling. OF CESTIUS PIUS: She had no favour: she had lived in the temple; and so she called only on the gods. The law would not defer the priestess all the way to the rock, were it not awaiting the gods' verdict. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: He described the height of the mountain, dreadful even to those who look down without fear, and added: even the executioner, drawing back, gives a push. She did nothing like a defendant; her innocence is stubborn; she, a priestess, thought it base to beg of any but the gods. OF MARULLUS: Is it wonderful if a maiden was overwhelmed without favour? For whose knees did she clasp with her hands? Whom did she entreat, she who begged even the gods reluctantly? THE DIVISION. Latro divided into these questions:

Hear from a madman examples for this charge: for ten and twenty years our youth has grown old amid wars; and can we not bear thirty days? I shall deliberate: the law wishes nothing to be done rashly; "it is a great matter," it says: deliberate, consider, take time. You broke into the house of a citizen — even, as you say, a merciful one. Die: this is not grievous to a guilty man; I have done no wrong: for your sake I long to die. A reason is demanded of me for another's fault, that lies in my power. "What then will you do?" I shall not pronounce before the last day. Why do you wonder if you won him over more quickly? It is easier to forgive a wrong than a crime. Come, into the open, old man, by whose pity I am made cruel: did you not think I should be deliberated with? Whence do you know what kind of son I have? I, at least, do not yet know what kind of daughter you have. No time is too narrow for a single word. "Now," he says, "the time is narrow": and have you leisure to accuse? OF VIBIUS RUFUS: Who, before me, was ever

If it is decided to plead for the young man with the colour that Latro used — that he should change nothing of his words, but say: "I wished to die out of weariness of my disownings and of unceasing misfortune, since I laid aside the dress of mourning only to take it up again with greater torment, and acquittal for me alone was not the end of peril but the beginning" — there begins to intrude, beyond the conjecture, that first vulgar and well-worn question in controversiae of this kind, whether it is lawful to have poison for one's own death. ALBUCIUS pleaded for the young man with that colour, that there was no poison. "When I thought," he said, "that I was hated by my father, I wished to test his feeling — how he would bear mention of my death: and so I held it openly, and in such a way that my father might interrupt." FUSCUS ARELLIUS used the same colour but differently; he did not say, "I wished to test my father," but:

I took them up, I reared them, I gave them back; let him choose. OF VIBIUS RUFUS. "Your children are safe," I said. After this violence of mine, the man kissed me. OF PASSIENUS. Give me the tablets of the will: I have more in the will than in the bargain. This will I do not mean to erase; if I cannot make my own sons heirs, I will make yours. My prayers I will transfer to your sons: this name, I think, I shall be allowed to use while I am at law. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. Do you bear this, excellent young men? I took you up exposed, I reared you, I sat by you when you were sick; you have made me an old man, and you leave me? OF ARGENTARIUS. In that violence I lost two sons.

THE DIVISION. Latro used in this controversia that well-worn question: whether a charge of madness can be brought against a father for any other thing than madness itself. "I am unrestrained, I am cruel, harsh — yet not mad. You owe it to your father to approve your own character, not to rule his. Say: 'You are foolish, you understand nothing'; I, if I can, will gather proofs of my sanity; I will say: 'In the senate I did not speak my opinion foolishly. What do I seem to you to have done madly? Did I plead the side ill?' You must gather many signs of madness; you cannot condemn a father for words, nay, for a single word."

whether the law concerns only the unchaste woman — that is, one who is thrown down and does not die; or also the condemned woman, who, if she has appeared innocent after condemnation, ought to be thrown down. Whether this woman is innocent; whether she was saved by the gods' help. CESTIUS subjoined these to this last question: whether the immortal gods take care of human affairs; even if they do, whether they care for individuals; if they care for individuals, whether they cared for this woman. He disapproved of ALBUCIUS, because he treated these not as particulars bearing on the question, but as philosophical problems. ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER divided thus: whether the penalty of the unchaste woman is to be thrown down, or to perish. Whether she was saved by the providence of the gods, or by chance; if she was saved by the will of the powers above, whether it was that she might perish more cruelly.

bidden to pardon thus? "Now," he says, "the time is narrow." Do you not think, then, that I reckon how much is left? "Now," he says, "the time is narrow." It would be narrow, if you had to entreat two men. "The time is narrow," he cries, "I do not know when to entreat." Then you ought to have entreated me first: I do not say because I am worthier to be entreated first, because I am your father; this, which is the least of it — I live nearer. To this, of course, that part of the law pertained: "and let him win over his own father." OF PUBLIUS ASPRENAS: Does anyone win over thus? Does anyone beg thus? It is plain that you are entreating now for the first time. I am mad: nay, if you want an argument, I will give you one: my son is going to die, and I have not yet changed my will. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: Many feelings draw me different ways: I must complain of some, blush for some, fear for some, and over all still deliberate. Not even that other man, though he is said to be too easily won over, would have pardoned, had he been entreated thus.

The division. Latro divided thus: whether there is violence or necessity in the matter. "There is no violence," he says; "violence comprises arms and chains and the utmost peril, none of which was present in your person." The other says: "There is violence and necessity where, will I, nill I, I must yield. And it was necessary for me; for I could not have one son unless I promised the other." It is answered: first, there is no violence where something must be endured for the sake of getting some object, but a bargain: as, I cannot have a house unless I buy this one; no other is for sale; the vendor saw this opportunity and presses it. Yet you will not rescind this purchase; otherwise the suit will extend to infinity. Another says: "It was necessary for me." Necessary for you? First, you could still have endured the prison; then, you could find another way, hope for another informer. Or could you not find one otherwise? Then I bestowed this the more on you.

If any father, even one not mad, can be condemned of madness for some blameworthy deed, whether this man can. This he divided into two: whether, even if he said it with this mind — that he wished his daughter to die — he should yet not be condemned. Here the accusation of the daughter follows the side opposed to the father, though nature itself had exempted her from public ills. Manlius punished his son, and a victor; Brutus punished his children, not made enemies but about to be: see whether under these examples it is allowed a father merely to speak more boldly.

This colour is generally intermixed with the epigrams I have set down; yet I shall make known what Cestius thought. Certain men spoke against the priestess: that the gods seemed hostile to her, in keeping her alive for this — that she might be the longer tortured. Cestius said he preferred it to seem done by chance rather than by the gods' will; for if once we admit that they intervened in this matter, it will be the more plain that the priestess was saved as a reprieve, not for a punishment; and so he did not approve that saying of Triarius: "Do you think your punishment remitted? Your case has been adjourned." That very adjournment, he said, which is wont to be made before judges, from which the word in the epigram was taken, is not the mark of one condemning, but of one in doubt.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: Wretched me, father! Nothing has been taken from your anger, much from my time. I am unhappier than if I had won over neither: I fear death after all have congratulated me. What shall I pray for you, best of fathers-in-law, in return for that pity of yours, by which you spared both me and my father, but a surviving daughter? OF PAPIRIUS FABIANUS: I cannot dissemble, father: that I won him over is your kindness; certainly when he was won over he said this: my grief, indeed, advised otherwise, but what shall I do against my father's judgement? I have pity. Have pity, father: you know how brief my respite is. "I have pity," he says; do you wish me to tell the truth — what he said? "On your father." Whence should I, wretched, coming from this father, fear a father?

And he went on to quote very many most eloquent lines of Publilius. Then he said that the author of this fault — which arises from the catching at a single word that signifies several things — was POMPONIUS, the writer of Atellan farces, from whom this fashion of imitation first passed to LABERIUS, and then from him to Cicero, who carried it over to a higher excellence. For — to pass over the innumerable things which Cicero said in his speeches or in conversation in this vein, and not to mention what Laberius said (since the mimes of Laberius have whatever they have of tolerable quality of this kind) — there is this: that Cicero, when at his games the deified Julius brought Laberius on stage as a mime, then restored him to the equestrian order and bade him go and sit among the knights; and all so crowded together that they would not receive him as he came up. Cicero was ill spoken of as being neither a sure friend to Pompey nor to Caesar, but a flatterer of both.

Whether, if there is violence and necessity in the matter, things done by violence and necessity are to be rescinded only if the violence and necessity were applied by the bargainer. "It makes no difference," he says, "whether I or you are compelled, provided I am not compelled by you; the fault must be mine, that the penalty may be mine." "No," he says; "for the law is not angry with the man who applies violence, but succours the man who suffered it, and it seems unfair to it that that should hold good which a man bargained for not because he wished, but because he was compelled. And it makes no difference," I say, "through whom it became necessary for him; for what is rescinded is made unfair by the fortune of the man who suffered, not by the person of the doer." Then whether violence was applied by this man. "You," he says, "applied violence to me, who would not inform unless I made the bargain." "It is not," he says, "to apply violence, to promise something under a fixed condition. If there is any violence, it was applied by you to yourself, in that to expose . . . and that he had come to entreat that he might give back to the father only as much as had been left over for the rearer."

Then: whether he did not say it with this mind — that he wished her to die. "I said it," he says, "in anger, when I wished to chastise, not to kill." CLODIUS TURRINUS said neatly: "Do not marvel if I use harsher words; I am not going to go beyond words; I will threaten, then forgive: the victor did so too."

There had declaimed before him this very controversia VARUS QUINTILIUS — then Germanicus's son-in-law, and still wearing the toga praetexta. He, when he had described the indignation of the bystanders that the punishment was so quickly withdrawn from their eyes, said: the immortal gods heard the prayers of the public vow: they called the unchaste woman back, that the punishment might not run past too quickly. CESTIUS said many things insultingly against this epigram: "Just so," he said, "did they call her back as one calls back the racing chariots? For you set down the comparison before, since she too had come out of the carcer." When he had said much, at last he added a thing we all disapproved: "By such carelessness your father lost an army." He was rebuking the son, but reviled the father.

OF CESTIUS PIUS: I fear death, and now I have no one for whom to perish. OF MARULLUS: If your hatred toward me is so stubborn, declare boldly what you will do; say you cannot be won over. Why do you keep me hanging in the uncertain expectation of death? Anxious even in my sleep, I shudder as though the axe were brought to my neck. If I cannot obtain to live, let me at least obtain not to die long. There is no cause for you to think the law narrow in its number of days: it is his law to make me die long. Answer, father: if you mean to save your son, the time has already been; if to kill him, the time is now. I cannot bear the fear longer, nor suffer these torments for thirty days: and over myself I have some power. OF BLANDUS: Has it fallen to you so meanly, that you alone, when your son is in peril, do not entreat?

Caesar had then enrolled many in the senate, both to fill up the order exhausted by the civil war and to repay the favour of those who had deserved well of his party. Cicero jested at both things, for he sent to Laberius as he passed: "I would have received you, were I not sitting in a narrow place." Laberius sent back to Cicero: "And yet you are accustomed to sit on two stools." Each most elegantly, but neither kept measure in this kind of thing. From these the imitation of this pursuit spread to many. But to return to the controversia, CASSIUS SEVERUS said that he liked that colour: "I wished to die"; and he said certain sententiae in the course of disputation: "The third time," he said, "when I was being disowned, I said: 'Nothing is worth so much; let this wretched life, which my father so often harries and assails, receive itself but once.' But again I said to myself: 'Save that life: you will do as you please when acquitted.' Why then do you not die now? someone says. First, the wretched do not always like the same thing; sometimes it is pleasant to contend with one's fortune and to wear it out. Then — do you wish the true reason why I do not die meanwhile? Because I think you wish it." JUNIUS OTHO seemed to have said a foolish sententia: "It matters little to me; for he wished to kill either me or my son."

For the rearer GALLIO followed this colour, that he had been moved by pity. "When I saw," he said, "a childless man without an heir, I said to myself: Why are you greedy? We can both be fathers. And he said that charming sententia: "And so now I pay the penalty for being merciful." MONTANUS VOTIENUS began thus: "If anyone sees me, judges, a moment ago the father of two children, now imperilled by anxiety, I am sure he says, 'A cruel informer.'" And he pleaded with his opponent in a subdued way: he asked him to be content with one; and he took up that objection: "I do not know," he said, "which one," and said: "Believe me, who know them best: choose whichever you will; for this very reason I made the bargain so, because it made no difference."

GALLIO made this question too: whether the girl did not perish for this — that the father answered her so harshly. "She perished," he says, "from longing for her husband; otherwise would she have paid for the bitterness of one word with death? Nay, headlong, rash, burning with insane love and stunned, the man whom she had followed, leaving her father, having seen her father, she followed."

PASTOR AIETIUS delivered this controversia before Cestius, being already a senator, and thought this the best colour: by her poisonings her body has so hardened that it beats back the rocks. Cestius much rebuked him and said: "Is this why I should invite my hearers to go and hear others? He does me as much harm who is either an athlete or a consumptive." And he was speaking against Albucius, who in those days had said in this controversia: "harder than the rock," and against Julius Bassus much, who had said: "a virgin from under the rock." Junius Otho the father I remember introducing a foolish colour — the less to be borne because he published books of colours: "Perhaps," he said, "she prepared herself for the punishment, and from the time she began to sin

LATRO divided thus: whether within the thirtieth day the ravisher can go to law with anyone — just as one cannot who is in custody, who is in prison. Even if he can with another, whether he can with the father, to whom the choice of life or death is given: "is he free to accuse one whom not to have won over is deadly?" Even if he can go to law with the father, whether he can for that which the law has given the father power to do: "for by that reasoning nothing is lawful, if either to be won over or to be accused is unavoidable for him." Then, if he can go to law, whether he ought. He treated the causes of anger: that he ravished, that he entreated another first, that he did not entreat me, that he even accuses. If not to be won over by a son is madness, whether one can yet be condemned for madness, when it is still uncertain whether he will be won over. Here he treated a father's feelings, giving hope. He did not approve Fuscus, who pleaded a little too openly: it is against the controversia to promise. The father can nonetheless be played both as good and as not yet won over.

HISPO ROMANIUS was by nature one who followed a rougher manner of speaking; and so he pleaded with this colour, so as to inveigh against him as a bad father, and call him one who exposed cruelly, who received back treacherously. "In this," he says, "he asks them back, not because he wishes to have them, but because he wishes to snatch them away; he is angry with me because I reared two, because I informed." And when he had described the savagery of the man who exposed them, he added: "Even now he seems to me of the same mind, the same hardness, because he thinks he owes nothing to the man who reared his children. The father is hard, he is cruel; do not believe so sudden a change after that ferocity. Let me not put to the test, in one son, . . ." CESTIUS had said in this controversia, in that question in which he said he had applied no violence at all: "What then? Who applied violence? You to yourself. There is no reason for another to say: Who applies violence to himself? It happens; behold, I myself have harmed myself." And he had said this: "It pleases me that the things done be recalled to nothing. What do I give that I may not have informed?"

SILO POMPEIUS set before this question that one, from which the passage was made to this: whether, even if she perished for this word of the father's, the father ought nonetheless not to be condemned: for not the outcome of any matter ought to be charged, but the intention. If after this word the girl had lived, could you condemn the father of madness? And after this word, if anything was done, it was done not by the father but by the girl. But her rashness ought not to seem the father's madness. After this question he made that one:

has learned how to fall." SILO POMPEIUS attempted this colour: "There is a certain modesty shown even to condemned priestesses: we blushed to take anything from a condemned woman's garment." HISPANUS said: "So you had thought you could be quit with one punishment, when on the rock you had named the gods?" TRIARIUS, when he had described the voices of the indignant, added: "What? Can you not die twice?" MARULLUS said: "She stood on the rock, she called on the gods; the public indignation arose: does she dare to name the gods, dare it in this place? And what has she now to beg of them, but a good death?" DIOCLES OF CARYSTUS said: "Once, and a second, and a third time, and until you fall down to where you were cast."

FABIANUS made this question, and dwelt much upon it: that an action for madness cannot lie except against one who rages from disease; for to this end the law was passed, that a father should be healed by his son, not ruled. Latro elegantly used to say that there are certain questions which ought to be reckoned among things already adjudged: such as, whether a brave man or a tyrant-slayer ought to receive whatever he chooses: since it has been pronounced that he ought not, no one now treats this question, just as no one treats that other — whether whatever a father commands ought to be done. Among these he thought was this one too: whether a father ought to be accused by his son for madness only when he rages from disease; for he said it was plain from the law both that the question is of a father's duty, and that certain controversiae are invented in which a father cannot be proved mad, and yet cannot be acquitted on account of too great impiety or foul lust. What then? he said, shall I never use this question?

ARGENTARIUS said, on the other side, that he was now more wretched than when he did not know his own children; and when he had described the torments of a father's heart, he said: "Even now I wish to bargain. What do I give that I may not get back my children? What do I give that I may not have recognized them?" CESTIUS was indignant that he was so often distorted by him and his sententiae changed. "What do you think Argentarius is?" he used to say; "he is Cestius's ape." He used to say it in Greek too: "My monkey." For Argentarius had been Cestius's hearer and was his imitator. He used to say in turn: "What do you think Cestius is but Cestius's ash?" And he used to swear thus: "By the shade of my teacher Cestius," while Cestius was alive. But he followed all Cestius's footsteps:

whether she perished for this. The colour on the accuser's side is simple: he says the father was hard, cruel; that to the public good this man was not the leader of his party. "He said it," he says, "with such a look, such firmness, that he seemed not only to bid but to kill." In this place TURRINUS CLODIUS said: "This after war — nay, after the edict?" And he added: "Now the state understands, general, how much it owes to you, to whom satisfaction was made without blood." All said that the husband married her against the father's will.

I shall use it when I am at a loss for others. ASINIUS POLLIO used to say that Latro seemed to do this like a forensic pleader, in cutting away foolish questions, but that in nothing was he more caught out as a schoolman. He gives up, he said, that question which is always strongest for fathers. I know that no one is given a guardian by the praetor because his father is unjust or impious, but because he is mad; and that to seek a guardian in the forum is the same as to bring an action for madness in the school.

equally he spoke extempore, equally he inserted many things insultingly; this one thing, however, he kept with the best good faith — that, though each was a Greek, he never declaimed in Greek, and always admired those who were not content with eloquence in one tongue, but, when they had declaimed in Latin, laid aside the toga, took up the pallium, and, as though they had changed their character, returned and declaimed in Greek; among whom was SABINUS CLODIUS, against whom, declaiming in one day both in Greek and in Latin, many witty things were said.

GALLIO said: "It did not yet seem to me that she knew what she had deserved. I wished her to understand her crime." CESTIUS with this colour: "She asked," he says, "defiantly, in the very manner in which she perished — not with downcast face, not with humbler words, not yet as one conquered: I recognized nothing of a daughter, nothing of one conquered. First, why does she send to me, not to her brother? Is she still angry with her brother?"

GALLIO used the earlier question and added this one: whether one can go to law against a father for madness for what he has done, not for what he is going to do. That no one is accused of injury because he is going to do an injury, nor of adultery because he is going to commit adultery, nor even of madness because he is going to be mad. "And yet you," he says, "do not go to law with me because you have not won me over, but because you are not going to win me over; for suppose I am won over today: I shall not be mad. Do I seem mad, who can be healed by a single word? The law gave thirty days, because it judged that someone might be harsher. Even if he is mad who is not won over by his son, is he so on the twentieth day too? Therefore you cannot condemn me on the ground that I have not been won over; for even now I can be won over. So, if you want the truth, you cannot go to law with me on this charge; at any rate, for thirty days I can be won over; after thirty days you cannot complain: either I have no crime or I have no accuser."

HATERIUS said to certain men who complained that he received small fees, since he taught two subjects, that those who taught translation-exercises had never received large fees. Maecenas said: "You could never tell to which side Tydeus' son belonged." CASSIUS SEVERUS said the most charming thing of all, who, when on returning from hearing him he was asked how the man had spoken, answered: "Badly — and worse." GLYCON said: "If you do not give me back both, you will lose what makes them a pair." GALLIO, however, said most elegantly on the father's side, when he handled the last point through the figure of a will: "Whenever I am dead, then let him be my heir: do you wish me to ask which one?" TRIARIUS said, on the rearer's side: "So I could take them up, I could rear them, but I could not keep silent?"

ARGENTARIUS said: "We won over the leader, we whose children had been on opposite sides; we said: 'Forgive; do not be stern, when you are allowed to be free from care.' What sin did I commit, that I did not at the first word receive my daughter as she came from the enemy's camp?" CLODIUS TURRINUS said: "I wished to give the brother a kindness toward his sister: 'I will speak the harder, that he may beseech me for his sister.' First, why does she ask me alone, when she ought to make satisfaction to two?" SILO GAVIUS said: "I wished her to be tortured with delay: 'Let her,' I said, 'ask a second and a third time: not even the gentlest victor forgave at once.'"

SILO POMPEIUS made the question GALLIO used, and added: the young man will accomplish nothing, even if he condemns his father; for he will perish nonetheless, since the law gave the ravisher no other way of safety than if he won over his father. Latro treated all these as limbs bearing upon some question, not as a question; just as this very point, he said, bears upon that question in which it is asked whether the ravisher can accuse his father within the thirtieth day. "For when I say: you cannot accuse one in whose discretion it is placed whether you die or live, any more than you can summon a magistrate to court, or pass sentence on your own judges, or any more than a soldier can pass judgement on his own general — I add: you cannot accuse; for it will profit you nothing, even if you condemn; you will die; for the law wishes you to perish unless you win him over; and you do not win him over even if you condemn." Why did he not place this in the position of a question?

LABIENUS said: "I was not won over at once; and had she lived I should not have been broken by her next prayers, nor even when asked a third time or a fourth. 'But the victor was quickly won over.' Do not marvel: it is easier to forgive war than parricide." HISPANUS said about her death: "A second time the husband has taken her from us." ALBUCIUS said: "I thought," he says, "I could safely speak the more boldly; for I did not doubt the brother would say to her: 'There is no reason for you to fear, he will be won over; if he is the harder, I will ask him myself'; and had you asked, young man, I should have done it. I refuse you nothing, no more than your sister refuses her husband."

He thought it weak. For it appears that the law does not require him to win over a father who has no one to win over. For suppose someone's father is so openly mad that he understands nothing: does the law wish him to be won over by his son? And yet a manifest madman is in the same position. FUSCUS thought this not strong enough as a question, strong enough as an argument; and that other question — that one cannot go to law with a father on the ground that he has not sinned but is going to sin — he placed in the treatment of equity, when he said: even if you can bring an action against me for madness, you ought not. For what wrong have I done? I have not been won over: the time has not yet passed, I can still be won over. How unjust it is that I am not yet guilty, and already a defendant!

MONTANUS VOTIENUS said: "There is no reason for you to think she fell to her father's anger: for him for whom she had lived she perished, she spent herself for him to whom she had bound herself." And the same thought in his arguments, when he said that even by her death she sought ill-will against her father, that she did not perish for the father's sake: "What then," you say, "for whose sake?" You know she had one for whom she could die.

All defamed the father of the ravished woman as colluding with the ravisher. GALLIO said: he ravished a freeborn maiden — if, that is, he ravished her at all. SILO POMPEIUS turned the same suspicion upon everything: "I won over," he said, "the father of the ravished woman." So then — when she had an easily-won father, you ravished her? HISPANUS said: everything was done quickly: this man quickly ravished, that one quickly forgave. Unless I am mad, something is to be suspected. ARGENTARIUS said: she was ravished and at once won over; nay, I am not sure whether she was won over first, then ravished. I hope you were more innocent than you wish to seem. You say you won him over; I think you were won over. Tell me, what did you arrange with your father-in-law? OF VIBIUS RUFUS: Tell me what you arranged, for how much he promised you the marriage. You will not?

Then, by Hercules, you will confess when the day comes. ASPRENAS said: "Now," he says, "not much is left of the thirty days"; if I counted the days from that point when you first won him over, they say thirty days have already passed. Latro said what is written among the epigrams: "I shall die"; tell the truth, then. CESTIUS declaimed with this figure, so as to entreat his father, as though the father of the ravished woman had been won over; then he passed to this epigram: have I a worse cause, if I have won before another judge? With the same figure HISPO ROMANIUS too declaimed, but passed over more softly: I know what can be answered me: it is easy to satisfy a household judge; I shall see to you, when you come to the father of the ravished woman.

In this controversia TRIARIUS had said: you will not know whether you win me over, unless the last day comes; and then, as long as it is allowed, I shall persist. Then, with the schoolmen's greatest uproar: but you, whoever you are, executioner, when you have raised the drawn axe, before you strike, look back at his father.
