Prettily ASINIUS POLLIO mocked this: let the son, he said, stretch out his neck, let the executioner raise his hand, then look back at the father, and say: shall I do it? — as is the custom with victims. But, jest aside too, he said a most true thing: that the executioner cannot come except at the time when the father can no longer be won over.

CESTIUS, on the other side, used this colour, because he had entreated the father of the ravished woman first: I did not wish him to be in suspense, I wished him to be at once at ease about me; he complains that I wished him to think rather of his son's marriage than of his peril. Latro used this colour: you know that men in peril act by another's discretion. Those companions who were around me, the friends of my father who had come to me, kept saying: let us go at once to the father of the ravished woman; in such a case those men are entreated; for the fathers of ravishers do the entreating.

SILO POMPEIUS followed a colour opposite to this: the harshness of my father was well known, he said; and so my friends advised that we go to the father of the ravished woman, lest it harm us with him that his own father was won over too slowly. HISPO ROMANIUS used a pretty colloquialism. "Day has dawned," he said, "friends; let us go to the father of the ravished woman; let us hurry, the other is at home." FUSCUS ARELLIUS said: the one more feared was entreated first. TRIARIUS, on the young man's side, said: I fear he may change, even though he has been won over. This thought SILO POMPEIUS not imprudently disapproved; for he said that a sentence once passed cannot be changed.

Some wished it to seem that the father of the ravished woman was won over quickly, some slowly. FUSCUS ARELLIUS said: I have consumed a great part of the law's time, and I do not complain of the delay: the father of the ravished woman was being entreated. CESTIUS did not approve this, and used this epigram in censuring the colour: while he wishes it to seem that the father of the ravished woman was long entreated, he brings it about that he seems to have been slow in entreating his own; but I would rather it seem that this man's father is slowly won over, than slowly entreated. HERMAGORAS was wont sometimes to pursue figures at length, sometimes to touch them briefly and more forcibly, as he did in this epigram, when he wished to raise a suspicion of collusion between the father of the ravished woman and the ravisher: "He has been won over," he says, "the father of the ruined girl, very quickly indeed: almost before the ruin."

ARTEMON said: "Tell me, what have you arranged with the father of the ruined girl? Tell me, how have you won him over? Are you silent? You are caught." GLYCON said: "If you pity me slowly, how will you save me? . . . a care chillier than death, I will not await your pity." This thought LEPIDUS, Nero's teacher, expressed more aptly: do you not have pity except on the last day? I shall have pity on myself before. DIOCLES OF CARYSTUS, on the father's side, spoke ethically: "Shall I then die? Die: for to what end did you ravish? To what end . . . ? To what end did you rage? And these things, too, either after setting an ambush, or some such thing."

THE LAW: A son shall be in the father's power. Whoever catches an adulterer with the adulteress may kill them both, provided he kills both bodies. THE THEME: A brave man in war lost his hands. He caught his wife in adultery, and called his son to kill them; the son refused. The adulterers escaped. He disinherits his son. OF PORCIUS LATRO: I only roused my adulterers. Wretched me! How long did they lie there after I had caught them? Shall I not disinherit you, whom I might kill? O bitter remembrance of my own valour! O grievous memory of my victory! That military man, but now laden with the spoils of the enemy, did no more than curse his adulterers: I alone of all husbands neither dismissed the adulterers nor killed them. Why do you laugh? I say I have hands. I called my son. You, the son of a brave man, who cannot draw a sword? Not even a trunk could I have been taken, save at home; yet such as I could, I struggled, and set my mutilated body against them. The adulterers went out stained only with my blood. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: O me, worthy either of a chaste wife, or of an unchaste one only while I am armed! You I call upon, my country, you who possess my hands. Who would not suppose either that I had no son, or that the son had no hands?

THE THEME: A man had two sons. One of them, having a child by a harlot, fell sick. The father came to him at the harlot's house. The dying son commended his child to his father, who took up the child. He is accused of madness by his other son. OF PORCIUS LATRO: What a woman I saw! She herself performed the offices, busy about the sick man's bed, running to every service, her hair not merely loosened but torn. Where, I said, is the harlot? Someone came to me suddenly to say: your son, before he dies, asks you to come. I did not wait for this man's leave: out of my senses, I ran. The rest, how I am to relate, I do not know: whether I stood or sat, what I said, what I heard, I do not know; this one thing I know — that I lay between my two sons. Come here, boy, my charge, my crime; I have, wretch that I am, no one to whom, when dying, I may commend you. OF CESTIUS PIUS: I took my grandson into my bosom.

OF CESTIUS PIUS. There is no reason for you to weigh a woman's feeling by the law with which she threatens; she does everything that her son may not be bound. About to sail, he left his son to his wife; and she was not yet blind. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. I brought your son down to you; so hold him, embrace him. I dare to say, this pair not even pirates would divide. If she wished her son bound, she would let him go where he hastens. So you, young man, will not even repay your mother the ten months' nourishment? If you will not feed your mother, wait at least to carry her out to burial. OF TRIARIUS. She has brought a law with which to threaten chains, a reason for which she fears. OF MARCELLUS AESERNINUS. If you persist, drag me too to the pirates: I shall obtain nourishment from them; they feed my husband too. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. The mother, if she is not fed, will perish; the father, even if he is not ransomed, is still fed. OF JULIUS BASSUS.

I should be happier if I were defending more defendants. OF TRIARIUS. These wounds which you see on my face I made after I was dismissed. OF JUNIUS GALLIO. I give thanks to my son, that he did not leave me alone with the tyrant. What his hands dared, I ordered; and so I am present for my own charge. "He was," he says, "the tyrant's friend." Or did my son only feign this in the citadel? I fall at your knees, judges — I, that stubborn man, who, when I was being beaten, did not beg.

OF PORCIUS LATRO. Estimate how great is that man's crime, in which the injured fathers are silent so as not even to acknowledge or take back their children, even when the wrongs are confessed. His cruelty was a tax — all the more so because all of us, except him, are merciful. You would be a beggar, had you not made so many beggars. That wretch brought it about that, by a new fashion, nothing was more wretched for the exposed than to be taken up, for the parents than to acknowledge them. OF CASSIUS SEVERUS.

OF CESTIUS PIUS: This man was conceived — by whom, we shall know when I have caught my adulterers. I never thought it would come to pass, while the republic stood, that a brave man should feel he had lost his hands. OF MARULLUS: I escorted my adulterers right to the threshold. I ran, wretch that I was, to the sword, as though I had hands. OF TRIARIUS: My arms fell with my hands: then for the first time I felt that I had lost my hands. THE DESCRIPTION OF THE BRAVE MAN FIGHTING. Good gods, and did anyone mock these hands too? OF PUBLIUS ASPRENAS: Summoned to kill the adulterers, he came to dismiss them. So have I lost my hands even for adulterers' sake? I stood mocked by my own adulterers; the deserter of his father, the procurer of his mother, who, I think, you now believe is no son of a brave man — a third man, the mocker, stood in the bedchamber.

Do you wish me to disinherit him too? I raised two sons; to that number I am now used. He accuses his father, defames his brother, persecutes an infant: I ask you, is it not better to love a harlot than no one? It is a madness of a new kind I am charged with: I should be sane if I did not acknowledge my own. He handed me the child and breathed his last; I had no one to whom to give it back. I offered myself to my kinsmen, I waited for someone to entreat for the disinherited man: none of the kinsmen dared, while the brother held back; they, of course, kept silent in this thought: shall we entreat, when the brother does not dare? "You have taken in," he says, "the son of a harlot": yes — of her who had taken in mine. I confess I was once mad: I did not know which son was to be disinherited; I cast out the better one.

Your father has both eyes and nourishment left. The other side. OF CESTIUS PIUS. I wish to imitate my mother: she taught me to love my own. With one man's chains she binds two. If, by my mother's example, I wish to be dutiful, I owe my father even my eyes. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. You will find your deserter with your father. OF VARIUS GEMINUS. What a fortune it is! To the conquered, mother, you proclaim chains; to the conqueror one must go to the pirates. Though I render my father everything, yet he had the better wife. How many think, because I am unwilling to go to ransom my father, that I am now in collusion with my mother! OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. For my mother I fear nothing, if I leave her with you; for my father, what do I not fear, if I leave him among pirates? OF BUTEO. I will surely tear out my own eyes, lest a wife render more to her husband than a son to his father.

OF MUSA. The tyrant was killed; by whom, do you think, but by the man who could beat his father? Will you cut off the tyrannicide's hands? What is this? The tyrant lies untouched. Fix the tyrannicide's severed hands on the citadel. Shall I not call him my avenger, my son, on whose account I was not even beaten by the tyrant with impunity? After he had seized the citadel, murderers followed him, poisoners followed, there followed whoever could beat his father. It was necessary to beat my father, just as, by Hercules, it was necessary to plunder temples, to rape virgins. I kept saying: "Son, strike harder; the tyrant is watching." If my son was such as you describe, I do not know to whom it would have profited more for the tyrant to live. O how much we owe to those hands, by which now nothing is necessary! He killed the tyrant: so do these angry hands strike. When he was killing the tyrant he said: "A brother strikes you, a father strikes"; so they strike who wish to. With you, my son of inconsiderate devotion, I complain: you struck your father more strongly than the tyrant ordered. In my anger I hurled into my own face the very hands of the corpse as it lay.

Here the blind, leaning on staffs, wander; here they carry round maimed arms; this one's foot-joints are wrenched and his ankles twisted, this one's legs are crushed, this one — with feet and legs unharmed — a woman has battered the thigh: savaging each in a different way, that bone-breaker cuts off one's arms, unstrings another, twists another, weakens the loins of another, beats another's diminished shoulder-blades into a deformed hump, and hunts laughter out of cruelty. Bring out, come now, your half-living household — trembling, crippled, blind, maimed, famished; show us your captives. By heaven, I wish to know that den of yours, that workshop of human calamities, that spoliarium of infants. To each is assigned his own calamity as though it were a trade: "This one has straight limbs, and if no one hinders it, his natural tallness will shoot up: let him be broken so that he cannot lift himself from the ground, but, the joints of his feet and legs loosened, may crawl; let this one's be torn out by the roots. This one has a comely face: a beggar can be handsome; let his other limbs be made useless, that the injustice of fortune, raging against its own gifts, may strike men's minds the more." Thus, without his guard, the tyrant dispenses human calamities.

OF FULVIUS SPARSUS: In war he lost his own hands, at home even his son's. This one man of all went forth to war as the substitute for his young son: in the battle-line he conquered, at home he was taken captive. He watches the adulterers wallowing amid the spoils of the brave man. "Young man, the time of your service is come." A shameful thing: he was deceived; as vainly did he run to his son as to his sword. The adulterers laughed at the brave man's mutilated hands, slipping down about his own arms. OF ARGENTARIUS: He did not come into the war, and refused his hands to his country before he refused them to his father. Gladly I have taken up his cause: for who would not avenge him? What is more unhappy than this — a man whom the adulterers laughed at, just when they ought to die? Shall a brave man, a trunk, behold in the city adulterers whole and sound?

OF PAPIRIUS FABIANUS: How little of a harlot's life I saw in that house! The woman sat by, with a sad face, afflicted, herself most like a sick person, her eyes cast down to the ground. "Father," he said, "did my brother say nothing to you?" Into my bosom he laid both his son and his soul. I carried it home. He calls it madness that I did not disinherit the infant. What was I to do? Refuse a son something, when he was entreating me for his son? I forgive you for being so hard: you did not see your sick brother. He, but lately born the successor of a great patrimony, was dying on a borrowed cot; no crowd of slaves stood about him, no crowd of friends; between an infant and a poor little woman the failing young man's breath was held back until I came. As I entered, he raised his already drooping eyes at my name, and held back his fleeing soul. "Father," he said, "that I have entreated for nothing till now I did not do from obstinacy; I had entrusted it to my brother." I will declare my crimes to you: I wished to call back to life your dying co-heir; I prayed the gods that he might be safe, and — though you call it madness — had he lived, I should have taken him in.

Latro declaimed this controversia as though it were wholly a matter of duty; he inserted no questions of law, but compared the misfortunes of father and mother with each other, and stated it as a thesis: whether a son ought rather to go to ransom his captive father, or to stay to feed his blind mother; and he so divided it as to say: "What the mother desires is useful to the father too." Last he treated that not even the father wishes it; certainly, if he knew the mother to be in this plight, he would not allow it. In the epilogues APOLLONIUS the Greek was vehement. BUTEO had raised a silly question first: whether the law which had been passed about supporting parents pertained only to the father. To them all privileges had been given, and the very penalty for not supporting was a sign of no womanly power. The matter is too silly to be refuted, and so I pass it over; this one thing only that Asinius Pollio said I will report: that in a case which calls for delicacy one ought never to attempt an indecent question.

OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. They were such that of them one could despise the tyrant, the other kill him. OF JULIUS BASSUS. I drove my son's clenched hands into my own face; I consoled him as he struck. OF PORCIUS LATRO. "Beat your father," he says. While I am careless, my son seized the chance to hurl himself headlong from the citadel. This is not to spare a father, but oneself. Endure, my son; you must go to the tyrant by way of your father. See, they hold the tyrant's bloody head; now cut off those hands. OF BLANDUS.

OF VIBIUS GALLUS. Behold the feeble limbs of the wretched, consumed by I know not what wasting; this one's hands cut off, this one's eyes torn out, this one's feet broken. Why do you shudder? Thus does that man show pity. So many limbs are broken to fill one belly, and — O new monster — the whole man is fed, the cripples feed him. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. "They would have perished," he says. Do they not survive more wretchedly than they were going to perish? "They would have perished," he says. Ask the fathers which they would have preferred. "Let his eyes be torn out," he says, "this one's hands cut off." What if some one of these is to be a brave man? Is to be a tyrannicide? What if a priest? Nor, I think, do I speak things incredible in this fortune; certainly from such a crowd the origin of the Roman race appeared. An excellent rearer reckons more put to cruelty's account than expended on pity. OF TRIARIUS. "They would have perished," he says.

OF JULIUS BASSUS: There is no reason for you to think he is being punished: he is sent back to his own; sent back, I say, to his mother — perhaps to his father too. He has earned the inheritance of the man whom he thought it kin-murder to kill. To no man did you ever owe more than to this brave man: so far did he fight for you, that he could not fight for himself. Young man, follow those you dismissed.

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: I was the more at ease, since I had thought his brother furnished him with everything, when suddenly it was announced that my son was at his last — and this not from his brother. O wretched me, that I have taken in my only grandson! OF ALBUCIUS SILUS: When he saw his wife, when he saw his father, he was looking round even for his brother. OF JULIUS BASSUS: To you, woman, I owe it that my son had a house in which to be sick. I am ashamed to say it: I was entreated to acknowledge my grandson. Madness cannot be understood from a single fault. No one is without a vice: in Cato moderation is wanting, in Cicero constancy, in Sulla clemency. In sum, we were three, we all sinned: I in that I disinherited, my son in that he kept silent, you in that you did not entreat for your brother. I am not content with one heir, I wish to have two, and — that I may covet it the more — I have had two. He sent for me, my affectionate son, when sick. Shall I not go? Believe me, you hear otherwise about a co-heir. Consider who entreats, for whom he entreats, whom he entreats; you will see that no one could refuse, save one who could also accuse his father.

HISPO ROMANIUS raised that question: whether the law about supporting parents did not pertain to mothers while the fathers were alive. "A son under paternal power," he said, "can be a slave to none but his father; from every other slavery he is free. Suppose you seek nourishment from one whom your father sends abroad, whom he bids to sail: the first claim is the father's, the second the mother's." ALBUCIUS made that not a question of law but of equity, yet in such a way that he joined law to it: whether the mother's duty came before the father's or the father's before the mother's. POMPEIUS SILO made that question: whether, whenever there was joint ownership between two, the whole power passed to the one who was present. "Suppose," he said, "you are a common slave: you will serve the master who is present. Suppose an estate is held in common: he will take the fruits who is present." And he subjoined to this a hard question: whether the father now has no right at all over the son. "As one who does not have the rights of a free man," he said, "does not have the rights of a citizen, so one who does not have the rights of a citizen does not have those of a father either; he has no power over you, the mother is in possession of the whole law; now the right over you is not common to her, but her own."

When I saw the tyrannicide coming down from the citadel, before anything else I kissed his hands. OF POMPEIUS SILO. Which of my sons do you approve? One killed himself, the other the tyrant. No one has a right over these hands; they are mine; these hands, even when they served the tyrant, obeyed me. So may it be granted me to die with my son surviving, as I called him a parricide who preferred to die. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. I beg you by the public security, by the joy of liberty just now restored, by your wives and children. No one heard me, as suppliant as I beg now, when I was being beaten. How feeble were his hands as he struck! I should not have thought him able to commit tyrannicide. These hands held out to me my saving food, these my drink; yet never did I feel hands more tender than when they struck me.

I think you have tested that we are not cruel; yet there was not one of us who, as he held out a coin to these, did not pray for death. Rise, you cripple: he tries and falls down. Rise, you mute one: but why are you roused? You cannot ask. Rise, you blind one: but to whose knees you should go, you do not know. O you, most happy of all the cripples before this trial — because you did not see that master; in this trial most wretched — because you do not see that defendant! The exposed have been nursed even by wild beasts, which would have been gentle enough had they passed them by.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF VIBIUS GALLUS: "You did not kill," he says, "your mother." Whom should I have been less bound to destroy by this crime than my father? My father ordered me to kill: the law forbids. I would not have set the law against my father, had not that law been on his side. I thought it the other kin-murder, to kill my mother before my father's eyes. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: O wretched piety, amid what a conflict of a parent's wishes did you stand! Not always are crimes within our right, and merciful nature unstrings even savage minds.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF PORCIUS LATRO: One whom the harlot more honourably substituted than bore. This man's father is uncertain; it would be well with him, if his mother too. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: He is mistaken who thinks I am moved by money. First, I am used to having a co-heir; next, long since I have already divided the paternal estate with that boy, because his father gave him much more than his own share. OF ROMANIUS HISPO: He fell in with a harlot who, among all her other evils, was even fertile. Truly a mime wedding, in which the rival came into the bedchamber before the husband. OF ARGENTARIUS: When he was disinheriting, he kept saying: shall I, of course, wait until you raise children by a harlot? The woman is, I am not sure whether, the more injurious to the father in that you took an heir from him, or in that you gave him one.

VARIUS GEMINUS divided thus: whether a son can not always be compelled to support his mother; then whether now he ought not to be compelled. "Not always," he said, "is a son compelled. I pass over those who cannot — the sick, the useless; suppose someone sets out to repel an enemy, on whose single service the public safety rests: will his mother hold him back? Suppose an envoy on a matter of the highest concern to the state, suppose on a treaty: will his mother lay hold on him?" And comparing the two duties part by part: "He," he said, "is abroad, you at home; he a captive, you free; he among pirates, you among citizens; he bound, you loosed. But you are blind: he is the more unhappy in this, that he sees; for what does he see? The marks of his captivity, and the slaughters and wounds and crosses of those who are not ransomed. But it is dangerous. Everything is; both to stay at home and to weep."

OF VOTIENUS MONTANUS. "Let him rather perish," he said. Since there was a man who spoke so bravely, scarcely was one found to kill the tyrant. "Son, strike harder," I said, "lest the tyrant perceive we are in collusion." He raised his hands, lightly poised; the son feigned the blows, the father the groans. If there is any faith in me, in anger I carried out my son for burial because he had not struck me. Necessity is a great defence for human weakness: this excuses the men of Saguntum, though they did not strike their fathers but killed them; this excuses the Romans, whom the disaster of Cannae forced to a levy of slaves; whatever it has compelled, it defends. He too would not have spared me, had he been my only son. He left me to a brother: would this one have left me to the tyrant? "Even now," he says, "the wounds appear on your face." Son, it harms you that you killed the tyrant so quickly. OF MENTO. Do you ask who made these wounds? The man over whose death I beat myself. So may it befall me, a free man, both to live and to die, so may my son's hands close my eyes, as I stood among my children the braver.

OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. So then, if in those times that executioner had appeared, would Rome not have her founder? I fear lest this profit the defendant — that no one of these wishes any to seem his own. OF JULIUS BASSUS. Look upon both sides, and succor the side that is more pitiable. Let it be permitted to see your hirelings: this one is blind, this one crippled, this one mute. To these you do not permit to die? Do you wish the judges to be merciful upon you after your own manner, by your own example? OF ARGENTARIUS. Whose prayers, though they are heard everywhere, in their own cause alone fail. "Let us add something to the takings:

THE DIVISION. Latro used this division: whether it was lawful for the son to take vengeance then; whether it was fitting; whether, if it was lawful and fitting, he is to be pardoned if he could not, his natural affection resisting. Whether it was lawful he divided thus: whether a son may avenge adultery when the husband is not present; whether he may when the husband is in that place as though he were not present at all. Whether it was fitting is a matter of treatment, which each man varies as he pleases; yet Latro arranged it thus: it was fitting, even had the father not ordered it, to kill the unchaste wife of a brave man; it was fitting, the father ordering it, even if he himself could have killed her; it was fitting, when the father both ordered it and could not himself do it. The modern declaimers attempted that question born of the law's word — "Whoever catches an adulterer with the adulteress, provided he kills both bodies, shall be free of penalty": whether no one can kill but the one who catches them; they attempted also this: whether a son can be disinherited for what his own law made lawful for him to do.

OF ALBUCIUS SILUS: Let friends come there, let kinsmen come: now they blush to enter a harlot's house. Woman — you who cannot honourably be named without a prefatory apology — give up that home-born slave, to be acknowledged by no one; but let the mother claim him. A most severe father disinherited even the son he knew to be his own. There was in the house a boy who called everyone "father." He adopted the son of the woman for whose sake he had even cast out his own. OF CESTIUS PIUS: I refuse no kind of judges: if they are severe, it will harm him that he took in a harlot's son; if merciful, that he disinherited his own. The father cried out: shall a harlot then come into my house, or — what is baser — her son? He went to her, he sent a public child into our house. Who was present at that wedding, but a man disinherited or to be disinherited?

Latro said that for the mother one must plead in a subdued and gentle manner. "For she seeks," he said, "not vengeance but mercy, and she stands face to face with a young man in whom she so demands dutifulness as to hinder it." And so he used to say that even rougher words must be avoided whenever such material arose; the very speech must be softened to suit the disposition of the feeling we wish to move; in the epilogues we must on purpose break our very voice too, and let our face fall, and take care that the orator be not unlike his speech; a gentler composition too suits such themes. CALVUS, who long maintained a most unequal contest with Cicero over the primacy in eloquence, was so violent and impetuous an actor that, in the midst of his pleading, the defendant Vatinius rose and exclaimed: "I ask you, judges, must I be condemned merely because this man is eloquent?"

The other side. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. He beat his father so long, until he should please the tyrant as a henchman. What? Can you not commit tyrannicide unless you have practised your hands in parricide? "My father is present," he says. So much the worse; for you struck not only a father, but a patron. OF JULIUS BASSUS. Since the age has so changed that a parricide's father is present, we are present for this man's advocacy. He defends a guilty man: do you at all recognize indulgence? His brother, who chose to perish rather than beat his father, is unhappy in that he did not join his cause with his brother's. This man exclaims: "I gave him no orders." I will satisfy you on his behalf too. "That I might strike harder for the state," he says, "I did it." Will you have the grace not to claim the same thing both for the state and for the tyrant? "My father," he says, "is present to me." But, by Hercules, his brother would not be present. You had something to flaunt before the tyrant: my brother chose to die. Whoever was to be beaten was handed over to this man. "The tyrant," he says, "I killed." But your father — how little less than to kill him was it!

take out this one's eyes, that one's hands." OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the father. "Let the tongue," he says, "be cut out: it is a kind of asking, to be unable to ask." Pity all these, judges, of whom you are wont to pity even single ones. OF CESTIUS PIUS. To undertake this case I was not even asked by those for whom I plead. For what do the wretched know how to ask except a coin? What sin has that wretch committed, other than that he was born? OF CLODIUS TURRINUS the father. Come, if anyone acknowledges his own, will you ask for maintenance as though you had reared him? There is no reason for you to fear, no one will acknowledge them. O wretched man, if anyone gives maintenance to his own! O wretched man, if he refuses! Do you so think we will refuse vengeance to these, to whom we do not refuse even that which they will give to you? And — what is most unworthy — though he is so cruel, he lives by the public pity.

The colour for the young man introduced by all who declaimed was one: "I could not kill" — drawn from that saying of Cicero's which he uttered in a like controversia, when a man was being disinherited who had received his unchaste mother to be killed and had let her go: "thrice not . . ." Latro described the stupor of his whole body at the spectacle of so unlooked-for an outrage, and said: "Father, your hands failed you, all of me failed me." And when he had described the darkness of his eyes, the swooning of his mind, the numbness of all his limbs, he added: "before I came back to myself, they went out." GORGIAS with a clumsy colour, but a sweet one; PAMMENES, of the new declaimers —

Latro divided thus: whether a father can be accused for any adoption, whether he ought to be for this one. All defamed the young man, as though by his slanders it had come about that his brother was disinherited; and so this epigram of FABIANUS is praised: I said nothing to you. And since this one thing harms the boy — that he was born of a harlot — all took pains, as far as the controversia allowed, to heal this fault and bring it about that nothing in her should seem to have been a harlot's but the name. MARULLUS said this becomingly, at the same time charging the brother with impiety: nothing, he said, in that house was a harlot's:

The same man afterwards, when he saw Asinius Pollio surrounded and being beaten in the forum by the clients of Cato, his own defendant, ordered himself to be set upon a boundary-stone — for he was tiny in stature, on which account Catullus too in his hendecasyllables calls him "that eloquent little manikin" — and swore that, if Cato did any injury to Asinius Pollio, his accuser, he would lay against him a charge of false accusation; nor was Pollio ever afterwards harmed by Cato and his advocates, either in deed or in word. He used besides to step beyond his own benches, and in his impetus rush sideways right into the opponents' party. And his poems too, though they are jesting, are full of a great spirit. He says of Pompey: He scratches his head with one finger. What would you suppose he wants? A man.

OF POMPEIUS SILO. I rejoice that the father is on this man's benches. For how else could I have brought it about that you should see his wounds? It matters little to me where he is: from this side the charge is made, from that it is shown. A witness who rises from the defendant's side is wont to be the weightier. Such, indeed, was the father, whom no other could beat but one who could be the tyrant's friend. The brother perished, lest he either commit parricide or look on it:

Come, wretches, and today for the first time ask on your own behalf. OF MENTO. The wretched wander about the houses of their own parents, and perhaps someone does not obtain maintenance from his father. None bring back more than whole slaves. "Why do you bring back so little? . . . could you not, that you might not ask, that you might not receive? I should not have left you breath, had I not been about to be crueler in leaving it. Your daily catch does not answer my hopes; it appears you do not yet seem wretched enough to men." OF GAVIUS SILO. "You," he says, "shall beg in that neighborhood, you shall approach that threshold"; and the cruel man points out to the wretched the houses of their parents. "This one does not easily obtain a coin: let something more even now be taken from him."

— said . . . GORGIAS said excellently . . . PAMMENES said . . . ARELLIUS FUSCUS said: greater was the crime you commanded than the one you had caught. ALBUCIUS did not narrate, but pleaded with this colour from beginning to end: ought I to defend myself? If anything is charged against me, I shall either deny it or excuse it. If you demand of me something beyond my strength, I shall say: pardon me, I cannot. A father pardons a son who refuses a voyage, if he cannot bear the sea; he pardons one who does not follow the camp, if he cannot, though the father himself be a military man. I cannot kill. Come now, recite the law itself: "let it be lawful for the husband, lawful for the father, lawful for the son." Why does it name so many, unless it thinks that some are unable? And in his description he said: when my father called me, "this," I said, "he thinks will be a punishment graver than death — if he shows the adulteress to her son." And he said this too: the adulterers went out between the maimed father and the stupefied son. SILO narrated with this colour: I did not think it lawful for me.

you would know it, had you been with me. ALBUCIUS spoke ethically, as many think — at least it was praised when he said: as I went out, the boy followed me. Messala did not approve this epigram: he has no confidence, he said, if he prefers to seem to have taken in the boy rather than to have brought him; by which reasoning the boy was adopted not because he ought to have been, but because he followed. Now Messala was of a most exacting talent in all branches of study, and at any rate a most diligent observer of the Latin tongue; and so, when he had heard Latro declaiming, he said: he is eloquent in his own language. He granted him talent, he objected to his diction. Latro did not bear this insult, and against Messala's most eloquent speech for Pythodorus he recited one equally well-composed, and declaimed the suasoria on Theodotus for three days. What he said I shall render in its place, when I come to the suasoriae.

His composition too in his pleadings is rigid after the example of Demosthenes: nothing in it is placid, nothing soft; everything is roused and surging. Yet here, in the epilogue which he delivered for Messius, then pleading his case for the third time, he not only composes gently, but even says: "Believe me, it is no disgrace to feel pity" — and the rest; almost everything in that epilogue is not only of a softened composition, but of a broken one. In this controversia a certain rhetor named FESTUS, of tiny stature, gave a Publilian sententia, at whom EUCTEMON, a man of most charming wit, said in Greek: "Before I saw you, I did not know that rhetors came at half-price." Now Festus's sententia was: "Your father," he said, "is a captive"; if captives move you, this woman too is a captive. And, as though we had not understood: "Do you not know that people are said to be 'captives in their eyes'?"

on that precipice, I say, he fled no less his brother than the tyrant. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. The father came down bloody, his face battered and mangled, scarcely to be recognized; you would think two men had struck him. He did what he ought, who had beaten his father: he killed a friend. OF CESTIUS PIUS. "I," he says, "was beaten; I remit the penalty." I should wonder, were it not that for so good a father there was a man who wished to die. He deserves that you avenge him against his will; or are cruel fathers alone avenged among us? "My father," he says, "ordered it." Then was your brother impious, who did not obey his father? If ever the henchmen obeyed slowly, the tyrant would say: "Did you not watch how he beat his father?" "Let the hands of him who has beaten his father be cut off": this law the dying tyrant praised. At the last the tyrant came between son and father.

OF JUNIUS GALLIO. "Keep his eyes that he may see whom to ask; keep his hands that he may have wherewith to receive the coin." Dire omens meet weddings, gloomy auspices public rites; on holidays especially, and solemn days dedicated to mirth, these half-living herds wander abroad. From a father, perhaps, someone carries the coin he received to the gods. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. I know, judges, that each man is wont to be driven to accusing by various causes: some have been provoked by ambition for the glory they sought from a condemned man, others have been drawn on by hatreds and feuds; I do not doubt there have been some who sought a reward. I am free of all the causes that impel others: for what glory is there in so squalid a defendant? What feuds, when one would be ashamed even to have contracted them? Or what reward, since those feed him who cannot feed themselves?

BLANDUS with this colour: from both sides I hear the name of son; my father asks a juster thing, my mother an easier. And this he added after the description: I will confess to you — I could not commit kin-murder before my father's eyes. CESTIUS pleaded with this colour: "my mother sprang forth at once," he said, "and bound my hands with her embrace. I give thanks to my confusion, that I saw nothing in that bedchamber but my mother and my father: my father begged me to kill, my mother to let her live; my father, that the guilty woman should not go unpunished, my mother, that I, the innocent, should remain so; my father recited the law on adulteries, my mother the law on kin-murder." And he gave this last epigram: if it is base not to have wished to kill my mother, I could not. ARGENTARIUS said: there is no reason for you to judge me by this present condition, that I have hands: then I had none. And he said this: she pays you the penalty — she has lost her husband, lost her son; I will not sit by her when she is sick, I will not maintain her when she is in want; all things are free for me — I no longer owe her my life.

On the young man's side not one colour pleased all. Some introduced his character such as they had received it, hard and harsh, among whom was ROMANIUS HISPO: he said this one thing must be brought about — that he should seem not hard but severe. In this part he spoke that famous epigram which Fabius Maximus used to carry about: a harlot comes constantly into the house, she does not depart, she is but little short of being a stepmother. CESTIUS pleaded with a pretty figure: "madness," he said, "is a thing contrary to sanity. I shall not seek outside, from the example of a sane man, a standard to which to hold the father: I shall compare him with himself. He was once sane: what then was he doing? He hated luxury, he chastised vices. Will you think this so severe an old man sane, if I show him to you in a brothel?" So he declaimed as to give the brother his father for accuser, and to convict him by comparing him with himself.

And he said this: "Send away that fruitless letter. You ought to hate it: this is what blinded your mother." And that most false thing, into which many fall: "For this very reason," he said, "she is the more to be wept for, that she cannot weep." And again: "Tears," he said, "the mother lacks, causes she has in plenty" — as though the blind were not wont to weep. I remember a certain CRISPUS, an old rhetor, in that controversia of the brave man who keeps his third son — when one son had lost his eyes in tyrannicide, the other his hands in battle — saying: "Rise now, you living corpses, and plead for your father." But why do I mock my own? The one has not eyes wherewith to plead, the other has not hands.

The division. Latro divided into these questions: whether everyone who has beaten his father is not to be punished. "In the law," he says, "nothing is excepted." But many things, though not excepted, are understood; and the letter of the law is narrow, its interpretation broad; some things indeed are so plain that they need no proviso. For what point is there in excepting by law, that it be no harm to a man who in madness struck his father, when he needs not punishment but a cure? What need is there to provide by law that an infant not be punished if he strikes his father? What need that the law provide against punishment if someone roused with violence a father lulled to sleep and collapsed under a sudden heaviness of the body, since that was not an injury but a healing? I am not yet speaking of the particular case, but of the general. If everyone who has struck his father in the way of duty can be acquitted, on this man's behalf I will plead the more spiritedly, that he is worthy of punishment unless he be worthy of a reward.

He is not one who knows not how to ask; he even teaches it. Which of your feelings I ought to wish for, I do not know: if you are nearer to mercy, I will show you the crimes of the defendant; if to severity, the defendant himself. This man we feed at public cost. The talion cannot be exacted from you: you do not have as many limbs as you owe. The she-wolf, forgetting her ferocity at the exposed infants, calm, is said to have offered them her teats as though to her own young. Thus the she-wolf came to the infants; let us await the man. I congratulate you, Rome, that a man did not fall upon your founders.

On the other side many things were most beautifully said; yet I am not sure our men will yield to the Greeks. In this controversia DAMAS said . . . This epigram has something corrupt about it. Latro said: how greatly did I then complain of my fortune, that I had not lost my eyes too! SILO POMPEIUS said: son, either tear out my eyes or lend me your hands. All said something pretty at that point where the adulterers were caught and dismissed. Latro said: I only roused my adulterers. ARELLIUS FUSCUS rather frigidly said the opposite epigram: I did not even rouse the adulterers by my coming in. VIBIUS RUFUS said: the adulterers did not rise for the husband. POMPEIUS said: young man, come, rouse the adulterers at last; since you came, they lie the more at ease. Latro said: you are mistaken who think I have no hands. I called my son: when he entered, he was greeted by the adulterer.

Latro spared the brother; he pressed the boy, and said he was not the son of the brother, and that not even the brother had wished to confess this; that those words were imposed upon a sick man. FABIANUS, of all these, followed the best colour, by which Messala said the young man's cause could be made not only good but even honourable: he charged the father with having disinherited the brother — not by a figure but directly. "He had done no wrong," he said; "he loves a harlot; it is wont to happen: he is young, wait, he will mend, he will take a wife." Why then did you not bring an action for madness at that time? "I was waiting," he said, "for your repentance; he will take him back soon." This he began to object in passing — that he had not taken him in, when he saw him living in a brothel. "You disinherited him," he said, "to mend him, not to increase his vices. You see, no vice of his:

On many a man composition has imposed by the pretty sound of a sententia; and so I remember LATRO PORCIUS, to reproach this carelessness of the schoolmen in listening — chiefly because TRIARIUS, by composition of prettily falling words, delighted many schoolmen and deceived them all — in a certain controversia, when his words flowed as with a great force and roused, thus rounded off a passage: "Among tombs are monuments" ("inter sepulcra monumenta sunt"); and when the schoolmen praised it with the loudest applause, he inveighed against them as he ought, and brought it about that thereafter they praised even what was well said the more slowly, while they feared a trap. GLYCON said: "Set me beside you, mother, take hold of your child: poor wretch, you do not even see whom you grasp. 'If you do not feed me,' he says, 'wait, that you may bury me.'" HYBREAS in this controversia said: "Child, even if you flee me, I will overtake you, begging." This seemed to some men corrupt, but ROMANIUS nevertheless . . .

If not everyone who has struck his father ought to be punished, whether this man ought. This question he divided into more parts: whether the man is safe who did it at the tyrant's bidding. Consider how many things the tyrant exacted. It makes for public innocence that not even this be permitted to tyrants — to make us guilty. The man who did this at the tyrant's compulsion was more wretched than the very man being beaten. She is not unchaste who is summoned by the tyrant; he is not called sacrilegious who carried the gifts of the immortal gods in his own hands to the tyrant, or who set up among the images of the immortal gods the deadly images of the tyrant.

So then, when you were thinking of the public mercy, could you be so cruel? "On the next day," he says, "this one brought in the most: another must be made like him; this one brought in enough: let another also be made wretched after this example. Go now," he says, "and seek maintenance for me. You," he says, "who have no eyes, ask by your eyes; you," he says, "who have lost your hands, ask by your hands; you, by those crippled limbs which you drag; let each go round begging by what he does not have." O wretched they who ask thus, more wretched they who are thus asked! Behold someone: "My son," he says, "if he were alive, would perhaps be like this one. Do I pass over my own?" Another: "Mine," he says, "could have fallen upon the same master. What if he has fallen upon him?" All heap up alms upon all, while each fears to refuse his own.
The other side. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS. "You crippled them," he says. The fathers had harmed them more.
LATRO divided thus: whether the state has been harmed.

FUSCUS said: son, your loyalty! Show that I have not lost my hands, while you are whole. The adulterer makes a controversia of you against me: come, and declare whose son you are. PUBLIUS VINICIUS both spoke prettily and not novelly — he took from everyone what was well said: I burst into the adulterers' bedchamber: why do I lie, wretch that I am? With the bedchamber open the adulterers were waiting. CESTIUS said: I called my son; the adulterer laughed, as though to say: he is mine. VIBIUS RUFUS said: my adulterer went out at his own convenience. HYBREAS expressed this thought excellently . . . DIONYSIUS, the son of that Dionysius who taught Cicero's son — a declaimer more elegant than vehement — expressed this thought both vehemently and elegantly . . . VIBIUS RUFUS said:

it belongs to his age, it belongs to love: take him back before he does something for shame of which he may soon die." At the last he objected to him that he had not carried his sick brother home with him. "He can," he said, "recover, if he sees his own household gods; or if not, at least he will die on his father's soil, his own, untainted. Why," he says, "were you not at your brother's?" I too complain of it. He, when he sent for you, thought he was sending for two. Would that I had been with you, father; you would have come back from there with a son — but your own." Of the adoption he complained last, and with this figure: you have taken from me the brother with whom I was born, with whom I was reared — to give me whom? This boy. I am indignant that this insult is offered to my brother — that this child should be called his father. But, to jest a little, FABIUS MAXIMUS was a most noble man, who first brought into the Roman forum this new-fangled disease from which it now suffers; of whom SEVERUS CASSIUS, before he was prosecuted by him, had said: you are as-if eloquent, as-if handsome, as-if rich; one thing only you are not "as-if" — a wastrel.

Whether the man is safe who did it at his father's bidding. "He did not beat him, but obeyed." And he said this in the narration: "My brother stood with defiant face; I understood he could not be compelled by the tyrant." Whether the man is safe who did it for the fatherland; and whether this man did it for the fatherland — that is: whether already at that time he had a design of tyrannicide, and struck with this mind, that he might make himself a way to the tyrant's friendship. MONTANUS made that last question too: whether, even if some fault was committed, it was redeemed by so great a service.

"First," he says, "the crime ought to be established, then this man sought out as the defendant. Whether the state has been harmed is not usually proved by arguments; the damages of the state are at once manifest, if the walls are thrown down, if the fleet is burned, if the army lost, if the revenues diminished: this damage which you object — who saw it? Tell me: when did he harm the state? When he crippled one exposed child? And yet even he who kills one is not held liable for harming the state, but for murder; even he who kills two, even he who kills more: tell me what number makes the state seem harmed. Two are crippled — the state is not yet harmed.

"They could have become leaders," he says. They could also have been temple-robbers and murderers; they could also have perished. "But he does a cruel thing, who out of his own resources ruined infants and forced the unhappy to beg." So does the trainer who forces young men to the sword, and he is not condemned for harming the state; and the pander who forces unwilling women to suffer outrage does not harm the state. I do not desire that the defendant be praised, but acquitted; let this harm him when he seeks office: a man can be both not honorable and an innocent defendant.

how at their leisure, how at their ease the adulterers passed before my eyes, before my son's hands! Latro, when he had described the adulterers going out, added: young man, follow your parents. NICETES that most beautiful epigram, in which I am not sure he did not surpass our men . . . But that saying of ALBUCIUS surely outdoes the Greeks: when he had described himself fighting in the battle-line, he said: wretched me, what hands the adulterer escaped! And this of Albucius's: "I could not," he said, "kill my mother." That you may be the more excusable, add "and my father." Albucius narrated as though the adultery were done with the son's knowledge; he made him suspect as though privy to it for his mother. PUBLIUS ASPRENAS said: the husband went out last, and gave place to his own adulterers. The same man said: you cannot kill your mother? At least you will kill the adulterer. Or is he too a father? NICETES had said . . . MURREDIUS, while wishing to imitate this epigram, said something most foolish: I left my fighting hands in the battle-line.

When MAXIMUS declaimed this controversia, he spoke a tricolon of the kind that infects the basilica. He was speaking on the father's side: we have all brought you something in our weakness, one the burden of another: a father is accused in his last years, a grandson in his first, one son is disinherited. These things I relate now and again because examples of things to be avoided ought to be set down as much as of things to be followed. In this controversia Latro said something contrary not to the controversia, but to himself. He was declaiming it in the hearing of Caesar Augustus and of Marcus Agrippa, whose sons — his own grandsons, Lucius and Gaius — Caesar seemed in those days about to adopt. Marcus Agrippa was among those who were not born noble but made so.

GALLIO made that question first: whether the avenging of a beaten father belongs to none but the father. "You will not," he says, "avenge me against my will. If I had been beaten by any stranger and were unwilling to bring an action for injury, no one would bring it in my name. And yet there is no difference: the punishment of the man who struck is greater, the right of the man struck is the same." Against this it is said that an action is given to all; for the injury is not private but public; and so the condemned man does not get off with a money-penalty or the penalty for injury, but loses his hands; that this example pertains to all fathers, to all sons, to the state itself: such are the men who become tyrants, and certainly such are the tyrants' friends.

Then: whether, if the state has been harmed, it has been harmed by this man. "Not by me," he says, "but by the parents who cast them out: this man, cruel though he be, however much he took from them, gave back life." On the other side he says: "They expose them one by one, you cripple all; they take away hope, you the very instruments of living." Then: whether he is liable for harming the state, if he did what he is allowed to do. "No matter can be condemned by the law," he says, "which is permitted by the law. If I demolish my own house, do you say that I harm the state?" And you could have described how inhuman it is for those walls of one's ancestors, carried down even into our own memory, to be cast down in the fashion of an enemy.

When Latro was speaking the young man's part and treating the commonplace on adoption, he said: now this man, from the lowest, is grafted by adoption into nobility; and other things to this effect. Maecenas signalled to Latro that Caesar was in haste; let him now end his declamation. Some thought this was malice on Maecenas's part; for he brought it about not that Caesar should not hear what had been said, but that he should mark it. Yet so great was the freedom under the deified Augustus, that there were men not lacking who reproached Marcus Agrippa — then all-powerful — with his low birth. He had been Vipsanius Agrippa, but had dropped the name Vipsanius as though it were a proof of his father's lowliness, and was called Marcus Agrippa. When he was defending a defendant, there was an accuser who said: "Agrippa — Marcus and what is between" — he wished Vipsanius to be understood — "come together: Agrippa, you shall have a thrashing; answer, if you please, Marcus." At any rate the deified Augustus seems to me worthy of admiration, under whom so much was permitted; but I cannot pity these men who think it worth more to lose their head than their jest. Latro deserved pity, who could not even excuse his slip. And nothing is crueller than to give offence in such a way that you will give more offence if you make amends.

And he made these last questions: whether, if he did it with a dutiful mind, he is not liable; whether he did it with a dutiful mind. And to that question of Latro's — "whether the man is safe who did it at his father's wish" — "now," he says, "he invents this for his son's defence, but at the time he did not wish it." And he added: "Do not say that the father wished the same as the tyrant. Do you ask which one he obeyed? The tyrant loved him as though he had obeyed him. 'The father,' he says, 'wished it.' So did you seem worthy of parricide not only to the tyrant, but to your father too?" When he had described him impious toward his brother, impious toward his father, he added:

If in my own fields I wished to cut down the orchards . . . Then: whether this was not allowed him to do. "It was allowed," he says; "the exposed are of no account; they are slaves; . . . it seemed good to their rearer." Finally, if it is not allowed, they have the law: each can sue by the talion, can sue for wrongs: but for harming the state no suit can be brought in the name of those who are outside the state. There can be no suit on behalf of all, on whose behalf, taken singly, there can be none.

"the tyrant too, at the time when you ought to have loved him, you killed." MONTANUS declaimed the accuser's part, and used this colour: that the father had been most indulgent to his children; that his excessive tenderness was known to the tyrant; and so that the tyrant, who sought grief for the chaste from unchastity, for the defiant from slavery, sought torment for a most loving father from his sons' impiety; and he brought in the son who was bidden first to strike his father speaking boldly: "What," he said, "if I do not strike? What will you do? Will you torture me? Kill me? What you command is more than what you threaten." There was a contest in one man, whether nature or the tyrant could do more. "'Strike,' he says: 'I do not strike'; 'scourge': 'I do not strike.'" This with the brother listening. And he said this: "When the tyrant promised friendship, he dreaded the reward of the tyrant's command more than the command." And when he had described the scars of the beaten father and his still disfigured face, he said: "You would think he had been struck by both sons."

I know that some think there is a question: whether the state can be harmed by a private man; SPARSUS, certainly, I remember declaiming so. But if anyone admits this, he will admit that one too: whether it can be harmed by a woman, by an old man, by a poor man — none of which is ever made a question, yet is wont to be said; just as, when that question is handled, whether the state has been harmed, so often the defendant, among the arguments that the state was not harmed, says: "It could not even be harmed by a private man, by a poor man, by a sick man, by an absent one." GALLIO made that question too: whether the state can be harmed in the exposed. "The state cannot be harmed," he says, "except in some part of itself; these are no part of the state; you will not find them in the census, not in wills." But this too runs into that one: whether the state has been harmed; for it is said: "It could not even be harmed in those whom it did not have."

MONTANUS, however, used to say that nothing could be better said than this: on this side the tyrant orders, on that the law forbids: you shall die unless you strike; die rather than strike. CESTIUS said: "The tyrant orders you to beat your father: that is nothing new. You refused to do it: do you think I will praise you? I, for my part, do not praise you; that glory is another's; you should have imitated your brother." ARGENTARIUS said: "You beat your father, when you knew both the law and your brother." MONTANUS said: "Parricide, you violated your father's body, your brother's kindness."

For him who crippled the exposed very few indeed spoke. GALLIO spoke, and used this colour: that a needy man, who could not feed even himself, much less others, had taken up those who, already abandoned and without hope, scarcely drew breath, to whom no wrong was done if something was taken away, but a kindness given if life was preserved. "Let them stir up ill-will because one lacks eyes, another hands; let them say these men live so wretchedly through him — provided they confess that they live through him." GALLIO attempted this too among the arguments: "So far," he says, "was this thing from harming the state, that it can even be seen to have profited it:

On the other side all declaimed with this colour, as though he had done it at his father's bidding. TRIARIUS said: "I ran upon my son's hands." BASSUS JULIUS said: "I beat myself with my son's hands." Haterius said: "I give thanks to the tyrant that he ordered my other son to be guarded, so that he could not die." CESTIUS said in the narration: "The tyrant orders him to strike, the instruments of torture are set out; what will he do? 'Let him die,' you say. You say this: rather than strike his father, let him kill him." FUSCUS ARELLIUS said: "I wish to embrace those hands, which deserved well of me even before the tyrannicide." GALLIO said: "Let him see how much the state thinks itself to owe you; I judge that I owe you more than it does: it is harder, what you did at my bidding." MONTANUS VOTIENUS said in the narration: "If you persist, my son, I will follow your brother: see whether you would rather beat your father or kill him."

fewer will there be who expose their sons." CLODIUS TURRINUS used this colour: that many fathers were wont to expose useless offspring. "There are born," he says, "some at once maimed in some part of the body, weak and fit for no hope, whom their parents cast away rather than expose; some too throw away house-slaves born under an unlucky omen or weak in body. Of these this man took up some, and with his own hand removed those parts which could make each the more pitiable: they beg a coin, and live by one man's mercy, are fed by all's. But it is a foul thing to keep beggars, to be fed by beggars, to dwell among cripples. Come, are you not ashamed to produce from this fellowship a defendant by whom you say the state was harmed?" And so he descended to the arguments, so as to say:

This controversia I remember was well declaimed by JULIUS SABINUS too. "Describe," he said, "describe the tyrant killed and yourself led down from the citadel with great glory. O you parricide, unless even after the tyrannicide you understand how much more honourably your brother perished than you killed." That I did not approve — that in a serious matter he attempted many witty things. He was, however, a most urbane man, as I have often told you, so that whatever he lacked in eloquence he made up in wit.

"How could this man harm it?" SILO POMPEIUS used that colour: that this man was merciful, that he wished to give life but could not feed them; and so was driven to this — that each should pay some part of his body for the whole. LABIENUS declaimed the part of him who crippled the exposed as eloquently as no one declaimed the other, though all the most eloquent men declaimed it as it were to test their own powers. That passage he spoke most vehemently: "It is strange that men have leisure for this thought, to care what a beggar does among beggars. Princely men," he says, "exercise their wealth against nature: they keep herds of the castrated; their catamites, that they may be fit for a longer endurance of unchastity, they mutilate, and because they are ashamed that the men are men, they bring it about that they be as few as possible.

I remember that, when Syriacus Vallius, an eloquent man, was accusing, and seemed likely to incur the charge of false accusation, Sabinus moved about gloomily among the ring of the judges and kept meeting Syriacus as he went and asking what hope he had; then, after the trial, when Syriacus thanked him for having taken so great care of him: "But, by Hercules," he said, "I was afraid we should have one rhetor too many." And when a witness produced was asked whether he had received . . . sesterces from the father, he said he had received the sesterces; whether he had them, he denied it; then, asked whether he was liable to a charge of false accusation, he said: "You yourselves know my carelessness: whether I have it I do not know; that I received it I know." And against Domitius, a most noble man, when in his consulship he had built baths overlooking the Sacred Way, and had then begun to go round the rhetors and declaim: "I," he said, "knew you would do this, and to your mother, when she complained of your idleness, I had said: 'First swimming, second letters.'"

These no one succours — these dainty and handsome cripples. It comes into your mind to take care who carries off from the wilderness infants destined to perish unless they are carried off; you do not care that those rich men cultivate their solitudes with workhouses of the freeborn; you do not care that they go round the simplicity of wretched youths and thrust each most handsome and most fit into the camp of the gladiator-school. It comes into your mind to pity these because they lack limbs; why not those because they have them?" And by this manner inveighing against the vices of the age, by an excellent figure he defended a defiled and infamous defendant by the impunity of greater crimes. This controversia is famous among the Greeks; many things were beautifully said by them, from which our men did not keep their hands; many things corruptly, to which they themselves too did not yield.

Two of his witty sayings I cannot pass over. He had followed the proconsul Occius Flamma into the province of Crete. The Greeks began to demand in the theatre that Sabinus hold the highest magistracy. Now it is the custom for a magistrate of the Cretans to let his beard and hair grow. Sabinus rose and made silence with his hand, then said: "This magistracy I have held twice at Rome." He had twice pleaded a case. The Greeks did not understand, but, praying well for Caesar, asked that Sabinus hold the office a third time too.

GLYCON said: "And do you ask maintenance for these, whom it is impious not to maintain?" P. ASPRENAS said this thought in the same way, using one word more apt: "These someone asks maintenance for, to whom he is cruel who refuses it." Akin to this thought is that one said by QUINTILIANUS: "I know not whether to call you more wretched because you receive maintenance, or because you give it; for you receive it because you are crippled, you give it to him through whom you are crippled." ADAEUS the rhetorician: "Weeping mothers contributed: 'If he is mine,' saying, 'for mine; if another's, that another may give for mine.'"

Then afterwards the whole cohort of his companions offended them: they were beset in the temple by the whole multitude, which demanded that Sabinus set out for Rome with Turdus. Turdus was among the most infamous and hated of men. When Turdus promised that he would go, that he might thus be able to get out, Sabinus, when silence was made, said: "I will not go to Caesar with a relish." Afterwards this was cast in Sabinus's teeth when he pleaded his case. Many things I remember he said eloquently, when he was brought from prison into the senate to ask that he might receive a daily ration. Then, complaining of hunger, he said: "I ask nothing burdensome of you, but that you should wish me either to die or to live." And he said this: "Do not, I beg, hear proudly a man in calamity: often the man who could have shown pity asks for pity."

This thought certain Latins said, but so that I think they did not openly borrow this sententia, but imitated it. BLANDUS said: "Some woman, asked, holds out a coin to a beggar. Surely if she gave birth, she exposed. O how wretched is the thought of her who holds it out! 'This one, perhaps, is mine.'" OSCUS said: "Some woman, because she has already cast away her own, gives a coin to more than her own." ARELLIUS FUSCUS said: "A mother, asked, feeds her son; wretched if she knows it is her own, wretched if she does not." ARTEMON said: "The children of others, sound, sail, till the fields; but ours, maimed, feed — does the whole one feed them?"

And when he had said that the wealthy followers of Sejanus were in prison: "I, a man as yet uncondemned, beg bread of parricides, that I may live." When he had moved men both by a tearful and an eloquent speech, he nevertheless returned to his jests: he asked to be transferred to the quarries (lautumiae); "there is no reason," he said, "why the very name 'lautumiae' should deceive any of you; for that is a thing not at all elegant (lauta)." This I have reported, that you might both know the man in some part and learn how hard it is to escape one's own nature. How could it be obtained of him not to jest in declamations, when he jests amid his own miseries and perils, in which that he ought not to have jested who does not know, that he could who would believe?

This sententia Latro said more strongly and more manfully, who cannot be suspected of theft; for he both despised the Greeks and was ignorant of them. When he had described the feeble limbs of all, and some bent, some crawling, he added: "By the good gods! Is anyone fed whole by these?" DAMAS the elder said: "Once the danger to the exposed was to be cast away, now to be reared." This thought CESTIUS rendered: "You have brought it about," he says, "that there was greater peril in being reared than in being exposed." FUSCUS ARELLIUS said it otherwise: "Those things were still feared in the infancy of wretched lot: wild beasts and serpents, and the cold hostile to tender limbs, and want; among the perils of the exposed we did not count the rearer."

MURREDIUS did not fall below himself in this controversia; for he introduced a most foolish colour: "He too," he said, "wished to follow his brother's example: while I hold him back, while I struggle, he seemed to have struck his father." Of those I heard declaim, I know that MENTO used the father not as advocate but as supporting witness; he brought in the tyrannicide himself speaking, and used this colour: not that he had been bidden by his father — for he said it seemed incredible to all that a father should have bidden himself to be beaten before the tyrant — but that he had entered upon a design of tyrannicide, so that through this he might come to friendship, through friendship to tyrannicide. This sententia of his was praised, when he described himself laying hands on his father: "Nothing in the whole tyrannicide did I do more difficult." And he said this: "The tyrannicide would have been accomplished then and there, had not my brother deserted me." And he said this: "You I then looked to — the temples, the laws, the state; for if I had looked to myself alone, I should easily have escaped the tyranny by that road by which my brother escaped."

GLYCON said a corrupt sententia: "Let someone knock at the door of the rich, that he may bring." And that one: "Come, weep you, and you lament. O harmonies of evils!" But our men too have raved well. MURREDIUS said: "A long line of the wretched is brought forward; the greater part drags itself without itself." And LICINIUS NEPOS: "That you might be solvent for punishments, how often must you be born again?"

That thing SPARSUS said, which Montanus called not only corrupt but contrary: "You alone have more limbs than you have left to so many men." For thus this man can seem to have harmed the state, if many are crippled; but it appears there are not many, if he has more limbs than he has left to the crippled. And that too Montanus said was corruptly said by him: "There came forth more beggars than limbs." I report the Greek sententiae for this — that you may judge, first, how easy is the passage from Greek eloquence into Latin, and how everything that can be well said is common to all nations; then, that you may compare talents with talents, and consider that the Latin tongue has no less faculty, less license.

The sententia of Labienus I have set apart, because men had spoken about it: but it descends to the daily reckoning of the beggars' takings: "You have brought in less today; give me the lash; I am glad I have not maimed them all. Why do you weep? Why do you beg? You would have brought back more had you begged so." He said this sententia too: "Give the wretched that one joy which they can take: let one of them see this man condemned, let one hear it." ARTEMON . . . GLYCON said: "For the wretched joy is left."

P. VINICIUS, the supreme admirer of Ovid, said that this thought was most eloquently set down in Naso Ovidius — which he said should be kept in memory for inventing similar sententiae. When Achilles was slain, this epiphonema is set down:
"What joy old Priam could have after Hector, this was."

CASSIUS SEVERUS had said: "Show us your captives." JULIUS BASSUS had said: "Show your hirelings." LABIENUS seemed to have said more fitly: "Show us your fosterlings." P. Asprenas said, when he had brought in one holding out a coin to a beggar: "O unhappy father!" — and he who says this is himself perhaps a father.

THE LAW: A ravished woman may choose either the death of her ravisher, or marriage to him without dowry. THE THEME: A man on one night ravished two women. One demands his death, the other marriage. — He was already preparing himself for a third, had not the night failed. He is accused of outrage, and defends an outrage; with one of the ravished women he goes to law, and the other he summons as advocate. Avenge it, fathers; avenge it, brothers; avenge it, husbands; let the severity of public discipline rise up, the stronger: now they are ravished in pairs. OF MENTO: On the next day there was weeping in this woman's house, the lamentation of a mother bewailing her hopes, when meanwhile from another house arose another outcry, another uproar. The people gathered, as if struck by some public terror; they could scarcely believe there were only two ravishers, when meanwhile the public enemy of chastity was brought forth, whom one night, with the wrong of one maiden, had not wearied. OF CESTIUS PIUS: One woman he ravished by wrong, the other he ravishes by patronage. As far as I suspect, you were not even ravished. Do you ask the proof? You are not angry. How comes this about? He wronged two, and only one complains. "I am compassionate," she says. Rejoice; you have one to avenge you. See what a husband you are to have: he is not content with one. ARGENTARIUS expressed the same thought with this addition: he is not content with one — no, not with one night.

THE THEME: A tyrant ordered a wife to be tortured to make her reveal her husband's plans against him. She kept silent. Afterwards her husband killed the tyrant. He divorced his wife, who had not borne children within five years, and is accused of ingratitude. OF PORCIUS LATRO: If she had been tortured along with her children, she would have revealed it. "Go up," she said, "kill the tyrant; if you do not kill him, I will reveal it." Suddenly a guard, laying hands on her, said: why do you delay? The instruments of torture are already set out. It is well, said the woman, I am not summoned to outrage. Daily the wife pressed her husband, demanded the tyrant's death: "it is time; go up; if for nothing else, that you may have children: I will not bear except to a tyrant-slayer. Do you wonder that I could not bear at the time when a tyrant could torture a matron? Go up, kill the tyrant; I would follow you as companion, had not the tyrant dismissed me useless. Go up: I have already done my own tyrant-slaying." That marriage was divorced by the tyrant-slaying which the tyrant did not divorce.

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. When I heard the outcry, if there is any faith in me, I thought adulterers had been caught by my father. Who would endure you coming into the forum as a voluntary witness, even if you came to speak for your son? Most wretched boy, although I myself am in peril, yet for you I fear more: too closely you tread in your brother's footsteps; and so now you do not agree with your mother. As long as my mother lived, my father was content with me as steward. Parricide is not easily committed. Do you wish to know how much nature avails? Even an infant speaks for his brother. OF TRIARIUS. With his father living, an adulteress; as he died, an accomplice; dead, a witness. One man is content with a single witness: I will give the boy. Another is not content with a single witness: I will give the people. She charges her stepson with parricide, her son with lying. The steward enters where he was wont.

OF JUNIUS GALLIO. A violent and ungovernable old man, I snatched a free man from my own bosom. What is hard for you to keep, give to his grandfather. How often, most wretched boy, will you hear from your stepmother: "Who are you, runaway? Have you been brought back?" I had a daughter — although this man has but one son — a fruitful one. How tenderly she divided her offspring! A son was born; she said: "This son is mine"; another was born; she said: "This is his father's"; a third was born; she said: "This is his grandfather's." When this man sought his son, there were those who advised and said: "Be silent; he deserved to be shut out." OF CESTIUS PIUS. What cause for seizing him had I, ungovernable old man? Had I killed his brothers? Forgive me if I tell only my daughter's dying charges: her alone of my own did I see die. I had a daughter: of all my own I must say "I had." The boy wandered in mournful and dingy bordered robe; all pitied him, and some I even heard saying: "What?

OF GAVIUS SILO. The unhappy old man saw the ruins of his prostrate, dismembered country; torn from his wife, torn from his children, he stood over the ashes of burnt Olynthus; already he is sad enough for fashioning a Prometheus. By Jupiter! — for whom better should I call upon against Parrhasius than him whom he imitated? — do I except only the Olynthian from your painting? No one, to paint a shipwrecked man, has drowned a man.

He is beaten: "It is too little"; he is burned: "even now too little"; he is torn: "this," he says, "is enough for an angry Philip, but not yet for an angry Jove." OF JULIUS BASSUS. A boy is brought forward . . . "it is superfluous," he says; "he cannot yet groan as much as suffices for a Prometheus." The Olynthian's last entreaty is: "Athenian, give me back to Philip." This is no gift, it is sacrilege. "He was my slave," he says. You would think Philip were speaking. They flee to the temple of Minerva as to the camp of the Macedonians. OF CLODIUS TURRINUS. "He is too little sad," he says.

OF POMPEIUS SILO: But how well he played the mime — how she bewailed herself as ravished, with what an outcry! How nearly we yielded her the choice! OF TRIARIUS: You would have perished, ravisher, had you not deserved to perish twice. OF JUNIUS GALLIO: Let the punishment be exacted of him, let it be set up in the public view, let him be flogged long, let him perish a whole day who sinned a whole night. Suddenly the disdainful ravisher steps up and says: "Now I do not even want the marriage." Foolish woman, you are deceived; shall I tell you what he said to you? For he said the same to her too: "While I was seeking you, I fell upon that one." OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: Let rivers flow backward, let the sun lead the sphere on a contrary course, let the sacrilegious man flee to the altars: the ravished woman avenges the ravisher.

OF CESTIUS PIUS: Suddenly the tyrant fell upon an unhappy wedding. Matrons were dragged off, maidens ravished; nothing was safe; none seemed then more fortunate than those who had no children. And so some women crushed the children they had conceived, some delayed their own fertility. As to this woman, do you give thanks to Fortune, that at that time she bore nothing?
