The tyrant suspected this man of some thought of tyrant-slaying — whether something slipped from him, or his face did not well veil his great designs. At any rate you cannot complain of your wife's chattering, since you know how she keeps silent. He sent his guards: "drag off," he said, "his wife, and," he added, "any children she has."

Say, boy, who killed your father; say boldly; you name the same man whom the people name. Night suits crime: surely the time for adulterers. Though he wished it, yet he would not have me have a stepmother. What was the light to me? When about to commit so great a crime, night must be drawn over it. "What," she says, "did I do wrong before?" It is not alike: remember that the inquiry is about a murderer; a murder can be an apprentice-piece, parricide cannot. You brought a light that you might mark out there the one you ought only to wound lightly. We see the sword driven into the breast: so would I have wounded my stepmother. Brother, I ask whether you saw the steward on the last night; I ask nothing of the earlier ones.

Has that boy no mother? No father? No grandfather?" OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. You owe three of my daughter's sons; one is mine: let him be nursed with me. What do you fear? That you will not be admitted when you come? It has pleased me to expound thus far; now fortune, or the stepmother, must be told. When the boy saw me, he clung to my embraces; I, wretched, kept kissing him, kept asking about his brothers; while I ask, while I weep, I had reached home. I beg that this may not make my case the worse — that the one I seized was an only son.

Is any Olynthian too little sad, except the one who has drawn an Athenian master by lot? Do you wish, Parrhasius, to see a sad man? I will show you greater torments: lead him to prostrate Olynthus, lead him there where he lost his children, where he lost his home; you surely know how sad a man you bought. We opened our city to the Olynthians — did we close our temples? Surely no Olynthian would have been tortured, if all the Macedonians had bought them. "Let him be tortured": this was not done even under Philip. "Let him die": this not even under Jove.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF POMPEIUS SILO: On the next day, when his night's mistake had been told him, while he thought he had fallen upon one woman, he stretched out suppliant hands to this first one, entreated her first, and won her over: for this reason, I think, she is the more angry with the ravisher. Of the two girls, the one wishes the ravisher to die, the other to be saved: the one judge condemns the defendant, the other acquits him; when the votes are equal, let the milder prevail. I will say what I think: she would be the more angry if he had ravished one only; she would say, "So then, was I alone thought worthy to be wronged by him?" OF ARGENTARIUS: Cite now Verginia, cite Lucretia: yet the Sabine women are more. Of the tribunes, the more powerful is the one who interposes his veto. That power is not hateful which conquers by mercy. Why do you delay, girl? Beg for your husband. This epigram was laughed at by Cestius as improper.

There come into the house the cruellest executioners, in whose faces were the tortures: the wretched woman is tossed about among the hands of the guards, and through the whole journey is not led but dragged. Will anyone wonder that she did not bear — even were she not tortured — when this man was thinking of tyrant-slaying? Boldly now we declare the plan; for now, I think, it is allowed. She married this man for children, but the tyrant quickly fell upon the unhappy wedding; this was a public divorce. The woman is dragged off to the citadel, harried among the hands of the guards and torn. Will anyone wonder, even were she not tortured, that she did not bear? Set on the rack, she looked back more often to her absent husband than to the present tyrant. How many mothers I heard at that time: what did I want, who have borne?

OF VIBIUS GALLUS. Shall I be silent about the adultery which even the people prosecutes? Shall I be silent about the parricide which even the boy prosecutes? I call you to witness, judges, I left my father safe. O great perversity of our age, turned to its opposite! A man has been found who could kill his father and could not kill his stepmother. Even if a man cannot kill his father, he can kill his stepmother. OF SEPULLIUS BASSUS. While I dig through the wall, someone will hear. Whose sleep do you wish to be the lightest — the boy's, the old man's, or the man of middle age's? The boy's? The brother will hear. The old man's? The father. The middle-aged man's? The stepmother. I would ask in what mean house he was born, if he had had any; but as it is, he escapes our inquiry by his obscurity. I do not wonder if you do not know how hard it is to kill a father, since you hold your own father uncertain.

OF VOTIENUS MONTANUS. You send out a herald; add to him all the marks: "This boy lost his mother, lost his brothers, has a stepmother"; I assure you, no one will give information who has any goodwill. You err, and grievously err: the sons you lost you do not seek; you seek the one you did not lose. Which, after all, is the juster complaint? The father asks the grandfather for one; the grandfather asks the father for two. OF VIBIUS RUFUS. That ravisher and ungovernable man — while my grandsons were dying I stood at his door: I have more to fear as a grandfather than as a defendant.

OF ARGENTARIUS. With this hospitality was the Olynthian received at Athens? And what besides? Did Parrhasius torture only the Olynthian, and not torture our eyes too? There he sets up the picture where perhaps we set up the tablet of the treaty. This is to make a Prometheus, not to paint one. He said to the torturers: "Strain him thus, beat him thus, preserve thus that very look which he now wears, lest you yourselves be the model."

THE DIVISION. In this controversia, on the first question no one agreed with another. Latro made this the first question: that a ravisher who has been ordered to die by the woman he ravished cannot be saved . . . "If," he said, "he must go as an envoy, he will perish; if he must do military service, he will perish; if he must lead by law, likewise he will perish; if he must marry the ravished woman, he will equally perish. If he had ravished you first, and you had chosen marriage, and then, after an interval, before you married, he had violated this other woman, would you deny that he ought to die at the ravished woman's bidding? And yet there is no difference, except that the ravisher is the more deserving of death, between whose two ravishments not even one night intervenes. If you had married the ravished man, and then, after the third day, he had ravished another, would you deny that he ought to die? And yet what difference is there, except that you would then defend a husband more honourably than now you defend a ravisher?"

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS: The apparatus of cruelty against the unhappy woman are unfolded, and those instruments, which break even men's spirits by the very sight, are set forth to wring out the secret of a woman's heart; the tyrant presses first with threats rather than tortures, and tortures by threatening: she is silent. She sees the tyrant's intent face, she sees his menacing eyes: she is silent. She could not have done you more service, had she borne children to you. Her limbs are cut with scourges, her body is torn apart with blows, and blood is wrung from her very vitals: she is silent. Whether she would have given you children I do not know; she gave you a tyrant-slaying. So then, woman, will you not bear? You are dainty, you fear the pangs of childbirth. The husband raged with indignation at the captured state, made braver both by his own resolve and by his wife's help: how shall I kill the tyrant? Which part is most exposed to one approaching? Where do the guards fail? Where does the nature of the place, with a weaker defence, not bar valour? Thus did husband and wife spend their nights. Do you wonder that five years passed, with the wife tortured and the husband busy? The tyrant still raged; wives were tortured before their husbands' eyes; mothers repented of their fertility.

OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. I ask you, woman, whether you think your son is to be believed? Let me be allowed to rear the boy: he will agree neither with his mother nor with his guardian. Three are in the bedchamber: the father you kill, the boy you scorn, the adulteress you know. The slaves and freedmen offered themselves one by one to the boy, and I stood before them all: the assassin lurked behind the adulteress. What did I do wrong before? Whose wife did I corrupt? But if I had done so, I could kill a man, my father I could not. I have good witnesses; I fear this one, in another's power. Look upon my father's body: how heavy the blow, how deep the sword was driven! So would I have struck the stepmother. OF CESTIUS PIUS. That you are an adulterer I will give not one witness, I will give an uncorrupted one, I will give many, I will give even boys. Did I strike my father as heavily as I ought to have struck the stepmother — but the stepmother not even as I struck my father?

OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. One perishes, another perishes: so often you accuse fortune, never the stepmother. An outrage! A boy is sought, for punishment, on the father's information. I came to my sick grandson; I was not admitted: this was the true violence. OF ARGENTARIUS. "What accomplices had the boy?" I do not know; I was not at home. Having lost my daughter, I wished to adopt one of my grandsons, but I said: "What need is there? Whenever I wish to see them, I will come home; whenever I wish, I will take one home; let us act as kinsmen: you have three sons, let us divide them"; and see how not unreasonable is the division I want:

OF CESTIUS PIUS. "I bought him," he says. Nay, if you are an Athenian, you ransomed him. If you do not know it, Parrhasius, in that temple we made vows on the Olynthians' behalf: are they thus to be paid? That cruel butcher of Greece did nothing more, even so, than sell him. A noble old man is brought forward, worn out by the long wasting of his miseries, his eyes drawn inward, as sad as if he had already been tortured. When he saw the chains brought to him: "They are superfluous," he said; "had I come to another master, I should flee to Athens." This I do not permit you with any Olynthian, unless you have bought a Lasthenes.

He made a second: whether the ravished woman who chooses marriage can grant the ravisher nothing more than that he not perish by her own law, while she has no right against another's law. You chose marriage: he will not be killed as your ravisher. But the same man, on the very night on which he ravished you, if he deserted his post, will be beaten with the cudgel; if he committed sacrilege, will be killed. Though you say, "What then? Shall I not marry?" — you grant the ravisher this, that you yourself do not kill him; you cannot grant that no one kills him. As a sacrilegious man, though saved by you, would perish, so the other girl's ravisher, though saved by you, will perish. If he had ravished you, and then, caught in adultery, were kept under guard to die more lingeringly, and you meanwhile, brought forth, had chosen marriage — for the choice is given even for an absent man — would you forbid him to be killed by the husband? What difference does it make by what law he perishes, except that you would more modestly interfere with another's law than with your own?

OF ROMANIUS HISPO: For what did you long for children? That there might be those to whom you could leave your patrimony? Ingrate — so, while she is safe, have you no heir? He omitted no kind of torture; all her limbs were mangled, wrenched in every direction, her body cut with scourges, burned with fire, racked with tortures. You will pardon, I think, a poor little woman if I say: she is weary. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: He hung back, nor could be driven by any exhortations to tyrant-slaying. In short, when you had seen his wife, you could pardon a man who was afraid. The tortures were constantly varied; the quenched fires were rekindled; the torturer was called for, under whom husbands had betrayed their wives. Suppose I make a bargain with you: if I keep silent, will you grant me five years? Why do you boast, as though it were not easier to kill a tyrant than to endure this? He is bound by a double benefit from his wife: both that he was not killed, and that he killed. He loathes as barren the woman he made so. OF JUNIUS GALLIO.

OF JULIUS BASSUS. For you the light was necessary, that you might not kill the woman for whose sake you were killing; for me it was superfluous, lest by the instrument of parricide I betray the parricide. If the nature of things allowed it, I should have had to forget my father while I killed him. With greater license we do the things we do not see, and, though the atrocity of the deed is no less, the dread is less. If I killed my father, my whole couch must be cleared for me; I have no one to obey, since I am a parricide. I cannot boast of avenging my father; my brother seized that office before me. OF BLANDUS. How hard for a son to wound his father, and how easy for a stepson to kill his stepmother! OF VARIUS GEMINUS. "You killed," she says, "your father."

of three I ask for one. Would that he sought all those he lost! OF BLANDUS. When I wished to hand over the boy, someone or other cried out: "Boy, now you are lost." I will keep nothing from you; why should I? to the herald too I revealed everything. OF MENTO. I seized my grandson, I have him;

OF TRIARIUS. You have spoiled the two greatest gifts of Prometheus, fire and man. Whomever the crier saw weeping, he knew to be a buyer; all pitied him; and perhaps Philip himself would have ordered him brought back, even had he seen an Athenian for buyer — which I do not doubt to be a fable. But let Parrhasius choose which he will: either too impiously he defamed Jove, or he imitated him. That man kept crying: "You are not yet sad enough, not yet, I say, have you added enough to your former look." Such was Philip at the auction.

He made a third: since what each woman chooses cannot both come to pass, whether that choice is to be preferred by which vengeance reaches both. The one who chooses death says: my choice avenges both you and me; yours does not avenge me; nor does my choice grant me what it grants you — the odium of a slain ravisher. The other answers: your choice does not avenge me. Do you call it my vengeance, that what I wish does not come to pass, and what I do not wish does? It will even be an insult to me, that you should be thought worthy to have a man killed in your honour, and I not worthy to have one saved in mine. In that way my choice avenges you too: surely the law wrote two penalties for the ravisher; one he will suffer; you will not go unavenged, for the ravisher will not go unpunished: he will have a punishment — a dowerless wife. She answers: not in the same way: he will die, but for both; he will be saved, but not for me. There he made a fourth question: if both choices cannot stand, which is the worthier. A last point, not a question but a treatment: that every ravisher would go unpunished, if this path of impunity were shown — that he who had ravished more women would be the safer; that everyone would find some lowly woman to lend herself to the choice.

The tyrant pressed: torture; that part too can bear it; apply fires: in that part the blood is already dried up; cut, scourge, tear out the eyes, see to it now that she does not please her husband — her womb. OF PAPIRIUS FABIANUS: I shall now describe the torments and the wretched endurance of the body amid the tyrannical tortures raging: the quenched fires were revived with blood; sometimes the torturing was broken off only that it might be repeated the oftener. Choice scourges, hot plates, the rack, whatever ancient cruelty had devised, whatever the new age had added — what more shall I say? The tyrant both tortured and, in tortuting, inquired about tyrant-slaying. O happy we! Because she had been drained by no childbearings, she kept silent. Then by her silence she did the tyrant-slaying — at any rate she made the tyrant-slayer. Her limbs torn and mangled, and not yet sufficing, she was not dismissed from the citadel,

I call you to witness, judges, these hands do nothing lightly. Did I not wish to kill you, or had I not the power? And yet you are wounded — wounded lightly. How carefully you have been preserved! Give your testimony, and show that thing, not a wound but an argument. Show the wound: how the assassin feared lest he kill! OF PORCIUS LATRO. Why do I bring a light? I shall commit parricide more bravely if I do not see my father. Can a man kill his father before his stepmother, and not be able to kill his stepmother even after his father? OF TRIARIUS. Who, for a parricide, keeps his hands clean, and begins where it is hard to arrive?

I would give him back, if the father were seeking him. THE DIVISION. MONTANUS VOTIENUS divided into these questions: whether there is violence in the matter. "There is no violence," he says: "what arms, what fight, what wounds has it? I want the escort of this 'tumult' described to me: what crowd is one boy and one old man? You seized," he says, "my son": nay, he took up his own grandson; nay, he could not shut him out when he came. Whether, if the violence is said to have been done for the sake of the man to whom it is said to have been done, the doer is not liable. Injurious violence is condemned; for violence is wont to be also salutary. If, when robbers were besieging someone, I had broken through his villa and with an armed band carried off his wife and children, could my kindness be accused? Physicians too bind, and apply violence to our bodies that they may heal them. Whether it was for the boy's good to be seized. Here the accusation of the stepmother and the attack on the father, who so patiently loses his own.

OF MUSA. I am about to tell of the fires, the lashes, the torments of the old Olynthian: someone now thinks I am complaining of Philip. The gods and goddesses destroy you! You have made Philip merciful. If you believe this man, he imitated an angry Jove; if us, he outdid an angry Philip. Paint Philip with crippled shank, with eye gouged out, with throat broken, tortured . . . by the immortal gods. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. With the last wasting of his limbs he dies amid the torments. Parrhasius, what are you doing? You do not keep your design; this is beyond Prometheus. As much must be suffered while Parrhasius paints as while Jove is angry.

ARELLIUS FUSCUS made this the first question: whether one who has ravished two women must in any case die. The law, he said, which says, "Let the ravished woman choose either the death or the marriage of her ravisher," speaks of those who have ravished single women; it did not suppose anyone would ravish two on one night. I do not ask what you choose; what you can most severely choose, I forestall. The ravisher must die. Why? To each ravished woman vengeance is owed. You cannot marry both; you can die for both. One part of the law applies to this ravisher, in which there is death. Suppose both had chosen marriage: what would happen? There would be a contest for marriage to the ravisher. Suppose he had ravished more than two: what would come of it? One would marry. The marriage would belong to one, the death to all. He who has ravished two owes death to both. Why? I will tell you. Let him choose what he wishes: if they choose either both marriage, or one death and the other marriage, what both women wish cannot come to pass; in one way only can what both wish come to pass — if both choose death: therefore let that be done by which alone the two can be avenged. Here he treated:

but flung out. What reason have you for divorcing your wife? Does she burden your fortune, costly in her expenditure, and, as is the fashion of the age, does a woman's ambition, as luxury flows ever for the worse, in mutual rivalry run mad with private extravagance even to public harm? Did she covet gems and little stones sought from a foreign shore, and gold and clothing that will cover nothing in a matron? If she were such, the tyrant would easily have corrupted her. Wait, she can bear; fertility does not answer to a set plan nor to a fixed day; the nature of things is its own master and is not arranged by human laws: sometimes it hurries and outruns our prayers, sometimes it is slow and delays. Wait; she will bear. What do you say: "it cannot be"? Why? Because she was tortured. You lay it to her charge that she became public property; you lay it to her charge that she was tortured; you lay it to her charge that she is barren. OF JULIUS BASSUS: The tyrant said: burn, cut her womb.

THE DIVISION. These controversiae, which have both a defence and an accusation, not all declaimed in the same order. There were some who defended before they accused, among whom was Latro. FUSCUS ARELLIUS said: "The defendant ought to end with the epilogue. Now the epilogue is best woven to the defence; and men favour the one who defends more than the one who accuses. Let the last part be the one that can send the judge away well-disposed." Some mingled accusation and defence, so as to enter on a comparison of the two defendants and, having at once repelled a charge, straightway transfer it; among whom was CESTIUS. This is not always expedient. At any rate, for the man who has the weaker side it is not useful to engage at close quarters: things that are not compared more easily lie hidden.

GALLIO made that question too, and thought a question should first be taken from the person rather than from the matter: whether action can be brought against a grandfather in a grandson's name. "No more," he says, "than against a father in a son's name, no more than against a mother. Nature has her own rights, and this difference between grandfather and father — that a grandfather may keep his own, a father may even kill them. You cannot," he says, "deal with me as with a stranger, so as to say: 'What have you to do with him? Who are you?' He of whom, dying intestate, your son will be heir, whom you will, when mad, put in chains. Certain rights are given us not by law but by nature. A grandfather will strike his grandson when he does some wrong and frolics too wantonly among boyish games, and no one will bring an action for injury against him.

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the father. Paint Prometheus, but making men, but dividing the fire; paint him, but among gifts rather than among torments. Among the altars he has set up the cross of the old Olynthian. Most wretched old man, perhaps some one of your slaves serves more happily; at any rate happier is whoever serves a Macedonian.

that it is not even a useful precedent that one who has ravished two should not in any case perish; that by this reasoning a most pernicious custom would be introduced into the state — that a man should not perish for this reason, that he deserved to perish more often. The remaining part of the controversia Fuscus divided into these: which choice is the more honourable, which the juster, which the more useful. CESTIUS divided this part of the controversia thus: which choice of the woman is the worthier to prevail; in which choice the ravisher is the more worthy to be placed. Cestius also attempted a conjectural question: whether this woman had colluded with the ravisher and been ravished for this purpose, to be set against the other.

OF ARGENTARIUS: Cut her womb, that she may not bear tyrant-slayers. OF TRIARIUS: Nature does not answer to a formula, nor does chance obey a prescription; fortune always prefers to be awaited rather than ruled. In one place an unforeseen ripening of the crops gives offence, in another a late delay is redeemed at great interest. Though the law fix the days, nature does not admit it. The tyrant said: reveal it; it is no fault of yours: she is silent. She is cut: she is silent; she is burned: she is silent. Which do you think is to be wondered at — your tyrant-slaying, or her silence? Some woman is said to have waited a long time for her husband: how great is the praise of having saved him, when to have waited was so great? Another, struck with longing for her husband, threw herself upon his burning pyre: would this woman not have burned with her husband, who burned for her husband? Another, for her husband's safety, died in his stead by a substituted death: do you believe this woman was overcome by tortures? She would have suffered death besides for her husband, had the tyrant demanded anything more. OF MARCELLUS.

In this controversia † there are even two or three defendants: for the stepmother is joined with the steward. And so on the son's side he said that one must accuse first, because the son had to defend one charge but to bring two — both adultery and murder. If anything is difficult on either side, it requires not colour but argumentation; and so, that I may not exceed measure, I will pass it by. About the stepmother's wound some said pretty things, some silly — nay, many silly.

And GALLIO made that last question, when he had handled those — "it is lawful for me to use force that I may do good"; then, "this was for his good" — whether the grandfather should be pardoned, since out of feeling for his grandson he was carried away to do it. Here he handled how unworthy it was that the man be condemned for this. LATRO put the two last questions differently and embraced more: whether, even if he used violence, he nevertheless cannot be condemned, if he did it with good intent; whether he did it with good intent. For he said the controversy with the grandfather was also about his intent, and that the father said: he did it not to save his grandson, but to defame my wife as a poisoner, and me as a man handed over to a poisoner, to whom his own children would be ill entrusted.

OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. If you set out to succor him, I complain that you bought only one; if to torture him, I complain that you bought any. Would, Philip, that you had held your auction with a reservation: that no Athenian should buy. Phidias did not see Jupiter, yet made him as it were thundering; nor did Minerva stand before his eyes, yet his spirit was worthy of that art, and conceived gods and displayed them. What shall we do if you wish to paint a war? Shall we set up opposing battle-lines of men and arm hands for mutual wounds? Shall the conquered follow the conquerors? Shall they return bloody? Lest Parrhasius's hand toy idly with colors, must we buy at the cost of a human slaughter?

Latro said that not everything which can be scattered as suspicion should also be indicated; that this was a colour, not a question; that a question is one which can be filled out with arguments. Cestius said that this too could be filled out with arguments. This thought, bandied about by the Latins, NICETES expressed: "the third night failed him." GLYCON said . . . Diocles of Carystus said . . . This thought VIBIUS RUFUS expressed subtly: I wish to make you ill-disposed toward your betrothed — he has a mistress. In this controversia ALBUCIUS said: "let him walk among males." So true is it that no vice is without its lover, that some thought this a witty thing; yet I marvel more that Albucius could say it than that any could praise it. Of the Latins, TRIARIUS said: I congratulate you, maidens, that the day broke sooner. ARGENTARIUS said: do you ask what put an end to his ravishing? The daylight. Latro: he was already preparing himself for a third, had not the night failed.

If, however, she had sinned in childbearing, it could be pardoned her; for she had married a busy man. You are crueller even than the tyrant you killed: he tortured, but sent her back to her husband. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS: Endurance had conquered cruelty; the blood now failed, the loyalty remained. At last she was flung out; she was abandoned with her hands wrenched, her joints dislocated; her limbs had not yet returned to their own members. Such a wife the torturer sent back to childbearing. He was called ungrateful because in his reward he made no mention of his wife. "Keep your things to yourself." He ought to have laid hands on him and dragged the man himself among her things; you owe a father nothing more than you owe a wife. Believe me, it was a greater thing to suffer the tyrant-slaying than to do it.

First I will report those that were prettily said. FUSCUS said: "The skin is grazed with a light wound; you would not believe it done by a stepson's hand, you would believe it a lover's." PASSIENUS said: "So lightly did that right hand wound you, which neither a wall nor a father withstands?" VARIUS GEMINUS said: "Give the sword to my witness: he will strike harder." CESTIUS said, when he had described how slight the wound was: "You would have hurt me," he said, "if you could have hurt your mistress." BRUTUS BRUTTEDIUS used a homely word with point: "He killed," he said, "his rival, and merely grazed his mistress." HISPO ROMANIUS said a thing of the same kind: "Show, stepmother, show that thing which your lover pinched." BASSUS SEPULLIUS said: "He killed the husband, he merely scratched the adulteress."

So Latro used this same colour for the father, to say that not even while his wife was alive had he been on good terms with his father-in-law, but that, after her death, the man had carried on open enmities against him: that, when the boy was ill, he had come with abuse, with shouting, both speaking and ill-boding nefarious things; that friends had advised him not to admit a man who came not for his grandsons' service but for the injury and insult of his son-in-law — a man who had never deigned to approach his grandsons when they were well; and that the physicians had urged him not to come and confuse the boy and fill him with suspicions.

If someone must be tortured, buy a guilty slave, that at one and the same time you may both take an example and a punishment. On one side Parrhasius is set, with his colors; on the other a torturer, with fires, lashes, racks. Do you think him too little sad, Parrhasius, whether he sees these things or awaits them? The wretch kept saying: "I did not betray my country. Athenians, if I have deserved nothing, succor me; if I have deserved it, give me back to Philip." Amid this it is doubtful whether Parrhasius paints the more zealously, or that man rages the more.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF ARGENTARIUS: "And yet I was tortured." You might justly object it, had I not avenged it. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS: With you, judges, I speak . . . THE DIVISION. The first question to make the defendant guilty in this controversia, if the material permit: "I did not receive . . . indeed, but I returned it"; or "I received it indeed, but could not return it"; or to flee at last to this: "not whoever has not returned a benefit is liable for ingratitude. The mind of the one who does not return must be weighed." ASINIUS POLLIO used to say that these questions should never be attempted unless the first could be manifestly maintained, by which we deny that we received a benefit; the whole case is lost, unless he wins on this point. For it is plain that a man is ungrateful who does not even confess that he received the benefit.

Of those who had said silly things, first there, before all, was your own MUSA, who, when he had described the stepmother's wound, added: "But, by Hercules, my father was pierced through like a wall." MURREDIUS: "He thinks it a defence of his case that he let blood." LICINIUS NEPOS said: "That is not a wound, but the bite of a sporting adulterer." SENIANUS produced a sententia of that stamp of fools: "He did not wound," he said, "his stepmother, but sprinkled her with her husband's blood" — although she is presented as wounded.

SILO POMPEIUS' colour was, as it seemed to Latro, one that worked against the controversia; for he said that the grandfather had come to the feeble boy; that to the sick men are not always admitted, especially to those who are gravely ill; that often even a father has not been admitted; that so to the grandfather too, coming unseasonably, it was said: "Now you cannot"; that he had at once gone off with abuse; and had done the same in the other case. Latro used to say that this colour was the best, if the matter stood thus, but that it could not be accepted, because it is laid down: "he was not admitted";

He tortures, he scourges: thus does this butcher temper his colors. What do you say? Does he seem too little sad whom Philip sold, Parrhasius bought? "Now torture him, now; it is well, hold him thus: this look should be that of a man torn, this of a dying man." OF PORCIUS LATRO. If you think well, adorn the altar of mercy with these gifts. Does no one of the Olynthians, then, serve more wretchedly than he who drew an Athenian master by lot? The wretch, wherever he had not seen Philip, thought it peace. "Bind him," he says.

Our GALLIO thinks that, whenever one can, this should be taken from the adversary; whenever one cannot, it should be shaken; whenever one cannot do even this, it should be passed over as though we grant it and could indeed make a controversia of it, but do not wish to. The same view pleased ATTICUS VIPSANIUS, a pupil of Apollodorus. This he added: whenever, he said, we cannot make a controversia of whether we received a benefit, let us make one of the degree: that it is not so great as he says — just as we do in criminal charges, whenever we cannot deny: we confess the crime indeed, but as worthy of a lighter penalty than the accuser alleges.

VINICIUS, a man of most exacting talent, who could neither say silly things nor endure them, used to deride this sententia of Senianus, and to compare with it a similar one said in a speech of Votienus Montanus. SENIANUS had said in this same controversia: "Nothing is more sure than a boy as witness, especially one of five years; for he has reached the age at which he understands, and not yet that at which he invents." "This definition," he said, "is ridiculous: 'Nothing is more sure than a boy as witness, especially of five years'; suppose a boy of four is no witness, nor one of six." And he used to add most charmingly: "You would think something was being transacted: everything in this sententia belongs to a circumspect man — definition, exception; but nothing is more unlovely than diligent stupidity."

that under this theme we understand that it was said to him not "Now you cannot," but "You cannot at all." GALLIO mixed both, and used, more openly, this colour, which otherwise may seem to overturn the theme. "It was said to him," he says, "'The boy is resting, wait a little; the physicians have forbidden anyone to be admitted.' You know they are wont to say: 'Not even if the father comes.' At once this man began to shout: 'I call to witness that I am not admitted,' and all but to give notice with sealed tablets. I had put off the grandfather, I shut out the accuser. Again," he says, "he came with abuse: 'Already you have killed one, you are killing the other.' Nothing is more wretched than when, out of someone's misery, ill-will is sought for him." He was not admitted when he said he did not wish to see his grandson, but to inspect him. Thus he pleaded: "I came, not to accuse this man, but to defend myself." GALLIO used this colour: "I did not admit the grandfather, because I had been told that he came in this mind — to seize the boy."

He kept saying: "Unbound was I under Philip." OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. Wait until a Euthycrates or a Lasthenes is captured. Phidias, Parrhasius, made everything without a torturer. Philip too was content to have sold him. A noble old man is brought forth, weeping, looking back upon his country: his look pleased that man; he had something like Prometheus even before the torments. He pleads his case carefully, as though before Philip: ". . . it is not for the Olynthian, I have lost my money." Go back to your model. For men's sake Prometheus was racked; for Prometheus's sake do not rack men. Philip was asked thus: "Let the Olynthians be allowed to live." Parrhasius must be asked otherwise: "Let the Olynthians be allowed to die." "I wish to make him sad." No one will make him so, if Philip did not.

Latro in this controversia did not hesitate to make the first question, whether he gave a benefit. This he divided thus: even if you knew and did not reveal, it is no benefit not to commit a crime; and then, you did not even know; for I did not reveal it to you, nor did I entrust so great a design — grievous even to manly minds — to a woman's chattering, which can keep silent only about what it does not know. Even if he did give a benefit, whether he received one in return. I killed the tyrant, I restored your liberty, I pursued the fullest vengeance, I killed the abominable enemy there where he had tortured. You will say I did it for the republic's sake: and you kept silent for the republic's sake. Let him be safe for what he did by law. Then the last treatment of equity:

The sententia of MONTANUS VOTIENUS he said was like this, and he derided it: "A dog is a sleepless and wakeful animal, especially a chained one, on the alert." Now he was not fair to Montanus himself. He had accused him before Caesar, at the request of the colony of Narbonne. But Montanus was so wholly a schoolman in spirit that on the very day on which he was accused by Vinicius he said: "Vinicius's pleading delighted me"; and he kept quoting his sententiae. Elegantly SURDINUS said to him: "I ask, do you suppose he was declaiming the other side?" A grave disease has invaded the schoolmen: when they have cited examples, they wish to reduce them to some theme of the controversia.

On the other side CESTIUS introduced this colour: that he had feared for the boy. "And not without cause," he says: "the stepmother had killed two." And he said: "I could wish I came to you a more guilty defendant; I could wish I had been able to seize all three." ARGENTARIUS used this colour: that the grandfather was begged by the boy. "He said," he said, "that he could not live if he were left in that house." HISPANUS used this colour: that he had been carried away by feeling. "I took up," he says, "my grandson; I could not be sated with kissing him, I could not be torn from him so quickly. Do not wonder: after a long time I had seen him."

This controversia a great part of the declaimers said in such a way as to divide not the controversia but the accusation — in the manner in which those are wont to arrange their pleading in the forum who accuse in the first place; in the school, because it is not spoken in two places, one must always not only speak but answer. They object that he tortured a man, that he tortured an Olynthian, that he imitated the punishments of the gods, that he set up a tablet in the temple of Minerva. If Parrhasius is not going to answer, they divide well enough. But nothing is more base than either to declaim a controversia in which nothing can be answered from the other side, or not to refute it if it can be answered.

whether what he did, he ought to have done. This he divided into two: whether he ought to have borne the now-certain barrenness of so good a wife; whether she is even certainly barren. The modern declaimers, after Moschus the Apollodorean — who was prosecuted for poisoning and defended by Asinius Pollio, and, condemned, taught at Massilia — made this question too in this controversia: whether benefits given between husbands and wives are liable to the law of ingratitude. It is no benefit but a duty, to do what you owe: so a son might say he confers a benefit on his father. This question our GALLIO too made. BLANDUS, in the last part of the controversia, where the matter of the republic is disputed, made the question whether the five years ought to be reckoned, the tyranny excepted. That time ought not to be charged against her as barren, in which mothers cursed even the children they had borne: let that time be charged against women in which they bear for the republic, not the time in which they bear for a tyrant. To this he subjoined, whether, even if the time of tyranny is usually charged against others, it ought not to be against this woman.

As this is sometimes to be done when the matter allows, so it is most foolish to wrestle with the material and to fetch things from afar, in the way that MUSA did in this controversia, who, when he was delivering for the son the commonplace about the indulgence of children toward their parents, came to the son of Croesus and said: "In his father's peril the mute man broke through the natural impediments of his voice, who had been silent more than five years." Because a five-year-old boy is presented, he thought that wherever five years were named a sententia could be made, because it had succeeded with Latro, who, when he had made sport of the slight wound, said: "Look at that scarcely visible scar: I ask you, do you not think a little boy did it — and not even a five-year-old little boy?"

ALBUCIUS used this colour, saying that he had not wished the boy to be reared in so ill-omened a house, from which two brothers of his had already been carried out; that for the one who afterwards died, among the causes of his death was his brother's fate. And he kept this colour, that he should say nothing against the stepmother, nothing against the father; he used to say that the grandfather would be most just, if he had wished only to defend himself. "What then? Why did you seize him? I loved him; to him above all, from the first, I had bound my heart. In your house I feared nothing but the house itself. If two had died in my care, I should have moved him out of my house." MONTANUS VOTIENUS said

GALLIO had in the Parrhasius case a division much like the one he had had in that controversia of which mention is made in this very book — of the man who crippled the exposed — with certain things removed. He divided thus: whether the state has been harmed. "What did he lose?" he says: "nothing. I do not yet make a controversia about the right. Olynthus lost one old man. Grant he is an Athenian: you will not sue me for harming the state if I kill an Athenian senator, but for murder." "So; but the reputation of Athens is corrupted; for mercy we have always been esteemed." Never is the public fame corrupted by the misdeed of one man; the reputation of the Athenians is too solid to be shaken in that way.

Latro, in his usual way, thought these were not questions, but limbs of that last part hanging from the question of equity. Whether she is even barren he fetched from deeper: not every woman who has not borne in five years is barren. For what? If someone's husband has been away almost the whole five years, it will be charged to the husband's absence abroad. What if the husband was sick? If this husband, tortured by the tyrant, had lain useless for intercourse with his own wife, would he charge the five years to her? You ask why she did not bear? It was tyranny; everyone complained to his own parents that he had been born. Here, because she was tortured; here, because the husband, busy with tyrant-slaying, had no leisure for his wife's pleasure.

GALLUS VIBIUS spoke a shameless sententia, when he was describing the murder: "He killed," he said, "the husband, hurt the stepmother, spared the boy: even now he thought him his own." For CESTIUS used to say that the boy must be much spared; and so he said, when he praised his testimony: "Were you born for a steward?" HERMAGORAS placed this thought more becomingly: "Was it according to the brother, or not?" Blandus's sententia was praised, when he had described the steward pointed out by the boy: "A finger that signifies much!"

that MARCELLUS MARCIUS told it thus: "The boy followed me. I do not accuse him to you; whatever it is, let it be at my peril rather than his: I seized him. 'Where is he?' he says. He is alive, he is safe; come and look at him when you will. 'Give him back,' he says, 'to his . . .' I cruel! Come, I will show you, if you wish, who took your sons from you before me." VARIUS GEMINUS said the same thought: "What devotion is this, either so late or so preposterous?

"The state has been harmed," he says. It has not been harmed, as I think. Suppose someone denied to an Olynthian a deposit: he would seem to have harmed not the state but the man. To the Olynthians you granted this — that they should be in the same standing as the Athenians. "You harmed the state," he says, "in that you set up this picture in the temple." They harm the state who take something away from it, not who add to it; who demolish temples, not who adorn them. The priests too sinned, then, who received the tablet. Yet why should they not receive it? The adulteries of the gods are painted; pictures of Hercules killing his children are set up.

BUTEO, a dry declaimer indeed, but a prudent divider of controversiae, held the contrary to Latro and agreed with Blandus. For it is one thing, he said, to say "she who has not borne within five years is not necessarily barren," another to say "she who has not borne within five years cannot at once be put away under the name of barrenness." Here the inquiry is about a condition of law, there about a hope of fertility. But he found fault with Blandus too; he said the inquiry should not have been made thus: whether the time of tyranny ought to be excepted; and then, even if not in others, whether in this woman . . . there should be a gradation. He himself divided the question in this part thus: whether any woman who has not borne in five years can be put away as barren.

EUCTEMON said: "Stepmother, I have found a good witness. O dutiful child! O child unworthy of your mother, but wholly your father's!" MURREDIUS, in mimic vein, spoke a foolish sententia, when he had said that the stepmother was disputing against her own son's testimony: "She does," he said, "what she is wont: for her lover she does not spare her own blood." NICOCRATES the Laconian, a dry and squeezed-out declaimer, said: "She spared her own witness, but scorned mine." HERMAGORAS, when he had said that the boy's condition was pitiable, being given back to a hostile stepmother and a steward, said that the steward was already crying out: "He is not ours."

You begin to seek your own with the third." MONTANUS VOTIENUS, a man of most rare though not most faultless talent, his own fault which he does not avoid in speeches he could not avoid in declamations either; but in speeches, because the material is more spacious, the repetition of the same things is less noted; in declamations, if the things said are the same, since they are few, they are marked. I remember him, on behalf of Galla Numisia before the Hundred Men, making his maiden plea. Galla was heir to a twelfth part of her father's estate. She was charged with poisoning. He said a thing most eloquent and likely to endure for all ages, than which I do not know whether anything better has been said in this kind of cause: "A twelfth is owed neither to a daughter nor to a poisoner." He was not content; he added: "In a father's will, a daughter's place is either her own or none." And now he added:

Then: whether he can be accused of harming the state for that which he was allowed to do. Prosecute by that law what was not allowed. You say to me: "This ought not to be done." For this matter the valuation is immense; and so there is no penalty; and only that is punished which is not allowed. It is fully and abundantly enough if the craftsman, ignorant of affairs, is innocent before the law. Whether this was allowed him to do. This is divided into that: whether an Olynthian, before an Athenian, even before the decree was made, could not be a slave. "He is my slave," he says, "whom I possess by the right of war; and what is acquired by the right of war is valid. It is to your advantage, Athenians: otherwise your empire is reduced to its old boundaries; whatever there is, was acquired by war."

There could happen what happened to the Athenians in war — that children and wives be deposited in some safer place: will this time be charged against women, in which they do not abandon their husbands but do not have them? What if the tyrant had forbidden this woman to bear within the five years? And when he had filled this out vehemently and proved that not all could be put away if they had not borne in five years, then he passed to this: whether this woman could be; and even here he still did not ask whether she ought to be put away, but whether she could. And this he said against Latro: how do you think this question falls under the treatment of equity, when the inquiry is what is lawful, not what is fitting? For this — whether she can — I fill out through those points: she cannot, because she had not conceived in the tyranny. Misery makes some time exempt from the laws. I do not say it is because she was tortured — this I still pass over and reserve for the treatment of equity. But she did not bear because you, occupied with the thought of so great a matter, gave no thought to children.

"You leave too much to the guilty, too little to the innocent." Not even thus could he sate himself; he added: "A daughter cannot cling so narrowly to a father's tablets, which she ought either wholly to possess or wholly to lose"; and many more besides which I do not recall from memory; some of these he carried into his speech, and added more than he had spoken. Nothing of these but is fine, if it stand alone; nothing of them, again, but stands in another's way. The same thing I remember he did in this declamation. "You err," he said, "father, and grievously err: those you lost you do not seek; the one you seek you did not lose." Then: "This boy, if he is found, perishes." Then: "Whoever favours the boy, let him pray he be not found." Then: "The boy, unless he follows his grandfather, will follow his brothers; cease to seek the one whom, if you find him, you will so lose that you cannot find him." And then: "The grandfather seized him, lest the stepmother seize him." And then: "The father seeks one only of his children — the one who is safe."

On the other side he says: "That slave can be another buyer's, not an Athenian's. For what if you had bought an Athenian from Philip? But you knew the Olynthians were joined to us by treaty." "That you may know," he says, "they were slaves, the decree of the Athenians was made afterward, by which they were ordered to be both free and citizens. Why was this right given them, if they already had it?" Then: whether by the decree it is not contained that they should become free, but that they should be judged to be free. "We decreed this — that the Olynthians are our citizens: so this man too was our citizen." "No," he says; "for the decree was made for the future. Surely you do not wish this to become law for the past? Surely whoever had an Olynthian slave will not be accused of having held a citizen in his slavery? If anyone then, amid the necessary services of slave-duties, struck or beat him, shall he be accused of wrongs?" And yet, as concerns the right, it makes no difference whether he killed or beat; for either it was not allowed to beat, or it was allowed to kill.

PASSIENUS, a most eloquent man and the first orator of his time, did not approve this subtlety of pleading: he said he agreed with Latro for this reason — that all these things would always have to be treated for their own sake, if this woman were bringing an action for unjust divorce; but as it is she brings one for ingratitude: so the inquiry is not whether she was lawfully, but whether she was ungratefully, put away; and so even matters of law fall under the treatment of equity. For when the inquiry is whether this woman ought not to have been put away even if it was lawful, it appears how much she ought not to have been put away, if it was not even lawful. And so ALBUCIUS acted most becomingly — for he was generally wont to arrange a declamation into certain figures — and pleaded first for unjust divorce, then for ingratitude: . . . he thinks . . . any benefit, by whom she was, as it were, unjustly put away. Hence he treated freely all the questions pertaining to barrenness and the reckoning of the five years, then passed into the accusation of ingratitude. CESTIUS introduced a simple colour for the husband:

GLYCON said this thought once, and in an uncorrupt manner: "This little boy, when he is found, then he will perish." Montanus has this fault: by repeating his sententiae he corrupts them; while he is not content to say one thing once and well, he brings it about that he has not said it well. And on this account and for other things in which an orator may seem like a poet, SCAURUS used to call Montanus the Ovid among orators; for Ovid too does not know how to leave what has come off well. Not to recount many things that Scaurus called "Montaniana," I will be content with this one: when Polyxena had been led off to be sacrificed at Achilles' tomb, Hecuba says: the very ashes of the buried man war against this race. He could have been content with this; he added: in the tomb too we felt an enemy. Nor content with this, he added: I was fruitful for the son of Aeacus. Now Scaurus used to say a true thing: it is no less great a virtue to know how to speak than to know how to stop.

On Parrhasius's side he made this colour: that an old man, useless, at the point of death, had been bought by Parrhasius: "If you wish the truth," he says, "he did not kill him, but used the death of one failing and in any case about to die. He tortured him, however: if for gain, object it; surely Athens has the price of this cruelty." In the arguments he said how much had always been allowed to the arts: that physicians, to learn the unknown force of a disease, have cut into the entrails; that today the limbs of corpses are cut up, that the position of the sinews and joints may be known. ALBUCIUS with this colour: that the man was calamitous, bereaved, openly wishing for death; that Philip would not otherwise have sold him, had he not thought it a punishment for him to live.

at the time my wife was tortured I was as yet thinking nothing of tyrant-slaying; afterwards I thought of it, and this very thing was my reason for thinking — the avenging of my wife. He pursued both points: that she could not charge her husband with her silence, and that the husband could charge her with the tyrant-slaying. Latro said that he had been thinking of tyrant-slaying even then, but had not revealed it to his wife. FABIANUS the philosopher introduced a colour more befitting a good man than a cunning orator. For he said that he had both thought of tyrant-slaying and revealed it to his wife, and that she at that time did what an honest woman ought to do, but now sins in thinking it a benefit to do right. This colour profited him in that other part too: if you think you gave a benefit in not betraying the tyrant-slaying, I gave one first in entrusting the tyrant-slaying to you. The divorce . . . from your . . . desire for children, which he ought always to have used as a husband, afterwards more as a tyrant-slayer.

SILO POMPEIUS thought it more convenient if Parrhasius had gone to the auction with this mind — to buy someone for this use; for then he can seem to have chosen the cheapest and most useless. FUSCUS ARELLIUS preferred that he had bought him indeed for other uses, but, when he was failing and wished to die, had spent him on that one thing which the artist could get from a corpse. GALLIO bound himself to neither, nor said with what mind he bought; but Gallio's colour is intolerable: for he said that he had bought the old man from the guilty Olynthians; and if he is allowed to invent this, I do not see why by the same means he should not say both that the man was privy to the betrayal of Lasthenes, and that he had tortured him for punishment's sake.

LUCIUS VINICIUS, the brother of Vinicius, strongly approved Fabianus's colour, and said the wife could be burdened in one way only — if the husband had never had any secret from her. If he says, he remarked, that he thought of tyrant-slaying after the tortures, then we owe the tyrant-slaying to the wife. She deserved better of her husband if, tortured, she made him a tyrant-slayer, than if she kept silent; but it appears he had thought something of tyrant-slaying, of which the tyrant suspected him so far as to torture him. If he says that he did indeed think of tyrant-slaying before the tortures, but did not reveal it to his wife, he will increase his wife's benefit; for she could the more freely reveal a tyrant-slaying that had not been entrusted to her; for the wife could detect the contriving of so great a design even without her husband revealing it. But if I follow this colour of Fabianus's, I shall accomplish much. If I have long thought of tyrant-slaying, I am more honourable, an old tyrant-slayer, driven to vengeance not by private but by public ills. If, when I was thinking of it, I did not conceal it from my wife, I shall more easily persuade men that I am no bad husband today, to whom I was always so devoted. At the last I shall attain this — that if she kept silent about what she had heard, it is no benefit but fidelity.

HISPO ROMANIUS excused him by ignorance: "A painter," he says, "shut within his workshop, who knew only these common laws — that nothing is not allowed to a master against a slave, nothing not allowed to a painter in painting — spent his own chattel upon his own work." "You do not tell all," he says: "it was an Olynthian who perished." But what does it matter to the case of what nation the slave was? "Do you dare," he says, "to call an Olynthian a slave, even after the war and before the decree? Otherwise what kindness did you do them, save that now it is allowed neither to torture nor to kill them?" The Greeks thought it impious to speak for Parrhasius: all accused him; they fell into the same thoughts.

This is the Lucius Vinicius than whom no Roman citizen had a readier talent in pleading causes: whatever long reflection was to furnish him, the first effort of his mind gave; he pleaded cases extempore, but did not need this recommendation — to seem to plead extempore. Of him the deified Augustus elegantly said: Lucius Vinicius has his talent in ready cash. HISPO ROMANIUS, maliciously and like an accuser, said: "I had told this man nothing; she, as was inevitable, suspected something from his face, something from his nightly wakefulness: whence the talk leaked out, you shall know. You see where the tyrant comes: not to my friend, not to my slave, but to this woman, who would have had no trouble, had she kept silent. You kept silent for your own sake too: you knew you would perish, if you confessed the tyrant-slaying." HYBREAS said: "Go up, then, advancing to the citadel, and, if you so desire, take now the sword."

GLYCON said: "Fire and man, Prometheus — your own gifts torture you." TRIARIUS, filching this in some part, twisted it. Such men, CASSIUS SEVERUS used to say, who did this, seemed to him like thieves changing the handles on others' cups: there are many who, by taking away a word or changing it or adding one, think they have made others' sententiae their own gain. TRIARIUS, however, turned it thus: "You have spoiled the two greatest gifts of Prometheus, fire and man." But the Greeks too stole it: EUCTEMON, who said:

"Prometheus, upon you someone brings fire and man" — more soundly than Glycon; ADAEUS: "Prometheus, someone painting you destroys a man"; DAMAS most corruptly: "Justly, Prometheus: why did you steal fire for man?"; CRATON most madly, who said: "Prometheus, now you should have stolen fire." This is Craton, a most charming man and an avowed Asianist, who waged war with all the Atticists. When Caesar made him a present of a talent — in which there are twenty-four sesterces by the Athenian reckoning — he said: "Either add to it or take from it, that it may not be Attic." He also, when Caesar would never hear him except in the month of December, said: "Do you use me as a furnace?" And when he was commended by Caesar to Passienus and did not pay court to him, and to one who asked why he did not embrace the favor of so great a man, he said: "While the sun burns, I do not light a lamp."

He often used to clash before Caesar with TIMAGENES, a man of acid tongue and one who was too free — I think because he had long not been free. From captive a cook, from cook a litter-bearer, from litter-bearer happy up to the most intimate friendship of Caesar, he so despised both fortunes — both the one he was in and the one he had been in — that, when Caesar, angry with him for many reasons, had forbidden him his house, he burned the histories of the deeds done by him, as though he too were forbidding Caesar the use of his own talent: an eloquent man and witty, by whom many things were said improperly but charmingly. That I may not exceed measure by running off, I return to Parrhasius.

NICETES said: "In fire, in iron, are you painting for us, or playing the tyrant?" HISPO ROMANIUS said: "Fire, iron, torments: is this a painter's workshop, or Philip's?" Sparsus's sententia in the description of the picture has something corrupt: "And wherever blood is needed, he uses human blood"; for he said what cannot be. That passage all attempted: "What if you wish to paint a war? What if a conflagration? What if a parricide?"

Of the Greeks DORION said madly: "What Oedipus will there be, what Atreus? For you will not paint unless you see the myths living." But there is nothing that can be less endured than what was said by METRODORUS: "Bring me no Trojan women, nor a Niobe. Apply the fire: not yet has he given me back my Prometheus." TRIARIUS said: "Not yet have you groaned worthily of an angry Jove." HATERIUS said more soundly: "Not yet does the look suit the story." And this: "Parrhasius, that all may be done according to the model, let him who has been tortured live." But, if you wish, hear that beyond which madness cannot proceed: LICINIUS NEPOS said: "If you wish to punish Parrhasius worthily, let him paint himself."

No less foolishly a certain AEMILIANUS, a Greek rhetorician — which kind of fool is the most lovable — out of dryness a simpleton, said: "Kill Parrhasius, lest, unwilling to paint, he find a model out of you." PAUSANIAS said: "Because of you, Parrhasius, those going out of the temple must purify themselves." OTHO the father, when he spoke for Parrhasius, was derided for this colour: "Because," he said, "Olynthus had fallen through traitors, I wished to paint Jove angry at his betrayer." GARGONIUS much more foolishly, as to why Parrhasius had painted Prometheus's punishment: "Should I," he says, "with Olynthus burning, not have hated the author of fire?" That famous

sententia of Latro is well known, which SPARSUS too, with certain words removed, said in the description of the torments: "'Parrhasius, I am dying'; 'hold him thus.'" This sententia they say DIOCLES OF CARYSTUS too said, not in the same way: "His disdain is past belief: at the look that pleased him he cried out, 'Stay.'"

SPYRIDION made the Romans speak honorably; for he raved far more violently than our frenzied men. He wished it to seem that vultures flew to Parrhasius's tablet — led by an elegant tale to a base sententia. For it is handed down that Zeuxis, I think, painted a boy holding a grape; and since the likeness of the grape was so great that it made even birds fly to the work, one of the spectators said that the birds judged ill of the painting; for they would not have flown to it if the boy had been like. Zeuxis, they say, smeared out the grape and kept that which was better in the picture, not that which was more like.

SPYRIDION likewise thought the vultures came into the temple as familiarly as sparrows or doves; for he had said: "Your painting devours its flesh-eating creatures." But I would not have the Romans beaten in anything: MURREDIUS will restore the line, who said: "Paint Triptolemus, who with yoked dragons furrowed the air." Among those who said something corrupt about Prometheus, APATURIUS too claims a place for himself; for he said: "Would that the fire had been stolen back to the gods."

THE LAW: [implied in the theme]. THE THEME: A young man, captured by pirates, wrote to his father about his ransom. The father did not ransom him. The archpirate's daughter compelled him to swear that he would marry her if he were released, and he swore. Leaving her father, she followed the young man. He returned to his father and married her. An orphaned heiress comes forward; the father bids his son put away the archpirate's daughter and marry the heiress; when the son refuses, he disinherits him. OF PORCIUS LATRO: Good gods — and was this girl too received in my father's hospitality? I forbid her my house — a woman to be forbidden the earth. A wife of fine promise, a daughter-in-law of fine promise, who can love a captive and hate even a father. "Captured," he says, "I lay in darkness." Tell, I beg, your father-in-law's kindnesses. Can I, judges, be at ease? My son says he owes his wife the murder of his father. OF CESTIUS PIUS: Who was present at your wedding? Her father? Then — the girl's father?

THE THEME: A father, himself luxurious, accuses his luxurious son. — Yet let the luxury of each be compared. You consume your father's patrimony; I, my accuser's. Sail, serve as a soldier, travel abroad, get as a young man, enjoy as an old. My accuser has feelings diverse and contrary to each other: he longs for the defendant to be condemned, and the charge to be acquitted. OF CESTIUS PIUS: We can agree; we are alike. Suppose yourself the father: say what you would have me do: if then you are honestly frugal, this too I imitate. Do I imitate you, or you me? I ask you, which began first? "You are luxurious," he says. Let us reckon up the patrimony. "But you are old," he says. This is what you say: your luxury began later, it will end sooner.

We should have consolation if a tyrant had made this marriage, not a father. Pay him honour now: make him part of the dowry, let him guard his mistress. Do you think him sane who preferred to imitate a tyrant rather than a slave? Our father, born of honourable parents — for how otherwise could he have held our mother's hand —

OF CESTIUS PIUS. There is no reason for you to think these tears either a daughter's or a defendant's: she weeps for her brother. It would not profit you, girl, even this — that your brother loved you — unless your mother had hated you. In this you killed me, stepmother, that you knew to choose an accomplice for the punishment. He said: "Let us sift out her past life." OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. Nefarious woman — a stepmother to her own daughter too — she could not even die without killing. Among gladiators too the victor's condition is worst when he fights with a dying man. No adversary should you fear more than one who cannot live, but can kill.

OF PORCIUS LATRO. I took up only what the thief would have left. I feared nothing so greatly, as a thief, as that the owner should not acknowledge his own property. Stir up ill-will against me, betray my theft — yet thank the magistrate, that, when I had reported my theft to him, he did not order the thief to be removed. I restored by the ruin of one wall the tottering condition of the state. OF OSCUS. He was anxious lest what he had lost should be sought. I lay information: I have many accomplices of the theft. To that . . . I have not this theft alone. Is it a theft, which the owner fears to acknowledge? I could have been not poor, I had something to sell for much: behold, I hold letters in which there are manifest proofs of treason, in which the plans of the enemy. I ask you: if it is a theft, I put it back. OF MUSA. Do you call it theft, which the man who had lost it denied was his? I committed a theft, but against the enemy. OF CLODIUS TURRINUS. Do you call it theft, where the man who had lost it bore punishment, the man who took it away a reward? To which of the two would you have permitted to speak, if at the same time both the thief had come and the owner? I could have sold the state for much, even to the traitor. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the father.

THE OTHER SIDE. OF JULIUS BASSUS: Today I should be a captive, had this woman not been the archpirate's daughter. When I said, "I have a father," I was set apart among the good captives. She is called the archpirate's daughter — born, I suppose, of some captive woman; certainly her nature had drawn her mind away from her father: she was merciful, she would entreat, she wept, she was moved by everyone's perils; nothing of the pirate could be found in her. I promised marriage, and, as a kind of sacred testimony, I inserted your name. In that place she did not desert me, into which even fathers feared to come. Fortune bound us more closely than that, orphaned, she could tear us apart. You should have seen my body covered with rags, all my limbs pressed with bonds, my eyes drawn back inward with leanness, my hands worn by chains and useless: who could love such a man but a merciful woman?

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: "But you," he says, "are old." How do you know you will not be a luxurious old man? Every vice is from you: that my hair drips with unguent is yours; that my toga is let down looser, right to the feet, is yours. What else is there that old men learn from you? And further: does our house not hold two luxurious men? I could not disinherit you more indulgently. May I not refresh my old years with a better life? This is my last service, and the one I most lay to your charge: for your sake I have even become luxurious. OF FABIANUS: Do not covet money. What shall I tell you? This is what increases discord, drives cities and the whole world to war, goads the human race, kin by nature, into frauds and crimes and mutual hatred; this is what corrupts old men. Some have said the highest good is pleasure and referred everything to the body. I have no need of instructors: I have an example, I have set before me to do whatever you do; I will sail if you sail, serve if you serve: say today what you think better. But I make this reservation: you shall not object to what you yourself have chosen. OF BLANDUS: He objects luxury; I might say to him: young man, I lived frugally as long as I had a father. You stopped before me, you had begun before me. OF BLANDUS.

if he had only been freeborn? OF CESTIUS PIUS. Sister, I wish you perpetual barrenness. When I said, "Let us free the slave," he said, "Let us wait for our sister's wedding." So, sister, in order that you may have honourable children, you must commit adultery? He made himself like a tyrant: his daughter like the raped, his freedman like the crucified. The master allowed his slave more than a tyrant. Whoever makes such marriages is either mad or a tyrant. Who can believe this — that it was to be wished by the daughter that the tyranny should not end, that the father should not return? If I ask the father what was the most grievous crime in the tyranny, if he is sane he will answer:

OF VIBIUS GALLUS. Most furious is the rage in death, and in the last despair the mind is driven to frenzy. Some beasts bite the very weapons, and through their own wounds rush at the author of their death. The gladiator, his discharge cut off, naked pursues the man whom, when armed, he had fled. Men flung headlong drag down not only what pushed them but what they meet, and by a kind of natural feeling of a desperate mind it is most welcome to the dying to die in company.

You captains of a thousand ships took Troy by a theft. If cities are well overthrown by theft, how much better are they saved? If I do not disclose whose it is, no one will know. OF VIBIUS RUFUS. Whose breast itself, had I been able, not his wall only, I would have pierced through. I have not yet fully accomplished my whole duty: the state is not so narrow that it can be crushed by one man. OF CESTIUS PIUS. Do not demand of me everything I know; there are many things, some to be told even in the assembly. Teach this theft to your children. I ask you, judges, by my theft: as often as I brought forward my theft, the owner is silent. I a thief? Behold a second wrong. "Did you not," he says, "pierce through the house?" Be silent, I would not . . . better. I am wont to tell, I would not deny for a price . . .

I deceived you, girl; I promised you other things: you shall come into my homeland with me, there I will requite you; here, chained, needy, squalid, what can I do? My father, your father-in-law — for so he already long since called you — your father-in-law, I say, will requite you. Some men have buried with their disgraces the images of grandfathers and fathers; some, born ignoble, have made a lineage for their descendants: in the former, not to have kept what they received is the greatest dishonour; in the latter, to have made what no one had given is praiseworthy. If men could make for themselves their lot of birth, no one would be lowly, no one needy; each would seize a fortunate house; but since we are not gods, nature rules us and sends upon each whatever chance she will.

"As an old man you are luxurious." I answer you: as a young man I sailed. "I," he says, "have already stopped, you not yet." I do not wonder if you stopped first; you had begun first. OF MENTO: Whatever joy you have received . . . truly I am luxurious. OF POMPEIUS SILO: If only my son is reformed — for luxury too can be feigned — let each be a defendant in his own order. Do you wish me to take a wife? If you had a stepmother, you would already have been disinherited. OF VIBIUS GALLUS: Your guests, at least, say: let us drink, we must die. If I understand it, this is said to no one in the house more than to me. I have shown you your own vices, which you did not see in yourself. Bind me, while you guard yourself. OF PUBLIUS ASPRENAS: Because I made no headway by rebuking, I wished to show him his own life. OF JUNIUS OTHO: I should have a bad cause, if I had another accuser; I should have a bad cause, if I had not you for a son.

that mistresses were given to slaves. OF FULVIUS SPARSUS. A husband is chosen whom a sane father would have given as part of the dowry. Your son-in-law deserved the cross by the very wedding. An excellent son-in-law, in whom there is nothing more glorious than that he is not among the crucified! A most grievous injury was done even to the slave himself: he was not permitted to keep his mistress a virgin. OF BLANDUS. He did an injury even to the slave, from whom he took away the glory of his self-restraint. By his own wedding he was set free. O marriage baser than any adultery!

OF VOTIENUS MONTANUS. While I avenge my son, I showed where she could most grievously harm me. A lie like the poisoning itself! Do you think it credible, parricide in a sister? I do not fear lest anyone believe this of a sister, which I scarcely proved against a stepmother. I took up a daughter, born to me as though to be a pledge of peace; I said: while she remembers her mother she will forget her stepmother. But she, while she remembers her stepmother, has forgotten her mother. "My daughter," she says, "is my accomplice." After this word you would think the torments relaxed: she became like the torturer. A sister gave her brother poison? How long we struggled to make it believed that the stepmother had given it to her stepson! Stepmother, you have attained what you wished: I now repent having condemned you. OF ARGENTARIUS.

From this we are to be judged — when we are our own. What was Marius, if we look at him by his ancestors? In his seven consulships he has nothing more illustrious than that he was his own founder. If hereditary images had raised up Pompey, no one would have called him "the Great." Rome bore Servius for her king, in whose virtues nothing is more illustrious than the lowness of his name. What do those men seem to you, called from the plough, who by their poverty made the republic blessed? Turn over whatever man you will as noble: you will come to lowliness. Why do I recount men one by one, when I can show you this city? . . . Bare stood the hills, and amid walls so widely spread nothing is nobler than a lowly cottage: gleaming above its gabled roofs with pure gold, the Capitol shines forth. Can you reproach the Romans that, when they might hide their lowliness, they display it, and think these things not great unless it appear that they have risen from small beginnings?

THE OTHER SIDE. OF JUNIUS GALLIO: I shall begin from the father's praises. He was a most temperate young man and passed that slippery time without disgrace; he took a wife, raised a son, brought him to manhood. He is already become an old man, save that he does not yet seem so to himself; his luxury has gone so far that I accuse him. An old man in love, an old man drunk, wreathed with garlands and anointed with unguents, driving himself back into past years and revelling more lustily in pleasures than a youth — is this not a portent? A luxurious young man sins; but a luxurious old man is mad; his age is drained, his vices run wanton. OF PAPIRIUS FABIANUS: You sink your ship in harbour. The one slips at the usual time, the other at the unusual; the one at another's expense, the other at his own; the one follows his years, the other fights against old age. Your luxury is not what you wish it to seem: you do not feign these things, but do them; you do not play the lover, but love; you do not sketch the drinker, but drink; you do not unteach the squandering of goods, but squander them. No one, I think, imitates the vices he hates. What general flees from battle himself, that his army may fight well? Who, to repress bribery, has himself bought offices? Who, to soothe sedition, has thrown the republic into disorder? He does not check vices who provokes them.

OF JULIUS BASSUS. The state being freed, do not wonder that you saw me sad: for us the tyrant even now lives. The virginity which she had kept under the tyrant she lost under her father. Say, gallows-bird, for whom did you keep my sister a virgin? Say, if you please, "For myself." "I did not violate her," he says, "when it was permitted me." So is he worthy of marriage because he is unworthy of the cross? From his own cell he will move into his mistress's bedchamber — or will the mistress move from her bedchamber into his cell? OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS.

I do a thing not new, judges: I avenge my children against a stepmother; I beg that, because I avenged my son, I may not lose my daughter. Unless you succour me, the stepmother has won, I am beaten. I do not know whether I married a worse wife or stepmother. This girl is the dearer to me, that she was so hateful to her mother. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS. If she were an accomplice, I should await no one: you know how I hate a poisoner. I pressed on with the torments, I said: "Die worse than you killed"; the fires did not seem to me to burn enough, the lashes not to cut enough; I said: "If I can add anything to your torments, I think I will order my daughter brought; let someone call her hither to her mother." Why are you frightened, girl? Why have you fled back to my bosom? Why have you taken fright as at a stepmother?

One ought to pity her because she is an orphan. And yet she has kinsmen, she has her father's friends, she has you, the bravest guardian of her weakness.
