All rich wives demand servitude: believe me, she will want to reign over her own riches; and yet it is fair that I possess the house which has acknowledged me. If we should begin to be freer, if a somewhat finer house should gleam upon her fancy, if we should treat her a little less fawningly, she will leave us: and then it is a torment to lack riches, when once you have felt them. You see the difference between two wives: this one, if she leaves us, will reclaim her own; the other, dismissed, will not carry off what she gave. Many have married women without dowry; some have not accepted dowries even when named; some have been content even with bought slaves, and, when they might have accepted riches, have preferred to buy those to whom they might give freedom, rather than to sell their own.

Latro divided thus: whether a father can be accused on this ground. Here he placed that common question which he was wont to disdain: namely, that this is by no means usually objected to a father; that luxury is no more objected than avarice, than irascibility; that not a father's vices are usually accused, but his disease. Whether, so that something besides madness may be objected to a father, luxury may not be. "Otherwise," he says, "you allow sons to disinherit." Here he spends from his own store. Even if a father can be accused on this ground, whether he can by such a son. Here the reproach of vices. So you object drunkenness to your father, drunk; so wantonness, having been condemned for an injury. Even if he can be accused on this ground, even by such a son, whether, if he used this device to chastise his son, he is to be condemned. For the young man says: you ought to have rebuked me by any other means. What if you wished to avenge adultery by committing it? It is base to chastise vices in such a way as to imitate them. Then, whether he is luxurious by design. For the son does not grant this: "otherwise," he says, "why, if you began to mend your son thus, do you not stop now that you had mended him?"

The violated are of better condition than the virgin: yet to them it fell to change their marriages. Why, tyrannicide, did you receive a reward? Even now some woman is married under the tyrant's edict. The man who had fled the tyrant's edict returns with an edict. It was by the father's madness that this was done — that he could not accuse the tyrant. "What?" he says; "that man kept my daughter a virgin for another." Now he is a husband, who even under the tyrant could be nothing more than a ravisher. The man who was destined to be part of the dowry was left as her guardian. The edict was published, and to escape obeying it we fled. Nothing in the whole stretch of public slavery seemed more unworthy, nothing less to be borne by gods and men. And so the tyrant was killed after this. The girl was betrothed; everything was done according to the tyrant's edict.

OF MARULLUS. Not even amid her punishment did she cease to kill: and shall anyone think this woman could not have given poison without an accomplice? The girl who is said to have killed her brother — what did she ever do wrong before? The stepmother too killed her stepson before her daughter. And she is of good hope; do you ask for proof? She does not please her mother. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS. Even toward your ashes the stepmother is hostile; the one thing she can, she persecutes — your sister. What can the girl yet know but her brother? Let it profit her before you that her father praises her, and let it profit her that such a mother accuses her.

A young man is sought for adoption: if he is willing to go, let him inquire what kind of ancestors that old man who seeks him has, and how many, how great his goods, whether he can pledge himself for a price great enough. Someone wishes to capture childless old men, and to spread his hopes over others' deaths: let him scrutinize their wills, examine their fortunes; but when he seeks a wife, let him see whether she loves her marriage, whether she values nothing more than her husband, whether she is merciful, whether she is brave, whether she can, if anything befall her husband, bear ills together with him: if she has been furnished with these two goods, she is dowered. We cannot be happy together: as we are wont, we shall be unhappy together. "Do," she says, "what he commands; I do not wish you to offend your father on my account. I will go alone." You will go? Where, unhappy woman? What regions will you seek? Is there any place for you? Your father has shut the seas against us, mine the lands.

CESTIUS, on the father's side, used to say that the pretence of luxury should be hinted at rather than professed. Thus, he said, it will appear that he was pretending, if he is still pretending now; if he stops pretending, he shows that he now has no need of that device, as though his son were reformed; but he did not grant that the son was reformed, and constantly said that he feared nothing more than this interval of luxury; that interrupted vices rise the more violently. Latro thought the pretence should be openly confessed. I begin, he said, to defend not only an honourable old man but a prudent one, if I make what could seem a vice into a device. Why should he hint, rather than say, that he is frugal? BLANDUS declaimed the son with this figure, and answered for the disinherited man.

OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. An excellent son-in-law, whose one glory is that, compared with the crucified, he is more frugal. The slave guarded his mistress better than the father his daughter. The kindly father so bestowed his daughter as the angry tyrant bestowed others' daughters. Your enemies pray that you may have grandsons. When the father was sane, he fled rather than see this marriage. Do you think it too small a proof of madness that he drove the tyrant to death, the fathers into exile, the slaves to the cross? How is it that you, who flee thus, give in marriage thus? You are more honourable as an exile than as a father-in-law. If you wish to find your son-in-law's kinsmen, you must go to the cross.

OF MENTO. Do you not pity this girl? She is more wretched than her brother: he, no doubt, had a stepmother. "My daughter," she says, "is my accomplice." I began to be tortured, the stepmother to torture. You have attained, woman, what you wished: alone of all I felt my stepmother more when I lost her. OF PORCIUS LATRO. I had a son so good that even a stepmother could love him, had she not fallen in with one who could hate even her daughter. To such depths have the ages fallen, that there is a girlish parricide? So, if she does not understand the magnitude of the thing, is she fit for parricide? "But she is a poisoner's daughter," she says. If parents are looked to, why should she not rather seem like the father whom she pleases than the mother whom she displeases? Finally, I do not refuse that in her case even the mother's imitation be required: at this girl's age the mother was neither a stepmother nor a poisoner.

OF CESTIUS PIUS: Those who are compelled by their fathers to take wives are wont to say, "We are not yet fit for marriage": I, on the contrary, shun a wife because I am too fond of my wife. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: An unruly evil is a rich wife. When the orphan has brought an immense weight of gold, when her money has loaded our coffers, what else shall we be but blessed slaves? The one gives you a son, the other a patrimony: father, which is the richer? She whom you would join to me is wealthy, father: O if you knew how rich this woman too once was! "She is an orphan," he says: and this woman too is an orphan; of the two orphans, the one is more to be cared for by me than the one whom I made an orphan.

CESTIUS used to say that the young man's part should be coloured more carefully: that he does a thing not blameworthy; for thus he does not remit to his father what was remitted to him by his father. And so he narrated in such a way as to charge his own luxury too to his father: that the discipline had not been severe, that there was no rule of a well-ordered house, such as could shape a young man's character and lead him away from the vices of his age. "In a manner," he said, "I was sent ahead to luxury by my father . . . an old man dripping with unguent and a reveller; and so I seemed to no one too luxurious, but rather a little out of his senses. Rightly do they not punish every luxury in the young: they stop quickly. I stopped, when I had this example of luxury. You ask what remedy I had? Age: I now thought that what I was doing no longer became me."

OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. From a slave he has become a son-in-law, from a mistress a wife, from a master a father-in-law. Who would not think this marriage a tyrant's? I accuse the father of the tyrant's crimes, the tyrant of the father's. What shall I complain of in the tyrant? He is like the father. What shall I not complain of in the father? He is like the tyrant. Most wretched sister, under the tyrant you longed for your father, under your father you long for the tyrant. You forced upon your daughter what the tyrant had only permitted. Now, father, if you are sane, we must go into exile. For what more wretched thing can befall than that condition in freedom which others scarcely endure in slavery? We fled lest we be slaves. He turned our happiness into calamity: for it was far better to bear insult with the rest than, when all were freed, to be cast back, alone, into tyranny. To the slave he gave freedom, to his daughter slavery. To the slave he gave his daughter, from her he took her innocence. I know not what he means by praising the slave's merit: he ought to have praised the tyrant. Our slave, not foolish, preferred his hide and his head to present delights. If he says that he merely feared so great a crime, I will praise him and will wish him even now this same mind.

OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. I married a wife as yet stained by no scandals, and I do not wonder that she was then innocent: she was still a girl. OF BLANDUS. Grant that she is wicked; surely she is like her own mother; before parricide she ought to commit poisoning. "My daughter," she says, "is my accomplice." The gods destroy you! Even while you are tortured, you kill. A slave under torture named Cato as accomplice in a theft. What are you doing? Do you believe the torments more, or Cato? OF BUTEO. If an accomplice is to be sought from you, girl, name your father. Why the stepmother so late, the girl so soon? "My daughter," she says, "is my accomplice."

THE DIVISION. In this controversia there was no dispute: nearly all agree. LATRO made this the first question: whether a father can disinherit a son on account of marriage, when the choice in this matter is free to each man. GALLIO subjoined this: even if he can order a son to take a wife, can he order one who already has one? Latro made a second: if the father has the right to disinherit even on account of marriage, whether this son was not free to obey, since he had sworn. This he divided into these: whether no one is bound by an oath to which he was driven by necessity; whether he fulfilled the oath by marrying her; whether, even if he did not fulfil it, one is not bound by the obligation who, under compulsion, does something against an oath — and that this man was compelled by his father. If, by reason of the oath, he can obey his father, whether he ought to. Here come the girl's deserts and character. With this colour Latro used for the father:

This thought CESTIUS himself expressed in a sound manner; Alfius Flavus, his pupil, who had said the same thing more wantonly, he rebuked. FLAVUS said it thus: that when he had torn himself from sloth, he gradually returned to frugality, and his vice became hateful to him. "This was," he said, "why I stopped: I felt," he said, "that I was growing old." CESTIUS said this was sweeter, indeed, but censured the last epigram. "It is incredible," he said, "that, being a young man, he felt himself growing old, and I should not wish him to seem to have been luxurious so long until he lost his sense of feeling."

Other women have found themselves honourable husbands; this one has such a husband as they had under the tyranny. My sister is a maidservant's rival, and, that the mistress might marry, the fellow-slave was thrown out of her little cell. There was no greater crime in the tyrant than the one it pleased you to imitate. O you, sister, wretched, that you did not suffer this under the tyrant! For by now you would have ceased to suffer. Do you think this a reward — that, because he did not violate his mistress, he may violate her as much as he wishes? But this man, as you will say, did you an injury, because he delayed your kinship; if he had not held back, perhaps we should already have grandchildren from him. Let us have, if we can, a son-in-law our equal; if not, then one not to be blushed at, who has some kinsman, who has some sacred things and an inner shrine into which a wife may be led, whom we may join to our house, not one whom we should strike off our census.

May you perish ill! And I thought you were one woman's stepmother only. OF TRIARIUS. "Your daughter," she says, "is your accomplice." After this word she seemed to herself to have conquered. She wept for her lost brother at his funeral; she wrung the tears of the whole people from her own; and so the stepmother wished her to perish worse than her stepson. "My daughter," she says, "is my accomplice." This was the stepmother's last poisoning. OF Q. HATERIUS. Succour her, I beg, lest, when she has been tortured because she killed my son, she also, while being tortured, kill my daughter. I always carry out my children for burial by the lie or the poison of one and the same woman. She does not weep as much as is enough for a defendant. How shall I wring tears from her? Bring me my brother's likeness: see the tears stirred by sudden longing: did she have such a face when her mother was being tortured?

that the girl was moved not by mercy but by lust, and therefore it was no kindness. In his arguments he treated this part elegantly: even if she had done a kindness, gratitude was not to be returned in this way; further, that a kindness is what is given by judgement, not what is given by frenzy or sickness. HISPO ROMANIUS said with another colour that she had followed not from love of the young man but from hatred of her father; he wished to strip from her even the recommendation of love. BUTEO used a far-fetched colour; for he wished it to seem that all this was done not against the father's will, but with his secret persuasion while he openly dissembled; that this honourable match was devised by the father, since in no other way was it possible; for they could not otherwise have escaped, save with the father conniving.

FUSCUS ARELLIUS said: I am not going to accuse my father, but to defend myself, lest I be ill-spoken-of for another's luxury. The device conceived while the son was luxurious is superfluous now that he is reformed. In his narrative he had this colour: that the father's mind had collapsed in a sudden frenzy. A harlot hanging from the old man's neck, a herd of parasites poured round my father, base brawls with rivals, and day added to a nightly drinking-bout. I too thought at first it was a device, not a disease: I stopped being luxurious; he will stop, I said, if he began for my sake. He persists in youthful vices, more shamefully luxurious and longer. What shall I do?

OF PORCIUS LATRO. We who had borne everything, this we flee. He summons the slave and, because he had not deserved the cross, bids him deserve it. So, gallows-bird, could you embrace your mistress? Did you think either that the tyrant would live forever, or that the father would forever be merciful? Most fortunate will those women seem to whom a tyrant's rape befell. So, no doubt, he did her a kindness, in that he guarded his mistress from defilement, himself from the cross? When the new bride was being led with the unlucky torch to her dowry-slave, if there is any faith in me, I shuddered as though the edict were restored. I was considering what husband to choose for my sister. I will confess plainly: I now disdained the matches which had been available before our departure; I said: "In that time other maidens too were virgins." "He did not violate her," he says, "under the tyranny." O happy us, if not even now!

The other side. OF TRIARIUS. If we hated you, we should allow you to live with such a daughter. The cubs of certain beasts are born with rabies; poisons are deadly from the very root. How much did it add to her crimes that a stepmother bore her? What of the girl who scattered her brother to delay her pursuing father? You have an example that suits both a sister and a virgin.

But Latro said it was not worth so much to strip from the freed young man his recommendation, as to strip from the abandoned father his odium. ARELLIUS FUSCUS declaimed excellently; for he ordered her to be put away not on account of marriage to the heiress, but to be cast out even if there were no heiress. He said not that the other woman pleased him more, but that this one displeased him; and this, which Latro had run past, he pressed: that he feared the girl, rash, born among pirates, reared among pirates, undutiful toward her father. GALLIO said what all the schoolmen had passed over: that he feared she might be a spy and might disclose to pirates all their opportunities — or at least might seem to; that he did not wish to be an object of suspicion to the republic. JULIUS BASSUS feared that the girl might seem to have improperly exacted the oath; lest the young man should have any freedom, he added that he had sworn by his father.

If I wish to mend my father in his own way, I must be luxurious. SILO POMPEIUS gave the young man an advocate; which Latro thought should not be done in an accuser's person, that someone should accuse a father through an advocate. RUFUS VIBIUS, on the young man's side: a merry old man! In his son's honour he gets drunk. In his narrative he used this colour: that the father was dissolute; that, his mind now slipping, he had begun to praise luxury; to say that those live more happily who let themselves love to the end; that one should have only what one has received; meanwhile to rebuke, as though they were not . . . "A boorish young man!" he said. "Premature severity," he said, "is not frugality but gloom: what will you do as an old man?" Do you not believe that this was said by a man who, even when he wishes to rebuke vices,

OF TRIARIUS. Come, is this not a reward — to watch, alone, the crosses of all? I am sure that, if the tyrant had had a daughter, he would not have written the edict. He proclaims a festal day, he orders the images of the ancestors to be opened, when most of all they should be covered. OF VARIUS GEMINUS. In the same hour he made him both freedman and son-in-law. You did what a tyrant does not compel except when he is angry, and does not even then make men slaves when he is compelled. What sort of son-in-law have you? — that I may render him his own praise — a thrifty slave, to be sure. Your slave-women will bear brothers for your daughter. As for the setting-out of the facts, the evils of the tyranny are indeed bitter, yet I will set out things still sadder that were done after the tyranny. I did not doubt that she would marry the tyrannicide. If she had been violated under the tyrant, we should have had this consolation: "It has not befallen you alone." I think the tyrant not yet slain; even now I see a tyrant's marriage.

The division. Cestius divided the conjecture into two parts, and first asked whether she needed an accomplice; then, if she needs or needed one, whether she had this one. But he did not keep measure; for he both handled at length that commonplace — that a sister cannot be driven to her brother's death — and meanwhile wished her to seem so much a girl as to be fit for no service. And so most elegantly did MONTANUS Votienus deride in this controversia the follies of the rhetors, that they declaimed as though this girl who is named were an infant, and did not understand that, were she such, she would not even be a defendant. "And so this," he said, "we ought to set before ourselves: a girl of an age at which a crime is perhaps credible." That, indeed, he used to say was intolerable which CESTIUS had introduced: the mother saying to the daughter, "Give your brother poison," the daughter answering, "Mother, what is poison?"

TRIARIUS, while catching at a manly epigram, said foolishly that he had sworn even by the orphan. For Cestius said it was a poor thing to abandon her now as an orphan, if he had even sworn by her. Latro said that to swear by the father too was foolish; for nothing is less fitting than that a man should swear by his father, when he is about to abandon her father. All gave the girl an honourable mother, all said with what mercy she had departed, moved by it, with what love. Pollio alone wishes her to have done it by judgement: for he said she could not live with pirates; that as soon as she found an honourable occasion of departing, she departed.

is luxurious? ARGENTARIUS declaimed with this colour: two men are luxurious in one house: one young, one old; one a son, one a father; both walk abroad in equally unrestrained dress. The one says this to you: I use the pleasures granted to my age and fulfil the law of youth; I began in good time; as soon as I have paid this first service of youth, as a debt and a customary thing, I shall return to good morals. I do what my father did, when he was young. Will he deny it? Of what kind his cause is, you shall see; let him do, if not what ought to be done, at least what is wont. The other says: I know I walk abroad a new marvel of the city, a luxurious old man, but this kind of chastising seemed more moving; to mend my son, I myself began to sin. So, if your grandfather were alive, that no one in the house might be luxurious, there would have been three of you luxurious.

OF MARULLUS. Now I shall know whether you deserved your liberty, if as a free man you do not deserve the cross. The thing I charge, the man who did it to more women was killed. OF P. VINICIUS. Now in our house there is a marriage of which I should be ashamed even if it were a rape. How wretched do you think those men, judges, for whom the two most wretched things had to be wished for — a tyrant and a ravisher? The one recommendation of your son-in-law is that once he thought himself unworthy of this girl. OF VALLIUS SYRIACUS. We are in such a condition, judges, that we must console our sister either because she was not raped or because she has married. And yet what did he deserve, while it was permitted him by his master to be a most innocent slave?

TRIARIUS made it much more foolish, because he did not invent it but corrupted it; for he drew it from Cestius's sententia: he had brought in the stepmother saying, "Give your brother poison"; he made her answer, "Mother, give some to me too." For what is so absurd as that a mother should so speak with a girl, "Give your brother poison"? Nor did he tolerate that sententia of Triarius which Haterius used differently, when he had come to the epilogue: "At this point the defendant ought to weep; does the girl weep? I will find how she may weep; let someone bring hither my brother's likeness." For she, if she is so much a girl as to say, "Mother, what is poison?" cannot be of such piety that the likeness of her brother should stir her to tears. So great, indeed, is the error in all pursuits, but most in eloquence, whose rule is uncertain, that some both understand their own faults and love them.

QUINTUS HATERIUS, on the father's side, raised a most beautiful image: for he began suddenly, in that rush of speech he was wont to use, to describe — as though he heard some uproar — all things laid waste and plundered, country houses burning with fires, the flights of country folk; and when he had filled everything with terror, he added: why have you shuddered, young man? Your father-in-law is come. The epigram of GLYCON is very slight and Greek: "Consume your own begetter: we have a father." He made tolerable that thing, when he described the force of an oath: that it is what sanctions treaties, by which armies are bound: "An oath is a bond, and even among pirates a sure pledge." ARTEMON dwelt upon the same thought, on the young man's side; when he had said his father was abandoned, he added: "Revile now the archpirate, the murderer, the temple-robber: add, if you will, the perjurer too."

On the father's side GLYCON SPYRIDION said: "I spend unwillingly, but you do not stop." AGROITAS OF MASSILIA said a far livelier epigram than the other Greek declaimers, who in this controversia jested like rivals. Now Agroitas spoke unpolishedly, that you might know he had not been among the Greeks, with strong epigrams, that you might know he had been among the Romans. The epigram that was praised was this: "On luxury we have disagreed: you spend with pleasure, I with pain." DAMAS SCOMBRUS: "Possessing . . . you are luxurious in luxury."

OF SEPULLIUS BASSUS. We made the wedding with the house shut up. The slave's mistress was led into common quarters with him: so did this fellow not touch my sister's hand except while being freed? OF ASINIUS POLLIO. Amid the wedding Fescennines they jested about the cross of our son-in-law. I remember spending a most wretched day, when the state began to be enslaved; I remember spending a most wretched day, when we fled into exile: among these days I count my sister's wedding. Most wretched sister, perhaps you are stepmother to your own home-bred slaves. "Father, I wish to take a wife: say which of the maidservants you betroth to me." Against. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. He saved his mistress. If anyone had informed the tyrant, he alone would have hung on the cross.

CESTIUS understood that he had said childishly, "Mother, what is poison?"; for he used to deride MURREDIUS, who, imitating this sententia in his epilogue, when he had begun to address the girl and said: "Compose yourself into the bearing of those in peril, pour out tears, let your hands fall to your knees, you are a defendant," had made the girl answer, "Father, what is a defendant?" And Cestius used to say: "If, to deride me, a charming man said this, then I too now know that I speak a foolish sententia; but I say many things not because they please me, but because they will please my hearers."

DIOCLES OF CARYSTUS: "But if comely flesh is changed by luxury." HERMAGORAS used to speak epigrams that were rare but pointed, and such as would deeply affect an attentive listener but slip past a careless and inattentive one. In this controversia he said: "O cruel fortune! We did these things commanding one another." BARBARUS said a common thought commonly enough: "You shall know, child, that the mind is still in its first bloom." More elegantly Hispo ROMANIUS composed this: my frugality pleases you, because I have kept my patrimony, because I have added to it, because I married in good time, always loved my wife, kept myself safe from every scandal. This I affirm — that in my whole life I have done nothing more frugal. A thing said by all, SYRIACUS VALLIUS said most quickly: son, let us stop when you wish.

The division. Latro divided into these questions: whether, even if he ought not to have given his daughter in marriage thus, he cannot for this reason be condemned for madness. "It is lawful," he says, "for me to give my daughter to whom I will: by that reasoning I shall be accused even if I send my son-in-law a notice of divorce. I gave my daughter in marriage badly: so have many others. What do you think of those who take their daughters away from . . . but he gave her badly . . . nor shall I be condemned for this. You ought to accuse a father who is mad, not to govern one who is sane. Whether I did this without reason, we shall see: it is enough if I did it with a sound mind." Then: whether he ought to have given his daughter in marriage thus. This he divided into this: whether, even if the slave deserved well, gratitude ought not to have been repaid him thus; then, whether he deserved well. About the slave's deed he disputed first, then about his intention. For of what sort is the deed? He did not defile his mistress. Increase the kindnesses: he neither killed his master nor, as an adulterer, gave his master poison. It is no kindness to abstain from crime. And the tyrant permitted men to ravish their mistresses, he did not compel them. Then preserve this kindness of his which you praise: otherwise he did an injury, if she was not rescued from injury but reserved for it. Yet there would have been this consolation, to suffer along with many. Finally, other women suffered under the tyranny, this one in freedom; the rest with their own people away, this one with them present; in the others it was called defilement, in this one marriage; in the others an end of the injury was awaited, in this one none; finally, the ravishers of those women were nailed to the cross, the ravisher of this one was set free.

And that of RUFUS VIBIUS he used to say was more tolerable, but itself too worthy of some reproach: he had said in the epilogue, "Nurse, take away the defendant." That in Haterius, who both promised an orator and proved one, he denied he could bear, which he had said: "This defendant must not be sent into exile, but carried"; "when he knew," he said, "that men condemned to deportation into exile are wont to be put up for contract." For what does he wish to be understood by this sententia? That the girl is wholly unable to walk, or unable to walk all the way to exile?

Then about the slave's intention. LATRO made this colour on the son's side, as to why the slave had not defiled her: that he feared punishment, that he knew it would come about, when the state was freed, that all who had defiled their mistresses would pay the penalty; and the last hour seemed already drawing near to a tyranny then driven to the height of madness, which never arises except from desperation. "And so, when he saw," he said, "slaves being nailed to the cross, he cried out: 'This I knew would come to pass.'" In his closing speech Latro said: "In the slave's name too I can complain of you, who made him, who had been thrifty, worthless." ALBUCIUS used this colour: "The girl was still unripe and not yet fit for injury, and for that reason we did not take her away — because, by the benefit of her age, she could not feel the tyranny."

it is true, but neither could her mother. SILO, on the father's side, made a comparison between the mother and the daughter, and declaimed the whole through this figure: "I will not," he said, "tell you what sort a poisoner ought to be. I shall waste effort if I begin to describe that she ought to be advanced in age, practised by use, hated by her husband, one who could kill even her daughter. It is superfluous to use many words; in this very case we have a model of a poisoner. Let us compare the two defendants with each other; nor is there reason for you to seek someone to lead your inquiry through all the parts of the comparison; I will tell you how I accused her. I charged her with her past life: can you charge this girl with hers?"

CESTIUS said: "I plainly will not detract from the slave his own praise: he had a good mind; he hoped it might come about that, if he kept her a virgin, he would be freed at his mistress's wedding." VARIUS GEMINUS said: "Perhaps he had a mistress; in her he found delight — for some men shrink from the embrace of virgins. Perhaps he knew she would not yield, and — the thing which sometimes makes even worthless slaves thrifty — he feared evil fortune." And he added this sententia, which was much circulated: "Would the gallows-bird have dared to lie with his mistress, unless the father had permitted him?" And he said this: "Was it for this, father, that you had returned from exile?

And so he went round everything and defended by comparing. That little question which had been handled in the first part by some — whether she needed an accomplice at all — he ran through thus: "The defendant kept saying through the whole pleading: 'Say what accomplice I had'; I denied that she needed one; I said: 'You were in the same house, the poison was known to the stepmother, the opportunity easy for one living together, you were not suspected, no one feared you on account of your sister.'" On the other side he used this colour: that the stepmother had given the stepson poison so that her own daughter might be sole heir; that the same girl had been both accomplice in the poisoning and its cause.

Into exile, then, why did we flee?" BUTEO wished the father to seem really deranged in mind, and in the narration said this: "How sad he came home from the tyrant's edict! How he wept in his daughter's bosom! I think that at that time his mind was shaken." VARIUS GEMINUS thus on the abstinence: "He did not dare to defile his mistress and drag her into his cell. Unless perhaps you prefer me to tell it thus: even then he had begun to hope for his marriage with his mistress."

He said all the declaimers had wished to say something new in that place where the stepmother named her daughter as accomplice. "HYBREAS said," he says: "'What then? Did she lie against her own daughter? No: but against mine.'" This sententia FUSCUS ARELLIUS, being one of the Asians, did not say by chance, but transferred it word for word: "What then?" he said. "Did she lie about her own daughter? Nay, about mine." More modestly did HATERIUS turn this sententia: "What then? Did she lie? Why should she not lie about her accuser's daughter?"

On the father's side Latro said that there was need rather of defence than of colour. VARIUS GEMINUS defended the deed itself: that great men had married freedwomen as wives. "M. Cato," he said, "married the daughter of his own tenant farmer." "But a freeborn one." I answer: "But Cato; there is more difference between me and Cato than between a freedman and a tenant." What advantages would a submissive and obedient husband have! He will fear no wantonness, no insult of words, no rival, no divorce. I shall always have my daughter at home;

CESTIUS said: "She named her stepson's sister." ALBUCIUS said: "What had she, that she should doubt whether to spare the daughter of the man by whom she was being killed, the sister of the man whom she had killed?" TRIARIUS said: "What then? Did the mother lie? Take away the name 'mother': after her condemnation she is a stepmother." BLANDUS said: "I will name the girl who stood by her father, who wept for her dead brother, did not weep when her mother was tortured." SILO POMPEIUS said: "'My daughter,' she says, 'is my accomplice.' After this I noted in her the same face I had seen when her stepson was dying."

for whom I long the more, because I was so long away from her. Then he praised the freedman's deed. ALBUCIUS even turned philosopher; he said that no one was born free, no one a slave; that fortune afterwards imposed these names upon individuals. "In short," he said, "you know that we too were lately slaves." He recalled King Servius. POMPEIUS SILO, using this colour, said: "My patrimony was exhausted by the injuries of the tyranny; I had no dowry to give." ARGENTARIUS wished it to seem that he had done it with the girl's consent. "She seemed," he said, "to favour him; certainly she ought to have."

MONTANUS VOTIENUS said that MARCELLUS MARCIUS, his friend, of whom he often makes mention in his writings as of an eloquent man, had said this sententia: "She found how, though condemned, to accuse, dying to kill, tortured to torture. This is no information, but a second poisoning by the stepmother." Latro had said, when he had described the torments: "I stood over her head not as accuser but as torturer; I myself put on the fires, I myself laid hands on to stretch the rack. Shall I not drink that woman's blood, not tear out her eyes? She snatched away my son; had I not crushed her the more swiftly, she would have carried off my daughter too." TRIARIUS said: "When I accused, I charged poisoning; in the last part, amid my prayers, I roused the girl to avenge her brother. This above all moved the judges, this above all offended the stepmother." ALBUCIUS said: "After she named my daughter she looked back at me — to know, no doubt, whether she had tortured me enough." NICETES said admirably in this same place: "'My daughter,' she says, 'is privy with me,' and added, 'in this.'"

GAVIUS SABINUS used this colour, so as to pull down his own dignity as far as he could and to confess his lowliness. "And for this reason," he said, "he could the more easily avoid being defiled, because no one directed his eyes toward our house. And I had considered," he said, "what to do, to whom to give her in marriage: I had to seek some freedman as a son-in-law. What then? Another man's freedman rather? This one I now know; I know what his feeling is toward us; if I die, I know I shall leave my daughter safe with him." And he added this sententia, which was much taken up:

MONTANUS, when he was treating that commonplace — that even wicked parents wish their children to be innocent — said: "That woman can pretend her daughter a poisoner, if she can make her one; it is harder to befoul one's children than to destroy them." And this: "Favour the age, judges; since it bears great crimes, let it not bear premature ones too; favour it, that no crime be committed but the usual one; favour it, that rather a stepmother not cease to commit parricide than a sister begin. I was able to condemn her, I was not able to escape her. You did it too late, stepmother: if you had said this before, you could have bargained for collusion; not rightly, when you were being condemned, were you so spirited; rightly you can do nothing. If there is any faith in me, an accuser, I feared snares for the defendant; nowhere did I let the girl from my bosom, I myself tasted all her food beforehand. O mortality, heedless of the future! After I had brought the stepmother to the torturer, I ceased to fear for my daughter.

I did not scorn as a son-in-law the man who had scorned a tyrant. ACCIUS POSTUMIUS used this colour: "Nothing," he said, "is more dangerous than envy; this wise men teach us to avoid as a pestilence: this I have avoided. There was great envy: everyone reproached us with the fortune of our children. The women hated my daughter, the fathers hated me, as though I were set apart from the common misery and reproached them with it: in the one way I honourably could, I made my daughter like the rest, my fortune equal to the public fortune; all envy is taken away; I have no daughter more honourable than yours, but I had a slave more frugal than you."

All used this colour — that the daughter was named by the stepmother to grieve the father. GALLIO said more: "Perhaps," he said, "she named her to conceal the true accomplices; perhaps, because the accuser pressed most fiercely, terrified by this fear she sought to put an end to the torments; perhaps, too, stupefied by the excessive pain of the torture, she did not know what she was saying." Last he said: "Perhaps for this — that she who was paying the penalty of poisoning might exact the penalty of the accusation." He added that thought: "I judge it from my own feelings: at the time when I raged with anger, with hatred, I looked round all the paths of vengeance, forgetting innocence; if the stepmother had had children of her own, I should have killed them. Against this very girl how often I wished to make an onset! But for this she was safe from me — that she was not safe from her mother."

pr.1. Question me on whatever you wish, and then let me return from these youthful pursuits to my old age. I will confess to you: by now the thing has become a weariness. At first I leapt to it gladly, as though I were bringing back to myself the best part of my life; then I began to be ashamed, as though I were spending a long while on no serious matter. This is the nature of the schoolmen's studies: lightly touched they delight, but handled and brought closer they breed disgust. Let me then drain my memory once and for all, and dismiss me — even if it must be by compelling me with an oath, by which I should swear that I have told what I knew and what I heard and what I judged to bear upon this matter.

pr.2. But I do not think it bears upon the matter how L. Magius, the son-in-law of T. Livius, declaimed — though for a time he had his own following, since men praised him not in his own honour but carried him along for his father-in-law's sake; nor how L. Asprenas or the elder Quintilianus declaimed: I pass over those whose fame was extinguished along with themselves. About SCAURUS, if you ask me — when you have heard him along with me — you are unfair. I have known no one whose talent the Roman people forgave more stubbornly. He used to speak carelessly: often he learned his case on the very benches, often while he was putting on his cloak; then, looking more like a man quarrelling than pleading, he wished to call forth some utterance from his opponents and to come to a wrangle: he knew his own powers. Nothing was more charming than he, nothing more ready: his manner of speaking was of the old style, the weightiness too of words not common, his very face and bearing of body marvellously fitted to oratorical authority.

pr.3. But from all this one may know, not how great an orator the idle Scaurus showed himself, but how much he threw away. Most of his pleadings were bad, yet in all of them some trace of a great and neglected talent stood out. Rarely was any pleading good — and even that one you would set down to luck. To such a pass had a long, nay perpetual, sloth brought him, that he wished to take pains over nothing, and could take pains over nothing. He published seven speeches, which were afterwards burned by a decree of the senate. The fire had done well by him; but there survive little books that war with his reputation — far looser, indeed, than the pleadings themselves; for when care abandoned those, heat assisted; these have less of heat, no less of carelessness. We heard him declaim, and most lately indeed under M.' Lepidus, in such a way that — which was the hardest thing of all — he was displeased with himself.

pr.4. You ask about T. Labienus? He declaimed not indeed before a crowd, but excellently. He did not admit the crowd, both because this custom had not yet been brought in, and because he thought it base and a mark of frivolous self-display. For he affected the censor's frown, though his spirit was of another kind: a great orator, who, having struggled out of many hindrances, had reached the fame of his talent because men confessed it rather than because they wished it. His poverty was utter, his ill-repute utter, the hatred of him utter. But that eloquence must be great which pleases men against their will; and since the favour of men reveals talents and the favour of men feeds them, how great must be the force that bursts out among obstacles? There was no one who, while he flung every reproach at the man, did not grant much to his talent.

pr.5. The colour of his oratory was of the old age, the vigour of the new, the polish midway between our age and the former, so that either party could claim him as its own. His freedom of speech was so great that it passed beyond the name of freedom, and, because he mangled ranks and men on every side, was called Rabies, "Frenzy." His spirit, among his vices, was huge, and, in the likeness of his talent, violent — one that had not yet laid aside its Pompeian breath amid so much peace. In his case a new penalty was first devised: for it was brought about by his enemies that all his books should be burned — a new and unwonted thing, that punishment should be exacted of studies.

pr.6. By heaven, this cruelty, turned to the punishment of talents for the public good, was invented after Cicero's day: for what would have come to pass, if it had pleased the triumvirs to proscribe Cicero's talent too? The immortal gods are slow indeed but sure avengers of the human race, and they turn great examples back upon the heads of those who invent them; and by a most just exchange of suffering, what each man has devised for another's punishment he often expiates by his own. What madness so great drives you on, men most demented? Plainly there is not enough cr+uelty of the known kind for punishments: you hunt up new ones against your own selves, by which you may perish; and if Nature has withdrawn anything from all suffering of the body — as the talent and the memory of a name — you find out how to bring these too back to the same

pr.7. bodily evils. To set a torch to studies, and to take vengeance upon the monuments of learning — how great and how unsatisfied a savagery, when other material does not content it! The gods grant us better — that these punishments of talents began in the age in which talents had ceased! As for him who had pronounced this sentence against the writings of Labienus, later, while he was still living, his own writings were burned — by an example now not evil, because his own. Labienus did not bear this insult, nor did he wish to survive his own talent, but ordered himself to be carried into the monuments of his ancestors and there shut in — fearing, no doubt, lest the fire which had been applied to his name should be denied to his body: he did not merely make an end of himself, but even buried himself.

pr.8. I remember that once, when he was reciting a history, he rolled up a great part of the book and said: "These things which I pass over will be read after my death." How great was the freedom in those pages, which even Labienus dreaded? A neat saying of CASSIUS SEVERUS, a man most hateful to Labienus, was reported at that time when the books of Labienus were being burned by decree of the senate: "Now," he said, "I must be burned alive, who have learned them by heart." I will show you a pretty little book, which you may seek from your friend Gallio. He recited the reply written to Labienus on behalf of Bathyllus the freedman of Maecenas, in which you may look up to the spirit of the young man, provoking those teeth to bite.

pr.9. But now, I think, you no longer used to hear anything — though my Mela knit his brow. He had much talent, no judgment: everything carried to the last degree of swelling, so that it lay not outside health but outside nature. For who could endure a man saying, about fountains, "they rain back from the sky," and, about the sprinklings, "perfumed showers," and, about the dressing of greenery, "embossed woods," and, about a painting, "rising groves"? Or that thing which I remember him saying about sudden deaths, when you had brought me there: "Whatever of birds flies, whatever of fishes swims, whatever of wild beasts runs about, is buried in our bellies. Ask now why we die suddenly: we live by deaths."

pr.10. Ought we not then, even though he had already been set free, to have satisfaction made to us out of his hide? Nor am I one of the strictest judges who would direct everything to the exact rule: I think much should be forgiven to talents; but vices are to be forgiven, not monstrosities. Yet if any things were said tolerably, I shall not withhold them, though they may not seem many: do you add the rest. OSCUS said not unhandsomely, but did himself harm; for, while he wished to say nothing except in a figure, his speech was not figured but distorted. And so not without wit did the rhetorician PACATUS, when he met him at Massilia one morning, salute him with a figure: "I might," he said, "have said, 'Hail, Oscan.'" He himself was far from eloquence, born to brand reproaches upon the talents of all. There was no one on whom he did not stamp something that could not be escaped.

pr.11. On that Passienus he imposed an obscene name, the first syllable changed into Greek — a declaimer subtle but dry; to that Sparsus, who kept a common school with a certain rhetorician, he said: "Can you understand a controversia, you who do not understand that you are washing a brick?" SPARSUS, however, used to speak violently, but harshly. He had set himself to the imitation of Latro, yet was never like him except when he said the same things.

pr.12. He used his own words, but Latro's epigrams. He had a contest with BASSUS, whom you too have heard, an eloquent man, from whom you would wish to take away the bitterness he pursued and the pretence of oratorical pleading. There is nothing more unbecoming than when a schoolman imitates the forum which he does not know. And so I loved CAPITO, whose declamation on Popillius is wrongly put under the name of poor Latro: he was a schoolman in good faith, and in those declamations which turned out well for him he is to be preferred to anyone after the first tetrad.

pr.13. You ask what I make the first tetrad? Latro, Fuscus, Albucius, Gallio. As often as these clashed, the glory lay with Latro, the palm with Gallio; the rest arrange as you please: I have given you the power over them all. Let these, the less famous, withdraw into their place — Paternus and Moderatus, Fabius, and any of neither bright name nor obscure. Since I have offered myself to you to your full content, allow me also to bring forth from my bosom some whom you do not know, to whom not talent but opportunity was lacking, that they might reach fame.

pr.14. GAVIUS SILO declaimed well, to whom Caesar Augustus, when he had often heard him pleading causes in the colony of Tarraco, gave full testimony; for he said: "Never have I heard a more eloquent head of a household." But while he set above all the head of a household, he was withdrawing the orator: he thought it part of eloquence to hide eloquence. CLODIUS TURRINUS too used to declaim with zeal, whose son is joined to you in brotherly love, a young man destined for the highest eloquence, if only he did not prefer to exercise what he has rather than to attain what he is able to.

pr.15. But Turrinus the father had taken much from his powers, while he followed the Apollodoreans and thought their school the supreme law of speaking; yet so much of his powers survived as would have been strong even if art had been wanting. He spoke epigrams that were excited, insidious, aiming at something. He never failed to make a controversia for Latro about the colour. Latro was never wont to dispute at a banquet or at any other time than when he could declaim. He used to say that some colours were at first sight hard, rough: that these could not be approved except in delivery. And so he denied that he could please anyone except as a whole; that he knew his own powers, and, in confidence of them, dared things fearful to others and abrupt; that he did not persuade the judge of many things, but carried them off.

pr.16. TURRINUS, on the contrary, approved nothing unless it was safe — not because he was feeble, but because he was circumspect. No one set out his cases more carefully, no one answered more readily; and so he owed to eloquence both his money and the dignity which he held, the first man in the province of Spain. He had been born, indeed, of a most splendid father, his grandfather being a guest-friend of the deified Julius; but in the civil war he raised again the weakened strength of his noble house, and so brought it to the highest dignity that, if anything was lacking to him, you may know it was opportunity. From him too his son — that is, my son, for I have never distinguished him from yours — has in his speaking his father's diligence, by which he deliberately blunts the powers of his own talent. This he follows in his very manner of life too — a young man who would rise to the summit, were he not content with a modest place; and therefore he is worthy that fortune should keep faith with desires so modest. That I have set down their names from no excessive favour but from sure judgment, you will know when I have reported their epigrams, either equal to those of the best-known authors or to be preferred.

HISPO ROMANIUS had said: "Shall I call this man a husband — a late ravisher?" This word, as not used among the ancients, displeased some men. In the same sense of the word, but so as to be beyond reproach, GAVIUS SABINUS used it, saying that the public vengeance against slaves had not yet been completed: "Even now in our house there remains a leftover ravisher."

FURIUS SATURNINUS, who condemned Volesus, had a greater name in the forum than in declamations; yet he used to declaim so honourably that you would know him not less fitted for this material, but less familiar with it. He, in this controversia, declaiming with the son of L. Lamia, said this sententia: "The father has become worse than a tyrant, the slave better than himself." Many tried to draw a sententia from the deed of purchase. ALBUCIUS said: "Bring me the tablets.

What is this? The father-in-law took the son-in-law by formal conveyance." TRIARIUS said: "'Not a runaway, not a vagrant': so, if we have a bad vendor, is our son-in-law a runaway?" BLANDUS said: "Let us read the warranty-tablets: 'free from theft and damage.' This is the praise of our son-in-law." GALLIO said: "He is free from theft, free from damage." SPARSUS said: "Show the tablets. What have we to do with this son-in-law? The former owner warranted that he was not a runaway. I congratulate you, posterity: you will not have a runaway father." VARIUS GEMINUS said: "'Not a vagrant'; I add, not a runaway; I add, free from damage and theft. Have I detracted at all from your son-in-law's nobility?"

Pollio used to say that he laughed because the declaimers had decreed that this man was at all events bought-and-paid-for. I think you wonder that in this controversia all the declaimers were of sound mind. They were not. NEPOS MAMILIUS, when he was urging the freedman to divorce the sister, said: "Repay us the favour, and do you too set my sister free." NEPOS LICINIUS did not yield to him; for he said: "Pass beneath these benches, slaves, pass over, freedmen — bought-and-paid-for kindred." And when he had taken up that elegant thought, bandied about by everyone — "Sister, I wish you barrenness" — he added: "Nor is there reason for you to wonder that I fear your offspring: I am quite sure that tyrants are born thus."

THE LAW: Children shall maintain their parents, or be bound. THE THEME: A man had three sons — one brave, one a tyrant, one an adulterer. The brave son was captured by pirates, and wrote to his father about his ransom. The father wrote to the pirates that he would give double the sum, if they cut off the son's hands. The pirates released him. He came home, killed the tyrant, killed the adulterer, and being now poor, his father seeks maintenance from him; he refuses. — Give me the letter of this hungering man. "Let his hands," he says, "be cut off." Upon whatever part of my body let his cruelty rather rush: the rest of my limbs are my own, my hands are the republic's. Do I, perhaps, ask the reward of a tyrant-slayer? Send me away such as you received me from the pirates. I have no cause to complain of fortune: behold the man who [betrayed?] my hands . . . flees for refuge. "If you cut off," he says, "his hands." If you are angry, write rather: if you kill him. As a tyrant-slayer I ask the tyrant's end. I do not fear that judges will bind the hands which the pirates loosed.

THE THEME: A man, going abroad, left his wife behind. While he was away, a handsome, rich, unknown young man moved into the neighbourhood, was repeatedly rebuffed by the wife, fell sick, died, and made the wife his sole heir on the ground that she was chaste and could not be corrupted. The husband, on his return, accuses her of adultery. OF PORCIUS LATRO: Although the morals of the state have now sunk so low that no one can seem too credulous in suspecting adultery, yet I have been so far from that vice that I rather fear someone may charge me with too much patience or too much dullness, in bringing so late a complaint. I do not accuse my wife of adultery save now that she is grown rich; I drag her as defendant from a house in which nothing of mine is left. While I have travelled so long abroad, and have fled no peril by land or sea, she has earned more within a single neighbourhood than I in a whole voyage over the sea. After such great profits of unchastity, if I can keep silent, I must confess that I was away for this reason — to vie with my wife in increasing my patrimony by travel. This, judges, is my torment — that, branded by your verdict, though she lose her doubled dowry, she will yet have more from her gains than the condemned must lose; so much has her rich lover poured out upon her, that even after punishment it pays to have been an adulteress. What I charged my wife as I set out, I know;

OF ALBUCIUS SILUS. What more do you require? The commander bore the punishment, the traitor the price. We saw this man gloomier when his son was proclaimed commander than when he was captured. Give an account, old man, how you returned safe, alone, with the gold, when even commanders are captured. The young man was proclaimed commander, all rejoicing except his father.

Of all the ills that fortune, by land and sea, has heaped upon me, both privately and publicly — tyrant and adulterer and pirates — I have experienced nothing harder than my father: the tyrant, though he feared my hands, did not cut them off; the wrong of my marriage took nothing from my body; the pirates, as though they lived by my favour, pitied me for nothing; one enemy alone I had who was inexorable. O happy republic, that, with my enemy removed, I did not sail before the tyrant was slain! "I begot you," he says, "I reared you": surely you rendered that service to the tyrant too, and to the adulterer. If you cannot ransom these hands through yourself, appeal to the republic. The adulterer was buried with his hands, the tyrant cast out with his. By great crimes the laws of nature perish: you are no more my father than those were my brothers. Hear a new word from a captive: I am safe, if my father has nothing. "Whatever you have, send for the ransom of your son": there is no reason for you to fear: you will not lack maintenance, when you have said you are the father of a tyrant-slayer;

the rest — how a handsome, rich, unknown young man moved into the neighbourhood of a handsome and, in her husband's absence, too free woman; how, by constant satiety of daily lust, day and night, his strength drained, he perished — ask of rumour. I ask you, judges, what was my duty: could I, with my honour safe, suspect nothing about an inheritance into which I am named even as confirming witness by my wife? I have come for nothing else than to complain of my fortune; for the case you know better.

OF CESTIUS PIUS. He received more gold than could be hidden. Do not wonder: he had sold both the commander and his son. "Beware of treason." We have already guarded against it at the elections. The enemy would have taken your gold from you, had they not given it. When the ransom was being discussed, all were in the senate-house except his rival. "Beware of treason." The dying man's information was brief, the son's was modest. OF BLANDUS. How did they let you go? If nothing else, you both begot a leader and wished to be one yourself. If we had not decreed it, you ought to have awaited our counsel; if we had decreed it, your duty. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS the elder. Whence those folds of the father so heavy? Do they perhaps bring back the bones of his son? The defendant, no doubt, awaits your verdicts — as though he did not know what you think of him. Not once were you among the enemy, but once we sent envoys. The commander does not dare to name you — as his father. OF JUNIUS GALLIO.

you begged for an adulterer son. Seek now how tyrants are made. OF CESTIUS PIUS: Give me my father's letters. You ask whence I have them, when you sent me none? "I will give double the money": it is plain — he is begging for an only son. "I will give double money": one sum for the son, the other for the tyrant-slayer. "If you cut off his hands": this is not lawful even with adulterers. "I had no money." But you can ask those men — and ask boldly: I fell among merciful pirates. Why do I not maintain him? Because, though my son was captured — it is surely too little if I say you did not ransom me — I cannot maintain him: I have lost my hands. Do you not believe it? Read the letters. You were giving double money — to the greedy you were giving it, to pirates you were giving it: so the pirates themselves excused themselves, when they cut off my hands: "your father ordered it," they said; "it is a great deed, but for a great price it is allowed."

It is time, judges, that a husband be believed about his wife — that so handsome a woman could be loved: a chaste woman could perhaps be loved thus, that she might not be solicited; and there is no cause for her to say: that was not in my power. You are mistaken, judges, if you do not think that a greater incitement to soliciting a matron is the hope of corrupting her than a face, however lovely and charming. If as much could be hoped in a beautiful woman as can please, all beautiful women would turn all eyes upon themselves. A matron who wishes to be safe against the wantonness of a solicitor should go out adorned only so far as may keep off the unchaste, if by nothing else, by the modesty of her years; let her keep her eyes cast down to the ground; against an officious greeter let her be inhuman rather than immodest; even in the necessary exchange of a return greeting let her be covered with much blushing. So let her pledge herself to modesty; let her deny her unchastity by her face long before she denies it by word. Into these guards of preserved integrity no lust will break.

He was an excellent young man, most modest, who would have yielded to his father if he could have done so with his duty unimpaired. Again we must judge between you — between father and son. The candidate came forward against his father: if we had known how to understand his silence, even then he had modestly given us information. You had authority among the enemy: it was plain that you were angry with the state. Our envoys were bringing gold; the father was carrying it off. You had said that they would come too late: they did not come too late; they met our commander. The commander accuses this man, we subscribe to the charge.

"I am needy," he says: you lie. Give me my father's property-list. "What then? Will you maintain a poor man?" Once released, perhaps I shall promise, when you ask: I make no bargain. Even now you seek my hands? Deny that the letter is yours, and you have an argument; say: I too am wont to beg even for an adulterer. "Whoever has not maintained his father," he says, "let him be bound": I feared more for my hands. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: What my father begged of me I do not know: by public vengeance I drove a bloody sword into a private tyrant. The pirates, when they had captured me, did nothing more than bind me. "I will give double money." What? Do you promise more than is asked? Whence have you such resources of patrimony? Even now do you speak as though from the tyrant's coffer? My brother corrupted my wife, whom not even the tyrant had violated. When the pirates fixed a price, I rejoiced, for my wealthy father could pay even if they had demanded double. They sent me back to the republic with my hands, to my father with his letters. OF POMPEIUS SILO.

Go forth composed, with smooth brow, to every allurement, a little more darkly than naked women with their garments laid aside, with speech exquisitely turned to every witticism, all but offering blandishments unbidden, so that whoever sees you may not fear to approach: then do you wonder if, when you have written out your unchastity by so many tokens — dress, gait, speech, face — someone was found who would not draw back from an adulteress running upon him? She ordered, I suppose, the solicitor's go-between to be seized and stripped, demanded scourges and lashes and every kind of torture, and barely restrained the weakness of a woman's hand from the wounds of a worthless slave.

This was our commander's testament. "Bring," he says, "some charges of his earlier life." I cannot: you had a modest rival; he was much silent. What greater charge can I bring against you? Your own son did not wish the state to be entrusted to you. There is no reason for you to say, "Whom did I send to the enemy?" — as though you could not go yourself. Why do you return so quickly? You begged us against your son longer than you begged the enemy for him. You did not stand motionless, you did not cling there as though you too were fastened up. Why do you withdraw so quickly? He is still alive, still speaking. About to withdraw, ask whether he wishes to give any charge. By his voice he convicts the treason, by his silence the traitor.

I bargained for my ransom, I wrote to my father. Whoever of you hung in suspense for your tyrant-slayer, I am sure, anxiously prayed that this letter might reach my father. "I am in want," he says. So suddenly? What ought not to be bought at all, he bought at double. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: I won my cause before those who owed nothing to my hands. Only then does this man complain of being in want, when he saw my hands. What wonder if the pirates did not think it base to take the wage a father gave? Be present, natural affection; if I have lived holily, if innocently, bring it about that this man, who hates my hands, may miss them. The letter seemed to me slowly loosed. This, surely, was wanting to an age filled full of our crimes, that someone should be told of as loosed by pirates, bound by his father.

How often did she implore her absent husband's name? How often did she complain that she did not travel abroad with him? No one asks a second time one who refuses thus. With whom did you complain? Before whom were you indignant? Do you think you will go far enough toward proving your chastity, if you only deny the outrage — which, for the most part, even the most unchaste woman, in hope of a richer reward, deliberately feigns? When did you write to your husband about the wrong done you, and, that your solitude might not lie open to the chance of a like wrong, beg his earlier return? And how much more becomingly should I have learned of the affront to my marriage-chamber by a wife's letter than by a solicitor's will! Most wretched of all the age's husbands, with my absence thus despised, I should even now not know my own wrong, had the man who did it wished to keep silent.

I understand at how great a peril I offend this man. For how will he avenge the accusation? By the cross. He is hard pressed by every argument: I will give those who saw, I will give those who heard, I will give the gold, I will give a witness, and — that no doubt may be possible about his rank — a commander. Let him say of this man what he will: "He is an enemy"; this man gave the information. Was there so much gold that it was plain even to those not seeking it, or were you so suspect that the treason, which we were bidden to beware of, put any man in mind of you? An excellent young man, an excellent commander, who did not cease to care for the state even on the cross, his son thought you unworthy of being told:

OF BLANDUS: This man, who has not the means to live, how dearly does he sell your tyrant-slayers! What do you say, pirate of your own son, schoolmaster of pirates, buyer of a cruelty of which not even a pirate is the seller? OF ROMANIUS HISPO: "The father greets the pirates": this greeting you snatch from your son. "I will give double": what need? I could have been loosed more cheaply. "that you cut off his hands": the pirates were astounded, and as they let me go, said: "tell your father that pirates do not sell everything." OF MENTO: Until now, judges, I have pleaded as though for my own hands; but the truth must be confessed: they have been given back to you. I exhibit, republic, the pirates' deposit to you: these your hands have been brought back safe to you. Do what you will. This one thing I ask: if they have sinned, hand them over to anyone to be bound: if you hand them to this man, he will bind them as he loosed them: he will cut them off.

So often solicited, did you not veil that face by which you could please? Did you not curse every ornament as the cause of such a wrong? What comes next to one who promises: being asked, she keeps silent about the outrage. Look at the adulterer's fortune; from it let that go unpunished which she gave to the adulterer, if there is anything she did not give. Why do I reckon up everything one by one? What did I, her husband, not send her from my own goods? Now, with all my fortune, I lie hidden among the adulterer's gifts! "Let her be sole heir." Why so? "You have it," he says; he wrote the reasons: "because, when I had appealed once, when I had appealed a second time, when I had appealed a third time, I did not corrupt her."

"Beware of treason." OF VARIUS GEMINUS. Do not expect everything from an accuser both preoccupied and modest: understand the defendant; you have heard the charges. Do you ask for charges of his earlier life? I have none: your son never wished to reproach you with anything. So quickly have your prayers tired? What will the poor wretch do? The commander cannot keep silent about the treason, nor the son speak of the traitor.

OF ALFIUS FLAVUS: As yet I know not what kind of father to wish for. A rich one? He maims. A poor one? He binds. Neither is good for my hands. "I will give double, that you cut off his hands." You had a son less cruel. OF MARULLUS: When the letter was brought, the pirates already began to loose me; when the double money in the letter was read out, "this," I said, "is the father I had praised to you." OF TRIARIUS: Where is that patrimony of yours which equips tyrants, which makes adulterers? Where is it? Certainly on me you spent nothing.

O we, born in too happy and golden an age, as they say! So even those who seek the unchaste honour the chaste? "Of all my goods, of all my money, let her be sole heir, because she could not be corrupted, because she could not be stormed by so many solicitations, because she so faithfully guarded her chastity." Conceal the testator's name a little while: do you not think it the will of a husband? Lo, suspecting no disgrace in my wife, amid mutual love — or at least so believed — if I, now about to die, seizing the tablets, wish to set an inscription upon her along with my gifts, it must be sought from the adulterer's will. "Let her be sole heir, though a stranger, though unknown; only because she is chaste, because she is uncorrupted." What?

OF PORCIUS LATRO. What is safe from this treason, which has already reached as far as the commander? I fear lest we beware as late as our commander, who did not understand the treason before he was betrayed; and never was peril more present: the state is without a commander, the traitor without a guard. For what reason is there why the enemy should spare you? You are both the father of our commander and you have gold and you are no envoy. If I should say to you, "Wait until envoys are sent; your son is being sent back to you officially," you would say: "A father's feeling does not bear delay; longing for my son hurries me on; even if I cannot ransom him alive, at least I will ransom him dead; never was an enemy so hard as not to be bent by a father's tears."

THE OTHER SIDE. OF JULIUS BASSUS: Even my victory will be unhappy: if I do not win my cause, I shall die of hunger; if I win it, I shall achieve only this — not to die of hunger. I married too fruitful a wife: she bore me three I know not what monsters, raging in various ways against each other and against me, judges: one able to crush his country, one to violate his brother, one his father. I call all my fellow-citizens to witness, judges: we served together; no one felt the tyranny more than I alone. I have the greatest proof — that I live: you would not have spared me, had you thought me a part of the tyrant. While they fought among themselves, the republic won. The remaining two, since they could not against us, exercised their tyranny upon each other. This one had some wife or other, whom he had got to know in the citadel. If I could bind you, I would have bound you when you set out.

Has this so censorious an adulterer no mother? No sister? No kinswoman? Or is none of them chaste? For this, of course, with such great riches he wanders through foreign cities in honour of unknown chastity. There, where he was born, no woman was chaste; and there, where he did business, because every woman was a prostitute, a chaste heiress was sought, by mistake, with a vacant will. I charge with adultery a woman whom I received in marriage, of whom I prayed for children in common, whom I would most gladly believe chaste. Will the age now give us up to every endurance, so that against a husband's complaint a wife is defended by a stranger's testimony? But, by Hercules, against the opinions of outsiders this was a most splendid defence: I please my husband.

Though I forgive you that you went so quickly, I will charge you that you returned so quickly. Say what he said to you. Or did he wish to say nothing to his father? "Beware of treason." This he meant: see that no one go out by night without the guards' knowledge, that no one reach the enemy without the state's knowledge, that no one return from the enemy's camp heavy with gold. Nothing is wanting to the information. If you ask anything about the treason, the commander will tell you; if anything about the traitor, the envoys.

You have no need of great expense to support your father: share with me your own maintenance. I do not wish you to maintain me as well as I maintained you; I do not wish you to pardon me: whatever you suffered, whatever you feared, I will suffer; demand the lash, tear at my wrinkles. Were you burned? Set fires beneath, and this half-dead face, which breathes only for its own reproach because it cannot be put out, burn away. If that is too little, do what you say not even the pirates did: cut off my hands. I exhibit them to you: these are the ones that write whatever they please. Where is your sword? Draw it. The tyrant was allowed to die by a wound; the adulterer was quickly dispatched with one blow: I, your father, ask as a kindness a like fate. Not even among the pirates did you fear hunger. No tyrant tortured anyone so.

But I, if you now accept this fashion of writing, will, in your sight, write thus: "let my wife be my heir, because, while I was abroad, she was loved to distraction; because she was left heiress by a strange and lustful young man; because she entered upon so infamous an inheritance." From two wills I send you to deliberate: which will you follow? The one by which she is acquitted by an adulterer, or the one by which she is condemned by her husband? The one fruit of chastity is to be believed chaste, and, against all enticements and all allurements, the only firm support, as it were, for women's natures is to have fallen into no scandal. It is perhaps a new and dreadful thing not to . . . into all men's esteem . . . then . . . from one who will give . . . experiences of various . . . a woman . . . one chastity . . . and yet she must take care both to be and to seem chaste.

pr.1. Day after day you press me about Albucius. I will put you off no longer, although I did not hear him often: throughout a whole year he would speak before the public only five or six times, and not many forced their way into his private practice-sessions — and even those he favoured he came to regret. He was one man when he committed himself to a crowd, another when he was content with a few. He used to begin seated, and only when warmth had drawn him out did he venture to rise. That untimely philosophy in his declamations strayed without measure and without end; rarely did he fill out the whole controversia. You could not say it was a division, you could not say it was a declamation: as a declamation much was wanting, as a division much was left over. When he spoke before the public he summoned all his powers, and for that reason he did not stop. Often, while he was declaiming, the trumpet sounded three times, because in every controversia he wanted to say not what ought to be said but whatever could be said. He argued tediously rather than subtly: he bound argument to argument, and as if nothing were firm enough, he confirmed every proof with further proofs.

pr.2. There was this further fault in his argumentation: he developed a question not as a part of the controversia but as if it were a whole controversia. Every question had its own proposition, its own development, its own digressions, its own bursts of indignation, even its own epilogue. So while expounding one controversia he was really delivering several. What then? Is not every question to be filled out through all its parts? Of course — but as an accessory, not as the sum. No limb is well-proportioned if it equals the body. As for splendour of language, I doubt whether any other man had so much. His strength was not great, but his diction was. He spoke at a rapid and outpouring pace, yet with preparation. The faculty of extemporizing, as those who knew him more closely affirmed, was not lacking in him, but he thought it lacking in himself. His sententiae — which Pollio Asinius used to call "white" — were simple, open, bringing nothing hidden, nothing unexpected, but resonant and bright.

pr.3. He moved the passions effectively, he handled figures admirably, he prepared his ground in a suspicious way. But nothing is so unfair as obvious preparation: it shows that some trick lies beneath. So restraint must be applied, that the preparation may be preparation, not confession. He filled a commonplace richly. You could not complain of poverty in the Latin tongue when you heard him: such a flow of cultivated speech poured out. He never tortured himself over how to say a thing, but over what to say. The power of unfolding sufficed him as far as he wished; and so he himself used to say, when he wished to show that he did not hesitate over the choice of words: "When the mind has seized upon the matter, the words come crowding round." Hence one could not admire any evenness in him. He was most brilliant — and the same man would speak of the meanest things of all: vinegar and pennyroyal and lanterns and depilatory and sponges. He thought there was nothing that could not be said in a declamation.

pr.4. The reason was this: he feared to seem a schoolman. While he avoided one fault he fell into another, and did not see that the excessive splendour of his style was not defended by these mean ingredients but befouled. But this is common to all men, that they would rather excuse their faults than escape them. For Albucius did not seek how not to be a schoolman, but how not to seem one. He took nothing away from his superfluous noise; he brought in these mean words to cover for the others. To this was added an inconstancy of judgement: whomever he had just heard speaking gracefully, him he wanted to imitate. I remember that, dropping everything, he sat with his notebooks at the feet of the philosopher Fabianus, who was much younger than himself;
