pr.5. I remember him stunned with admiration for Hermagoras, withering away in imitation of him. He had no confidence in his own talent, and hence his constant changing. So, while he transfers from one style to another — now wishing to be plain and to stick to bare facts, now rugged and forceful rather than polished, now brief and neat, now lifting himself too high, now sinking himself too low — he made sport of his own genius and as an old man spoke far worse than he had spoken as a young one. For age availed him nothing toward improvement, since his pursuit was always new. The use of homely idiom is, among the virtues of oratory, a thing that rarely succeeds: it needs great moderation and a certain occasion. He used this virtue with mixed results: often it turned out well for him, often he came to grief. And yet it is no wonder if a virtue so near to a fault is grasped with difficulty. No one ever showed this more becomingly than our Gallio.

pr.6. Even as a young lad, when he declaimed, he used this style aptly and fittingly; which I admired the more, because tender youth shrinks from everything not only that is mean, but that resembles the mean. Fortune rarely answered to Albucius, but his reputation always did: however much one regretted having heard him, one was glad to hear him. He was a gloomy, anxious declaimer, one who feared for his own delivery even after he had spoken: so completely was no moment free from care. This anxiety drove him from the forum — that, and the cruel outcome of a single figure. For in a certain trial before the Hundred Men, when it was said that an offer of an oath had at some point been made by the opposing party, he introduced a figure of this kind, by which he might turn all the charges back upon his opponent.

pr.7. "Does it please you," he said, "to settle the matter by oath? Swear — but I will administer the oath: swear by the ashes of your father, which lie unburied; swear by your father's memory"; and he developed the commonplace. When he had finished, L. Arruntius rose from the other side and said: "We accept the condition; he will swear." Albucius cried out: "I did not offer a condition; I spoke a figure of speech." Arruntius pressed on. The Hundred Men were already hurrying to the last business. Albucius cried out: "By this reasoning figures of speech are abolished from the nature of things." Arruntius replied: "Let them be abolished; we shall be able to live without them." The upshot was this: the Hundred Men declared that they would give judgement for Albucius's opponent if he swore; the man swore. Albucius could not bear this insult, but, having sworn, laid upon himself the penalty for false accusation: never again to plead in the forum. For he was a man of the highest probity, who knew neither how to do an injury nor how to suffer one.

pr.8. And he used to say: "What reason have I to plead in the forum, when more people hear me at home than hear anyone in the forum? I speak when I wish, as long as I wish; I am counsel for whichever side I wish." And although he would not admit it, it delighted him in declamations that figures could be spoken without danger. Yet not even among the schoolmen could he escape the insults of Cestius, a most biting man. When in a certain controversia Albucius had said, "Why is it that a cup, if it falls, is broken, but a sponge, if it falls, is not broken?" Cestius said: "Go to him tomorrow; he will declaim for you why thrushes fly and gourds do not fly."

pr.9. When Albucius, in that controversia about the brother who set adrift in an unrigged ship the brother condemned for parricide, had said, "He placed his brother in a wooden sack," Cestius, about to speak the same theme, set out the controversia thus: "A certain man, when his brother had been condemned at home by their father on the stepmother's accusation, and he had received him for execution, placed him in a wooden sack." A great laugh from everyone followed. But the declamation did not go well even for Cestius himself; for he said few good things. And when he was not praised by the schoolmen, he said: "Does no one put these men in a wooden sack, so that they may arrive somewhere on earth where cups are broken but sponges are not broken? I see what you want: to hear sententiae rather than jokes. So be it: hear the sententiae spoken in this very controversia."

The other side. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS. What is the price for which I sell this — that as a father I should watch my son on the cross, as a son my father from the cross? For so much did I sell both the commander and a parricide? All congratulated me, on my defeat more lavishly than on my designation — too ostentatiously. Now they repent. The man who sold both his son and his country received gold so scant that a single old man could carry it.

OF PORCIUS LATRO: Son, I beg nothing more than to be spared hunger; yet if you are inexorable, this I ask as a kindness: that I may die either as an adulterer or as a tyrant. The fortune of us both was equal at that time: you were bound, I in old age was immobile and most like one bound; you in solitude, I in the solitude of all my own; you did not see the light, I even hated it. This one thing is between us, that you received food even from the pirates. OF BLANDUS: I was pleading not for an adulterer but for my house, that he might not kill his brother, defile a tyrant-slayer, bespatter a father. As I begged, and interposed these very hands, he all but cut them off. This epigram was laughed at by Latro as childish: this much was provided for it, that he might seem to have left someone of his own whom he did not kill. OF VIBIUS RUFUS: These, surely, are the hands that wrote the letter: I offer them; cut them off and maintain me. OF POMPEIUS SILO: "Let children maintain their parents, or be bound." To you I transfer my own law:

In this controversia, although it is conjectural and has, as it were, a fixed and well-worn road, there was nevertheless some disagreement among the declaimers. Latro always contracted, and whatever he could safely leave he passed over. So he both lessened the number of the questions and never dragged in the commonplaces; and even those which he had taken up he did not develop at length, but forcefully. This at all events was his precept: that a declaimer ought, like a praetor, to do certain things for the sake of lessening the suit. This he did in this controversia; for he did not trouble to say that no treason had been committed, but that he himself was no traitor. "For he too is suspect to the judge," he said, "who defends more than himself; and I do not wish," he said, "to fight with the son's voice, so as to say that the commander and son lied — especially when hatred against the son is charged against the father." ALBUCIUS divided the declamation into two parts: first he denied that there was any treason; then:

you may bind me, but maintain me. THE DIVISION. Generally they used this division: whether the law weighs the case neither of father nor of son, but that every father is to be maintained by his son — He said that this law was written for bad fathers; good ones are maintained even without a law. If not all are to be maintained, whether this man is to be maintained. This question Latro divided into these: whether he is to be maintained, since he did not ransom his son from the pirates. Here he asked whether he could not have ransomed him, or would not; then, whether he is to be maintained even though he wished his son's hands cut off;

supposing there were, that it did not pertain to him. SILO POMPEIUS introduced this colour against the father: that he had done it out of hatred of the state, by which he had been rejected, and out of hatred of his very son, whom he hated both because he had stood against him and because he had conquered. VARIUS GEMINUS said that the father had sought the command at once with this design, that he might betray it. "A grasping man and gaping after gain — for his ways were known — conquered by that rival by whom it was not right to be conquered save by a most base man. Before the elections," he said, "he had been ready to take money to destroy his son; after the elections he was ready to give money to destroy his son. When the leader was captured we said," he said, "'This cannot happen without treason.' We excused ourselves to the commander: we said that we had persevered toward the ransom, although the father had deterred us. At this point he answered: 'Beware of treason.'"

lastly, whether he wished them cut off. HISPO ROMANIUS made this separately, as a question of law: whether one who has not ransomed his son cannot seek maintenance from him. But, as GALLIO said, both questions contain this, and the first too, in which it is asked whether every father is to be maintained; for it is said: what if a man has blinded his son? What if a man has not ransomed him? And when one comes to the other question, in which it is asked whether this father is to be maintained, nothing else can be said why he should not be maintained, but that he did not ransom him, that he promised double for his hands to be cut off. The Greeks' improper question it will be enough, in such controversiae, to note once or twice: whether a father may use this law against a tyrant-slayer, as though his hands were sacred and public, against which not even the pirates think anything is permitted to them. Our men have removed this kind of question.

BLANDUS said that, taking ill the shame of his defeat, he had wished his son killed, so that he himself might be put in his place. HISPO ROMANIUS: "His revenge," he said, "he sold to the enemy. So easily," he said, "did he go out, reach the enemy by night, and return, that you would know he had not done it then for the first time." ARGENTARIUS said: "Carry to the senate your son's instructions. He must have told you many things; to the envoys too he entrusted some; perhaps he told his father the traitor's name; inform us. 'He told me,' he says, 'nothing.' The whole question is removed. Do you ask whom he named? See to whom he told nothing." For the father, on the elections, this was Latro's colour:

SILO POMPEIUS used not only the points the rest used, when he said this father ought not to be maintained because he had not ransomed his son and because he had wished his son's hands cut off, but he passed from the private causes to the public cause; for he said that a man pernicious to the republic ought not to be maintained — one who had had a tyrant for a son, who had not killed him, who longed for him when lost, who would avenge him; and he denied that this man had any other cause of pursuing the tyrant-slayer save public liberty, and he described the character of the man as impious, bloody, who, because he could not through his children, exercised tyranny through pirates: and, that he might say this the more freely, he gave the son an advocate. And this in this part was praised, while Silo declaimed: he had begun to treat this — that a tyrant's father ought not to be maintained; with all favouring him, that he should be starved to death; and when he had long pressed that he was a tyrant's father, he added: dare to demand that this profit you, that you are a tyrant-slayer's father. BLANDUS, when he declaimed this thought the next day, turned it into irony, and, when he had objected that he was a tyrant's father, added: do not turn from him;

"I feared lest anyone should defeat my son; and so I declared my candidacy, that by my authority I might deter future rivals; then I yielded to my son." ALBUCIUS used this colour: "Some said," he said, "that the commander ought to be a young man such as Scipio had been, others an old man such as Maximus was; the old man, they said, would do nothing rashly. I gave the people the opportunity of both." CESTIUS used this colour: "I knew my son's faults; I knew he was a keen young man, brave, but inconsiderate and rash. And so I sought the command both for the state's sake and for my son's, whom I did not think fit to bear so great a burden."

he has something to set against it: he is an adulterer's father too. The colour for the father one man and another introduced differently. FUSCUS confessed he had been angry with him for killing his brother before his father's eyes, and pressed this point vehemently, since no tyrant, no pirate, had done this. "I was angry," he said, "for this very reason, that by this crime you had defiled even your tyrant-slaying; it is plain that you rage against your own by a kind of disease." And he kept this tenor of pleading: "I was angry, and to this day I am angry, nor do I complain." Nor did he stoop to entreaties or beg, but used a father's right. This he added, to excuse the cruelty of the letter: I wrote to the pirates not with the intent that your hands be cut off, but to reproach you with your bloody hands, stained with a brother's blood before your father's eyes. And I wrote in safety; for I knew the pirates would not do it unless they had received money, which I would not send: and so they did not cut them off; and had they hoped for it, they certainly would have. But it was plain that those letters were the letters of an angry man, not of one promising. At the end he described how wretched he would be, taking maintenance from those hands which a little before he had watched killing his brother, and added — what he said his teacher delivered to the highest applause — that line of Homer suited to Priam: "And he kissed his dread, man-slaying hands, which had slain many of his sons." SILO POMPEIUS too confessed his anger.

FUSCUS ARELLIUS said that he had become a candidate for this, that the enemy's spirits might be broken when they heard that the state could choose a leader even from a single house. HISPO ROMANIUS thought one ought to plead plainly: "These colours," he said, "are silly, when rivals are presented." And so he conducted his case with this colour, complaining of the outcome of the elections: that all the young men had conspired, as though it were a contest about comparison of age; and so the old man, not canvassing, was easily beaten. "Of me," he said, "you cannot complain; I cried out: 'A commander of this age is not useful to you.' There remained in him," he said, "even after the elections the same defiance: he referred nothing to his father, communicated nothing; and so he was captured." And when he had described how unskilfully he had drawn up his line, how his rashness had been crushed by ambushes in unexplored places, he added: "This is what I kept crying out to you: 'Choose an old man for commander.'"

For he said he would not be believed, if he denied he had been angry; but he gave not the cause of his anger that FUSCUS gave; he said those grievances were to be passed over in which the son would glory; he gave this cause: that he had been abandoned by his only son, that against his will he had sailed away, seeing his father an old man, orphaned, now almost in want; that even then he had fled to avoid maintaining him; and he brought the father to prayers, and in the epilogue entreated his son. And SPARSUS too I remember declaiming with this colour — a man sane among schoolmen,

OTHO JUNIUS the elder said that, agitated by certain omens and dreams foretelling this fortune, he had become a candidate. Now Otho was one of the dreamers: wherever his colour failed him, he related a dream. About the fact that he went out without the senate's knowledge, LATRO gave this colour: that he had not awaited the decree, but, frantic and thunderstruck, had at once rushed forth. ALBUCIUS used this colour: "It is always by decree of the senate that a leader is appointed. It was long to wait; in short, I hurried and did not arrive in time."

and a schoolman among the sane. CESTIUS used a far different colour; he said it was not anger in the father, but cleverness: "I had nothing," he said, "wherewith to ransom him. Whom should I ask for money in so greedy a city, in which not even sons maintain their fathers? I used a stratagem: I knew the pirates were not cruel, but greedy. I wished to bring it about both that they should despair of his being ransomed, and that, for this reason, thinking him superfluous, they should let him go. Whether I planned wisely I do not know; meanwhile I planned luckily: after those letters which he accuses, he was let go." Latro removed himself entirely from these colours, and called up his powers with so great a force in the whole pleading that he held men astounded; for he used this colour: I know not what I wrote. Long ago my mind was struck from me. From the moment I saw one son in the citadel, another in adultery, a third in kin-murder; from the moment I was sprinkled with my dying son's blood; from the moment I was left alone, orphaned, an old man — I hate my own. This colour was to be approved by his powers; for how great a force is needed, that a man should make himself pitiable by accusing himself?

VARIUS GEMINUS said that he had preferred to go alone; for the enemy are not moved by the authority of envoys, but are often bent by the tears of fathers. SILO POMPEIUS said: "I thought it more useful that he be ransomed with private money: for he could be valued at less than if he were ransomed as a commander." ARGENTARIUS said: "Nothing was so unfair as that envoys should be sent for the ransom; for they would never have given back the man whom they had thus judged to be missed officially. And so I ran on ahead, meaning to plead and to say this: 'The army despises him, the state abandons him.'"

ALBUCIUS mixed all the colours and, that this might be free, gave the father an advocate, and would not narrate. He began from the proposition: a father has sought maintenance from his son; then, when he came to defend the writing that he would give double if they cut off the hands, he first used the Latronian colour: "this," he said, "I answer: he knows not what he did, he was driven into madness by his ills." Here he introduced a philosophical commonplace, how minds are overturned by great calamities; then he took up an anthypophora: "you lie; nay, he was angry. You compel me," he says, "to say that he was rightly angry with you." He went through everything; this among other things he objected to him: that he had either not known, or had dissembled, that his brother was seizing the citadel; he wished thus to strip from his tyrant-slaying too its recommendation. Then he returned to that Cestian colour: "but I think he did from policy what he did. What then? What yet does this man say? Why he wrote it? He says nothing; he weeps, he wishes to die, but not of hunger." In this declamation ALBUCIUS uttered that epigram,

BLANDUS said: "As I was considering what to do — whether to be content with a father's tears or to support my prayers with a public escort — at last it came into my mind that the Trojan king went to ransom his son without envoys and with gold." SEPULLIUS BASSUS said that he had not awaited the senate, because he thought there would be those who would say the man ought not to be ransomed — a thing that had happened often enough among the Romans; and so he had wished to ransom him before anything could be decided about not ransoming. CESTIUS said: "I did not seek secret by-ways and a hidden route: a traitor, I came by the same road as the envoys." On the son's voice ALBUCIUS made this colour:

doubtful among admirers and mockers: do you give the bread to your dog that you do not give your father? GLYCON said excellently: "Pity him, who runs the risk of nourishing a father." GARGONIUS was a hearer of Buteo, and afterwards his successor in the school too, of a dull but most pugnacious voice, of whom the buffoon Baros said a most charming thing: "you have the voice of a hundred hoarse men." This man thought he had devised a clever colour for the father: "I dictated," he said, "'I will give double, if you do not cut off the hands': one syllable, 'not,' fell out by the copyist, and he wrote 'if you cut them off.'" A thing worthy to be uttered in that voice. ARTEMON said: "Child-loving father, does anyone shrink from punishing you too?" ADAEUS said: "We saw a swift-sailing skiff. And was anyone of the sailors in that skiff a father?" NICETES said: "'I will give double, if you strike off the hands.' The pirates asked: 'Did you ever play the tyrant?'"

"He was ashamed," he said, "that he had been captured; he sought some defence for his fortune; he wished it to seem that this had befallen him not by his own fault but by treason: and so he could not add the name." FUSCUS ARELLIUS said that his mind, already estranged by his sufferings and wandering, had poured out these words without arguments, without a defendant. VARIUS GEMINUS embraced everything: "It can be," he said, "for this reason, it can be for that; I advise you the same thing:

beware of treason. If you wish to beware of it, make old men your commanders." This too, both in this controversia and in every one, CESTIUS used to say must be avoided: whenever some saying is set down, that we should not run to it as to a sententia. Just as in this case, at Cestius's school, a certain hearer of his began thus: "That I may begin with your leader's words, judges: beware of treason"; and so he ended his declamation, saying: "I end with the words with which the commander ended his life: beware of treason." This kind of sententia Cestius called echo, and to a pupil who used it he would at once exclaim: "Hail, Echo!" As in that suasoria in which Alexander deliberates whether to sail the Ocean, when a voice had been heard, "How far, unconquered one?" — from that voice a certain man began his declamation, and on this he ended; Cestius said to him as he ended: "With you I shall cease, and from you I shall begin." And to another, when, after describing Alexander's victories and the nations subdued, he set at the last: "How far, unconquered one?"

— Cestius exclaimed: "And you, how far?" OTHO the elder used this colour for the father: for he said that it was distressing to the commander that the envoys were looking at him nailed up; and so, to detach them from this spectacle and to relieve his own shame, he had said the thing which, on hearing, they would make them hurry away. And so he had said not "Let them beware of treason," but "Beware" — as though for the envoys themselves there was danger lest they be betrayed.

THE LAW: A son shall be in the father's power. THE THEME: A man had a son, brave in war. After he had thrice fought bravely, the father wishes to disinherit him, that he may keep him at home. OF PORCIUS LATRO: Most wretched father, I should no longer see my son, did I not disinherit him. Braver than is enough for the law or the fatherland, he did not return to me a third time, but was carried back. What is left over for the fatherland, I claim for the father. My son flees me — and indeed to the enemy. How long shall I, trembling, await the news of battles? Son, for myself I ask exemption. OF CESTIUS PIUS: I disinherit my son that I may have him. My exemption profited the republic no less than his military service: I took a wife. Thus he descends into the narrative. A third time I heard, as though the gods were warning me, that the young man should set a limit to his own good fortune. I sought leave for one battle: let happen, I said, whatever I fear, if I send him into the line again; I have made a bargain with the gods. "I am not afraid," he says. This is why I am afraid. It is cast at me that my son hates me. OF ARELLIUS FUSCUS THE FATHER: O me, already weary while my son fights!

Apart from the fact that in every crisis liberty is dangerous, the girl has deserved that we keep silent: she was merciful to us, even before we asked. Liberty is inhuman, if we conquer against the judge. You ought not to be allowed to choose more than once. All excessive power is most healthfully confined within narrow limits. Let him who can condemn be able to do it once; let him who can kill be able to do it once; or if any repetition can be admitted, it must be admitted only into repentance of death. Set before yourselves that face of punishment — the executioner, the axe: even this once permitted is too much. "I was won over, I sheathe the sword: I am angry, I take back my choice."

Great are the omens: do you think it nothing, that the father of a brave man should fear? Wretched me: now you are too well known to the enemy; now even the law fears I know not what on your behalf. Do you wonder if what is enough for the law is too much for a father? "Do you," he says, "reproach me with luxury?" Nay, I can even urge you toward pleasures. How long will you lie on the hard couch of the camp? How long break your sleep with the trumpet? How long live bloody? Let us be cheerful: the vows of three victories must be paid. So many battle-lines you have withstood, so many wounds; I can complain even of the republic: late are you discharged. Now and again I hear you saying, "I prefer glory to life"; this, then, is what kills me — that to die is so easy for you. At last rest from one war. OF POMPEIUS SILO.

And is it not better to die only once? Kill now not the ravisher, but the husband. OF PORCIUS LATRO. Is it more dangerous to deny a rape than to commit it? The young man had been led into such confusion that he did not know what he had done. Yet he did not shrink from marriage with the girl; he only favoured himself so far as to marry as an innocent man. And so he sought nothing else than freedom, that he might marry more honourably. So, before you, judges, is it safer to sin than to blush? He would have been more worthy of punishment if he had sinned in a way that he could remember. Rise, young man, and without any regard for your shame cast yourself at the girl's feet; come too, friends and kinsmen, and you, mother, and you, father. What is it, girl? Do these men's tears move you at all? "No," she says; "let the magistrate come to him." I do not dissemble: I fear you, girl, if you wish to be entreated nowhere but where you can kill. I am punished more heavily now, when I am ashamed of having sinned, than when I sinned. The woman who pardons after the injury grows angry after the mercy.

My reason for disinheriting is that I may not live without my son, whom I should long since not see, did I not disinherit him. My disinheriting is in the power of the disinherited. OF ROMANIUS HISPO: What is more vexing than one who wearies out his own good fortune? What do you wait for, until you are cast out of the camp? OF MENTO: The republic blushes to use a soldier so scarred. So great a valour ought not to fall without a successor: a wife must be taken; but even now I warn you, do not raise but one child. OF CORNELIUS HISPANUS: I did not begin to hold you back until the republic discharged you. No wound can now be impressed on you save through a scar. Until now you have been longer with the enemy than with your father: at home only have you been healed. OF JUNIUS OTHO THE FATHER: The best end of valour is to stop before you fail.

OF CESTIUS PIUS. He comes to you, by your kindness, to keep the girl's kindness. He chose marriage; nor did he yet know what a modest husband he was going to have. You let the ravisher go; will you kill the husband? The judge said: "What have you, that you deny so obstinately? She chooses marriage. Is then what he did in ravishing less than what he did in denying?" OF Q. HATERIUS. "I shall not choose death," she said, "but I wish it to be lawful for me even to choose death." The power that delights in this is cruel. OF BLANDUS. So have we denied the injury more dangerously than we did it?

THE OTHER SIDE. "Thrice bravely . . ." certainly the disinherited are allowed to fight. OF ALBUCIUS SILUS: What sudden uproar has resounded here? Does the general call? I come. I laboured most in the front line. I am ashamed: men thrice conquered serve as soldiers. OF PUBLIUS ASPRENAS: "How long," he says, "will you risk yourself?" It is well, judges: my father thinks me worthy to be safe. A senator, after his sixty-fifth year, is not compelled to come into the senate-house: is he forbidden? A man of praetorian rank may wear the bordered toga on festal or solemn days: is it necessary? Whatever is given under the name of reward or honour, is free both ways; otherwise it ceases to be a reward, on which necessity is laid. I obey that father of mine who used to say that by glory we are made immortal, who used to kiss the wounds of those returning from the line.

OF JUNIUS GALLIO. On a certain night — what shall I say? now it is shameful even to deny it. Night, wine, error — why are you angry, girl? Now I dare not deny. My case was not pleaded carefully: while you feared nothing, you the more easily entrusted me to the girl. We must confess our fault: we caused delay to the marriage. Whether she had still been violated or not, she seemed worthy of marriage who could not kill a man. I was taking thought for you, that you might not be said to be married to a ravisher: if it had been allowed you, you would have had a more honourable husband. Did you deny it? O shameless man! So did you not cry aloud, before the magistrate's tribunal, in the people's sight, in the middle of the forum, "I raped a virgin"? You can have no husband so compliant as this: he will now deny nothing.

To these new and contrary commands, do you think I can be suddenly turned about? It is not so. That feeling rules within us which first entered the mind. Luxury, avarice, sloth, unchastity, fear, are not unlearned, and daily all these are either chastised or punished: so tenacious are we even of our vices. Believe me, father: I am not my own master, when that battle-cry has arisen: it bids me charge the enemy, cleave the opposing ranks with the sword; this onset, this ardour of spirit, adorned your house with thrice-won spoils of the enemy; to this you owe those thanksgivings; for the sake of this you love me even when you disinherit me. Now my spirit is not steady, now my tongue is not steady; I have been caught up in another's work; the very toga does not sit upon my shoulders.

OF VARIUS GEMINUS. I will set out the order of events to you as though I had learned it from a man who does not know what he did. OF VIBIUS GALLUS. Where are you who used to say, "It is no concern of yours: confess"? He confesses because you thought it more honourable to marry a ravisher. "Let him be my heir," she says, "if any child is born within ten months." Does she deny it at all? Rise, young man, say, "I raped, I violated"; begin to know what you do not know: do you wonder that she does not believe you? There is much about which she is afraid.

Should you bid me go to besiege an enemy, to seize a position for a camp, to cut off the enemy's supplies — you command leisure to a spirit that is not at leisure. As often as any uproar has arisen, the eyes of all the citizens are turned upon me, they look to my hands; and yet — the truth must be told — the fatherland owes me nothing: I never fought save under compulsion. Do you think it matters at all where we are, what course of life we lead? The same perils stand round us everywhere, and there are as many roads to death. Sometimes continued toil makes men stronger: often what had strengthened, sloth has consumed. OF MARULLUS: Let me confer some service upon my country: until now my military service has been the duty of the law. I will fight even disinherited, nor will I fear that my service may be useless to my country. Even the Athenians conquered under a disinherited general. How great is the difference between me and him?

The other side. OF P. ASPRENAS. I do not know in which trial my opponent was the more shameless. In the earlier he aimed at this — to pay no penalty for the rape at all; in this he aims to choose himself which of the two punishments fixed by the law he wishes to pay. For he confesses that he preferred to go unpunished rather than to marry a wife; to marry a wife rather than to die. Before, he tried to overturn the law of violation; now he wishes to transfer it: he asks the advocates — let not this free him from fear, the fact that he knows the clemency of his own judge. He kept crying that he was innocent; if he had committed any sin, he did not refuse to die. The people stood by the ravisher, and nothing made the violated girl's case more suspect than the leniency of the choice. If now your defilement is clear to you, there is a certain modesty next to innocence — to offer oneself to the laws: but you did not even deserve death by that denial. Did you not know whether you had sinned? You wished to be innocent. You have your case: return to your parents, girl, since indeed you so often beg, who ought yourself to have been begged.

He wiped out his disinheriting by valour; I earned it. THE DIVISION. The first question was made by all, a common one: whether a son can be disinherited for the very reason that he is his own master; then, whether he ought to be. This belongs wholly to treatment. The Greeks are wont to attempt that first question, which has not gone to Roman ears: whether a brave man can be disinherited. But I do not see what they will bring forward, why he cannot. For the fact that he is brave, and so often, brings him not more right, but more recommendation.

LATRO made three questions: whether, he asked, that choice was lawful. "It was not lawful," he says; "for it was not established that you were a ravisher." "It makes no difference," he says, "whether he denied it. For he was a ravisher even if he denied it, and so the choice was lawful." Whether, if the choice was unlawful, it can be recalled. "The choice," he says, "is given to the girl once; it is unchangeable, the moment it is uttered. The judge cannot recall the verdict he has given on a defendant; the examiner will not change his pronouncement; nothing is so civic, so useful, as that a power which is great should be brief. If she wishes to recall both her second choice and then her third, it will never be settled what is to happen, since she can always rescind by a following choice what she had chosen." He made a third question: whether, if a choice can sometimes be recalled, it ought now to be. Here is the defence of the young man, because he denied that he had violated her.

The colour on the father's side some made the harder; for they wished the father to seem hateful to his son: so that the son would rather live with the enemy than with his father. Almost all: that the young man is insatiable of glory, and for that very reason is to be moderated and restrained by his father. Some took refuge entirely in the father's tenderness, and did not argue in the way SILO POMPEIUS argued, who divided thus, so as to say: even if you had no father, you ought to stop; since you have a father, you ought to stop, because your father forbids it;

FUSCUS both changed the order of the questions and increased their number; for he made the first question: whether the raped girl cannot choose more than once. "She can," he says; "for the law does not add how often she may choose, but from which choices: 'either this,' it says, 'or that'; it does not add, 'no more than once.'" Against this he says: "The law bids you choose one of the two; if today you choose death, you will do what was never done: you will have chosen both." "Even if it is not lawful," he says, "more than once, I have not yet chosen: for that is a choice which is made lawfully; that one was not made lawfully. If the praetor had been absent, would you call it a choice? If the ravisher had been absent? The ravisher was absent: that is not a choice; it is mere talk." Whether the choice was confirmed by the previous trial. The ravisher says: "It was argued before the judges whether the choice ought to be valid or not; it was judged that it ought to be valid: let it be valid." "No," says the girl; "for the question was whether I had a right over the ravisher; it was judged that I had: I must use it. I cannot have the law before I have the ravisher." He made a last question, of equity: whether the choice ought to be valid.

or in the way GALLIO did, who divided this part thus: this I command for the republic's sake, for your sake, for my own sake. The latter two you see how he could fill out: that he commanded it for the republic's sake he treated thus: first, that the way to valour might lie open to more young men, the opportunity of acting bravely ought not to be seized by one alone. Then, that it is expedient for the republic not to seem to depend on one man; that the enemy's spirits would rise and his own people's be broken, if the thrice-brave man should fall by chance. Last, that it is useful to the republic that the thrice-brave man be kept, that there may be one to be shown to the youth; that he can now be more an ornament than a defence. That old thought — "now even the law fears something for the brave man" — Gallio placed here: "this too," he said, "either distrusts or takes counsel for the thrice-brave man."

Passienus divided this last part thus: whether, if the young man with evil intent toward the girl denied the rape in order to escape the marriage, he deserves to undergo once more the fortune of the choice he refused. Then: whether he acted with evil intent. VARIUS GEMINUS added to the last question, or part — in which it is asked what ought to be done — these two things which he thought could be asked: whether, if the girl is certain to choose the young man's death, the choice ought not to be allowed her, since she would use her power so cruelly; then, whether she will choose death. "What reason have you," he says, "to wish to choose, except that you do not wish the marriage? This we not only endure, but ask for."

They did not even follow that treatment which BLANDUS used, who said: military service is for you superfluous, it is invidious, it is dangerous. It is superfluous, because you are not compelled — nay, you are forbidden by modesty. One serves for glory's sake: you have won glory; for exemption's sake: you have won it; for reward's sake: there are three rewards at home; and so he passed on to say that it was invidious for one man so often to wish for honours and intercept them from all; how dangerous a thing envy is, how great men it has crushed; here examples. That military service is dangerous he gathered in the same place as the rest; this one new point he added about the law, that the man could no longer act bravely, because all the enemy would single him out: "evidently for this reason the law discharged the thrice-brave man: it knows that he is now marked out by the enemy."

The colour for the young man introduced by LATRO was this: that he should say he had been drunk and did not know what he had done; that even today he rather believed than knew about his own deed; that he had refused, not so as not to marry a wife, but so as to marry of his own will; and that the judges had not listened anxiously, but had been lenient, as though the matter concerned the marriage. VARIUS GEMINUS confessed the rape, and said that nothing was so contrary to the young man's interest as still to deny it: he would offend not only the raped girl, but the judge. CESTIUS neither followed Latro, who said he had not known and did not even now know, nor Varius Geminus, who confessed, but denied the rape more openly. "The truth," he said, "could not be found out; the judges followed that sententia: 'If he raped, it is shameful that the girl go unavenged; if he did not rape, it is not shameful that he become her husband.'" SILO POMPEIUS said that the young man, modest by nature and of rustic shyness, had not endured to confess. The colour did not please LATRO: "He will be the less pardoned," he said, "if he knows that he raped her and knowingly lied." SILO argued against this, that no one could be made to believe that a man does not know whether he raped her.

These things, then, being passed over, those who brought on a loving father pleaded in this manner: "I cannot bear it, I cannot endure my longing for you." Here AESCHINES, of the new declaimers, when he said: not glory has made me more desirous of you, not your valour admired by all; I will confess, he said, a father's feelings, which let each man interpret as he will: "thus would I love you even disinherited." He seemed, while expressing tenderness, not to have preserved the father's dignity. It pleased Latro rather to hold the father back by reason than by feeling, since in reason feeling too has some place.

HISPANUS CORNELIUS: "I did not wish," he said, "to take her husband from her, but to give her a more honourable one. She is worthy," he said, "so merciful a girl, that she should not seem to have married a ravisher." HISPO ROMANIUS said that those comrades who had urged him on by night had stood round him and said: "It is not the girl you raped; it was another." He feared lest he do an injury to the girl he had raped. ARGENTARIUS said: "I could wish you had chosen death: this man would not have been judged a ravisher. It is not your case that presses him, but the choice, while each several judge says: 'What has he that he should so refuse? You would think his life were at stake; and he himself says he is not unwilling to marry a wife, but refuses the title. Of course, when conquered he will marry the wife. There is no need to judge anxiously concerning one whom we must congratulate even when condemned.'" SILO used this colour: that the young man, suddenly confused and in so great an uproar, had not been sufficiently in command of himself; and that he had denied it because he was confused, and persisted because he had denied it.

pr.1. . . . I was looking round, however, to see whether anything had escaped me. Of your own accord you brought up the mention of Votienus Montanus; and I should like you from time to time to offer me certain names by which my memory may be called forth, which, as an old man's, wilts of itself, but, when prompted and at times provoked, easily gathers itself together. MONTANUS VOTIENUS so never declaimed for the sake of display that he did not declaim even for the sake of practice. When I asked him the reason, he said: "Which do you want — the honourable one or the true one? If the honourable one, that I may not get into a bad habit. The man who prepares a declamation writes not in order to win, but in order to please. And so he hunts up every allurement; he abandons argumentation, because it is tedious and has the least bloom in it; he is content to soothe his hearers with sententiae and elaborations. For he desires to win approval for himself, not for his case."

pr.2. And this fault follows declaimers right into the forum — that they desert what is necessary while they pursue what is showy. There is added also this, that they invent opponents however foolish; they answer them both what they wish and when they wish. Besides, there is nothing to chastise their error with any loss; their folly is cost-free. And so a dangerous stupor, scarcely to be cured even in a man about to plead in the forum, can hardly be shaken off, having grown while it was safe. What of the fact that they are sustained by frequent applause, and their memory has grown used to resting at fixed intervals? When they have come into the forum and the applause has ceased to take up their every gesture, they either fail or falter.

pr.3. Add now that bile is roused by no one's interruption: no one laughs, no one deliberately speaks against them; the faces of all are friendly. In the forum, if nothing else, the forum itself disturbs them. This thing which is commonly told, whether it be true, you can better know: that LATRO PORCIUS, the one model of declamatory excellence, when he was pleading for a defendant in Spain, his kinsman Rusticus Porcius, was so confounded that he began with a solecism, and could not recover himself — longing for the hall and the wall — until he obtained

pr.4. that the trial be transferred from the forum into the basilica. To such a degree are talents delicately nursed in school exercises, that they cannot bear the shout, the silence, the laughter — in short, the open sky. But practice is not useful unless it is most like the work for which it trains; and so it is usually harder than the real contest. Gladiators learn with heavier weapons than they fight with; their master keeps them armed longer than their adversary. Athletes wear out two or three opponents at once, that they may more easily withstand single ones. Runners, though their speed is judged within a small space, often run in training the distance they are to run once in the contest. The labour by which we learn is deliberately multiplied, that it may be lightened by which we decide.

pr.5. In school declamations the opposite happens: everything is softer and looser. In the forum they accept their side, in the school they choose it; there they coax the judge, here they command. There the mind must be braced amid the roar of a crowd murmuring together, and the voice carried through to the judge's ears; here the faces of all hang upon the speaker's face. And so, just as men coming out of a shady and dark place are blinded by the brightness of clear light, so these men, passing from the schools into the forum, are confounded by everything as new and unwonted, nor are they hardened into orators until, mastered by many insults, they have toughened by real labour their boyish mind, grown languid through scholastic delights. LEPIDUS, an excellent man, who by no declamatory pursuit . . .

ASPRENAS followed a far different colour; for he said he did not refuse the republic a brave man's services, but reserved them for necessary occasions. If some great war should befall, then even veterans are called to arms. And that epigram of his was much praised in this place: "now let those serve who must; you will serve, if there be need." So, he said, the Roman people came to Scipio Aemilianus, when a greater war at Numantia had loomed than the other generals could sustain; a great interval was given to Scipio between Carthage and Numantia. So they came to Pompey, when the pirates had closed the seas. Great defences are not to be used up. Here Asprenas too spoke an epigram about the law: "evidently for such occasions the law set aside the thrice-brave man."

On the son's side some introduced a colour to make him eager for glory and warlike. NICETES indeed used this phrase: "we shall present him to the judges as a war-lover," and so pleaded that he should complain that his hands were idle, that they were unarmed. This colour did not please Latro: he preferred that the young man should serve by judgement rather than by disease. "This," he said, "is what the father may effectively say — that his son detracts from the glory of his own deeds, rash, bloodthirsty, whom neither a father can hold back nor the law discharge."

Some made a bargain with the father — like Mento, who said he wished to serve but once more, that he might seem to have rendered the republic something beyond the law. Some declared perpetual military service: as long as his strength held, the brave man would not fail the republic. Latro did not approve this colour; he denied that the father's hope in his son should be cut off forever. VIBIUS RUFUS pleaded with the same colour as Mento, but added this: that there reached him those voices of the envious: "did he fight any longer than he had to?" Some thought this too was a thing composed and feigned between us — that I should wish to serve, and you forbid it.

Latro pleaded vehemently on the father's side, and added: even when he is disinherited I will not let him go out; I will lay hands on him, hold him, and at the last fling this corpse of mine before the threshold as he goes out: that you may reach the enemy, trample on your father. PLANCUS, a great lover of Latro, thought this thought was said more forcibly by Latro, more tenderly by LESBOCLES the Greek, who said: "thus shall I lie, like a wall: leap over the trench and your father." FUSCUS ARELLIUS brought on the father with religious awe and terrified by omens; he said that his teacher, in describing the perils of the coming battle in this controversia, began from this line of Homer: "Strange man, your own valour will destroy you." GLYCON said: "you shall see how I despise this death for my country's sake." DIOCLES OF CARYSTUS said: "if you succeed, you will add one deed of valour; if you fail, you will lose three deeds of valour."

GLYCON said: "it is not easy to be sent off well by one who is weeping." AESCHINES — not the orator, for then there was no zeal for declamation, but this one of the new declaimers — said, when he was warning his son of the danger and saying he was touched by presentiments: "a father's soul, somehow, is most prophetic." DIOCLES OF CARYSTUS spoke an epigram which could please not only in declamation but even in some more solid kind of writing, when he was treating the commonplace on the changefulness of fortune: "there is but one safety against fortune — not to tempt her too often." DORION said a thing somewhat loftier than terse and restrained oratory admits, but by which he splendidly expressed the father's astonished feelings: "What desire is this, child, to drink things bloodied, to eat things bloodied? I fear, somewhere, a pitched battle; I fear, somewhere, a bond; I fear, somewhere, an array. I fear for the whole world. Why, child, do you blush?\"

pr.1. When I was calling to mind whatever good declaimers I had ever heard, there came to me, among others, Fabianus the philosopher, who, while still quite young, was of as great repute in declaiming as he was afterwards in philosophical disputation. He trained under Arellius Fuscus, whose style of speaking he imitated, but afterwards spent more labour to escape its likeness than he had spent to reproduce it. The exposition of Arellius Fuscus was indeed splendid, but laborious and intricate; its ornament was too studiously sought, and the arrangement of its words softer than a mind preparing itself for such holy and strong precepts could endure; there was the greatest unevenness in the speech, which was now meagre, now, by excessive licence, wandering and diffuse: the openings, the arguments, the narratives were spoken drily, while in the descriptions all freedom was given to every word, provided it glittered. There was nothing keen, nothing solid, nothing rugged; a splendid style, more wanton than rich.

pr.2. From this Fabianus quickly separated himself, and the rankness, indeed, he cast off when he wished, but obscurity he could not escape; this followed him even into philosophy. Often he says less than is enough for the listener, and in his supreme and most simple faculty of speech there yet remain traces of the old faults. Some things end so suddenly that they are not short, but cut off. Now Fabianus generally uttered sweet epigrams, and whenever any subject fell to him that admitted a reproach of the age, he was inspired with a great rather than a keen spirit. He lacked oratorical strength and that fighting blade; but a splendour, as if spontaneous, attended his unlaboured speech. The speaker's face was gentle, and, in keeping with the calm of his character, relaxed; there was no straining of the voice, no vehemence of the body, while his words flowed as though unbidden. Evidently a spirit by now composed and at peace, when it had repressed true feelings and driven anger and grief far off, could not well imitate the things it had escaped.

pr.3. He was better suited to suasoriae; the features of places, the courses of rivers, the situations of cities and the customs of peoples no one described more abundantly. He never came to a stop for want of a word, but with the swiftest and easiest flow his speech, in all its wealth, washed round every theme. These things, my dearest son Mela, I relate the more gladly, because I see your mind shrinking from public duties and turning away from all ambition, craving this one thing — to crave nothing. Only study eloquence: from it the passage to all other arts is easy; it equips even those whom it does not train for itself. And you have no reason to think a trap is being laid for you, as though I were contriving that the favour of a successful pursuit might hold you. I, for my part, am no hindrance to a good mind: go where your spirit inclines, and, content with your father's rank, withdraw a great part of yourself from fortune.

pr.4. You had, indeed, a greater talent than your brothers, most capable of all good arts: and this very thing is a pledge of the better talent, not to be corrupted by its own goodness, so as to misuse it. But since your brothers are bent on ambition, and prepare themselves for the forum and for honours — in which the very things that are hoped for are to be feared — I too, otherwise eager for that advancement, and an encourager and praiser even of a perilous industry, provided only it be honourable, while two of my sons sail the open sea, keep you in harbour. But the practice of declamation will profit you in those things you turn over in your whole mind, just as it profited Fabianus: who, that he might at last hear Sextius, nonetheless kept declaiming, and so diligently that you would think he was being trained for that study, not preparing himself through it for another.

pr.5. He had also Blandus the rhetor for a teacher, who was the first Roman knight to teach at Rome: before him this fairest of disciplines was confined among freedmen teachers, and by a most unworthy custom it was base to teach what it was honourable to learn. For the first Latin rhetor at Rome was Plotius, when Cicero was a boy. Under Blandus he studied longer than under Arellius Fuscus, but when he had now deserted to philosophy, in that time when he studied eloquence not for eloquence's sake. I know that, when you have heard his epigrams, you will wish to hear many more. But neither did he have leisure for declamations for long, and I, being so much younger than he, heard him as often as it fell out, not as often as I wished. Into this little book, therefore, I shall gather whatever of his sayings I retain.
